a 64-byte line only when `c ≡ 3 (mod 4)` -- **one pair in four**, which is milder than it first looks
but still trades one line fill for another on a quarter of the wins. Measured share of nonzeros whose
run starts on an even column: 0.503 transformer, 0.513 rn50, 0.461 suitesparse -- so half the runs
begin at an odd column, and a quarter of those cross.

Net for the transformer family: about 0.20-0.26 loads saved per nonzero out of 11.5 instructions,
which is **1.7-2.3%** against deficits of 8-25%.

**So the wide-load lever is not worth building for the family that carries the deficit.** It keeps
its value on the SuiteSparse family -- 6-7% before alignment, 3-4% after -- which is the largest
single estimate on the table and still smaller than the gap. This is the third time in this sequence
that the right shape has turned out not to be the right size, and all three were settled without a
machine: the reach enumeration for `RAISE_ON_FLOORED`, the emitted-loop count for chain49's arms, and
now this.

### The comparable subset, pre-registered before redwood's ladder lands

redwood can address 46 of MKT's 50 matrices (chain114). Restricting MKT's published curve to those
46 *before* the second host reports, so the comparison cannot be chosen after the fact:

| k | bytes | f32 all 50 | f32 subset 46 | f64 all 50 | f64 subset 46 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 30 | 27 | 30 | 26 |
| 2 | 8 | 43 | 39 | 31 | 29 |
| 3 | 12 | 42 | 38 | 29 | 27 |
| 4 | 16 | 30 | 27 | 10 | 10 |
| 8 | 32 | 15 | 15 | 3 | 3 |
| 16 | 64 | 3 | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| 20 | 80 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

The four dropped matrices contribute at most four cells, all at widths 1 to 4, and nothing above k=9.
The curve's shape, its crossover and its zero at 80 bytes are identical. **Both curves stay in the
record**: the 50-matrix one because it is what the reframing was derived from, and the 46-matrix one
because it is what the two hosts will be compared on. Rewriting the first retroactively would make
the derivation unreproducible.

## chain116: the prefetch arm reaches three of five widths, and the GCN guard had two more ways to measure nothing

Two pieces of desk work while MKT runs `mr4h` and redwood works through its queue. Both are of the
kind this sequence keeps finding cheaper than a machine: read the dispatch, read the harness.

### Which widths the prefetch arm can actually move

`SCORCH_SPMM_ROW_PREFETCH` guards one site, in `scorch_spmm_row_regblock`. The row loop's dispatch
order is halfvec, then exact-width, then the width-1 gather, then the general register block, so the
guarded prefetch is reached at:

| dtype | width | kernel | prefetch present |
|---|---|---|---|
| float32 | 1 | `narrow_exact` (K1) or `gather_f32` | no |
| float32 | 2, 3 | `narrow_exact` | no |
| float32 | 4 | `regblock` on the 128-bit type (`halfvec_exact`) | **yes** |
| float32 | 5..32 | `regblock` | **yes** |
| float64 | 1 | `narrow_exact` when the mean-degree test passes, else `regblock` | mixed |
| float64 | 2, 3 | `narrow_exact` | no |
| float64 | 4..16 | `regblock` (`HALFVEC_F64` ships 0) | **yes** |

`scorch_spmm_row_narrow_exact` and `scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32` contain no `__builtin_prefetch` at
all, and neither does `scorch_spmm_multirow_regblock`. The other three prefetching kernels --
`regblock_deep`, `regblock_pf`, `regtile` -- are either hook arms that ship off or serve widths above
the band. So of the widths the arm runs, **k=1 and k=2 are structural nulls and k=4, 8, 16 are live**,
and both stage scripts now carry this table so the analysis cannot read a null as a neutral result.

Against the byte curve that is 48 of the below-MKL float32 cells (30 at k=4, 15 at k=8, 3 at k=16)
and 13 float64 cells. Not the whole deficit -- widths 1 to 3 carry more of it than that -- but the
largest share any single mechanism on the table addresses.

**And the mapping itself says the prefetch is not the cause of the deficit.** The kernels that own
8 and 12 bytes, where the below-MKL count is at its worst, do not prefetch; the one that owns 16 to
64 bytes does. Whatever explains widths 1 to 3, it is not this. The arm's question is narrower and
still worth asking: whether the prefetch is spending issue slots in the part of the band it serves.

### The queued GCN redesign had two ways to report DONE having measured nothing

chain112 prescribed the fix for the whole-model guardrail -- three small graphs, short alternating
passes, every repetition emitted -- and the stage was written and queued. Reading it before it ran:

1. **`gcn_reps_run.py` puts a relative `"bench"` on `sys.path`, and the build tarball has no
   `bench/`** -- it carries `src`, `tests`, `tools`. Every pass would have raised `ImportError`,
   written a header-only CSV, and the stage would have printed its row counts and finished. Fixed by
   symlinking the repo's `bench` into each build tree, which also fixes the data root for free:
   `bench_gcn` resolves `DATA_DIR` and `WEIGHT_DIR` from its own `__file__`, and that resolves
   through the link to the populated `data/` and `weights/` rather than to a fresh download inside
   the build tree.
2. **`benchmark_dataset` prints `SKIP` and returns** when `load_canonical_weights` raises. A missing
   weight file is not an error to it. Added a pre-flight that imports the bench and asks for all
   three weight files once, and a refusal on a row count below 100.

That is the fifth and sixth entry in this project's list of drivers that would have reported success
having measured nothing, and again the check that catches them is the one that looks at the OUTPUT.

**The third fix is not a bug, it is the control.** The stage's framework list was `scorch` and
`scorch (fused)`. PyTorch was what proved the *previous* design invalid -- its two arms read 1.66x
apart on pubmed under defines that cannot reach it -- so dropping it would have removed the only
thing that can tell a real regression from a drifting host. It is back in the list.

### And a second unit for the same guard: the SpMM at the widths a GCN calls

The whole-model number is the workload claim, and it is the one the performance convention asks for.
But the unit the change lives in is the SpMM, and there is already a harness that interleaves per
cell and rotates which build leads. So the small graphs' adjacency now also goes through that
harness at the widths the model uses -- hidden 16, and the class count: 7 cora, 6 citeseer, 3 pubmed,
which is 12 to 28 bytes and squarely inside the band -- with 32 along as the out-of-band control.

The normalization is imported from `bench_gcn`, not restated. A guardrail that recomputes the matrix
it guards keeps passing after the bench stops agreeing with it, which is the failure this project has
now hit in four separate forms.

## chain117: the deficit is two mechanisms, and at widths 2 and 3 we run a scalar kernel that costs more than doing more work

The byte curve counted cells. Re-reading the same MKT ladder for *times* rather than counts splits
those cells into two mechanisms with nothing in common, and finds the largest single kernel deficit
in the project sitting at the two widths that carry the most cells.

### First, a method correction on my own analysis

The first version of this fit the deficit against nnz over the cells that are *below* MKL. That is
conditioning on the outcome: at small nnz a cell only enters that set when a fixed cost dominates,
so the intercept is biased up by construction. It produced "70-98% of the deficit is fixed cost" at
almost every width, with R2 of 0.1-0.4 -- a flat cloud being read as an intercept. Refitting over
**all** cells, and reporting a non-parametric statement alongside it, changes the answer.

### Mechanism one: a per-call floor, which decides the small and middle thirds

Five smallest matrices on the corpus, float32, ours/MKL in microseconds:

| matrix | nnz | rows | k=1 | k=2 | k=4 | k=8 | k=16 | k=32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| large_A_07 | 19637 | 4249 | 26.1/14.3 | 26.6/19.5 | 25.2/21.8 | 26.7/41.8 | 27.7/41.8 | 29.1/45.6 |
| as-735_G_517 | 19979 | 7716 | 27.2/21.2 | 27.3/23.7 | 27.9/27.4 | 30.4/44.3 | 30.4/44.3 | 31.8/49.4 |
| rn50 bottleneck | 23596 | **256** | 14.8/12.1 | 15.7/13.5 | 16.3/14.9 | 16.6/18.3 | 16.5/19.9 | 18.2/31.9 |
| as-735_G_683 | 24077 | 7716 | 28.3/23.1 | 28.0/24.9 | 28.4/28.0 | 31.9/44.6 | 30.8/44.2 | 32.7/50.7 |
| deter6 | 24771 | 4255 | 25.8/20.7 | 26.8/24.4 | 25.9/25.3 | 26.9/42.4 | 26.1/42.1 | 28.8/43.8 |

**Thirty-two times the arithmetic costs three microseconds.** Our time is flat in k from 26.1 to
29.1 while MKL's rises from 14.3 to 45.6. And the floor tracks ROWS, not nnz: 4249 rows costs 26 us,
7716 rows costs 28, and the 256-row DLMC matrix with *more* nonzeros costs 15. So there is a
per-call floor of roughly 14 us plus about 2.8 ns per row, and at k=1 MKL's is about 12 us lower.

It is not the ABI validation: `checked_csr_view` memoizes its O(rows) and O(nnz) structural scans on
the index pair, so in a batch loop only the O(1) checks re-run. Whatever the floor is made of, it
decides every below-MKL cell on the small and middle thirds at k=1 and at k>=4 -- and we win the
largest third at those widths, by 22.7 us at k=1 and 17-185 us from k=8 up.

### Mechanism two: widths 2 and 3 float32, where the deficit grows with nnz

Same corpus in thirds by nnz, float32, median over each third:

| k | small third gap | middle third gap | largest third: ours | MKL | gap | cells below |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | +5.8 | +3.1 | 309.5 | 332.2 | **-22.7** | 4/18 |
| 2 | +3.6 | +10.5 | 450.7 | 283.6 | **+167.1** | 17/18 |
| 3 | +3.2 | +8.3 | 574.6 | 378.7 | **+195.9** | 17/18 |
| 4 | +1.2 | -0.6 | 374.2 | 364.2 | +10.0 | 10/18 |
| 5 | +0.2 | +1.8 | 553.3 | 546.7 | +6.6 | 12/18 |
| 8 | -3.4 | -3.3 | 536.0 | 553.6 | -17.6 | 2/18 |
| 11 | -6.3 | -10.6 | 719.6 | 904.7 | -185.1 | 0/18 |

The fit agrees: at k=2 and k=3 the deficit is 0.0199 and 0.0254 us per thousand nonzeros with R2
0.903 and 0.943 -- the only two widths in either dtype where a per-nonzero model explains the gap.

**And the absolute times name the cause without any model. On the same matrices we take 574.6 us at
k=3 and 374.2 at k=4.** More arithmetic, less time, by 53%. k=4 is the only one of the three that
runs a vector kernel: `halfvec_exact` instantiates the register block on the 128-bit type. Widths 2
and 3 run `scorch_spmm_row_narrow_exact`, which is scalar by construction -- K scalar loads and K
scalar FMAs per nonzero where the vector form needs one of each.

### The emitted loops, x86-64 AVX2 at the extension's flags

| symbol | insns | packed FMA | scalar FMA | spill-st | reload | nnz/iter | insns/nnz |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hv_full_k4` (shipped at k=4) | 23 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2.0 | **11.50** |
| `hv_over_k3` (unmasked load, masked store) | 23 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2.0 | **11.50** |
| `hv_masked_k3` (128-bit, 3 lanes of 4) | 27 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2.0 | 13.50 |
| `v_masked_k3` (256-bit, 3 lanes of 8) | 27 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2.0 | 13.50 |
| `exact_k3_u2` (shipped at k=3) | 231 | 6 | 6 | 4 | 4 | 8.0 | **28.88** |
| `exact_k3_u4` | 444 | 16 | 4 | 16 | 15 | 17.3 | 25.62 |
| `exact_k3_u8` | 908 | 32 | 8 | 61 | 57 | 34.7 | 26.19 |
| `exact_k2_u4` (shipped at k=2) | 330 | 12 | 0 | 8 | 8 | 12.0 | 27.50 |
| `exact_k2_u8` | 627 | 24 | 0 | 28 | 27 | 24.0 | 26.12 |

The scalar kernel costs **2.3 times the instructions per nonzero** and spills at every unroll it can
pick. The divisor is stated per symbol here rather than inherited from `count_hot.py`, which divides
scalar FMAs by four because it was written for the k=4 question; at K=3 three scalar FMAs are one
nonzero, and reusing the old divisor would have flattered the scalar kernel by a third.

Subtracting a common per-nonzero term for the A stream reconciles the two measurements: if about
40 ps/nnz is the shared cost of streaming A, then 103.5 - 40 = 63.5 at k=3 against 67.4 - 40 = 27.4
at k=4 is a ratio of 2.3, which is the instruction ratio exactly.

### What that indicates, and the one measurement that stands against it

`SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI`'s own comment says the exact kernel "wins 6-8% at k=2 and k=3 on both
dtypes". That measurement was against the **masked 256-bit** block, which is what the alternative
was before the half-vector type existed -- and `halfvec_under`, the value that would route 2 and 3
to the 128-bit block, cannot fire today at all: it requires `!exact_width`, and exact owns those
widths. **So widths 2 and 3 have never been measured on the 128-bit block**, because the two
constants have to move together and no arm has moved both.

Three arms, in increasing order of what they need:

1. `EXACT_HI=1` alone -- widths 2 and 3 to the masked 256-bit block. This is the arm the old
   measurement already rejected, and it is worth running only as that measurement's control.
2. `EXACT_HI=1 + HALFVEC=2` -- the masked 128-bit block. 13.5 instructions per nonzero, and the
   mask is 3 lanes of 4 rather than 3 of 8.
3. `EXACT_HI=1 + HALFVEC=2 + an unmasked load` -- 11.50, identical to the kernel that reaches
   parity with MKL at k=4. B is only read and the extra lane is discarded at the masked store, so
   the only cost is reading up to `LH-K` floats past the end of B, which can only happen when a
   nonzero names the last row of B. `A1_crd` is validated sorted, so a row's last coordinate is its
   largest, and one compare per ROW -- `A1_crd[pA_end-1] != J-1` -- decides it. Rows that touch the
   last column keep the masked kernel. That is one compare per row against 15 instructions per
   nonzero saved, on 85 of the corpus's below-MKL float32 cells.

The masked-load cost is the whole question between arms 2 and 3: `vmaskmovps` is multi-uop and
cannot fold its address, which is the only way the old 6-8% measurement and this instruction count
can both be right.

## chain118: the retired arm was the largest kernel win in the sequence, and a geomean over the wrong corpus hid it

chain110 retired mr2h -- `EXACT_HI=1` with multi-row -- because MKT liked it and redwood reversed it
at width 2. Both readings were geomeans over all 50 (MKT) and 298 (redwood) matrices. Splitting the
**same measurements** by whether the kernel is most of the call changes the verdict completely.

The split is `nnz >= 1e6`, and it comes from chain117's floor measurement, not from this arm: the
DLMC transformer family is 512 rows and 26214 nonzeros and takes 22.4 us at k=1 and 24.5 at k=16 on
MKT, so its arithmetic is invisible next to a ~22 us per-call floor, while af_2_k101 at 17.5M
nonzeros spends over 99% of the call in the kernel. **A kernel change cannot move a floor, and
pooling the two dilutes it away.**

Geomean of `c0/mr2h` (above 1 = the arm is faster), with the same-code `c0/c0b` pair beside it:

| | MKT big (18) | MKT small (32) | redwood big (37) | redwood small (261) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| float32 k=2 | **1.1588** (17/18) | 1.0327 | 1.0157 (28/37) | 0.9675 |
| float32 k=3 | **1.4657** (18/18) | 1.1094 | **1.1581** (36/37) | 1.0521 |
| float64 k=2 | 1.0850 (11/18) | 1.0845 | **0.9566** (9/37) | 0.9433 |
| float64 k=3 | 1.2263 (14/18) | 1.1244 | 1.0294 (27/37) | 0.9936 |
| same-code floor | 1.015-1.026 | 0.994-1.002 | 0.998-1.009 | **0.923-0.980** |

Read the bottom row first. On redwood's 261 floor-dominated matrices the c0-against-c0b floor moves
**7.7%** -- the harness against itself, on the same object -- and the "reversal" that retired the arm
is a 3.3% reading inside it. The float32 k=3 column, meanwhile, is 1.4657 on MKT and 1.1581 on
redwood against floors of 1.026 and 1.009, improving **18 of 18 and 36 of 37 matrices**.

Per matrix at MKT float32 k=3, largest first, with the arm's own ratio against MKL:

| matrix | nnz | c0 us | c0/c0b | c0/mr2h | mr2h/MKL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| msdoor | 19173163 | 1577.6 | 0.988 | 1.614 | 0.860 |
| af_2_k101 | 17550675 | 1501.6 | 0.987 | 1.681 | 0.918 |
| halfb | 12387821 | 1123.6 | 1.118 | 1.886 | 0.690 |
| Hardesty1 | 12143314 | 1342.1 | 1.149 | 1.504 | 0.912 |
| fcondp2 | 11294316 | 1002.1 | 1.085 | 1.900 | 0.680 |
| pwtk | 11524432 | 922.3 | 1.056 | 1.761 | 0.834 |
| ... | | | | | |
| connectus | 1127525 | 186.6 | 1.041 | **1.023** | 1.076 |

**Fifteen of the eighteen go from losing to MKL at k=3 to beating it.** The one that barely moves is
`connectus`: 512 rows at mean degree 2202, which is the matrix family the whole-row partition's
balance ceiling already owns -- it cannot be helped by a kernel.

### What ships, and what it needs

Width 3 wants the vector kernel on both hosts and both dtypes. Width 2 wants it on float32 on both
hosts and does **not** want it on float64 on redwood, where it improves 9 of 37 matrices at 0.9566.
A single `EXACT_HI` has to give up one of those; `EXACT_HI_F32=1` with `EXACT_HI_F64=2` gives up
neither, and that pair is now expressible -- the constant is split per dtype, defaulted to the
combined value, and the instruction stream is unchanged (164121 instructions, identical).

It is not shipped as that pair yet, for two reasons worth stating. The numbers above are a
**re-analysis of an arm that ran for a different purpose**, and mr2h moves two things at once --
multi-row and the exact band -- even though `mr2` alone is null at k=3 (MKT 1.0128, redwood 0.9881),
which attributes the effect to the band. And the split, though motivated independently, was applied
after seeing the data. So the isolating arm is queued on both hosts with the split **pre-registered
in the stage script**: `hi1` (EXACT_HI=1 alone) and `hi1hv` (also HALFVEC_F32=2, so widths 2 and 3
run the 128-bit block rather than the 256-bit one -- a value that has never been able to act,
because `halfvec_under` requires `!exact_width` and the exact band owns those widths unless
EXACT_HI is lowered). It runs on the 298-matrix corpus rather than the 50-matrix residual family,
with the target group taken at nnz >= 1e6 and 24 seeded controls below it.

MKT's queue was reordered to put it first: measuring `mr2i` before it would decide the smaller
question with the machine and the larger one from a re-analysis. `mr2i` -- `EXACT_HI=2`, which keeps
the exact kernel at width 2 -- is exactly the arm that gives up MKT's 1.1588 and redwood's 1.0157 at
float32 k=2 to protect redwood's float64 k=2, which is what the per-dtype pair does without the
trade.

### The lesson, which is the third form of it in this project

A cell count and a geomean over a corpus that is two populations answers neither population's
question. The corpus here is 36% kernel-dominated and 64% floor-dominated at narrow k, and the two
respond to a kernel change by 1.47 and by 1.11. This is the same defect as measuring a kernel swap
on a corpus selected for already losing, and as pricing a lever off a mean run length when 41% of
the mass sits at length one: **the summary statistic was computed over the wrong set, and it was the
set that made the arm look small.**

## chain119: the floor is the declared pool, at least on one host -- and a pre-registration for the prefetch arm

### The floor, decomposed locally

chain117 left the per-call floor unexplained after eliminating three candidates: the ABI validation
memoizes its O(rows) and O(nnz) scans on the index pair, the whole pybind-plus-eight-kwargs call
floor is **1.62 us at one row** (1.22 positional, so the kwargs path costs 0.4), and the recorded
team-width cost is too small to be 20 us. The fourth candidate is the one the harness passes in.

`nthreads_override` is the caller's pool, and `mrgate.py` passes 32 on MKT and 24 on redwood, which
is what `ops.matmul` also passes. Sweeping it on the M5, on a 512-row 26214-nonzero matrix at k=1:

| declared pool | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | default (pool 6) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| us, 512 rows / 26214 nnz | **6.81** | 8.00 | 15.15 | 26.90 | 50.37 | **57.88** | 8.08 |
| us, 4249 rows / 19637 nnz | 10.91 | 10.69 | 12.87 | 30.67 | 52.36 | 59.51 | 10.74 |
| us, 32768 rows / 262144 nnz | 108.01 | 62.15 | **38.57** | 47.13 | 69.67 | 74.87 | 38.18 |

**Eight and a half times**, on work that one core finishes in seven microseconds. The third row is
the control: on 262144 nonzeros the sweep has a real minimum at four, so this is not "threads are
always bad", it is a team whose width is set by the caller's pool rather than by the work.

And the per-row dispatch cost, from a sweep that holds nnz at 32768 and spreads it over more
non-empty rows (R2 0.997-0.999):

| declared pool | 1 | 2 | 4 | default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ns per row | 1.603 | 0.814 | 0.430 | 0.607 |
| intercept us | 6.73 | 9.89 | 13.51 | 11.82 |

So the per-row cost is real but small -- about 6.4 cycles single-threaded -- and it parallelises.
The floor is in the intercept, and the intercept grows with the declared pool.

**This does not yet explain MKT**, and the honest statement is that it cannot: the recorded
per-worker team cost is 4.75 us on the M5, 0.26 on redwood and **0.06 on MKT**, so 32 workers there
should be about 2 us against a 22 us floor. Either that figure describes widening a warm team rather
than entering a region, or MKT's floor is something else. A 40-minute sweep is queued first on both
hosts to say which, and it is queued first because of what it would mean.

### What it would mean, which is why it goes before the kernel arms

If the floor tracks the declared pool, then **every arm ever read on the floor-dominated part of
this corpus was measuring a thread policy, not a kernel** -- which is the same defect chain118 found
in the pooled geomeans, one layer down. It also stops being a harness question: `ops.matmul` passes
`torch.get_num_threads()` the same way the harness does, so a user on a 64-core machine multiplying
a small sparse matrix pays it. And the fix would be a work-based team cap rather than a kernel
change, which is a different part of the code from everything else in this sequence.

Three cautions, all from the record. Thread interventions here have been rejected four times
(`chain59`, the adoption's 24-to-1 cliff, the physical-core cap, the auto-probe). The pool cap that
did ship matches `torch.get_num_threads()` floored and capped by rows -- 512 rows over 32 threads is
16 rows each, so the row cap does not bind on the shapes that lose. And the same intervention has
reversed sign across hosts before: 1.53x faster on the M5 and 1.32x slower on MKT.

### mrhv is correct on x86

The full suite under the multi-row half-vector kernel: **1108 passed, 72 skipped**, 48 minutes, on
top of the 81 shape/density/width numeric cases and the 33 constructed ragged cases. The kernel is
new code on the hot path, so this is the gate it needed.

### Pre-registration: what the prefetch arm should read

Written before it runs, at the peer session's suggestion, because there is a real prior in each
direction and that is exactly when a pre-registration earns its keep.

*For removal helping:* the prefetch and its guard are 9 of 23 emitted instructions per two
nonzeros, 11.50 instructions per nonzero become 7.00; two nonzeros of run-ahead is about four cycles
against a ~40-cycle L3 hit, which the depth hook's own comment already doubted; and the multi-stream
gather result is a null at every stream count (0.968-1.001), so these kernels are not starved for
outstanding loads in a way more run-ahead fixes.

*Against:* the deep-unroll history, where a +4% turned out to be the prefetch's absence rather than
the depth -- but that was nvec=2 on a different kernel, so it is a prior and not a result here. And
the gather pattern defeats the hardware prefetcher, so the software one is the only run-ahead there
is; if it is covering anything at all, removing it will show.

*The prediction.* Removal reads **between 1.00 and 1.08 on the live widths** (float32 k=4, 8, 16 and
float64 k=4, 8, 16), largest at k=4 where the loop is shortest, and inside the same-code floor at
k=1 and k=2, which the dispatch map says are structural nulls. Specifically: **not** the 1.39 the
instruction count alone implies -- chain117 already showed a 2.3x instruction ratio cashing out as
1.54x in time, because the A stream is a common per-nonzero cost neither arm avoids. If the arm
reads inside the floor at every live width, these kernels are latency-bound at the widths that lose
and the instruction budget is not the thing to spend effort on; if it reads above 1.08, the loop is
issue-bound and the unmasked-load variant at widths 2-3 becomes worth building rather than merely
worth costing.

### The floor arm, five arms rather than three, and its guardrail in the same allocation

Queued on both hosts, and on MKT deliberately held **outside** the serializer's order until the
sweep says the mechanism is there -- one edit to release, one `scancel` to drop.

Five arms, because the pair is ambiguous on its own. `ADOPT_GRAIN` and `BASE_WORK_TRUE` are two
gates whose cliffs point opposite ways: the adoption over-threads a tiny product today, and pricing
it on real arithmetic under-threads a real layer. A null on the pair could be both fixes working or
the two cliffs cancelling on a corpus that straddles them, and no guardrail distinguishes those
readings, so the set is `ag15k` (the adoption alone), `bwt` (the base bound alone -- the arm already
measured neutral, kept as the control that says so on this corpus), `agbwt` (the candidate), and the
`c0`/`c0b` pair. The peer session asked for this; it is right, and the extra arm is nearly free
because `bwt`'s number already exists.

Three pre-registered groups, each with its own widths and its own reason:

| group | matrices | widths | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| floor | the 24 smallest | 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 | the target: where the floor is most of the call |
| big | every one at nnz >= 1e6 | 1, 4 | the harm case: grading on real arithmetic can take threads a product needs, and at k=1 the real measure is 16x smaller than the proxy |
| gcn | cora, citeseer, pubmed | 3, 6, 7, 16 | the guardrail, at the widths a two-layer GCN calls |

The guardrail runs **in the same allocation and on the same builds** as the arm, rather than as a
separate job ordered before or after it. That is the stronger form: the concern that a guardrail
ordered later would be the weakest instrument in the chain at the moment it matters is exactly right,
and sharing the allocation removes the ordering question instead of answering it.

The `gcn` group is not a proxy. It is the normalized adjacency `bench_gcn` itself builds, exported by
importing its own `load_dataset` and `compute_normalized_adj` on the host that has the datasets and
shipped as npz -- cora 13264 nonzeros, citeseer 12431, pubmed 108365. **The header's own worked cliff
is in it**: a Cora output layer is 13264 nonzeros at k=7, which the ungraded adoption gives 24
workers, one grain size gives 6, and another gives 1.

## chain120: on the unselected population the residual is 97 cells of 2980, median 2.25 us, and almost none of it is the kernel

Every MKT count in this document runs on `c94_keys.txt`: 50 matrices chosen *because* they were
below MKL. redwood's 298-matrix corpus is not chosen that way, so it is the only honest denominator
either host has -- and now that the deficit is known to be two mechanisms, the count can say which
one owns each cell. Below-MKL means **both** same-code builds read below MKL, which is the rule this
host's crossing statistic needs.

| float32 | floor group (nnz < 1e6) | kernel group (>= 1e6) | float64 | floor group | kernel group |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| k=1 | 1 of 261 | 0 of 37 | k=1 | 3 of 261 | 0 of 37 |
| k=2 | 5 of 261 | 0 of 37 | k=2 | 4 of 261 | 0 of 37 |
| k=3 | 19 of 261 | 0 of 37 | k=3 | 5 of 261 | 0 of 37 |
| k=4 | **31 of 261** | 1 of 37 | k=4 | **16 of 261** | 1 of 37 |
| k=8 | 5 of 261 | 1 of 37 | k=8 | 4 of 261 | 1 of 37 |

**The kernel-dominated matrices already beat MKL nearly everywhere on this host: 0 or 1 of 37 per
width.** So chain118's 1.16-1.47x at widths 2 and 3 is a speed win on cells we were already winning
here, and its cell-count value was a property of MKT's selected corpus. That does not retract it --
the arm is real and improves 36 of 37 of redwood's big matrices -- but it reprioritises it.

### What is actually left

97 below-MKL cells of 2980 across both dtypes and five widths, **3.3%**. Median deficit **2.25 us**
where MKL itself takes 18.2; median ratio 1.099. Rows, median: **512**.

The 32 cells at the float32 peak are the DLMC transformer family, every one of them, and they are
floor cells by their own profile -- our time at k=8 over k=1 is **1.03** (a floor cell stays near 1;
arithmetic-bound would be near 8). Our times run 13-19 us across all five widths while MKL's run
14-21, so the crossing at k=3-4 is where MKL's dip meets our peak: two comparable flat floors whose
wiggles differ by a microsecond.

The tail is three known things, not a fourth mechanism:

| cell | nnz | rows | deg | ours | MKL | EXACT_HI=1 | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ffn_conv2, f64 k=2 | 104857 | 512 | 205 | 73.3 | 31.8 | 0.623 | **RETRACTED, chain121: A/A spread 40.4 us** |
| connectus, f32 k=8 | 1127525 | 512 | 2202 | 168.0 | 126.8 | 1.132 | **A/A spread 32.3 us** |
| nw14, f64 k=2 | 904910 | 73 | 12396 | 104.5 | 76.6 | 1.292 | stands (A/A 1.9 us) |
| bottleneck_3, f64 k=1 | 94620 | 2048 | 46 | 37.2 | 17.2 | 3.689 | **RETRACTED, chain121: A/A spread 14.3 us** |

`nw14`, `connectus` and `lp_osa_14` are the whole-row balance ceiling's three matrices, already
diagnosed and already exhausted on thread count and B footprint. **The two cells this section called
apparent defects are retracted in chain121: neither can support a size claim, because on both of
them the two same-code builds disagree by more than the deficit.**

Only **4 of the 97** cells sit on matrices above 1e6 nonzeros, though they carry 18% of the total
deficit. The exact-band arm flips **7 of 97**.

### What this changes

The goal as set is a cell count, and on the honest population it now reads: *beat MKL on about 50
cells that lose by one to two microseconds on fifteen-microsecond calls, plus three matrices with a
known structural cap, plus a handful of narrow-k float64 cells a queued arm already fixes.* That is
per-call overhead engineering, not kernel engineering.

So MKT's **census moved ahead of the exact-band arm** in its queue. Until that host has its own
unselected denominator, every cell-count claim about it is a claim about a corpus selected for
losing -- and that corpus has now misled this work twice, once in the byte curve's monotone shape
and once in the pooled geomean that retired mr2h.

One caution on the floor arm, from this same data. Grading the adoption by real arithmetic helps
where `work_true` is small, and on these cells `work_true` is 400000 units at k=4 -- so `ADOPT_GRAIN`
at 15000 leaves them at the full team and changes nothing, while a grain large enough to cut them to
six workers is large enough to cut a Cora output layer to one. Worse, the arithmetic argues against
the cut: at redwood's recorded 0.26 us per worker, the optimum team for 400000 units is about 21, not
6. **The floor arm's premise is strong on the M5, weak on redwood, and unmeasured on MKT** -- which
is exactly what the sweep queued first on both hosts is for, and a reason to read its answer before
releasing the arm rather than after.

## chain121: half the residual cannot be sized, and the two apparent defects were both A/A spread

chain120 read ratios off cells the crossing rule had admitted. The rule -- both same-code builds must
agree a cell is below MKL -- protects which **side** of the line a cell is on. It says nothing about
the **magnitude**, and I reported a cell at 3.689x whose two same-code builds differ from each other
by 1.62x. A cell can support a size claim only when its A/A spread is small next to the deficit
claimed, and applying that test:

| cell | deficit | A/A spread | c0/MKL | c0b/MKL | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ffn_conv2, f64 k=2 | 41.5 us | **40.4 us** | 2.307 | **1.035** | cannot be sized |
| connectus, f32 k=8 | 41.3 us | 32.3 us | 1.326 | 1.071 | cannot be sized |
| nw14, f64 k=2 | 28.0 us | 1.9 us | 1.365 | 1.341 | **stands** |
| bottleneck_3, f64 k=1 | 20.0 us | 14.3 us | 2.165 | 1.334 | cannot be sized |
| nw14, f64 k=4 | 20.4 us | 7.2 us | 1.231 | 1.312 | stands |
| lp_osa_14, f32 k=8 | 19.1 us | 7.9 us | 1.582 | 1.340 | stands |

**45 of the 97 cells have an A/A spread under half their deficit.** Their median deficit is 2.21 us
and their median ratio 1.096 -- so chain120's characterisation of the population survives; what does
not survive is its two named defects.

And the survivors are one family. Every sizeable one is `nw14` (73 rows, degree 12396), `kl02` (71
rows, 2993), `lp_osa_14` (2337 rows, 136) or `connectus` (512 rows, 2202) -- stable in both builds,
1.09 to 1.58 in each. That is the whole-row balance ceiling, diagnosed already: these matrices hold
about a tenth of themselves in a single row, so whole-row partitioning caps them near 40% of the
machine, and thread count and B footprint were both exhausted on them.

**So the honest statement of what is left on an unselected corpus is:** 45 sizeable below-MKL cells
of 2980, median 2.2 us against MKL's 18.2, of which the sizeable ones are four matrices with a known
structural cap and the rest are two comparable per-call floors whose wiggles cross. There is no
defect to fix. The kernel wins measured in chain118 remain worth landing on their own terms -- they
are 1.16-1.47x on matrices where the kernel dominates -- but they are speed, not cells.

The general form, and the third time this project has hit it: **a statistic that qualifies a cell for
one claim does not qualify it for another.** `an_stable.py` was written to make the crossing count
reproducible and it does that correctly. Reading a ratio off the cells it admits is a different
question, and it needs its own test -- which is now `an_resid_stable.py`, and which should have run
before any cell was called a defect.

### And chain118 re-tested against the same rule, since retracting one result with a test obliges applying it to the others

Per matrix: is the arm's gain large next to that matrix's own same-code spread? Geomean of `c0/arm`
over the big group, all matrices against only those that pass:

| | all | passing | passing / total |
|---|---|---|---|
| MKT float32 k=3 | 1.4657 | **1.4970** | 17 of 18 |
| MKT float32 k=2 | 1.1588 | 1.1738 | 16 of 18 |
| MKT float64 k=3 | 1.2263 | 1.2970 | 14 of 18 |
| MKT float64 k=2 | 1.0850 | 1.0950 | 16 of 18 |
| redwood float32 k=3 | 1.1581 | **1.1714** | 35 of 37 |
| redwood float32 k=2 | 1.0157 | 1.0144 | 28 of 37 |
| redwood float64 k=3 | 1.0294 | 1.0374 | 25 of 37 |

**The effect is larger on the cells that pass**, on six of seven columns -- excluding the unstable
ones sharpens the result rather than deflating it, which is what a real effect does and what
chain120's two cells conspicuously did not do. float32 k=2 on redwood remains the marginal column
(1.014 against a 1.0008 floor, and only 28 of 37 stable), which is the same conclusion reached from
the pooled numbers and the reason the shipping pair keeps float64 width 2 with the exact kernel.

The harness that produced this table printed one geomean under two labels on its first run. Fixed
before the numbers above were read, and worth recording: a script written to check for mislabelled
numbers had one.

## chain122: the shipping arm was built against a tree that did not contain its constant, and the seven-waiter chain fired a stage onto a live measurement

Two defects, both in the harness, both caught before they produced a number. Recording them
because each is a general form, not a one-off.

### A `-D` naming a macro the tree does not read

`shipcand` is three float32 constants: `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32=1`, `SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32=2`,
`SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2`. The per-dtype pair is new -- it was added earlier in this session
and committed as 2537d60. The tarball staged on both hosts predates it.

So `-DSCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32=1` named a macro no source file read. It compiled without a
warning, changed nothing, and left `shipcand` byte-identical to `hvmr`, which sets the other two.
Both arms would have been timed, and the interaction the whole arm exists to measure -- the band's
top lowered so that multi-row can reach widths 2 and 3 -- would have been reported as reproducing
at 1.00 against its own duplicate.

The existing check did not catch it. mrbuild.sh already refused a candidate whose `.text` equals
c0's, on the grounds that its define did not take. `shipcand` passes that check: its other two
defines took, so it differs from c0. It differed from c0 in exactly the way `hvmr` does.

Two checks added, and the second is the one that matters:

- Every macro a config names must appear somewhere under `src/scorch/csrc` in the tree about to be
  compiled. Verified locally: fires on the stale tarball, passes on the fresh one, and fires on an
  invented macro name.
- **Two configs with different define strings must produce different `.text`.** Comparing each arm
  against the baseline is not enough when arms differ from the baseline in overlapping ways.

The fresh tarball carries the split, and the job that is now running prints the positive control:

| build | defines | `.text` |
|---|---|---|
| c0 | | `dcdd393cb7e1ffc1` |
| c0b | | `dcdd393cb7e1ffc1` |
| hi1hv | `EXACT_HI=1 HALFVEC_F32=2` | `7f0013cdc04716a4` |
| shipcand | `EXACT_HI_F32=1 HALFVEC_F32=2 MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2` | `f8e4b7e69b114a5e` |
| hvmr | `HALFVEC_F32=2 MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2` | `e8a902fe4b913241` |

`shipcand` and `hvmr` are distinct, which under the stale tree they were not. Correctness: 120
cases each over dtype x rows x density x width, zero mismatches, all three arms.

Note for the analysis: `hi1hv` lowers the band for *both* dtypes (it predates the split and sets the
unsuffixed `EXACT_HI`), while `shipcand` lowers it for float32 only. The two are not a clean
one-knob comparison at float64.

### Seven waiters, each keyed on the previous one's process name

redwood's queue was seven `nohup` scripts, each polling `pgrep -f` for its predecessor's *name*.
Killing the first to reorder the queue satisfied the second's wait condition, which launched the
byte-curve stage on top of the running measurement: an mrbuild compile at `-j16` for about two and a
half minutes alongside a live timing arm. The intruder was killed; the arm it overlapped
(`ex4b float64 p2`) is re-measured rather than kept and caveated, and its own floor arms `c0` and
`c0b` come later in that group's rotation (`mrhv ex4b c0 c0b mr2`) so they never saw the compile.
Re-running the one arm restores the group.

Replaced by a single sequential runner holding the stages in one process, keyed on the pid of the
stage actually running rather than on any name, with a refusal that will not start a stage while any
timing process is alive. Dropped from the order: `mr2i` (superseded by `shipcand`, which contains
the mechanism it tested), the floor sweep and the floor arm.

Two smaller things in the same hour, both the same shape as the above:

- `pkill -f "[r]w_mr2i_after.sh"` killed the shell that issued it. The bracket trick stops a pattern
  from matching *itself*, but the loop that built the pattern had the plain name in its own argv, so
  the pattern matched the ssh command text. Killing by pid has no such failure mode.
- Two `zsh`/`tail` poller pairs from eight days ago were still resident and were killed.

## chain123: the audit for sign-selected corpora, claim by claim with the corpus named

Prompted by a fair question: an admission rule that selects on which side of MKL a cell lands makes
the side reproducible and bounds nothing about the size, so a magnitude read off such a corpus is
unsupported. That is what retracted chain120's two cells. The question is whether any *surviving*
magnitude claim in this file rests on the same footing.

**Scope, stated so the result is not read as more than it is.** This enumerates the magnitude claims
reachable by searching for corpora defined in loss terms -- 228 mentions of below-MKL, the five
places this file already names the hazard, and the sections whose headings promise a size. It is not
a line-by-line re-read of nineteen thousand lines. A claim absent from the table below has not been
cleared; it has not been examined.

| claim | corpus it was computed over | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| chain118 f32 k=3 MKT, 1.4657 pooled / 1.4970 passing | pre-registered nnz >= 1e6 target group, 18 matrices, split fixed before any timing | clean |
| chain118 f32 k=3 redwood, 1.1581 / 1.1714 | same split, 37 matrices | clean |
| chain117, the per-call floor being flat in k | five named matrices, absolute microseconds, no admission rule | clean |
| chain117, the per-nonzero deficit at f32 widths 2-3, R2 0.903 / 0.943 | **all** cells at each width (`an_fixed2.py`) | clean as re-fitted |
| — its first version | below-MKL cells only (`an_fixed.py`), which biased every intercept up and read 70-98% fixed cost at almost every width | **withdrawn** |
| the non-monotonicity, 1515.7 us at k=3 against 864.9 at k=4 | five named matrices, both widths, absolute times | clean |
| chain65, the k=1 extension worth +19.5% | 212 matrices in six **degree** bands, 1060 cells, per-band A/A floor, and the two losing bands reported alongside | clean |
| the regblock at 0.9033 "on the losing band" | degree >= 256 within a stratified corpus, every band tabulated on both hosts | clean; the phrase is loose, the measurement is not |
| MKT reading 0.64 of MKL on 30-100 us kernels | **split by how each matrix got in**: `gbkeys` (selected for already losing) reported separately from a 50-matrix size-stratified random draw, and the load-bearing figures are the stratified ones | clean by disclosure |
| the five cells of per-cell thread headroom, 12-37% | cells where a forced count beat both the policy and MKL -- sign-selected *and* in-sample | clean by disclosure; the text states it is not a policy, and gives clears-against-breaks in both directions |
| chain120's `ffn_conv2` f64 k=2 and `bottleneck_3` f64 k=1 | cells admitted by the both-builds-agree rule, which selects on side and not size | **withdrawn** (chain121) |
| chain120's residual census, 97 of 2980 and median 2.21 us | the unselected 298-matrix corpus | clean as a count; the file already notes that any *size* claim about the residual is a claim about a subset chosen by sign |
| the 236-cell autotune board, 0.675x -> 1.878x | four pre-existing matrix sets (the ones the 195-cell tiling study used) plus N=16 and 64 | clean |
| MKT's 113-of-250 caller-path count, and every MKT count in this file | `c94_keys.txt` -- 50 matrices (38 SuiteSparse, 12 DLMC) **selected because those cells were already below MKL** | clean by disclosure, and the disclosure is the best in the file: it names the right use (of the cells we knew we lose, how many still do -- the correct denominator for measuring a fix) and the wrong one (a census) |
| the shipping candidate | pre-registered split plus a three-graph GCN guardrail | pending, both hosts |

Two withdrawals, both already on the books before this audit and neither newly discovered. Nothing
else in the table needs re-measuring.

**The `c94_keys.txt` row is the one to carry forward into how the shipping candidate is reported.**
Every MKT count in this file runs on a corpus selected for already losing, and redwood's 298-matrix
corpus is not, which is why the two hosts' cell counts are not comparable and why this file already
says so. The consequence for the candidate is specific: on redwood's unselected corpus the
kernel-dominated group is already at 0 or 1 of 37 below MKL per width, so chain118's 1.16-1.47x at
widths 2 and 3 is a **runtime** win on cells we were already winning there, and its cell-count value
was a property of MKT's selected corpus. Both are real; they are not the same claim, and the standing
goal is a cell count. Say which one the candidate delivers on which host rather than pooling them.

The reason the rate is that low is visible in the file itself: it names this hazard in five separate
places, twice as grounds for *declining* to run something -- a degree ladder whose pooled geomean
would have been dominated by matrices where the knob provably cannot act, and a thread-count arm
that was given thirty unselected matrices specifically so it would not inherit a corpus chosen for
losing. The lesson was learned expensively once and has been applied since.

What the audit does not settle, and is the honest residual: "clean by disclosure" is weaker than
clean. Two entries above are sign-selected corpora whose text says so. That is the right treatment
and it still means the numbers cannot be lifted out of their paragraphs. Anyone quoting the five
headroom cells or the `gbkeys` band without the sentence next to them is quoting a selection effect.

## chain124: the decision rule for the shipping candidate, registered before its data is read

Three runs are in flight and none has been read: MKT (17 of 20 arms at the time of writing), the M5
ARM regression check (8 of 12), and redwood (queued behind a repair). Writing the rule down now
because a rule chosen after seeing the numbers is not a rule, and this file has an expensive
precedent for post-hoc reading.

The candidate is `EXACT_HI_F32=1` + `HALFVEC_F32=2` + `MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2`, shipped as a set
because the three interact (1.036 and 1.013 separately, 1.466 together at MKT float32 width 3).

| what the three runs show | what ships |
|---|---|
| MKT wins at widths 2-3, redwood same sign, M5 neutral, GCN guardrail neutral | the flip, globally, per-dtype as measured |
| MKT wins, redwood **smaller but same sign**, others neutral | the flip. Same sign with a host-dependent size is the expected case, not a failure: chain118 already measured 1.4657 on MKT against 1.1581 on redwood over the same split. Report both sizes, pool neither. |
| any **regression on redwood** beyond its own floor | **no flip.** Report it as a finding. A host-conditional default is not on the table -- this library does not tune per host -- so the constants stay where they are and the mechanism stays behind them. |
| a regression on the **M5** beyond its floor | an **ISA-conditional** default: x86 takes the values, ARM keeps the current ones. Precedent is in the tree already, where `HALFVEC` carries per-dtype defaults for the same reason, and in this file, where the ARM-only k=1 extension was scoped the same way. |
| a regression on the **GCN guardrail** at width 3 | **not a reason to drop the arm, and not a reason to tune around it.** The win is measured on `nnz >= 1e6`; cora, citeseer and pubmed are 13K, 12K and 108K nonzeros, all three orders below it. So the remedy is a structural gate at the same threshold the split already uses, which is *provably* inert on every GCN and autoencoder shape rather than tuned to miss them. That is the house rule for a sub-regime win and it applies here without modification. |
| the candidate's `.text` differs from a build of the flipped defaults | **no flip until that is explained.** The arm was built from `-D` defines and the flip changes header defaults; those must reach the same code. This is a check on the object, not an inference from the source -- the same discipline that caught the unread define this morning. |

Two things this rule deliberately does not do. It does not let a large MKT number outvote a small
redwood one, because the standing goal is a cell count on an unselected corpus and MKT's corpus is
selected for already losing (chain123). And it does not treat the M5 as a confirmation: that host
has two matrices above 1e6 nonzeros, so it can refute the candidate and cannot support it, and its
result above ~1.5M nonzeros is absent rather than neutral.

## chain125: MKT's verdict on the candidate -- two constants earn their place at different widths, and the third is unmeasured

Job 17278858, 42 matrices on the pre-registered split (18 target at nnz >= 1e6, 24 seeded control),
5 arms, 2 dtypes, 2 passes, plus the GCN guardrail in the same allocation. Every gate passed: five
distinct `.text` digests, 120 correctness cases per arm with zero mismatches, 2520 corpus rows and
144 guardrail rows per build.

### Every arm at every width, target group, geomean of c0/arm

| dtype | k | c0b (floor) | hi1hv | hvmr | shipcand | us: c0 -> shipcand |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| f32 | 1 | 0.9830 | 0.9974 | 0.9777 | 0.9800 | 95.4 -> 97.8 |
| f32 | 2 | 0.9851 | 1.0341 | 0.9698 | 1.0229 | 122.2 -> 117.5 |
| f32 | 3 | 0.9921 | **1.2347** | 0.9758 | **1.2212** | 157.1 -> 127.0 |
| f32 | 4 | 1.0145 | 1.0008 | 1.0011 | 1.0003 | 115.0 -> 115.4 |
| f32 | 8 | 1.0092 | 0.9991 | **1.3386** | **1.3351** | 144.0 -> 108.4 |
| f64 | 2 | 1.0031 | **0.8336** | 0.9918 | 0.9903 | 111.9 -> 114.8 |
| f64 | 3 | 0.9990 | 0.9803 | 0.9939 | 0.9840 | 141.7 -> 143.4 |

**Each constant owns a different width, and the ownership is unambiguous.**

- **k=3 belongs to the band.** `hi1hv` 1.2347 against `shipcand` 1.2212 -- multi-row adds nothing
  there. 17 of 18 matrices pass the spread test. Cell count: **34 of 42 below MKL becomes 16**, and
  `hvmr` (no band change) stays at 35, so the eighteen recovered cells are the band's.
- **k=8 belongs to multi-row.** `hvmr` 1.3386 against `shipcand` 1.3351, and `hi1hv` is 0.9991 --
  the band is irrelevant there. 17 of 18 pass. This reproduces chain74's independent finding that
  multi-row is a float32 win at k=8.
- **k=2 is not resolvable.** 1.0229 against a cross-build floor of 1.5-2.2%. The band alone reads
  1.0341, which is the same story one standard error better and still not clear of the floor.
- **k=1 and k=4 are null**, and both sit below their own floor.

### The per-dtype split is vindicated by measurement rather than by argument

`hi1hv` sets the **unsuffixed** `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI=1`, so it lowers the band on float64 too.
Float64 at width 2: **0.8336**, and its below-MKL count goes from 15 of 42 to 34 of 42. A 17%
regression and nineteen cells lost. `shipcand`, which sets only the `_F32` constant, is 0.9903 there
-- inert, as designed. Same source line, opposite sign by dtype, which is the entire reason these
are two constants.

### The GCN guardrail passes, and on float32 it is a win

Twelve cells per dtype at the widths a two-layer GCN calls. Float32: `shipcand` at or above 1.0 on
all twelve, with pubmed at width 3 reading **1.2122** (43.0 -> 35.5 us). Float64: 0.9632 to 1.0190,
worst cell citeseer width 6 at 0.9632 against its own same-code floor of 0.9825 -- about 1% below
its floor, in a code path the candidate does not touch, on a 25 us kernel. That is a binary-layout
effect and it is the honest cost of any code change, not a defect in this one.

### What this does NOT establish, and why nothing ships yet

`SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32=2` has **no measurement of its own in this job.** Both arms carrying it
also carry something else. And there is a specific reason to suspect it: chain118 measured the band
with multi-row and *without* halfvec at 1.4657 at float32 width 3, where this job's band *with*
halfvec reads 1.2347. Cross-job comparison is exactly what this file forbids -- different tarball,
different job, and a 1.5x discrepancy has been traced to that before -- so this is a question and
not a finding. But it is a question about a constant that would ship.

The decisive arm is the band **without** halfvec, in one job, against the band with it. Queued as
`bandf32` (`EXACT_HI_F32=1` alone) and `bandmr` (`EXACT_HI_F32=1` + `MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2`), so
`shipcand` minus `bandmr` is exactly halfvec's contribution and nothing else.

Per chain124's registered rule the flip also still needs redwood, and the object check comparing a
build of the flipped defaults against this arm's `.text`. Two of three constants are earned; the
third is unexamined, and shipping a constant nobody has measured is the thing this file exists to
prevent.

### One methodological note that changes how these numbers are read

The cross-build floor here is **1.5-2.2% on float32**, while the same-code spread *within* one
object is 0.2-1.0% -- two to four times smaller. The cost of being a separate object is most of the
floor. That is why 1.0229 at width 2 is not a result and 1.2212 at width 3 is. It also means the
rotation cannot balance: five builds across four (pass, dtype) groups leaves the order incompletely
crossed, which is consistent with the floor being *signed* (c0b reads 0.983-0.985 at widths 1-2
rather than straddling 1.0). Widths whose effect does not clear that margin by several times should
not be read at all.

## chain126: the candidate is a large float32 regression on ARM, at exactly the widths it wins on x86

The three constants have no ISA condition, so flipping their defaults changes the ARM build too, and
every confirming measurement was x86. The M5 was measured over 60 matrices in six nnz bands
(13.1K to 1.51M nonzeros), widths 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, both dtypes, two passes, 3600 rows per build.

### float32, geomean of c0/arm by nnz band, `[n/15]` = matrices clearing their own same-code spread

| k | b1: 13.1K-32.8K | b2: 32.8K-73.7K | b3: 78.6K-133K | b4: 134K-1.51M |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.9842 [8/15] | 0.9854 [3/15] | 1.0158 [2/15] | 1.0669 [4/15] |
| 2 | 0.9472 [12/15] | 0.9195 [8/15] | **0.8268** [14/15] | **0.7041** [14/15] |
| 3 | 0.9710 [11/15] | 0.9257 [10/15] | 0.9264 [3/15] | **0.8250** [13/15] |
| 4 | 0.9874 [7/15] | 0.9806 [3/15] | 0.9996 [2/15] | 1.0363 [7/15] |
| 8 | 0.9792 [7/15] | 0.9713 [5/15] | 1.0110 [2/15] | 1.0440 [6/15] |

The ARM cross-build floor is 1.0392-1.0438 on float32 -- about 4%, roughly twice x86's 1.5-2.2% --
and a 0.7041 with 14 of 15 matrices clearing their own spread is nowhere near it. **This is a 30%
regression at width 2 and 17% at width 3, on the same build that gains 22% at width 3 on MKT.**

Opposite signs on the same source. That is not a surprise in this kernel: the thread raise wins on
x86 and loses on ARM, tile-ijk's inner loop is +22% on ARM and was rejected on x86, and `HALFVEC`
already carries per-dtype defaults for the same reason. ARM has no gather instruction, so what the
exact band displaces there is a NEON register-block tile rather than `vgatherdps`, and the two
displacements are not the same trade.

**chain124's registered rule fires: the default must be ISA-conditional.** x86 takes the values,
ARM keeps the current ones. That was written down before this data was read, which is the only
reason it can be applied to it.

### The float64 half of this run is not readable, and the reason is worth recording

The float64 cross-build floor reaches **1.3641** in the largest band -- c0b apparently 36% faster
than byte-identical code. That is an order effect, not noise: three builds rotated across four
(pass, dtype) groups is `i % 3` over four values, so c0 leads twice and never gets the compensating
position. The spread test caught it -- 0 to 4 of 15 matrices clear their own floor in those cells,
against 13 and 14 for the float32 regression -- so the analysis refused the numbers rather than
reporting them, but the design should not have produced them.

Fixed in the isolation run now going: five builds over six groups, so every build leads at least
once.

### What is still unknown, and the experiment for it

"ARM regresses" is not actionable while all three constants move together. The isolation run on the
M5 uses the same nesting as the x86 job -- `bandf32` then `bandmr` then `shipcand`, each adding one
constant -- at widths 2, 3 and 8, so each successive difference is one constant on both ISAs. If it
is halfvec on ARM as well as being the unmeasured constant on x86, then one arm accounts for both
open questions and the remaining pair may well ship globally. If it is the band, then the band is
x86-only and multi-row's width-8 win can be examined on its own.

Until that returns, the shippable claim is: two constants earned on x86 at named widths, one
unmeasured, and a global default refuted by ARM.

## chain127: the no-regression gate, with each item's current status -- and a correction to chain125

Bobby's instruction: be more careful, and ship no regressions. Nothing has been flipped, committed
as a default, or pushed. But the near-miss was procedural, not just lucky: the plan described to him
would have flipped a **global** default on x86-only evidence, and the ARM check that refuted it was
added mid-flight because the macros turned out not to be ISA-gated. That is a habit, not a gate.
This section is the gate.

### A correction to chain125 first

chain125 called float64 on MKT "inert, as designed" on the strength of geomeans of 0.9903 and
0.9840 against floors near 1.00. **That was wrong**, and the reason it was wrong is a test this file
already knows how to run.

Counting cells where an arm is slower than `c0` by more than that cell's own same-code spread gave
163 of 444 on MKT and 186 of 600 on the M5 -- alarming numbers. They are mostly the test's own
noise: a per-cell spread is a single-draw estimate, so a small one admits any deficit. Running the
identical test on a **same-code arm** (`c0b`), with both arms judged against the same independent
yardstick `|c0(ours) - c0(oursb)|`:

| host | dtype | same-code arm | candidate | excess |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MKT x86 | float32 | 88 of 222 (40%) | 86 of 222 (39%) | **-1 pp** |
| MKT x86 | float64 | 109 of 222 (49%) | 137 of 222 (62%) | **+13 pp** |
| M5 ARM | float32 | 95 of 300 (32%) | 154 of 300 (51%) | **+20 pp** |
| M5 ARM | float64 | 61 of 300 (20%) | 60 of 300 (20%) | **-0 pp** |

So the raw count was 40% artifact and there are **two** populations, not one: the known ARM float32
regression, and **a real float64 regression population on x86** in a dtype whose constants the
candidate never sets. chain125's "inert" claim is withdrawn. Its width-3 and width-8 wins stand --
those clear their floors by 10x and pass the spread test on 17 of 18 matrices -- but the float64
half of that section was read too generously.

The mechanism for the x86 float64 excess is **not established.** It is plausibly binary layout: the
float64 source path is unchanged, and this project has measured a dead branch adding ten x86
instructions and reshuffling every stack slot. Two things argue for layout rather than a gating
bug -- the effect appears on x86 and not on ARM, where a genuine `_F32`-macro leak would appear on
both. But that is an argument, not a measurement. Static confirmation was attempted and abandoned
honestly: `spmm_csr_double_v2_core` is a three-instruction thunk, the kernel is inlined into a
larger function, so a symbol-level instruction comparison cannot isolate the float64 path cheaply.

### The gate. Every row must pass before any default moves.

| # | requirement | status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | x86 float32: zero regression population beyond the same-code control | **PASS** (-1 pp on MKT) |
| 2 | x86 float32: the claimed win present, clearing its floor severalfold | **PASS** (1.2212 at width 3 against a 1.7% floor, 17 of 18 matrices) |
| 3 | x86 float64: zero regression population beyond the control | **FAIL** (+13 pp, mechanism unknown) |
| 4 | ARM float32: zero regression population | **FAIL** (+20 pp, up to 0.7041) |
| 5 | ARM float64: zero regression population | **PASS** (-0 pp) |
| 6 | GCN / autoencoder guardrail neutral-or-better on both dtypes | **PARTIAL** -- float32 is a win (pubmed width 3 at 1.2122); float64's worst cell is 0.9632 against a 0.9825 floor |
| 7 | second x86 host agrees in sign | **PENDING** (redwood) |
| 8 | every shipped constant has a measurement of its own, not shared with another | **PENDING** (halfvec, job 17279494 and the M5 isolation run) |
| 9 | a build of the flipped defaults has the same `.text` as the measured arm | **NOT RUN** |
| 10 | any region left unmeasured is named, and the change is provably inert there | **NOT MET** -- ARM above ~1.5M nonzeros is unmeasured, because the local cache holds two matrices above 1e6 |

Four of ten pass. **Nothing ships.**

### The remedy for rows 4, 5 and 10, which is better than measuring harder

For ARM the right answer is not a better measurement, it is **provable inertness**. If the constants
are gated so the ARM build is byte-identical to today's, then ARM neutrality stops being a claim
about 60 matrices and becomes a property checkable with a digest -- and row 10's unmeasured region
above 1.5M nonzeros stops mattering, because nothing there changed. The precedent is in this tree
already: `SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32`'s own comment records that "the kernel is inside the AVX2 block,
so both values are inert on ARM by construction", and the NEON work was proven x86-inert by
`objdump` rather than by timing.

**Which yields a prediction, registered now, before the isolation runs return.** If halfvec is
already AVX2-gated, it cannot be causing the ARM regression, so on ARM `shipcand` must equal
`bandmr`, and the regression must belong to the band or to multi-row. If instead `shipcand` differs
from `bandmr` on ARM, then that comment is false and there is a second defect to find.

Rows 3 and 6 are about float64 on x86, where the source path does not change but the object does.
If more passes do not dissolve the +13 pp, the honest options are to declare the cost and let Bobby
weigh it against a 22% width-3 win, or to abandon the flip. Not to describe it as inert.

## chain128: the gate is designed and held; the float64 blocker gets the control it never had

Bobby's decision: hold the ISA gate as the intended shape, do not write it until the isolation runs
confirm the attribution, and treat the float64 population on x86 as a separate blocker that closes
on its own. Recorded because both halves constrain what may be committed.

### Why the gate is one constant and not three, and why it is not overfitting

Checked in the source rather than assumed:

| constant | ARM status | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32` | already inert | its dispatch is inside `#if defined(__AVX2__) && defined(__FMA__)` |
| `SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32` | already inert | its kernel is inside the AVX2 block, as its own comment claims |
| `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32` | **live on ARM** | the exact kernel is guarded `(AVX2 && FMA) \|\| __ARM_NEON`, with a second call site under `defined(__ARM_NEON) && !defined(__AVX2__)` |

So the ARM regression can only come from the band, and a gate is one value at one site.

**It is not overfitting, and the reason is that the constant is not a magnitude.** It decides *which
kernel* handles widths 2 and 3, and the two instruction sets hand that work to different kernels --
the masked 256-bit register block at one call site, the NEON path at the other. A constant whose
optimum depends on which kernel it displaces, where the displaced kernel differs by instruction
set, is mechanistically ISA-dependent rather than host-fitted. The house rule endorses precisely
this: gate a sub-regime win behind a condition that provably cannot fire where it hurts. Four
precedents in the tree -- `HALFVEC` inside the AVX2 block, the NEON row kernel proven x86-inert by
`objdump`, the E-core recruit built to be byte-neutral on x86 all-physical-core pools, and the
float64 register kernel with ARM deliberately unchanged.

Note the sign: ARM currently *gains* about 30% at width 2 from the exact kernel. Leaving ARM alone
preserves a win rather than forgoing one.

**What would make it overfitting, stated so it can be held against this work:** gating on ISA
without knowing which constant regresses and why. That is "it broke on ARM so we turned it off
there" -- a shrug with a `#if` around it. Hence the gate waits on the isolation run, whose
prediction is sharp because two of the three constants are already ARM-inert: on ARM `bandf32`,
`bandmr` and `shipcand` must all read the same. If they differ, one of the inertness claims above
is false and there is a second defect to find. Also prefer keying the gate off the existing
capability guards rather than `__x86_64__`, so it stays correct if a future instruction set gains
the same capability.

### The float64 blocker: the control that did not exist

Float64's source path is untouched by all three constants, yet its regression population on MKT is
13 points above its own same-code control. Two candidate explanations -- binary layout, or a leak
where some shared non-template path reads a `_F32` constant -- and no data separating them, because
**`c0` and `c0b` cannot: they are two builds of identical source at the same fixed path, and
mrbuild refuses if their `.text` differs.** They measure run-to-run noise and say nothing about
layout.

`c0pad` is the missing arm, added to mrbuild and queued as job 17282530: identical source, identical
flags, built at a path **one character longer**, which shifts embedded strings and every
RIP-relative displacement while emitting the same instructions. The harness verifies it is a
control by requiring the same `.text` **size** with a **different** digest -- same size and
different bytes is what a layout shift is, and what a semantic change is not. It is exempted from
the distinct-defines-imply-distinct-code rule, since it shares c0's empty defines by design.

This deliberately does the thing the harness exists to prevent. Building each arm at one fixed path
is why three earlier build-identity failures were spurious; `c0pad` inverts that on purpose to
measure the effect those failures were confounded by.

**Reading rule, registered now.** If `c0pad` reproduces float64's excess, the effect is layout, it
is not attributable to the candidate, and the honest report is that any change to this file costs
float64 that much on this host. If `c0pad` is clean and `shipcand` is not, there is a leak to find,
and that is a defect rather than a cost.

## chain129: the candidate is two constants, not three -- halfvec is a loss, and the ARM regression is provably the band

Two isolation runs, both complete, both with the arms nested so each successive difference is one
constant: `bandf32` (`EXACT_HI_F32=1`), `bandmr` (plus `MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2`), `shipcand` (plus
`HALFVEC_F32=2`).

### MKT, job 17279494: what each constant is actually worth

Target group, geomean of c0/arm, floor 1.006-1.013:

| f32 | c0b | bandf32 | bandmr | shipcand | band adds | multirow adds | **halfvec adds** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| k=1 | 0.9945 | 1.0000 | 1.0111 | 0.9915 | +0.0% | +1.1% | **-1.9%** |
| k=2 | 1.0134 | 0.8897 | 1.0608 | 1.0405 | -11.0% | +19.2% | **-1.9%** |
| k=3 | 1.0121 | 1.0551 | **1.2729** | 1.2458 | +5.5% | +20.6% | **-2.1%** |
| k=4 | 1.0112 | 1.0120 | 1.0016 | 1.0073 | +1.2% | -1.0% | +0.6% |
| k=8 | 1.0062 | 1.0117 | **1.3542** | 1.3483 | +1.2% | +33.9% | -0.4% |

**`SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32=2` does not earn its place.** It is -1.9%, -1.9% and -2.1% at widths 1,
2 and 3 against a floor near 1.2%, and neutral above. It was in the candidate because chain104 and
chain110 measured it in company, never alone. Dropped.

**Multi-row is the win and the band is its precondition, not an effect.** The band alone *regresses*
width 2 by 11% and gains 5.5% at width 3; multi-row alone cannot reach widths 2-3 at all while the
exact band owns them. Together: +19.2% and +20.6%. chain125 credited width 3 to the band on the
strength of `hi1hv` ~ `shipcand`; that comparison held halfvec fixed in both arms and so could not
see that the band's own contribution is small and negative at width 2.

Cell counts agree, float32, 42 matrices: at width 3, `c0` 34 of 42 below MKL becomes **22** with the
band alone, **15** with band plus multi-row, and 16 once halfvec is added. At width 1, `bandmr` 16
against `shipcand` 18. `bandmr` dominates `shipcand` on every width and ties nowhere worse.

**The candidate is `bandmr`: `EXACT_HI_F32=1` + `MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2`.** Two constants.

### The M5: the ARM regression is the band, and the other two are provably inert

The three ARM objects have **identical `__text` digests** (`110d587ad036b7d1`). Multi-row's dispatch
and halfvec's kernel are both inside AVX2 blocks, so on ARM all three arms are the same binary --
inertness proven by digest rather than measured over 60 matrices. The residual differences between
them (0.43% and 0.80% worst case) are therefore a pure noise reading between identical objects, and
usefully consistent with the 1% cross-build floor.

So the ARM regression belongs entirely to `EXACT_HI_F32=1`:

| ARM f32 | b1 13-44K | b2 44-130K | b3 131K-1.5M |
|---|---|---|---|
| k=2 | 0.9640 | 0.9197 | **0.7229** |
| k=3 | 0.9867 | 0.9470 | **0.8349** |
| k=8 | 1.0126 | 1.0123 | 1.0066 |

float64 is neutral throughout (0.9873-1.0081), and the rotation fix worked: those floors read
0.993-1.001 where the previous run's reached 1.3641.

**This is what licenses the ISA gate**, and it licenses it for exactly one constant. `MULTIROW_ROWS_F32`
needs no gate -- it is already AVX2-only. So the shipping change is one gated constant and one
ungated one, and the ARM object can be required to be byte-identical to today's.

### A statistic of mine that does not reproduce, and chain127's row 3 revised

chain127 recorded x86 float64 as FAILING on a regression population 13 points above its same-code
control. **The same arm, same digest, reads -32 points in this job.** The control itself moved (49%
to 55%). A statistic that swings 45 points between two runs of the same object on the same host is
not measuring the object.

So row 3's status is **unresolved**, not FAIL and not PASS, and the number that produced it is
withdrawn. Note what does reproduce: the geomeans. `shipcand` at float32 width 3 read 1.2212 then
1.2458; at width 8, 1.3351 then 1.3483. The per-cell-population count is the fragile instrument and
the geomean with a per-cell spread test is the sound one -- which is the same lesson as chain121,
arriving from the opposite direction. The `c0pad` layout control (job 17282530) still runs, because
the layout question is worth an answer even though the evidence that motivated it has evaporated.

### Three defects in the interlock, all mine, all found by testing it rather than trusting it

The stage lock added in chain122 had three:

1. **Its trap did `read -r P`** -- and `P` is the pass tag in every stage script. Firing the handler
   overwrote p1/p2/p3 with the lock's pid, so every arm afterwards was written under one bogus tag,
   collapsing the interleaved pass structure. Caught by seeing `--pass-tag 12006 --slice gcn12006`
   in a live command line. Variables are now prefixed.
2. **The `INT`/`TERM` handler did not exit**, so `kill` was caught, cleaned up, and *resumed* the
   stage. That is why redwood survived being killed. INT and TERM now exit 130 and 143.
3. **`STAGE=name . stage_lock.sh` does not persist `STAGE`** -- a prefix assignment on the `.`
   builtin is temporary -- so the trap referenced an unbound variable and aborted *inside the
   handler* under `set -u`. Captured into a variable assigned inside the sourced file, where
   assignments do persist.

Also learned, and it explains defect 2's symptom: **a stage blocked in a long `python` call defers
its own trap until that call returns**, so stopping a stage means killing the child first and the
script second. And `pkill -f` matched the ssh command text carrying the pattern -- the same defect
as chain122, committed twice in one day. Kill by pid.

The partial redwood run written under the corrupted pass tag was discarded rather than repaired.

### Gate status

Rows 1, 2, 5 pass. Row 3 is unresolved rather than failed. **Row 4 now has a licensed remedy**
rather than a failure: the ARM regression is one constant, and gating it makes the ARM object
byte-identical, which also satisfies row 10. Rows 7, 8, 9 pending -- and row 8 is now satisfiable,
since every constant that would ship has been measured alone.

## chain130: the gate is written, and both ISAs' objects are verified by digest

Two constants ship, float32 only, x86 only, gated inside `#if defined(__AVX2__) && defined(__FMA__)`:

```
SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32     3  ->  1
SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32   0  ->  2
```

`SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32` stays at 1. It was in the candidate and is not in the change.

### The object checks, which are what make this safe rather than argued

The measured arms were built by passing `-D` defines to a tree whose header defaults were unchanged;
the flip changes the defaults instead. Those must reach the same code, and it is checked rather than
inferred -- both builds at one fixed absolute path, since a directory one character longer shifts
every embedded string and every RIP-relative displacement.

**x86** (job 17283152, three builds, no timing in the job at all):

| build | `.text` digest | bytes |
|---|---|---|
| the measured arm, pre-flip tree + defines | `b2ed1412c6e6e767` | 1096738 |
| **the flipped tree, no defines** | **`b2ed1412c6e6e767`** | 1096738 |
| the pre-flip tree, no defines | `f58dcf626cfa0c5f` | 1073666 |

Identical to the measured arm, and different from what it replaces, so the defaults took effect.
**Consequence worth stating: the 120-case correctness check that `bandmr` passed applies to the
shipped object literally rather than by analogy, because it is the same object.**

**ARM** (M5, built at the same path as the reference): `f1b096cb6ef90d6f` before the flip and
`f1b096cb6ef90d6f` after. Byte-identical. ARM neutrality is a property of the preprocessor, not a
claim about 60 matrices -- which also retires the gate's row 10, because the region above 1.5M
nonzeros that this host's cache cannot reach is a region where nothing changed.

The x86 object is 23072 bytes larger, which is the multi-row kernel being instantiated.

### Gate status

| # | requirement | status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | x86 float32: no regression population beyond the control | PASS (-1 pp) |
| 2 | x86 float32: the win present, clearing its floor severalfold | PASS (+19.2% / +20.6% / +33.9% at widths 2 / 3 / 8; 34 of 42 below-MKL cells at width 3 become 15) |
| 3 | x86 float64: no regression population | **UNRESOLVED** -- the statistic that failed it swung 45 points between two runs of the same object and was withdrawn |
| 4 | ARM float32: no regression | PASS by construction (byte-identical object) |

| 7 | second x86 host agrees in sign | **PENDING** -- redwood running the same nested arms |
