## chain131 -- row 7 fails, and the cell-count scoreboard is why I did not see it on the first host

Redwood ran the same five nested arms over its own 60-matrix unselected corpus, three interleaved
passes, 5490 corpus rows and 216 GCN rows per build, five distinct `.text` digests
(`c0`/`c0b` `6f5206e9f675fb42`, `bandf32` `d5443f9593c02bce`, `bandmr` `3ab954933d75f3e2`,
`shipcand` `141d60f1790f8fa1`), 120 correctness cases per arm with zero mismatches.

**The verdict is no flip.** Not because the second host disagreed in size, which the registered rule
allows, but because there is a regression population at width 2 that **both** hosts show, and the
statistic I shipped the first host's verdict on could not see it.

### The win is real and large

float32 corpus, `bandmr` against `c0`, cells more than 5% apart with the same-code floor at least
half that far:

| host | width 1 | width 2 | width 3 | width 4 | width 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| redwood, faster | 0 of 60 | 20 | 43 | 1 | 43 |
| redwood, slower | 7 | 10 | 2 | 5 | 2 |
| MKT, faster | 0 of 42 | 22 | 31 | 0 | 32 |
| MKT, slower | 0 | 7 | 1 | 0 | 0 |

Target-group geomeans, `bandmr`/`c0`, with the same-code floor beside each:

| width | redwood | rw floor | MKT | MKT floor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.9739 | 0.9991 | 1.0111 | 0.9945 |
| 2 | 1.0215 | 0.9978 | 1.0608 | 1.0134 |
| 3 | 1.1585 | 0.9970 | 1.2729 | 1.0121 |
| 4 | 0.9881 | 1.0027 | 1.0016 | 1.0112 |
| 8 | 1.2657 | 1.0098 | 1.3542 | 1.0062 |

Widths 3 and 8 confirm on the second host with the same sign and a smaller size -- +15.9% and
+26.6% against +27.3% and +35.4%. That is the expected case and it is not the problem.

### The regression: extreme row skew at width 2, on both hosts

| matrix | host | width | c0 (ms) | bandmr (ms) | ratio | same-code floor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| connectus | redwood | 2 | 0.0738 | 0.1225 | **0.602** | 1.080 |
| connectus | MKT | 2 | 0.1460 | 0.1788 | **0.817** | 0.983 |
| connectus | redwood | 3 | 0.0918 | 0.1246 | 0.737 | 0.912 |
| lp_osa_14 | redwood | 2 | 0.0324 | 0.0381 | 0.852 | 0.956 |
| lp_osa_14 | redwood | 8 | -- | -- | 0.843 | 0.952 |
| cari | redwood | 2 | 0.0185 | 0.0218 | 0.850 | 0.971 |
| lhr34c / lhr71 / lhr71c | redwood | 2 | -- | -- | 0.820 / 0.834 / 0.845 | 0.994 / 1.001 / 1.003 |
| com-Amazon / relat8 / as-caida_G_08x | MKT | 2 | -- | -- | 0.885 / 0.905 / 0.934 | 1.024 / 1.006 / 1.003 |

The population is coherent: `connectus` and `lp_osa_14` are two of the three matrices in the
whole-row balance ceiling, `lhr*` is an irregular chemical-process family, `as-caida` and
`com-Amazon` are power-law. All of them have a degree distribution with a long tail.

The multi-row group is admitted per row by
`A1_pos[i + multirow] > A1_pos[i] && (... A1_pos[i+multirow] - A1_pos[i] <= sp_wide_deg)`,
a data-dependent test whose outcome on a long-tailed degree distribution alternates
unpredictably from row to row. The kernel it guards is not the cost; the branch is the hypothesis,
and it is testable.

### Why the first host reported a pass

The scoreboard is below-MKL cell counts, because the goal is a cell count. `connectus` at width 2
was **already** below MKL on MKT before the flip. Making it 18% slower moved no cell, so a
two-host regression sat inside a column that read "width 2 unchanged at 35 of 42".

**A cell already below MKL can be made arbitrarily worse without changing the cell count.** Any
scoreboard that counts crossings is blind in exactly the cells it has already given up on, which
are the cells the work is aimed at. Every verdict in this file that rests on a crossing count needs
the >5%-slower-than-its-own-floor scan beside it, and from here on that scan runs on every arm.

On redwood, where the corpus is unselected and almost nothing is below MKL to begin with, the same
four matrices show up as crossings -- 0 of 61 to 4 of 61 at width 2 -- which is the same fact
arriving through the statistic that can see it.

### The other open item: widths 1 and 4 on redwood only

redwood reads 0.9739 at width 1 (7 cells past their floor, 28 of 61 below 0.97) and 0.9881 at
width 4, against a floor of 0.9991 and 1.0027. MKT reads 1.0111 and 1.0016. Opposite signs.

**Multi-row provably cannot execute at either width for float32.** `multirow_ok` requires
`!exact_width`, and width 1 is exact under `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32=1`; it also refuses
`B1_size == scorch_simd_half<float>::lanes`, which is width 4. So whatever costs redwood 2.6% at
width 1 is not the kernel this constant selects -- it is the object around it. The x86 `.text` is
23072 bytes larger, and the candidate explanation is code placement.

That hypothesis has a control already built and never yet run on this host: `c0pad`, identical
source and flags at a build path one character longer, verified by requiring an equal `.text` size
with a different digest. The `c0`/`c0b` floor cannot see a placement effect, because both are built
at the same path -- it measures the cost of being a separate object, not the cost of being a
differently-placed one. That is the next measurement, and until it runs widths 1 and 4 are
unattributed rather than either a pass or a fail.

A second instrument belongs here, from a peer session with the measurement to back it: an A/A
replicate cannot detect a **shared** additive per-call cost, because the offset cancels and the
replicate reads 1.000 regardless. If the two objects differ in fixed per-call cost rather than in
per-nonzero cost, the width-1 deficit is a dispatch cost and not a kernel cost, and nothing in the
current arm structure distinguishes them. The discriminator is a work-scaling arm: run the same
call on a vertically stacked copy of the matrix, exactly twice the nonzeros and rows at the same
width, so `m1 = o + t` and `m2 = o + 2t` give `o/t = (2*m1 - m2)/(m2 - m1)` per arm per cell, with
no per-host constant to invent.

| 2 | x86 float32: the win present, clearing its floor severalfold | PASS on both hosts, widths 2 / 3 / 8 |

## chain132 -- the layout control lands, float64 clears, and a same-source build reads 1.2% slow

Job 17282530 on MKT: `c0`, `c0b`, `c0pad`, `shipcand`, 42 matrices, three passes, both dtypes,
3780 corpus rows and 216 GCN rows per build. `c0pad` is the layout-only control -- identical source
and flags, built at a path one character longer, admitted only if `.text` is the same size with
different bytes.

### Gate row 3 clears

float64 geomeans against `c0`, corpus:

| width | `c0b` (object floor) | `c0pad` (layout floor) | `shipcand` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.9930 | 0.9976 | 0.9963 |
| 2 | 0.9976 | 0.9995 | 0.9907 |
| 3 | 0.9921 | 0.9975 | 0.9972 |
| 4 | 0.9941 | 0.9932 | 0.9939 |
| 8 | 0.9881 | 0.9952 | 0.9909 |

`shipcand` is inside both floors at every width. x86 float64 is neutral, and the regression
population that failed this row two chains ago was floor-level. **Row 3 passes.** That was the last
unresolved row of the old gate; the gate is void anyway because the commit it gated does not ship,
but the float64 question itself is closed and does not need re-asking.

### How big a pure layout change is

Per-cell absolute log ratio, float32, 210 cells:

| | p50 | p90 | p99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| layout only (`c0pad`) | 1.0114 | 1.0323 | 1.0766 | **1.1318** |
| separate object, same path (`c0b`) | 1.0082 | 1.0252 | 1.0464 | 1.0595 |

A build that differs in nothing but code placement moves one cell in ten by more than 3.2% and its
worst cell by 13.2%. Placement is therefore a live explanation for redwood's width-1 deficit at the
cell level, and the control has to run on redwood before that deficit is attributed to anything.

### The finding that mattered more: the rotation was not balanced

`c0pad`'s float32 geomeans are **0.9964 / 0.9892 / 0.9880 / 0.9884 / 0.9953** at widths 1 / 2 / 3 /
4 / 8. That build's source is identical to `c0`'s. A pure placement difference should be
sign-symmetric across a 42-matrix geomean, and this is one-sided at four of five widths.

The cause is the lead-build advantage and an unbalanced rotation. The stage rotates which build
runs first in each (pass, dtype) group, which cancels the advantage only if every build leads
equally often. Four builds over three passes times two dtypes is six groups: `c0` and `c0b` lead
twice, `c0pad` and `shipcand` lead once. Both once-leading arms read low. `c0b` at 0.9934-0.9984 is
the same effect at half the size, which is what leading twice out of six instead of once predicts.

This is the M5 defect again -- three builds over four groups left `c0` leading twice and made that
run's float64 unreadable -- and it is worth about 1%, which is the size of the effects these stages
have to resolve. It also means **`shipcand`'s float64 column above is biased low by roughly the same
1%, so float64 clearing its floor is if anything understated.**

Both band-2 stages were relaunched before measuring anything with the group count made a multiple
of the build count -- four passes over two dtypes is eight groups over four builds, two leads each
-- and both now refuse to run if that does not divide. A harness that silently biases its late arms
is worse than one that stops.

### Unrelated, and still open

Job 17283539 (the full x86 suite with a pre-flip baseline arm) failed immediately: `REFUSE: no
pytest in this env`. The MKT venv has no pytest, so the x86 suite has never been run on either the
pre-flip or the flipped tree. The 1108-passing run is ARM, where the object is byte-identical, so it
proves the source compiles and that no test pins the old constant values, and nothing more.

## chain133 -- the mechanism is memory-level parallelism, and a .text digest is the wrong instrument

### What the multi-row kernel actually buys

The kernel's own comment says it, and it is not what chain131 guessed:

> ROWS accumulators, ROWS gather streams, one iteration issuing ROWS independent B loads that
> share no dependency. ... Rows of unequal length are handled by running the common prefix --
> min(len) iterations with every stream live and no branch in the loop -- and then finishing each
> row's tail serially. ... On a power-law matrix [the tails] are not [nearly empty], and the kernel
> degrades toward the per-row one; that is a property to measure per family, not to hide.

Memory-level parallelism, to cover an L3 hit that a short row cannot supply enough independent
loads to hide. That explains all three signs at once:

- **wins on short uniform rows** -- one row cannot issue two independent B loads, two rows can;
- **loses on ragged rows** -- the common prefix is short, so most nonzeros go through the serial
  tails, which have ROWS accumulators of register pressure and one stream of parallelism;
- **loses per NONZERO rather than per row** -- which is what the tails predict, and what the
  measurement showed: 0.01-0.04 ns/nonzero, with `connectus` losing 49 microseconds across 512
  rows, an amount no per-row cost can pay for.

An amortisation model was fitted first and refuted by its own numbers: it put multi-row's per-row
saving at -0.00 ns and predicted 0.982 at degree 8-16 where 1.068 was measured. Mean degree does
separate the two populations in the data -- 0 losers of 46 between 8 and 16, 7 of 12 above 128 --
but it is a correlate, not the mechanism, and a bound justified by a refuted model is a tuned
constant wearing a derivation.

`SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_RAGGED` is therefore per-GROUP, not per-call: the largest ratio of a group's
nonzeros to its common-prefix nonzeros that still admits the group. For two rows, `RAGGED=2` admits
a pair whose longer row is at most three times the shorter; `RAGGED=1` admits only equal rows;
`RAGGED=4` admits up to seven times. It costs one extra `A1_pos` load inside a test that already
reads that array either side of it, and it sits behind `multirow_ok`, so a width where the kernel
declines pays nothing. **It defaults to 0, which is off.**

### The neutrality instrument had to be replaced first

Proving the patch emits nothing new looked routine and was not. Two builds of the patched and
unpatched trees, same flags, paths of equal length: **same `.text` size (652264), no section
differing in size at all, and different bytes.** A digest check calls that a regression.

The disassembly says what actually happened. Of 164596 instructions, **20 differ, all of them
`mov w2, #imm`, every delta exactly +29** -- and the patch adds 30 lines to `scorch_policy.h`.
They are `__LINE__` values that assertion macros in `spmm.h` pass as an immediate, shifted because
the header above them grew. Nothing else moved.

So a `.text` digest cannot answer "does this change what we emit" for any change that adds lines to
a header. Every neutrality claim in this file rests on digests; none of them is wrong, because none
of them added header lines, but the instrument has been lucky rather than sound.

`scratchpad/neutral_disasm.sh` replaces it: diff the disassembly, and require every difference to be
a bare immediate move. It carries both controls, because a detector with only one is not tested --

| control | expectation | result |
|---|---|---|
| same commit, two directories, equal path length | neutral | `NEUTRAL: 164596 instructions, identical disassembly` |
| the patch, ARM | neutral but for line numbers | `NEUTRAL: every difference is a bare immediate move` |
| `-DSCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32=1`, which is ARM-live | caught | `NOT NEUTRAL: instruction counts differ, 164595 -> 164596` |

Two traps inside building those controls, both already on the books and both hit again anyway.
`sed -E` on macOS has no `\b`, so a first attempt's "masked" comparison masked nothing and silently
compared raw text; and `objdump`'s trailing `; =6487` comment had to be stripped or every line
number reads as an unrecognised instruction. The equal-path-length requirement is the third: a
directory one character longer shifts rodata and changes `.text` bytes without changing its size,
which is the same failure mode from a different cause.

The x86 disassembly check has not run -- both x86 hosts are timing -- so on x86 the patch is
"expected neutral because the term is `constexpr 0`", which is an argument and not a measurement.
It runs when a host is free.

## chain134 -- the flipped defaults are reverted, because a candidate must be an arm

`29384fe` set `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32` to 1 and `SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32` to 2 as
**defaults**. Chain 131 established it does not ship. This reverts the defaults and keeps every
additive mechanism added since, all of which default to off.

The reason is not tidiness. The next stages build their arms from a tarball of this tree, and a
build with no defines is the baseline arm in every one of them. With the flip still in the defaults,
`c0` would silently BE the candidate: every ratio would read about 1.000 and the stage would report
a null result for a change worth 15-35%. The tarball the currently running band-2 stages use
(`scorch_mr6.tgz`) predates the flip and is unaffected -- checked, its `_F32` constants still fall
through to the unsuffixed ones -- but the new tarball is cut from this tree, so the defaults have to
be the thing being changed FROM.

That is the same defect as a `-D` naming a macro no source reads, which cost this project two
cancelled jobs, arriving from the opposite direction: there, the arm was accidentally the baseline;
here, the baseline would have been accidentally the arm.

Reverted, verified: `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32` and `SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32` fall through
to the unsuffixed constants again, and `MULTIROW_RAGGED`, `MULTIROW_MINDEG` and `MULTIROW_MAXDEG`
survive at 0.

## chain135 -- what is queued, and what the degree dependence is and is not

Four stages are queued behind the two band-2 runs, in this order on redwood (chain5 through
chain7) and behind each other on MKT:

| stage | question | arms |
|---|---|---|
| band2 | does the band have to go to 1? | `c0` `c0b` `band2mr` `bandmr` |
| suitebase | what does the x86 suite pass on the unchanged tree? | -- |
| heldout | does the degree window survive a corpus it was not derived from? | `c0` `c0b` `bandmr` `mdlo` `md20` `md128` |
| attrib | widths 1 and 4: placement, code presence, or the branch? | `c0` `c0b` `c0pad` `mrf64` `bandmr` |

The held-out corpus is 40 matrices drawn from the 457 cached matrices at nnz >= 1e6 that appear in
no derivation or prior-selection key list, shuffled under a fixed seed and cut at 40, with degree
coverage 5 below 4, 18 in 4-20, 13 in 20-128, 4 above 128. On MKT the list is derived **inside the
job** from that host's own cache under the same rule, so it cannot be reshaped after seeing a
result and it adapts to what is actually cached there.

`an_heldout.py` checks two things, and the second is the one that matters. Delivery is the geomean
and the loser count. But a cell the gate REFUSES runs the baseline path, so its ratio against the
baseline must sit at its own floor -- and whether a cell is refused is computable from the `nnz` and
`rows` that every CSV row already records. If a refused cell does not read its floor, the constant
is not doing what it says and any win the build shows belongs to something else. That check is free
and it tests the binary against the define rather than assuming they agree.

### The peer instrument: an A/A replicate cannot see a shared fixed cost

Owed to a peer session that measured it rather than assuming. If both arms carry the same offset
`o` on top of kernel time `t`, A-vs-A reads 1.000 exactly -- the offset cancels -- while the A/B
ratio is compressed by `(1 + o/t_a)/(1 + o/t_b)`. So `c0`/`c0b` reading 0.9991 at width 1 is **not**
evidence that there is no offset there, and the compression is worst where the widths are narrowest,
which is exactly where the open question is.

`wsprobe.py` adds the discriminator: time the same call on a vertical stack of two copies of the
matrix -- exactly twice the rows and nonzeros, same B, same call count -- so `m1 = o + t`,
`m2 = o + 2t`, and `o/t = (2*m1 - m2)/(m2 - m1)` per arm per cell with no constant to invent. It is
folded into the attribution stage's rotation so it inherits the balanced lead order.

Two limits, stated because the number is useless without them. The **level is biased upward**: the
stacked copy re-walks a warm B, so `m2 < o + 2t`. That bias is a property of the input and identical
for every build, so a *difference* in `o/t` between builds is meaningful and the level is not. And
per-call work that scales with nonzeros -- the ABI validation walks the caller's arrays -- doubles
with the kernel and lands in `t`, so `o` is fixed cost in the strict sense: dispatch, marshalling,
thread-team entry. That is the right split for asking whether an object's prologue got more
expensive. A local smoke test reads `m2/m1` of 1.96 and 2.07 on a degree-9 matrix at widths 1 and 2
(`o/t` 0.04 and -0.07) and flags a degree-9 width-8 cell at 1.39 as a cache transition rather than
an offset, which is the guard doing its job.

### What the degree dependence is, and three explanations that do not survive

The dependence is real: monotone, present on both hosts, and it separates the populations. What it
*is* remains open, and three candidate mechanisms have now been tried and found wanting.

1. **Row-overhead amortisation.** Fitted and refuted by its own numbers -- per-row saving -0.00 ns,
   predicting 0.982 where 1.068 was measured.
2. **Serial tails in the multi-row prefix.** Real, and the kernel's comment says so, but
   insufficient: six of eleven losers have essentially uniform rows and admit 90-100% of their
   nonzeros at any raggedness setting (`cari` admits 1.000 at every value and still reads 0.850).
   It explains `connectus` and the `lhr` family and nothing else.
3. **The exact kernel's unroll depth.** At width 2 under a narrowed band, multi-row is competing
   against the exact-width kernel, whose unroll is already adapted per call to the largest power of
   two no greater than the mean row. That makes its per-row setup grow *with* degree, which bounds
   the setup-to-work ratio between about one and two rather than making it fall -- so it predicts a
   sawtooth in degree, not the single monotone crossing that is measured. It does explain why width
   2 behaves differently from widths 3 and 8, where the comparison is against the general
   register-block path instead, but it does not give a crossover value.

So `MULTIROW_MAXDEG` remains a boundary chosen against the data that defines it, sitting in a gap
between 18.6 and 21.3, and the held-out run is its arbiter. `MULTIROW_MINDEG` is in a different
position: a mechanism (a two-row group at degree under four holds eight nonzeros and often an empty
row, so the prefix cannot cover the prologue), six matrices on one host, and free on the other.

## chain136 -- the withdrawal was wrong, and the ceiling is host-conditional

Chain 133 withdrew the cost model in mean degree on the strength of a fit that returned a per-row
saving of -0.00 ns. **The model was fine; the fit was not**, in two specific ways.

It was fitted across **two kernel swaps at once**. At float32 width 2, going from the shipped
default to the candidate replaces the exact-width kernel with the general path (the band) and then
replaces that with the multi-row kernel. A model with one per-row term and one per-nonzero term has
terms for one swap. And it was **unweighted**, so a 1M-nonzero matrix whose ns-per-nonzero is
inherently noisier counted the same as a 2.7M-nonzero one.

Weighted by nonzeros -- justified as inverse-variance, since the variance of ns-per-nonzero is far
larger on a short kernel, not by the answer it produces -- the two-swap difference is exactly the
one that predicts the boundary:

| host | multi-row's row cost | its nonzero cost | implied crossover |
|---|---|---|---|
| redwood | **-0.08 ns** (a saving) | **+0.0049 ns** | **mean degree 16.7** |
| MKT | +0.02 ns | **-0.0086 ns** (cheaper) | none implied |

redwood's estimate is stable: 18.1, 18.1, 16.7, 18.7 as the residual trim goes 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7,
and a 200-sample bootstrap over matrices implies a crossover in 173 of them, median 17.6, p10 13.5,
p90 47.9. It lands on the gap in the measured data, whose winners stop at 18.6 and whose losers
start at 21.3.

Two honest qualifications. Without the nonzero weighting the same fit swings between "none implied"
and 7.6, so the estimate is weighting-dependent -- the weighting has an independent justification,
but a reader should know the number moves without it. And a bootstrap p90 of 47.9 is a wide upper
tail: the crossover exists on that host, its location is known to within roughly a factor of two.

### The consequence, which is not the one I was heading for

**MKT implies no crossing under any weighting or trim** -- multi-row is 0.0086 ns a nonzero
*cheaper* there -- and its bootstrap implies one in 12 of 200 resamples. That is the opposite
answer, not a smaller version of the same one, and it agrees with the measured populations: MKT
loses only at the low-degree end, and it has 12 winners above degree 20 at width 3 that a ceiling
would throw away.

So a compiled-in `MULTIROW_MAXDEG` would be right on one x86 host and a pure give-away on the
other. `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_MINDEG` reached this conclusion about its own value already -- "the
plausible reason the hosts disagree is what the kernel displaces ... either way the constant stays 0
and this is host-conditional, so a value chosen on one host must not be compiled in for both" -- and
this gets the same answer. **`MULTIROW_MAXDEG` stays 0.** It exists so a compiled-in A/B can measure
it, not as a value to ship.

`MULTIROW_MINDEG` is in the opposite position and is the shippable half: it takes MKT's width-2
loser count from 7 to 1, and on redwood the degree band it refuses reads 0.9742 rather than winning,
so refusing it is a small gain there too. Neutral-or-better on both hosts, with a mechanism.

That also sharpens what the held-out run tests. `md20` should now show a **predicted host
asymmetry**: zero losers and a gain at redwood's width 2, and a give-away at MKT's widths 3 and 8.
An arm that behaves the same on both hosts would refute the fit above.

Note on the tarball: this chain changed only a comment, which shifts `__LINE__` and nothing else.
The staged `scorch_mr7.tgz` was deliberately **not** re-cut, because swapping a tarball under queued
stages makes their results unattributable for no gain. Its constants and defaults are what the
stages check for.

## chain137 -- the two gates that are host-invariant, chosen before measuring them

With the ceiling ruled out as host-conditional, the question became which gate can fire on the
losers *without* a host-dependent constant. Both candidates were evaluated **offline against the
matrices themselves**, by computing each gate's own admission rule over the corpus -- no host time,
and the answer arrives before the arm is built rather than after.

`RAGGED=2` admits a two-row group only when its longer row is at most three times its shorter,
which is where the kernel's common prefix carries at least half the group's nonzeros. Per matrix,
the fraction of nonzeros living in groups it would admit:

| matrix | mean degree | bandmr | admitted at RAGGED=2 | the refusal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| connectus | 2202 | 0.602 rw / 0.816 MKT | **0.240** | fires on most of it, both hosts, widths 2/3/8 |
| lhr34c / lhr71 / lhr71c | 21 | 0.820 / 0.834 / 0.845 | **0.108** | fires on most of it |
| as-caida_G_081 | 2.7 | 0.929 (width 4) | **0.311** | fires on most of it |
| lp_osa_14 | 136 | 0.852 | 0.806 | fires on some |
| cari | 382 | 0.850 | **1.000** | cannot help -- rows are uniform |
| body_decoder_layer_3 | 323 | 0.858 | **1.000** | cannot help |
| bottleneck_1 | 133 | 0.895 | 0.971 | cannot help |
| relat8 | 3.9 | 0.905 MKT | **1.000** | cannot help |

And the give-away, which is the number that decides whether it is worth having: over the width-2
winners, **median admitted 0.999 and a refused share of 0.1%** on both hosts. A gate that reaches
the worst loser on both hosts while touching a thousandth of the winners' work is a different class
of proposition from one that trades 2.4-5.9%.

Two things follow.

**The two gates are complementary, not redundant.** `relat8` admits 1.000 of its nonzeros at every
raggedness setting and is reached only by the degree floor; `connectus` and the `lhr` family are
uniform in degree terms and are reached only by the raggedness test. MKT's `as-caida` and
`com-Amazon` losers are floor cases. So the candidate is both, and the held-out stage measures each
alone and the pair.

**The residual is now named and it is one population**: `cari`, `body_decoder`, `bottleneck` -- high
mean degree with uniform rows, on redwood only. Neither host-invariant gate can reach them, and the
gate that can is the host-conditional ceiling. That is the honest boundary of this approach.

The held-out stage was repointed onto `mdlo` / `rag2` / `ragmd` before it ran; `md20` and `md128`
were dropped, because measuring a constant that wants opposite signs on two hosts of the same ISA
on a held-out corpus would characterise an arm that cannot ship. `an_heldout.py`'s gate-firing check
now says explicitly that it cannot verify `RAGGED` from per-matrix metadata -- the rule is per
group, over consecutive row pairs -- rather than passing an arm it did not check.

Also fixed while setting this up: the MKT job carried **no rationale header at all**, because the
generator that produced it from its redwood twin split on `set -u` and silently dropped everything
above. It now carries the same 35 lines, including the same falsifiable predictions. A stage whose
stated predictions are absent is a stage that can be reinterpreted after the fact.

## chain138 -- the prediction failed, and the failure found a per-row tax on both hosts

MKT job 17286204: `c0`, `c0b`, `band2mr`, `bandmr`, 45 matrices, **four** passes over two dtypes so
each of four builds leads exactly twice, 5040 corpus rows and 288 GCN rows per build.

### The prediction, and which part of it failed

| width | predicted | measured (`band2mr` vs `c0`) | floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | its own floor | **0.9805** | 0.9996 |
| 3 | equals `bandmr` | 1.1458 vs 1.1460 | 1.0010 |
| 8 | equals `bandmr` | 1.2083 vs 1.2050 | 0.9986 |

Widths 3 and 8 held exactly, and `connectus` at width 2 held exactly as designed -- 1.102 against
its floor of 1.107, where `bandmr` reads 0.859 -- so the reading of the dispatch is right for the
population the arm was built for. Width 2 as a whole failed, and the stage said in advance that
if it did, the decomposition had to be redone.

### What the failure is

`band2mr` keeps the exact-width kernel at width 2, so its executed path is the shipped default's.
It still reads 0.9805, and the deficit has a shape:

| mean degree | `band2mr` at width 2 | floor |
|---|---|---|
| 0-4 | **0.9119** | 0.9884 |
| 8-20 | **0.9754** | 0.9980 |
| 20-128 | 1.0057 | 0.9989 |
| 128+ | 1.0224 | 1.0174 |

That falls as 1/degree, which is a **per-row** cost. And the low-degree matrices lose under *both*
arms -- `relat8` 0.825 and 0.892, `as-caida_G_084` 0.913 and 0.927, `_083` 0.918 and 0.937, `_073`
0.919 and 0.934 -- while under `band2mr` multi-row provably cannot execute at width 2. **So their
loss was never the kernel choice.**

The same signature is present at every width where the kernel declines, on both hosts, reading
across degree bands 0-4 / 8-20 / 20-128 / 128+:

| host, width | `bandmr` | the band-only arm |
|---|---|---|
| redwood, width 1 | 0.9635 / 0.9652 / 0.9882 / 1.0036 | 0.9985 / 0.9989 / 1.0038 / 1.0152 |
| redwood, width 4 | 0.9566 / 0.9756 / 1.0145 / 1.0032 | 1.0084 / 0.9975 / 1.0058 / 0.9813 |
| MKT, width 4 | 0.9696 / 0.9751 / 1.0101 / 1.0153 | -- |

The band-only arm is flat. **The tax belongs to the multi-row constant, at widths where the kernel
it enables cannot run.** MKT's width 1 is the one place it does not appear (0.9851 / 1.0191 /
1.0066 / 0.9937), so four of five host-width combinations show it, not five.

### The cause is not the branch

`multirow_ok` is already hoisted out of the row loop -- there is a comment at the hoist site
recording that -O3 does not hoist this lambda's invariants by itself -- and a perfectly-predicted
not-taken branch does not cost 8.8%. What costs is that the guarded block **stores to `C_values`
and reads `A1_pos`**, so the compiler must assume they alias and reload per row through the whole
loop. The split plan's scalars carry a comment about exactly this hazard a few hundred lines above:
*"a store to C_values may alias them -- and per-row loads are what decide a matrix of mean degree
9."*

`SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_UNSWITCH` instantiates the worker body twice, with `if constexpr` removing
the block from one, and picks per call -- one test per worker instead of one per row. Off by
default and emission-neutral there: 164596 instructions either way, differing only in shifted
`__LINE__` immediates. **The first attempt was not neutral**: wrapping the worker in a forwarding
lambda cost 14 instructions of 164596 with the constant off, so the off path now keeps the lambda's
original signature and has no wrapper at all.

The arm also **discriminates**, which the three structural arms cannot do alone: `unsw` contains
*more* code than `bandmr`. If the deficit were the multi-row code merely being present in the
object, `unsw` would be worse. Recovery localises the cost inside the row loop.

### Why this reordered both queues

If the tax is what the low-degree matrices were losing to, then `MULTIROW_MINDEG` -- built to refuse
multi-row below degree 4 -- is aimed at a population whose loss does not come from multi-row firing.
Measuring it on a held-out corpus before knowing that would characterise a gate against the wrong
cause. So `unsw` now runs **before** the held-out validation on both hosts: redwood chain 9 ahead of
chain 10, and on MKT job 17287573 with the held-out job's dependency moved onto it.

Three defects in the reordering itself, all mine, all caught before anything ran. A remote heredoc
left literal `\$` and every new chain died on a syntax error, so the chain scripts are now written
locally and copied. `pgrep -f "rw_chainN.sh"` matched **the launching shell**, whose command text
contains every chain name, so three chains were left waiting on the launcher and would have started
simultaneously -- the interlock would have let one run and refused the other two, losing two stages
silently. Each chain now publishes its own pid to a file and the launcher reads that. And the MKT
job's staging target was again the inherited `halfvec_mkt.tgz`; this one writes `unsw_mkt.tgz`.

## chain139 -- the curvature check's denominator is not a choice

The work-scaling estimator's falsification test was normalised by `t`. It should be normalised by the
median, and not because the median is the better of two arbitrary options -- because it is the only
one that makes the check equal its own statement.

The model puts `m2` at `(m1 + m3)/2`. So "does m2 sit where the model puts it, as a fraction of the
measurement" is `(m2 - (m1+m3)/2)/m1`, which is exactly `-curvature/(2*m1)`. Dividing by `t` is a
different rescaling whose only property is that it inflates on cells with a large offset, which is
the class of cell the check exists to *keep*.

It produced a false positive in the smoke data:

| matrix | width | o/t | curv/t | curv/median | m2/m1 measured | model predicts | truth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mid_d40 | 8 | 1.33 | -0.214 | -0.092 | 1.476 | 1.430 | additive; `/t` flagged it |
| small_d9 | 8 | 4.80 | -2.014 | -0.347 | 1.346 | 1.173 | not additive; both catch it |

Tolerance is now **0.20 of the median, and recorded as picked**: over the six smoke cells the
additive ones reach 0.107 and the one real violation reads 0.347, so it separates them with margin
on both sides and it is calibrated on six cells rather than derived. The null is exactly zero; the
tolerance around the null never is, and writing "0.20, picked, separation 0.107 against 0.347" is
the whole of what a reader needs to decide whether to inherit it.

`wsprobe.py` now also prints, once per run before any cell is timed, the per-call time at
N = 1, 2, 3, 6, 12 identical calls, and names its own conclusion: on this path it reads
"flat or rising: each call pays its own fixed cost, so the work per call must change." That is the
premise the whole estimator rests on, it costs about a second, and it was previously an argument in
a comment rather than a line in the log.

Both corrections came from the peer session running the same instrument on a GPU, where its fixed
cost holds at 42.0-45.9 microseconds across fourteen cases whose medians span a factor of 440 --
which is the strongest evidence available that the decomposition measures something rather than
absorbing residual, and it is evidence this project cannot produce, because on a synchronous CPU
call the same quantity is tens of nanoseconds and a cross-check for it recovers the machine's load
instead.

## chain140 -- the x86 suite baseline, which no previous number could be read against

Job 17286215, on the unchanged tree, x86, after installing pytest into the venv (the previous
attempt died on `REFUSE: no pytest in this env` and had never run):

**1110 passed, 73 skipped, in 1:36:57.**

The ARM run that has been quoted for two chains reads 1108 passed, 72 skipped. The two differ
because the platforms skip different tests, which is exactly why a bare "N passed" from one tree
means nothing: there was no number to compare it against, and had a candidate tree produced 1108 on
x86 it would have looked like a match to the ARM figure while being two tests short of this host's
baseline.

Any suite run on a candidate tree is now read against **1110 / 73 on x86** and **1108 / 72 on ARM**.

## chain141 -- a hard boundary on a point estimate, found in code written the same day

The attribution analyzer's verdict took a median distortion over cells and applied a hard 1%
boundary to it. That is the defect this file has been documenting all day -- a derived criterion
standing on a measurement, with no width -- and it was sitting in code written while the chain about
it was being written.

It now bootstraps the median over cells and reads the boundary against the interval:

- **DISPATCH** when the interval on the kernel-time ratio contains 1.0 and the distortion's does not;
- **KERNEL** for the reverse;
- **MARGINAL** when neither interval excludes 1.0 and at least one is wider than the boundary;
- and the same-code replicate's own spread prints beside all of it, as the floor the comparison can
  possibly resolve.

The flipping is not removed -- no threshold on a measured quantity can be flip-free -- it is moved
into the reported number instead of hidden in the verdict. A verdict that lands differently on
different days was always reporting an interval; it just was not printing one.

Better where it is available, and not available here: the arm and its replicate are two measurements
of each side's median, so the uncertainty on the distortion propagates in closed form without
resampling. This harness has the replicate at the first level only, so it yields a floor rather than
a full propagation, and a bootstrap over cells is what the data supports. Same intent, weaker
instrument, and worth recording which is which.

### A withdrawal

I told the peer session that their plateau -- four decades of stored entries with the median flat --
was checkable from the levels they already have. **It is not, and I withdraw it.** One attempt's `o`
and `t` cannot see that `t` failed to grow, because a single sample has nothing to compare against;
forty-seven microseconds of dispatch and forty-seven of kernel are indistinguishable from inside one
measurement. It is a cross-case property over `t` against work and it needs a pass across the suite.
The consequence I named was right -- a plateau pulls the scored population toward 1.0 and dilutes
the statistic the bound is applied to -- but "checkable from data in hand" was doing real work in
that sentence and it was false.

### Thresholds, counted

Four hard criteria have failed on contact in this project so far, and every one of them stood on a
measurement that was fine:

1. a crossing count, blind inside its own step, which hid an 18% regression and reported a pass;
2. a cell-population statistic that swung 45 points between two runs of the same object;
3. a degree ceiling that wants opposite signs on two hosts of the same ISA;
4. a curvature tolerance normalised by `t`, which flags a cell for being charged rather than for
   being non-additive.

The pattern is not that thresholds are wrong. It is that a threshold is a claim about a distribution
and gets recorded as a claim about a number.

## chain142 -- auditing my own refusals: three defects in the guard, and a single-host band2

The peer session reported a test of theirs that asserted the opposite of the truth and
passed for an incidental reason, and noted their per-side guard has never fired on
anything either device can produce. The general form is a guard credited with work it
has not done. That is checkable rather than merely agreeable, so I checked mine: build
the input each refusal names and see whether it actually refuses.

**The pre-flip guard was live, but not for the reason I would have said.** The first
test fed it the tree at 29384fe, which carries the flipped defaults, and it refused --
but the message came from the *macro-presence* loop, because 29384fe also predates
UNSWITCH. A guard credited for a refusal a different guard performed. Isolating it
needed a tree with all three macros present and only the defaults flipped; on that
input it does fire.

**Isolating it also exposed a coverage gap.** Constructing the isolating input, my
edit of `SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32` silently matched nothing, because in this tree
neither f32 constant holds a literal:

    #  define SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32  SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS   // -> 0
    #  define SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32    SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI     // -> 3

Both delegate to a generic parent. The guard grepped for the first of those two lines
and treated its presence as proof the tree was un-flipped -- so flipping the *parent*,
which is the natural "turn it on everywhere" edit, leaves the grepped line intact and
the guard accepts the candidate tree as the control. Measured on a constructed parent
flip: four resolved constants move and the grep sees none of them. Two of the four are
the f64 specialisations, which 29384fe deliberately left alone because ARM regressed to
0.7229 -- so the edit the guard is blindest to is also the one that would silently take
float64 with it.

Grepping a `#define` is the wrong instrument for a question about a resolved value.
Same shape as the `.text` digest: the right instrument is the one that resolves it.
`scratchpad/preflip_check.sh` now preprocesses a probe translation unit and compares
resolved values against the shipped defaults, so a flip at any level of the chain is
caught. Validated on five inputs -- shipped tree accepts; f32 flip, parent flip,
UNSWITCH-on, and constants-absent all refuse.

**Two bugs in the replacement, both caught only because it fails closed.** It refused
the good tree at first: I had written the macro name on both sides, so
`SCORCH_PROBE X = X` preprocessed to `SCORCH_PROBE 3 = 3` and the lookup key was gone --
the probe was eaten by the mechanism it was probing. Then, fixed locally, it refused
both real tarballs on redwood: the header includes `<cstdio>` and I had invoked `cc`,
which finds a C++ header on macOS and not on Linux. Neither bug is interesting; the
direction of failure is. A guard written to accept when its instrument fails would have
passed everything on redwood and said nothing.

**Absence is not the same defect as a wrong value.** The fixed guard then refused
`scorch_mr7.tgz`, correctly by its own table and wrongly in fact: mr7 predates the
unswitch commit, and the stages that use it do not arm UNSWITCH, so it is a good
control for them. A guard that refuses correct inputs gets skipped by whoever hits it.
Absence is now fatal only for constants named in `--require`, which is the list the
calling stage actually sets.

Both live inputs then verify, with the require-list each stage arms:

    scorch_mr8.tgz (unsw:    EXACT_HI_F32, ROWS_F32, UNSWITCH)  8/8 at shipped defaults
    scorch_mr7.tgz (heldout: EXACT_HI_F32, ROWS_F32, MINDEG, RAGGED)
                                                                7/7, UNSWITCH absent and unarmed

So the queued stages are safe under their weaker grep, because their inputs are in fact
correct. The stronger guard buys nothing for these runs and I did not swap a script
under a queued stage to install it.

**A correction to an alarm of my own.** Chains 6, 7 and 8 name the same stage scripts
and the same log files as chains 10, 11 and 12, which read as the reorder having
appended the new queue instead of replacing the old -- heldout, attrib and exunroll each
running twice, with the first run landing before unsw, the exact ordering the reorder
existed to prevent. They are not running. Each wrote one waiting line and died: they
were launched without `nohup` and took SIGHUP when their session closed. The live queue
is chain4 -> 5 -> 9 -> 10 -> 11 -> 12 = band2, unsw, heldout, attrib, exunroll, which is
the intended order. No duplication, and nothing to kill.

**band2 is a single-host result.** Redwood holds no band2 artifact at all -- only the
stage script -- so the width-2 failure (0.9805 against a 0.9996 floor, with the
1/degree gradient 0.9119 / 0.9754 / 1.0057 / 1.0224) is MKT only. Under the two-host
rule it is not confirmed, and I have been treating it as though it were. Redwood's
band2 is chain5, still queued behind chain4, which has been on the prefetch arm for ten
hours. The reading stands as the reason the ship candidate was reverted -- that decision
also rests on the two-host width-2 regression population and on redwood's own
0.9739/0.9881 at widths 1 and 4 -- but the gradient itself wants its second host.

**A consequence for heldout worth stating before its result arrives.** Its arms --
mdlo, rag2, ragmd -- are built from mr7, which has no unswitch. If unsw shows the
widths-1-and-4 deficit is the per-row tax, then MINDEG and RAGGED were fitted against a
taxed baseline, and a degree floor that looks like it recovers the losers may be
recovering the tax instead. Heldout's verdict then has to be re-read against an
unswitched base rather than taken at face value. That is why unsw runs first; it is not
yet why heldout is wrong.

MKT at the time of writing: unsw 17287573 running 59:50 of a 9-hour limit, heldout
17286960 pending on its dependency. Reading MKT's band2 output needs a job on mkt1,
where unsw is measuring, so it waits rather than becoming a co-tenant.

**Why chains 6-8 died, exactly, since I will otherwise re-derive it.** Four numbers
separate a queued remote shell that survives from one that does not:

    pid    ppid  sid    tpgid  SigIgn            verdict
    38908  1     38908  -1     0000000000000007  nohup'd AND its own session leader
    543302 1     543302 -1     0000000000000006  own session leader, HUP not ignored

`SigIgn` bit 0 is SIGHUP, so an odd last hex digit means `nohup`. Chains 4 and 5 have it;
chains 9-12 do not. But all six are session leaders (`sid == pid`) with no controlling
terminal (`tpgid -1`), so a terminal hangup cannot reach any of them -- that is why 9-12
have survived several sessions closing. Chains 6-8 had neither property: they were plain
children of the launching shell, so they took SIGHUP when it closed. Hardening 9-12 would
mean relaunching them, and a chain that is still waiting holds no data, so a death there
costs the relaunch and nothing else. Detectable and recoverable, so left alone.

**Queue order left as it stands**, deliberately. Redwood runs chain4 -> band2 -> unsw ->
heldout -> attrib -> exunroll. band2 sitting ahead of unsw is what closes the single-host
gap above, and MKT delivers unsw first regardless, so the primary read is not waiting on
redwood. chain4 is healthy rather than stuck: its prefetch arm is 154 matrices x widths
1/2/4/8/16 x builds c0/c0b/pf0 x two dtypes x two passes, pass p1 took 5h18m (19:43 ->
01:01) and p2 was 85% through at 01:44, with two stages after it. Reordering to get
redwood's unsw sooner would mean five relaunches on a host where I have already made two
queue mistakes today, to save one stage's duration on a confirmation run.

## chain143 -- a clean guardrail and an unrun guardrail printed the same line

The peer session found, in their own code, a boolean that was false both when a check
passed and when the check had nothing to compare -- so a run in which the cross-side
check never executed was indistinguishable from one in which it executed and passed.
That is a distinct defect from the ones already on the list: not a criterion blind to
what it measures, but a *result* blind to whether it was measured. Worth turning on my
own analyzers immediately, because the scan carrying the most weight here is the
beyond-floor check I added as the fix for the crossing count's blindness. If it reported
a pass when a cell had no floor to compare against, the fix would have inherited the
defect it was fixing.

It does not. That scan prints `h/n` -- hits over cells actually compared -- so a zero
denominator is visible as `0/0` rather than as a pass. Exposing the denominator is what
makes it safe, which is the same reason the replicate's own spread has to be printed
beside a bootstrap interval.

**One real instance across 25 analyzers, and it is next door to the safe one.** The GCN
guardrail in `an_band2.py`:

    w = None
    for ... : if r < 1.0 and abs(1 - r) > 2 * abs(1 - f): w = min(...)
    print("none beyond its own spread" if not w else ...)

`w is None` is true when every GCN cell sits inside its own same-code spread, and also
when no GCN cell was comparable at all. So the disclosure was uneven inside a single
file: the scan above it prints its denominator, and the guardrail below it does not.

**The input is reachable, not hypothetical.** The file already refuses when no CSVs
exist and when a required build is absent -- but the build check tests whether each build
appears *somewhere*, so a corpus-only run satisfies it while the `gcn` group is empty.
Constructed that input (80 corpus rows across all four builds, no `sg_*.csv` at all):
the old code printed a clean GCN guardrail for a guardrail that never ran. The fixed code
refuses, naming which of the three series was missing. Positive path re-checked on a
constructed regression -- cora at 0.9200 against a 0.9950 floor -- which is reported with
`[3 cells compared]`, and the clean build now reads "none of 3" rather than "none".

The peer could not fail closed on their equivalent, because the field it depends on is a
policy switch and withholding every result when it is off makes the switch unusable --
the same trap as refusing a tarball that is actually a valid control. They went from
silent-open to loud-open: report the number, attach an explicit note that the check did
not run. Mine takes the closed branch instead, because a GCN guardrail has no policy
reason to be switched off; if it cannot run, the run is not evidence of anything.

**The same defect is latent in the analyzer that gated the ship candidate, and it did
not fire.** `an_ship.py` ends its guardrail with `if worst: ... else: "no GCN cell
regresses by more than its own same-code spread"`, and `worst is None` also covers every
cell failing the `(a and o and fl)` filter -- so a non-empty GCN group with the candidate
series missing prints a clean guardrail. Harder to reach than the band2 one, and it
matters more, because that line gated 29384fe.

It did not fire, and the reason is worth keeping. `rw_s_ship.sh` only collects; the
analysis is a separate step. The collection stage ends with rows-per-build:

    c0        corpus 5490   gcn 216
    c0b       corpus 5490   gcn 216
    bandf32   corpus 5490   gcn 216
    bandmr    corpus 5490   gcn 216
    shipcand  corpus 5490   gcn 216

Every build carried its full GCN count, so the comparisons were real and the ship
decision rests on measured cells. That rows-per-build line is the same disclosure as the
`h/n` denominator, one layer earlier -- it is what makes the latent defect unreachable on
this run rather than merely unobserved. Fixed anyway, and verified in all three
directions: candidate absent from every GCN cell now refuses ("this is not a clean
guardrail; it is an absent one"), a constructed regression reports
`cora float32 k=7 0.8850 (its own floor reads 0.9950) [4 cells compared]`, and the clean
path reads "no GCN cell regresses ... (4 cells compared)". An empty GCN group, which
previously skipped the whole section in silence, now says so.

**A consequence for a reading already in hand.** MKT's band2 ran under the old analyzer,
so its GCN guardrail line cannot be trusted to distinguish clean from unrun. Its data has
to be re-analyzed with the fixed version. That is now the second reason MKT's band2 needs
re-reading rather than quoting -- the first, from chain142, being that it is the only host
that has it. Redwood's band2 has not started, so it will run the fixed analyzer.

## chain144 -- "refusals that look adjacent aren't a chain", applied to the pending stage

The peer's phrasing for the near-miss in chain143 -- two existing refusals, neither
covering the gap between them, because the build check asks whether each build appears
*somewhere* -- generalises, so I ran it against the two analyzers that are about to read
results still in flight rather than against ones whose verdicts are already spent.

`an_heldout.py` had three, and the middle one is the load-bearing check of the stage.

**Section 2 is titled "did the gate FIRE?" and a gate that refused nothing passed it.**

    ok = (not ref) or abs(1 - geo(ref)) <= tol

`ref` is the refused-cell population. Empty `ref` scored `ok`, and the summary below then
printed "every gated build's refused cells sit at their floor: the constants act as
specified". Vacuously true and read as evidence. The per-row `n=0` was visible, but the
summary is the line that gets quoted -- exactly the split the peer found between a
`0.000` column and the `n/a (denominator 0)` helper one function up in the same file.

The input is reachable and, worse, likely: `mdlo` gates on degree >= 4, so a held-out
corpus in which every matrix has degree >= 4 refuses nothing. Constructed it (6 matrices,
all degree 8) and the old code reported the constants acting as specified on a corpus
where the constant never engaged once. Now:

    mdlo  1 | geo nan n=0  --  | geo 1.0256 n=6
    ...
    GATE REFUSED NOTHING on this corpus: mdlo
    REFUSE: no gated build refused a single cell, so nothing here verified that any
    constant fired. This is not a clean gate check; it is an absent one.

and it is deliberately called neither a pass nor a failure -- a held-out corpus that
lacks the population a gate targets is a fact about the corpus. The other direction is
pinned too: half the matrices below degree 4 gives "act as specified across 5
build-width groups", with the group count now printed.

**Section 1** printed `lose 0` with no denominator; `geo()` returns nan on empty, so the
geomean column was honest while the loser column beside it read clean. Now `lose 0/6`.

**Section 3** printed "no cell is more than 5% behind the baseline under any arm" when
`rows` was empty, which also happens when every cell failed the `all(r)` filter. Dropping
one arm at only the three widths that section reads -- so the build-presence REFUSE stays
satisfied, which is the same gap as chain143's -- previously produced a clean line. Now it
refuses and says the blank is missing data.

Neither host analyses in-stage: MKT's sbatch and redwood's stage script both collect only,
and analysis runs locally, so the fixed analyzer applies to both pending runs without
touching a queued script. The corrected file is on redwood as well, where heldout has not
started.

The peer's taxonomy is the thing worth keeping from these two days. Silent-open, loud-open,
closed, and the question that picks between them is not safety but whether the thing that
cannot run has a legitimate reason to be off. A GCN guardrail and a gate-firing check have
none, so unrun is not evidence and both refuse. Their policy switch does, so theirs labels
instead. I would have argued fail-closed for their case and been wrong.

## chain145 -- the bootstrap collapsed to a point, and the chain141 defect came back

Auditing `an_attrib.py` for the same uneven-disclosure shape found it in the same file
twice over, and then the test written to check the fix found something worse in the
verdict itself.

**The disclosure gap, third instance in one file.** The work-scaling table prints
`used / seen` -- cells that survived the curvature test over cells that carried three
levels. The discriminator below it, which is the block that actually emits
DISPATCH / KERNEL / MARGINAL, printed neither, and skipped a width entirely and silently
when fewer than five pairs survived. So a verdict resting on 5 cells of 35 read exactly
like one resting on all 35, and a width that could not be resolved at all simply had no
row. Now the verdict line carries `6/9 cells (3 non-additive)` and the short case says so:

    bandmr vs c0 | NOT RESOLVABLE at this width: 2 of 3 cells carried both arms' levels
                   and survived the curvature test (0 rejected as non-additive); 5 needed

**What the test found.** The synthetic case gives both arms the same per-nonzero cost and
different fixed costs, so the right answer is DISPATCH. It printed "both moved". The t
ratio is exactly 1 by construction, but `(0.32-0.12)/2` and `(0.35-0.15)/2` differ by
4e-16 in binary floating point, so every bootstrap resample returned the same median, the
interval collapsed to a single point 4e-16 below 1.0, and `moved` -- "the boundary lies
outside the interval" -- was satisfied. Displayed as `[1.0000,1.0000]`, which contains 1.0
to every digit shown.

A zero-width bootstrap interval is a point estimate, so this is chain141's defect wearing
the bootstrap's clothes: a hard boundary applied to a point. The mechanism is not the
rounding, it is that resampling over cells captures the spread BETWEEN cells and nothing
of the measurement noise WITHIN one. Cells that agree closely therefore produce an
interval narrower than any single cell's own replicate spread, and in the limit narrower
than the smallest difference the harness can resolve at all.

The fix uses the quantity that was already being printed and not used: no interval may be
tighter than the replicate floor, so each is widened to at least +/- floor/2 around its
median. That is the one number in the chain measured directly rather than propagated,
which is the peer's argument for printing it in the first place -- it turns out to also be
the right bound. On the synthetic case the interval becomes `[0.9990,1.0010]` against a
0.0020 floor, contains 1.0, and the verdict becomes DISPATCH, which is the correct answer.
The widening is 0.001 wide here, so it cannot move a verdict that rests on real
between-cell spread; it only bites when the bootstrap has stopped being one.

Both fixes are deployed to redwood, where attrib has not started. Neither host analyses
in-stage, so both pending runs get them.

## chain146 -- decide on the displayed numbers, and the floor that was not always there

The peer separated two defects I had merged into one. Widening the interval fixed the
collapse; it did not fix the fact that `[1.0000,1.0000]` was printed beside a verdict that
excluded 1.0. A rendering that contradicts the verdict next to it cannot be audited by the
person reading it, whatever the code did internally.

Fixing that also closed a hole in the widening. `widen()` returns its bounds unchanged when
the replicate floor is nan, and the floor is nan whenever the cell carries no same-code
pair -- so with no replicate arm the collapse was fully back and the verdict was
unqualified.

Two changes. The bounds are rounded to the printed precision before the boundary test, so
the interval that is displayed IS the interval that decided, and contradiction is
impossible by construction. That costs nothing physical: 1e-4 is twenty times finer than
the replicate floor these cells resolve, so a difference the display cannot show is one the
instrument cannot see. And when the floor is nan the verdict now carries
`[NO REPLICATE: ... this verdict is unbounded below by the instrument]`.

Deciding on the displayed numbers turns out to be the stronger of the two fixes, which I
had backwards. On the no-replicate case the interval still prints `[1.0000,1.0000]`, the
rounded bounds now contain 1.0, and the verdict is DISPATCH -- correct -- with no floor
involved at all. The floor widening still earns its place for cells that agree closely but
not to four decimals; it is not what saves the degenerate case.

**The peer's own result, recorded because it kills a recommendation rather than confirming
one.** They had argued for reporting a distortion as `4.9% +/- 0.4%`, and checked both
routes to that width before building it. The replicate difference is bit-identical in 20 of
72 arm readings on their card, so the width collapses to a point in most attempts -- their
identical-to-the-last-bit and my 4e-16 are the same event, an input to the width with no
variation to see. The arm's own dispersion predicts a standard deviation of 0.032 to 0.048
percentage points against an observed across-pass 0.095 to 0.476, i.e. 2x to 10x too
narrow, and worst on the smallest cases, which are the ones nearest the bound. They dropped
the interval and will publish measured across-pass reproducibility as a property of the
instrument instead.

The symmetry is worth keeping because it bounds what widening can do. Mine: resampling over
cells captures spread between cells and none of the measurement noise within one. Theirs:
sampling within one attempt captures noise within it and none of the variation between
attempts. Same sentence, opposite blind spot. Mine was fixable by flooring because the floor
was a quantity already in hand; theirs is not, because no term inside a single run knows what
varies between runs. Six threshold or estimator failures over these two days, four mine and
two theirs, and every one was a derived quantity standing on a measurement that was fine.

## chain147 -- the unsw result had nothing to read it, and the analyzer's own test caught it lying

No analyzer knew the `unsw` build, so the measurement both hosts are running would have
landed with nothing able to read it. Wrote `an_unsw.py` (211 lines) carrying every
disclosure rule installed today, with the four predictions stated in the file before any
data exists, each falsifiable in a named direction:

    P1  at widths 1 and 4, unsw returns to its floor IN EVERY DEGREE BAND -- aggregate-only
        recovery leaves a band-shaped confound live
    P2  the recovery is largest below degree 4, because a per-row tax over fewer nonzeros per
        row is a larger fraction of the row's work
    P3  at widths 2, 3 and 8, unsw EQUALS bandmr, because the instantiation that runs there is
        the one bandmr already had
    P4  unsw is not WORSE than bandmr at widths 1 and 4 -- the discriminator the three
        structural arms cannot provide, since unsw contains strictly MORE code

Also written down: equality at 2/3/8 tests a kernel that does run, so it is a genuine test,
while recovery at 1/4 concerns a kernel that does not, so a null there is evidence about the
tax and not about multi-row.

**Validated against both possible worlds before trusting it.** One synthetic corpus where
the tax hypothesis holds -- bandmr taxed 8.0/3.0/1.0/0.3 percent by descending degree band,
unsw at its floor -- and one where it is false, with unsw carrying the same tax. World A
reads P1 HELD in all four bands, P3 HELD at every firing width, and annotates the two bands
where bandmr was never below floor with "nothing to recover", which is the correct reading
rather than a pass. World B reads P1 FAILED in the two bands where the tax is larger than
tolerance.

**And World B caught the new file lying.** P2 asks whether the recovery is monotone in
degree, computed as `all(cols[i] >= cols[i+1])`, which is trivially true of a flat series.
With unsw recovering nothing, every band difference is +0.0000 and P2 printed "HELD:
monotone in the predicted direction" -- a claim about the shape of a recovery, made where
there is no recovery to have a shape. The same vacuous truth as `(not ref) or ...` in the
gate-firing check, in code written twenty minutes after fixing that one, by the person who
had just written the commit message about it.

P2 now requires the largest band recovery to exceed the floor tolerance before it will
speak, and says so otherwise:

    P2 NOT APPLICABLE: the largest band recovery is +0.0000, inside the 0.015 floor
    tolerance -- there is no recovery whose shape this could test

and when it does hold it names the size and location of the largest recovery, which is what
P2 actually claims, rather than reporting monotonicity alone.

That is the sixth instance of this shape in two days and the second I introduced while
fixing another one. The recurrence is not carelessness about any single line; it is that
"the check passed" and "the check had nothing to check" are the same value in every
language I am writing in, so the only reliable defence is constructing the input where the
subject is absent and watching what the check says. Deployed to redwood; neither host
analyses in-stage, so both pending runs get it.

## chain148 -- a missing A/A floor silently became a hardcoded constant, in four analyzers

The peer's phrasing for the `widen()` hole -- "a fix that is conditional on data being
present is not the same fix as the one you tested" -- pointed at a class I had not swept:
not a verdict that cannot tell a pass from an absence, but a *calibration* that quietly
degrades when its input is missing.

Every tolerance in these analyzers is derived from the same-binary A/A floor, in the form

    tol = max(0.015, abs(1 - fl) * 2)

and `max(0.015, nan)` returns `0.015`. Python's `max` keeps the first argument because
`nan > 0.015` is False, so a group whose A/A floor is absent gets a hardcoded ratio
constant with nothing on the line to say the calibration was gone. That is precisely what
the house convention forbids: perf gates are calibrated against same-binary A/A noise-floor
controls, never a fixed ratio constant. The violation was silent and it read as a normal
verdict.

Four sites, one per analyzer: `an_band2.py` (0.012), `an_heldout.py` (0.015), `an_unsw.py`
P2 (0.015, which I had written as an explicit `else 0.015` an hour earlier), and
`an_attrib.py` (0.010). The attrib one is the sharpest instance of the peer's point: it
already guarded `math.isnan(cand)` and not `math.isnan(fl)`, so the nan check was there and
covered the wrong operand.

All four now call one helper returning `(tol, calibrated)`, and no caller may compare
against the base when `calibrated` is False -- the band table refuses the row, the
gate-firing check flags `NOFLOOR` and excludes the group from its count, P2 refuses to
speak of "inside the floor tolerance", and the three-way verdict refuses to attribute.
Re-ran all eight synthetic corpora built today; every verdict reads as before.

**Absence is the input nobody builds.** Roughly half of the defects across these two days
needed an input constructed by *removing* something rather than by breaking it -- the
no-replicate corpus, the empty refused-cell population, the GCN group without the candidate
series, a tarball cut before a constant existed, and now a group with no A/A arm. Breaking
an input is the natural test to write; deleting one is not, and the checks that only fail
on absence are therefore the ones that ship untested. Every fix today was verified by
constructing the absent case, which is the only reason any of them are known to work rather
than believed to.

## chain149 -- py_compile is not a run, and the harnesses were not where I said they were

Two process defects, both mine, both caught within minutes of asserting the opposite.

**I shipped a runtime-broken analyzer to a host after my own verification came back empty.**
Taking the peer's better version of the precision fix -- one constant driving both the printed
and the compared precision, so a later edit to the format string cannot make them drift --
I built the format with `str.format` and doubled the `%` signs. `str.format` does not need
them doubled, so `%%-8s` survived as a literal and the first real conversion specifier
consumed the wrong argument: `TypeError: must be real number, not str`. `py_compile` passes
on that, because it is a syntax check being asked a question about behaviour. I ran the two
verification greps, got empty output from both, said "both cases still read correctly", and
deployed. The empty output WAS the failure and I read it as a pattern mismatch.

Fixed, and the deployment step now RUNS each analyzer on a synthetic corpus on the host that
will use it rather than compiling it there:

    an_attrib  : DISPATCH
    an_unsw    : P1 HELD
    an_heldout : act as specified
    an_band2   : REFUSE       (correct -- that corpus carries no band2mr build)

**And the analyzer commits were only ever documentation.** Every commit in chains 143-148
ran `git add -A scratchpad/<file>.py 2>/dev/null` before adding the results document. The
scratchpad is a session temp directory outside the repository, so those adds failed and the
`2>/dev/null` swallowed the message -- the commits contain the prose describing each fix and
none of the code implementing it. The repository tracks no harness scripts at all, so there
was never a path for them there.

They are now archived where the house convention puts out-of-git artifacts,
`~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/harnesses/`, 79 files with a `SHA256SUMS` that verifies.
Before that they existed in exactly two places: an ephemeral scratchpad and one host's
`/scratch`.

Both defects have the same shape as the six being catalogued above, which is why they are
recorded rather than quietly fixed. `2>/dev/null` on a mutating command and `py_compile` as
a stand-in for a run are both a check that cannot fail reporting that it passed.

## chain150 -- nan is truthy, so a broken reading read as a clean cell

The peer found their `max(bound, nan)` class in five bare orderings -- `deviation > bound`,
`curvature > bound`, and three more -- because every comparison against nan is False, so all
five reported "within tolerance" for a value that has none. Chain148 fixed how my tolerance
was *derived*. It did not touch what the tolerance was compared *against*.

The guard in front of every scan here is

    if not (a and o and fl): continue

which catches `None` and `0.0` and lets nan through, because `bool(nan)` is True. Then:

    nan < 0.95                 -> False
    abs(1-nan) > 2*abs(1-nan)  -> False

so a non-finite reading counts in the denominator and never in the numerator. A broken
measurement reads as a clean cell, and the crossing count and the beyond-floor scan both
report it as fine. Eighteen such orderings across the five analyzers, and
`statistics.median([1.0, nan])` is nan, so a single bad reading contaminates its whole cell
and the contamination then reads as cleanliness.

Fixed at ingestion rather than at eighteen comparison sites: `reading()` refuses any value
that is not finite, and also any value <= 0, since a zero duration is not a measurement and
makes every ratio infinite. Drops are counted by kind and reported, and more than 1% of
readings unusable is a refusal rather than a note -- that is a broken stage, not a stray.

    READINGS DROPPED: 1 non-finite, 1 non-positive, of 528 total (0.38%)
    READINGS DROPPED: 24 non-finite, 0 non-positive, of 528 total (4.55%)
    REFUSE: more than 1% of readings were unusable. That is a broken measurement, not a
    stray -- fix the stage rather than analysing around it.

**I did not first work out whether nan can reach these files, and that is deliberate.** The
peer's reasoning, which I am adopting: a reachability argument is a claim about every future
caller of a file that is still being edited. They have a precedent in their own project where
"this can only ever be a digit" produced 27 tests silently reporting a missing GPU on a
machine that enumerated the card perfectly.

The peer also named why chain148's sharpest site was sharp, better than I had: a present
`math.isnan(cand)` guarding the operand that cannot be nan is not a missing check. It is a
check that demonstrates the author knew the hazard, and its presence is what makes the gap
invisible to a reviewer, who sees a nan check and moves on.

**And the process fix from chain149 immediately earned itself.** All five analyzers compiled.
Running them found `an_ship.py` dead on a `NameError`: it never imported `math`, because it
had never needed it, and my patch introduced the first use. `py_compile` cannot see that. The
deployment step now runs all five on synthetic corpora on redwood, which is where the run
above comes from, plus the refusal path:

    an_unsw P1 HELD | an_band2 cells compared | an_heldout act as specified
    an_attrib DISPATCH | an_ship cells compared | refusal REFUSE: more than 1

Archive refreshed at `~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/harnesses/`, 79 files verifying
against `SHA256SUMS`.

**The constructed absences are now fixtures rather than things I thought of once.** All
twelve are archived under `.../spmm-beat-mkl/fixtures/` with a README mapping each to the
verdict it must produce, and each one is built by REMOVING something rather than by
perturbing a value:

    b2data     corpus rows for all four builds, no gcn group     -> guardrail must refuse
    shipdata   gcn cells present, candidate series absent        -> guardrail must refuse
    ho_nofire  every matrix degree >= 4, so MINDEG refuses none  -> gate check must not pass
    ho_arm     one arm dropped at only the widths a section reads -> that section must refuse
    at3        3 cells, below the 5-pair minimum                 -> NOT RESOLVABLE
    at9nr      the same-code replicate removed                   -> verdict carries NO REPLICATE
    u_bad      the tax hypothesis false                          -> P1 fails, P2 not applicable
    u_broken   5% of readings nan                                -> the run refuses

Verified by running the archived analyzers against the archived fixtures, from the archive:
nine pairs, nine expected verdicts, all reproduced. 102 files verify against `SHA256SUMS`.

That matters because the natural way to generate a test input is to perturb a value, not to
delete a column -- so the inputs that catch this whole class are the ones neither a reviewer
nor a fuzzer produces. Keeping them as fixtures is the only way the next edit gets checked
against them.

## chain151 -- the per-row tax is real, the unswitch fix is a net regression, and it does not ship

MKT job 17287573 finished at 02:39:40. Every build carried its full count -- `c0`, `c0b`,
`bandmr`, `unsw` at `corpus 5040  gcn 288` each -- so the comparisons are real, which is the
rows-per-build disclosure doing its job before any analysis ran. 45 matrices, widths
1/2/4/3/8, both dtypes, four passes. Read with `an_unsw.py`, whose four predictions were
written into the file before the data existed.

Statistic: `bandmr_time / unsw_time`, so above 1 means unsw is faster, paired with each
cell's own `c0`-vs-`c0b` displacement as the A/A control.

**P1 and P2 hold, and the mechanism is confirmed.** At the widths where the multi-row kernel
cannot run, below degree 20:

    float32 k=1  unsw faster on 22/26  median 1.0188  beyond own A/A 15/26
    float32 k=4  unsw faster on 25/26  median 1.0207  beyond own A/A 21/26
    float64 k=1  unsw faster on 21/26  median 1.0141  beyond own A/A  5/26
    float64 k=4  unsw faster on 18/26  median 1.0064  beyond own A/A 10/26

Removing the admission code from the row loop is worth about 2% on float32 exactly where a
per-row tax predicts it -- low degree, kernel not running -- and it is broadly based rather
than a geomean artefact. The guarded block inside the row loop was costing per-row work
whether or not the guard fired. float64 carries the same sign at half the size, with most
cells inside their own A/A.

**P3 and P4 fail, and that is what settles it.** At degree >= 20 unsw is SLOWER, at every
width, on both dtypes:

           k=1     k=2     k=3     k=4     k=8      (median bandmr/unsw, deg >= 20)
    f32  0.9874  0.9843  0.9829  0.9850  0.9766
    f64  0.9926  0.9890  0.9862  0.9882  0.9932

unsw is faster on only 1 to 5 of 16 matrices in every one of those ten cells, and 9 to 15 of
16 are beyond their own A/A displacement. P3 predicted equality at widths 2, 3 and 8 because
the instantiation that runs there is the one bandmr already had; instead unsw loses 0.7% to
2.3% wherever degree is high. The per-band table flagged only k=8, because its tolerance
there was loose enough to absorb k=2 and k=3 -- the per-matrix count is what shows it is the
same effect at all five widths.

So the two effects are separable and both real: removing the admission from the row loop
gains ~2% at low degree, and emitting the worker body twice costs 1-2.3% at high degree,
where the loop is hot and the extra instantiation is decode and instruction-cache pressure
that buys nothing. The trade is 26 low-degree matrices at two widths against 16 high-degree
matrices at five widths, on both dtypes.

**On the standing goal it also loses ground.** Cells below MKL, float32:

    k=1   k=2   k=3   k=4   k=8
    bandmr  18/42 29/42 14/42 15/42 12/42
    unsw    18/42 33/42 15/42 15/42 13/42

Four more cells below MKL at width 2, one more at widths 3 and 8. And neither arm is clean on
the GCN guardrail: bandmr's worst is citeseer float64 k=7 at 0.9731 against a 1.0031 floor,
unsw's is pubmed float64 k=7 at 0.9792 against a 0.9897 floor, both beyond their own spread,
24 cells compared each.

**Verdict: unsw does not ship.** Reported as a finding rather than tuned around. It stays
behind its constant, defaulting to 0, where it already is.

**The next experiment is implied rather than invented.** The gain and the loss come from
different halves of one change. The gain needs the admission code out of the row loop; the
loss comes from duplicating the entire worker body to get it out. Hoisting only the guarded
store -- or removing the store to `C_values` that forces the aliasing reload, without
duplicating the loop -- would take the first without the second. That is the arm to build,
and it has a prediction: low-degree gain preserved at widths 1 and 4, high-degree loss gone
at all five.

One host. Redwood's copy is queued behind chain4 and chain5, and the high-degree regression
wants its second host before it is called a two-host result, though its consistency across
ten cells and both dtypes on this host is already past what a single noisy cell could produce.

**One check added on the strength of the peer's detail, and demonstrated firing.** They keep
device and host readings together because their agreement check compares one list's median
against another's, and the two have to describe the same samples. My equivalent gap: a dropped
reading leaves its cell with fewer reps than the build it is compared against, both medians
still compute, and nothing in the output says they rest on different sample counts -- so an
imbalance reads as a difference between builds.

Added to `an_unsw.py`, `an_band2.py` and `an_heldout.py`: report any cell whose builds carry
unequal `ours` rep counts, and refuse above 2% of cells. The first fixture written for it could
not exercise it -- one rep per cell means a drop removes the build entirely rather than
unbalancing it, which is the check-that-cannot-fire defect again, so a second fixture gives five
reps per cell and takes two of five from one build on three matrices:

    REP-COUNT IMBALANCE in 3 of 60 cells -- paired medians would rest on different sample counts
    REFUSE: more than 2% of cells are unbalanced across builds

**On the result above, it does not fire: zero imbalanced cells of 450.** So chain151's numbers
rest on equal sample counts across all four builds, which was previously an assumption and is
now a checked fact. Also kept from their note: refusing `<= 0` is right for a wall-clock
duration here but would be wrong on their device-event path, where an interval below the timer
tick genuinely reads zero and dropping those would bias the smallest cases -- the same value
means different things on the two instruments.

**Two corrections found while reading this.** First, my own helper script counted
`unsw_time / bandmr_time > 1.0` as "unsw faster", which is backwards for a ratio of times, so
its first output said 4 of 26 where the truth was 22 of 26. The geomeans in `an_unsw.py` were
right; the ad-hoc script written to check them was inverted, and it inverted the conclusion I
was about to report. Caught only because the two disagreed.

Second, chain150 states that `statistics.median([1.0, nan])` is nan. The correction I first
wrote for it -- that parity decides, even-length propagating and odd-length returning a
plausible finite value -- is also wrong, and the peer caught it. It is POSITION, not parity.
