Python's sort orders with `<` alone and every comparison against nan is false, so where the nan
ends up depends on where it started. Measured on 3.13.12, thirteen reps being exactly the count
this harness uses:

    median([1.0, 2.0, nan])              = 2.0
    median([nan, 1.0, 2.0])              = 1.0
    median([1.0, nan, 2.0])              = nan
    median([1.0]*6 + [nan] + [2.0]*6)    = nan     <- 13 reps, nan in the middle
    median([nan] + [1.0]*6 + [2.0]*6)    = 1.0     <- 13 reps, nan first
    median([1.0]*6 + [2.0]*6 + [nan])    = 2.0     <- 13 reps, nan last

So with 13 reps you get either outcome depending on arrival order. The operational conclusion
is unchanged -- a bound cannot be relied on to catch it, so refuse at ingestion -- but the
parity version was worse than merely wrong: it implies some sample count could make you safe,
and none can. Recorded because the wrong version was already written down.

The peer reports `statistics.stdev` raising `AttributeError` on their version where mine raises
`ValueError: inf or nan encountered in data`, so that symptom is version-dependent. None of
these analyzers computes a standard deviation, so the silent path is the only one they had.

## chain152 -- a finiteness check on a derived statistic protects nothing

Three things, and the middle one overturns the fix I had just written.

**The parity claim was wrong and is corrected above.** It is position, not parity: Python sorts
with `<` alone, every comparison against nan is false, so where the nan lands depends on where
it started. With thirteen reps -- this harness's count -- a nan in the middle gives nan, first
gives 1.0, last gives 2.0. The operational conclusion is unchanged, but the parity version
implied some sample count could make you safe, and none can.

**`max` over measured values discards a non-finite second argument and propagates a first.**
`max(0.006, nan)` is 0.006; `max(nan, 0.006)` is nan. Two sites here take a max over measured
quantities. `an_gcnguard.py` is safe by accident -- it filters with `a == a` before the max,
which excludes nan because nan is unequal to itself. `an_resid.py` was not:

    aa_reach = max(abs(q(aa, A.lo) - 1.0), abs(q(aa, A.hi) - 1.0))

A failed low quantile would have handed back the high one alone as the measured A/A reach --
narrower than anything measured, order-dependent, nothing on the record -- and `aa_reach` is
the control that decides whether a below-MKL cell is real.

**And the fix I wrote for it was the wrong fix.** I guarded the two components for finiteness
and skipped the cell otherwise. Built the corpus to prove it fires: nine reps, one nan in the
A/A pair of three cells. It did not fire, and the poisoned cell reported a FINITE A/A reach of
0.002. The nan never reached a quantile position; it only perturbed the sort order, and the
quantiles came from finite neighbours. So an ordering-based statistic returns a plausible
finite value from poisoned input, and checking the statistic for finiteness protects nothing.
Moved to ingestion, like the other five, where the drop is now reported:

    READINGS DROPPED: 6 non-finite or non-positive, refused at ingestion

I would have committed the output check and believed it worked, because it is the obvious fix
and it fails closed. Only building the input showed it never runs.

**Pairing by repetition index is structurally immune to the imbalance problem.** `an_resid.py`
computes `set(a) & set(b)` over rep indices, so a dropped reading removes that pair from both
arms and no median rests on samples the other lacks. The analyzers that compare two
independently-computed medians -- `an_unsw`, `an_band2`, `an_heldout` -- are exposed, which is
where the imbalance check belongs and where it now lives. Worth stating because it decides
which files need the check rather than adding it everywhere.

**The imbalance check now separates two conditions**, on the peer's point that only one is a
defect. An arm can be legitimately short because a pass produced fewer rows for it; refusing
that is a guard that refuses correct input. So the split is on whether the cell actually lost a
reading, and both branches are demonstrated:

    u_imbal  five reps, one build given three by the stage, nothing refused
             -> REP-COUNT SHORT BUT INTACT in 3 of 60 cells, and 0 refusals
    u_lost   five reps, two of five NON-FINITE for one build
             -> READINGS DROPPED: 6 non-finite (0.25%)
             -> REP-COUNT IMBALANCE FROM REFUSED READINGS in 3 of 60 cells
             -> REFUSE

The 0.25% drop rate sits under the 1% ingestion refusal, so the two checks catch different
things in sequence rather than one masking the other.

On the chain151 result none of this fires: zero dropped readings, zero imbalanced cells of 450.
Those numbers rest on equal sample counts of finite readings, as checked facts.

Archive at `~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/`, 106 files verifying, fixtures README updated
with the three new constructed inputs.

## chain153 -- the heldout job died 39 seconds in, and the guard was right to kill it

The MKT queue emptied, which I first read as heldout having run. `sacct` says otherwise:

    17286960  heldout   FAILED   1:0   00:00:00   2026-09-06T02:40:19
    17287573  unsw      COMPLETED 0:0  01:58:20   2026-09-06T02:39:40

Exit 1 with zero elapsed, 39 seconds after unsw completed -- so the dependency was satisfied and
the job died in its opening commands. The log, at the `/matx` staging path its `#SBATCH -o` names:

    note: /matx/u/bobbyy/staging/heldout_keys_mkt.txt not staged
    note: /matx/u/bobbyy/staging/gcn_keys.txt not staged
    excluded as derivation/prior-selection keys: 110
    size-filtered candidates: 913
    held out at nnz >= 1e6: 473
    selected 40; degree median 25.8; below 4: 5, 4-20: 14, 20-128: 14, above 128: 7
    REFUSE: no gcn key list

The guard was right. Without the list the GCN guardrail would not have run, and an eight-hour
heldout verdict with an absent guardrail is precisely the thing chains 143 and 144 exist to
prevent -- it would have printed a clean guardrail line under the old analyzer. Failing in 39
seconds beat succeeding in eight hours.

**But the dependency it enforced should not have existed.** `gcn_keys.txt` contains three fixed
strings -- `gcn/cora`, `gcn/citeseer`, `gcn/pubmed`. The unsw job, which ran fine, generates them
inline with a `printf` and then checks the matrices themselves are present. heldout instead
hard-depended on a staged file with constant contents, and that cost a run. Now it generates the
list and checks the real input:

    gcn guardrail inputs: 3 graphs, all present under /scr/bobbyy/mklsweep/csrcache

The npz files were there the whole time -- I had checked `/scr/bobbyy/suitesparse/gcn/` and found
zero, which is the wrong path; unsw extracts `gcn_npz.tgz` into the csrcache, where all three sit.
Checking the wrong path nearly had me conclude the GCN guardrail could not run on this host at all.

**Two things fixed while the job was not queued, which is the only safe moment.** The sbatch's
pre-flip guard checked both delegation lines rather than one, so it was stronger than the `.sh`
stages' version, but still could not see a parent flip. Replaced with the resolved-value probe
over six constants, and -- unlike chain142, where I verified the guard against reconstructions --
this one was tested against the exact bytes the job reads:

    redwood/local  8f5775f57fab187202d56a9c8c1a99572aa77b121ccea24ab26c99bc2380a7d1
    MKT staging    8f5775f57fab187202d56a9c8c1a99572aa77b121ccea24ab26c99bc2380a7d1

and on good / parent-flipped / f32-flipped / constants-absent it accepts, refuses, refuses,
refuses.

**And the header was asserting a corpus the job derives differently.** It claimed 510 candidates
at nnz >= 1e6 with degree coverage 5 / 18 / 13 / 4. The job actually found 913 size-filtered, 473
held out, and selected 5 / 14 / 14 / 7, because the cache has grown since the header was written.
A header that states a corpus the job then re-derives is a stale claim that reads as a
specification. The counts are gone from the header; the job prints its own coverage and that
printed line is the record.

Resubmitted as 17290869.

## chain154 -- the held-out corpus rejected both windows, and rejected my reading of the failure first

MKT 17290869 ran 03:06 to 05:19 on 43 held-out matrices, six builds at `corpus 3600 gcn 216`
each, rotation balanced at 6 groups over 6 builds. Every guard cleared, including the new
resolved-value policy check and the generated GCN key list.

**Delivery, float32, geomean against c0 with losers beyond their own floor:**

     k | floor  | bandmr           | mdlo             | rag2             | ragmd
     1 | 1.0014 | 0.9965 lose 4/40 | 0.9933 lose 4/40 | 0.9579 lose 15/40| 0.9594 lose 13/40
     2 | 0.9999 | 1.1221 lose 5/40 | 1.0795 lose 5/40 | 1.0434 lose 5/40 | 1.0187 lose 5/40
     3 | 0.9983 | 1.3379 lose 2/40 | 1.2873 lose 5/40 | 1.2418 lose 5/40 | 1.2138 lose 5/40
     4 | 0.9608 | 0.9503 lose 2/40 | 0.9532 lose 2/40 | 0.9314 lose 10/40| 0.9322 lose 9/40
     8 | 1.0054 | 1.4264 lose 0/40 | 1.3551 lose 0/40 | 1.3218 lose 0/40 | 1.2890 lose 0/40

`bandmr` -- band plus multi-row with no window at all -- is the best of the four at every
width. Both refinements are worse everywhere, and `rag2` turns width 1 into 15 losers of 40.
Neither ships.

**The mechanism, and it is the exact failure a held-out corpus exists to catch.** The window
MINDEG=4 was derived from corpora that showed low-degree matrices losing under multi-row. On
matrices that had no part in choosing it, those same low-degree matrices *gain* from multi-row,
and the window takes the gain away. Isolated to the refusal alone -- arm against its ungated
sibling, on only the cells the rule refuses:

    mdlo vs bandmr  float32  k=1..8  1.000  1.352  1.364  0.998  1.692
    mdlo vs bandmr  float64  k=1..8  0.989  1.003  1.010  1.016  1.037
    ragmd vs rag2   float32  k=1..8  1.005  1.211  1.203  1.002  1.232

Refusing costs 35%, 36% and 69% on float32 at the three widths where multi-row fires, is
neutral on float64, and does NOTHING at widths 1 and 4 -- which are the widths whose deficit
motivated the window in the first place. It neither helps where it was aimed nor is neutral
where it fires. The five matrices are `debr_G_16` at mean degree 4.0 and four of the
`Spielman_k100/k200` family at 3.0, reading 0.62-0.71 against c0 under mdlo where bandmr reads
0.889-1.005.

**The gate itself is not the defect, and my check said it was.** Section 2 shipped with the
premise "a refused cell runs the baseline path, so build/c0 should read ~1.000", and on that
premise it printed GATE DID NOT FIRE AS SPECIFIED for nine build-width groups. The premise is
wrong: a refused cell still carries `EXACT_HI_F32=1`, which c0 does not, so its reference is
bandf32 and not c0. The answerable firing test is the admitted cells against the ungated
sibling, where the same code runs on both -- and there mdlo matches bandmr to within 0.7% at
every width and both dtypes (0.9932 to 1.0079). The gate fires exactly as specified.

So the check conflated two opposite conclusions under one verdict:

    "the gate did not fire"           -- the constant is not doing what it names
    "the refusal path is not neutral" -- the constant fires, and refusing is expensive

The data says the second and the check reported the first. Now separated: the firing test runs
on admitted cells against the sibling, the refusal question is answered against bandf32 when a
stage carries it, and declared unanswerable when it does not -- this stage has no bandf32 arm,
so its refused-cell deviation is the band and the refusal together and is reported rather than
attributed. That is a stage design gap worth fixing before the next window is tested.

**And the width-1 and width-4 deficit survives everything.** `bandmr` still reads 0.9965 with
4 losers and 0.9503 with 2 losers there, on held-out data, and neither window moves it. Chain151
found the per-row tax is what causes it and that unswitching fixes it at low degree while
costing more at high degree. So the deficit's real fix remains open, and these two windows were
the wrong instrument for it -- they were fitted to the symptom's population rather than to its
mechanism.

Note the width-4 floor: 0.9608, a 3.9% same-code spread, giving a 7.8% tolerance. Width 4 is
weakly resolved on this corpus and its numbers should not be leaned on.

One host. Redwood's heldout is chain10, still behind chain4, chain5 and chain9.

## chain155 -- the other half of the unswitch result, and four defects in verifying it

chain151 left one experiment implied rather than invented. The unswitch gained ~2% at the widths
the multi-row kernel declines by removing a per-row reload of `A1_pos[i]` and `A1_pos[i+1]` --
the guarded block stores to `C_values` and the compiler cannot prove that store does not alias
`A1_pos` -- and it paid for that by instantiating the whole worker body twice, which cost 1-2.3%
at mean degree >= 20 at every width on both dtypes. The gain and the cost come from different
halves of one change, so `SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_HOIST` takes the first without the second: read
the row's own bounds ONCE, before the guarded block, and keep them in registers.

Committed as `b9e7910`, default 0, with its predictions in the constant's comment. **P2 is the
one carrying the discrimination**: if degree >= 20 is neutral here then the duplicated
instantiation really was the high-degree cost, and if it is not then chain151's explanation for
why unsw failed was wrong. P1 alone would only say the fix works.

**Emission-neutral at the default, proven and reconciled.** 185452 instructions on both sides,
20 differing lines, every one a bare immediate move into `w2`, single delta +27, and exactly 27
lines were added to `spmm.h`. So `__LINE__` shifted and nothing else -- no instruction added,
removed or reordered. Compiles clean at HOIST 0 and 1, with and without
`SCORCH_SPMM_SPLIT`, and introduces no new diagnostic. The `A1_pos[i + 1]` read stays behind the
region test, because under `REDIRECT` the claim index runs past the row region where `A1_pos` is
not indexed by it -- the same ordering hazard the multi-row guard's own comment records getting
wrong once.

**Four defects in my own verification of it, all caught, all the same shape as the rest of the
session.**

*The hoist landed 400 lines from where it belonged.* `s.index()` found the first of eighteen
occurrences of `#if defined(__AVX2__) && defined(__FMA__)` in the file, not the one inside the
row loop. Redone as a line-number insertion with three context assertions -- the row loop above
it and the `#endif` before it -- because the file also has a SECOND row loop at 6098 with its own
AVX2 block, and that one must not be touched.

*The compile check compiled `/dev/null`.* `-fsyntax-only ... -x c++ /dev/null` returns 0 for any
value of any constant. It reported "driver ok" twice for a tree whose hoist was in the wrong
scope. Same class as py_compile standing in for a run, one layer down: a check that cannot fail.

*The neutrality check compared two empty files and printed NEUTRAL.* `-S -o -` inside a flag
variable produced nothing, stderr went to /dev/null, and the diff of two zero-line files is
empty. I caught it only because I had printed the line counts. It now refuses under 1000
instructions per side, which is the rule `neutral_disasm.sh` already carried and this ad-hoc
check did not.

*`sed 's/[[:space:]]\+/ /g'` silently did nothing,* because BSD sed has no `\+`. The whitespace
was never collapsed, so the pattern matching "bare immediate move" matched none of the 20 lines
and declared them NOT NEUTRAL. Same family as the `\b` trap already recorded: a GNU regex
extension failing open on macOS.

**And a fifth, in the guard itself.** `preflip_check.sh --require SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_HOIST`
returned OK on a tarball, and the require did nothing at all -- HOIST was not in the table of
shipped defaults, so the name silently matched no check. A `--require` that cannot be honoured now
refuses, because the caller believes a check ran that never did. Verified: a bogus name refuses,
mr9 passes with 9 constants, and mr7 -- which predates both HOIST and UNSWITCH -- still passes with
7 and both absences listed as unarmed.

**Two stale references in the copied sbatch, one of which would have lied about the cause.** The
correctness loop still read `for B in bandmr unsw`, so it would have tried `$R/unsw/src`, failed
to import, and refused with "unsw disagrees with a dense reference" -- blaming correctness for a
stale build name. It now derives the candidate list from `BUILDS` minus the controls and refuses
if that is empty. The completion marker still said `MKT_UNSW_DONE`, which is the string the
poller greps for.

Submitted as MKT 17295447. Tarball sha256 `88cb4b24...803d7c` identical local and staged.

## chain156 -- the hoist is rejected, and it falsifies chain151's mechanism

MKT 17295447 finished at 11:04:47. Four builds at `corpus 5040 gcn 288` each, same shape as
17287573, so the two are directly comparable. `bandmr_time / candidate_time`, above 1 meaning
the candidate is faster, per matrix rather than per geomean:

    deg < 20, float32      hoist                      unsw (chain151)
      k=1                  faster  1/26 median 0.9103 | faster 22/26 median 1.0188
      k=4                  faster  0/26 median 0.9492 | faster 25/26 median 1.0207
    deg >= 20, float32
      k=1                  faster  1/16 median 0.9877 | faster  3/16 median 0.9874
      k=8                  faster  3/16 median 0.9893 | faster  1/16 median 0.9766

**All four predictions failed.** P1: hoist does not reproduce the gain at the non-firing widths
-- it is 9.0% and 5.1% SLOWER, faster on 1 of 26 and 0 of 26 matrices, against A/A floors of
about 0.7%, so 7 to 13 times the floor and unanimous. P4: it is worse than bandmr there, which is
the same finding stated as a comparison. P3: at the firing widths it is 1.5-1.7% behind bandmr in
the 4-20 band. P2: it is not neutral at degree >= 20 either -- 0.7-1.3% slower, faster on 1 to 6
of 16 -- though it is consistently LESS bad there than unsw (0.9893 against 0.9766 at k=8).

**P2 was the prediction carrying the discrimination and it fired in the falsifying direction.**
The claim it tested was chain151's account of why unsw gained: that the guarded block's store to
`C_values`, which the compiler cannot prove does not alias `A1_pos`, forced a per-row reload of
`A1_pos[i]` and `A1_pos[i+1]`. If that were the mechanism, keeping those two values in registers
would reproduce the gain. It does the opposite, by 5 to 9 percent, on essentially every matrix.

So the reload was not the mechanism. The likely reason it was never a reload: at the non-firing
widths `multirow_ok` is a runtime false, and it is the FIRST term of the guard, so `&&`
short-circuits before `A1_pos` is read at all. There was no reload to remove. What the hoist adds
instead is two unconditional loads and a live boolean in the hot loop on every row, which
lengthens live ranges and costs most where rows are short -- which is exactly the shape of the
damage, worst at low and mid degree.

That leaves what unsw actually did as something coarser: removing the branch and its block from
the instantiation changes the scheduling and register allocation of the whole row loop. That is a
real effect -- 22 of 26 and 25 of 26 matrices measured it -- but it is not a specific cost that
can be paid for separately, which is why the cheap version of it does not exist. The 1-2.3%
high-degree penalty was the price of the second instantiation, and hoist being less bad than unsw
at high degree while duplicating nothing is consistent with that half of the story surviving.

**Verdict: hoist does not ship.** Reported as a finding rather than tuned around; the constant
stays at 0, where it is emission-neutral. Combined with chain151 and chain154, three consecutive
attempts on the width-1 and width-4 deficit are now rejected: unswitching (net regression), the
degree window and the raggedness window (both worse than no window at all out of sample), and now
the hoist (regression, and it refutes the mechanism).

**What is actually established about that deficit, stated without the refuted part.** It is real
and it survives a held-out corpus: `bandmr` reads 0.9965 with 4 losers of 40 at width 1 and 0.9503
with 2 of 40 at width 4 on matrices that had no part in any derivation. It is float32-specific and
concentrated below mean degree 20. Removing the multi-row admission code from the instantiation
cures it and costs more elsewhere than it saves. Its microarchitectural cause is now unknown --
the reload explanation is dead, and no measurement has replaced it.

One host. The unsw and hoist arms are both queued on redwood behind band2, and the two results
that matter most for a second host are now unsw's high-degree penalty and hoist's low-degree
regression, since those are what the ARM instruction stream could plausibly change.

**One defect in the analyzer, fixed before reading the numbers.** `an_unsw.py` hardcoded `"unsw"`
as the candidate build, so it was parameterised to detect whichever build is not one of the three
controls -- and to refuse when there is not exactly one, since with none there is nothing to test
and with several the verdicts would silently describe only the first. Five verdict strings still
named `unsw` in their message text after that, so the first hoist run printed "P1 FAILED: unsw
0.9668" for the hoist build. A label that names the wrong build is the same defect the copied
sbatch had an hour earlier, and it would have gone into this section verbatim.

## chain157 -- the second host revises chain151: the gain is two-host, the penalty mostly is not

redwood finished band2 at 09:47 and unsw at 12:23 (63 matrices, 7320 corpus rows per build).
Heldout is running there now. Both results change what chain151 concluded.

**The low-degree gain is two-host and holds firmly.** unsw against bandmr, above 1 meaning unsw
faster, per matrix:

    deg < 20, float32     MKT (Zen4)                  redwood (hybrid)
      k=1                 faster 22/26 median 1.0188 | faster 34/38 median 1.0163
      k=4                 faster 25/26 median 1.0207 | faster 32/38 median 1.0201

**The high-degree penalty that killed it does not replicate.** At degree >= 20, float32:

      k=1                 faster  3/16 median 0.9874 | faster  9/22 median 0.9986
      k=2                 faster  3/16 median 0.9843 | faster 11/22 median 0.9996
      k=3                 faster  4/16 median 0.9829 | faster 10/22 median 0.9979
      k=8                 faster  1/16 median 0.9766 | faster 11/22 median 1.0017
      k=4                 faster  4/16 median 0.9850 | faster  5/22 median 0.9864

Four of the five widths are neutral on redwood where MKT read 0.977 to 0.987. Only width 4
carries the penalty on both hosts, and there it is about 1.4%. On float64 redwood is
neutral-to-faster, including 19 of 22 at 1.0218 for width 2.

So chain151's verdict -- "net regression, does not ship" -- was a single-host verdict, and the
second host declines to confirm the part that condemned it. The honest statement now: a ~2%
low-degree gain confirmed on two x86 hosts, a high-degree cost that is Zen4-specific at four
widths, and a two-host ~1.4% cost at width 4. That is not a clean rejection and it is not a ship
either. The width-4 penalty is the blocker, because it is the one finding both hosts agree on.

This is the two-host rule working in the direction I do not usually get to report: it stopped a
rejection, not a claim. Had unsw been measured only on MKT it would be recorded as a failed
experiment.

**And it sharpens the chain156 result rather than overturning it.** The hoist still fails on MKT
by 9.0% and 5.1% at the widths where unsw gains, unanimously, so the reload was still not the
mechanism. What changes is the other half: chain156 reasoned that unsw's high-degree cost was the
price of the second instantiation. If that cost is largely absent on redwood, then the
duplication is not intrinsically expensive -- it is expensive on Zen4 -- and the explanation has
to be about that machine's front end rather than about instantiation in general. The hoist arm
has not run on redwood yet; it is not in any queued chain, so that is a gap to close before the
mechanism question is settled either way.

**band2 is now two-host and it agrees.** redwood, float32 geomean against c0:

    k | floor  band2mr bandmr
    2 | 0.9984 0.9883  0.9999
    3 | 0.9958 1.1023  1.1102
    8 | 0.9949 1.1746  1.1824

band2mr sits about 1% below its own floor at width 2 and slightly below bandmr at widths 3 and 8,
which is the same direction MKT measured (0.9805 against a 0.9996 floor at width 2). The single-host
gap flagged in chain142 is closed, and it closes against band2: lowering the band to 2 does not
help on either host. `29384fe` stays reverted.

## chain158 -- width 1 is not two-host, and the neutrality instrument now reconciles the immediates

**A correction to how the deficit has been summarized.** Comparing `bandmr` against `c0` at
float32 with the same analyzer on both hosts:

    width | MKT      floor    | redwood  floor
      1   | 1.0089   0.9891   | 0.9766   1.0006
      4   | 0.9894   0.9951   | 0.9907   1.0028

Width 4 is below its floor on both hosts. **Width 1 has opposite signs** -- MKT clears its floor
there, redwood sits 2.4% below. The doc already recorded this at the level of the individual
prediction table ("second x86 host agrees in sign: FAIL at widths 1 and 4", and "MKT's width 1 is
the one place it does not appear"), but the running summary has been saying "the width-1 and
width-4 deficit", which asserts two hosts for a fact that has one.

It sharpens rather than weakens the target. `unsw`'s surviving penalty was also two-host *only* at
width 4. Two experiments, different comparisons, both isolate width 4 as the single cost the two
machines agree on; width 1 is a property of redwood.

### Three owed x86 neutrality claims, not one

The tarball lineage, by line count of the two headers:

    tarball  adds                              spmm.h        scorch_policy.h
    mr6      (baseline)                        6681          --
    mr7      MULTIROW_RAGGED + MULTIROW_MINDEG 6725  (+44)    (+71)
    mr8      MULTIROW_UNSWITCH                 6753  (+28)    (+57)
    mr9      MULTIROW_HOIST                    6780  (+27)    (+25)

Three constants were added at default 0, each with the argument that it emits nothing there, and
**every one of those arguments was checked on ARM only** -- where neither the multi-row kernel nor
its dispatch is compiled, so it is the weaker ISA for exactly this question. The +27 matches the
hoist commit's ARM reconciliation exactly, which is the check that the lineage is read correctly.

The old `rw_s_attrib.sh` covered only mr6->mr7, had **no A/A control** -- which
`neutral_disasm.sh`'s own header says the verdict requires -- and printed "neutrality unchecked"
and continued when a build failed. An unrun check rendered as a clean line, again.

### The instrument was doing the weaker half of its own argument

`neutral_disasm.sh` checked that every difference is a bare immediate move, and stopped there. But
an immediate that changed for a *real* reason -- a folded constant, a literal branch target --
matches that pattern too. The strong claim, the one the hoist commit actually made in prose, is
that every changed immediate moved by exactly the number of lines added, which only a `__LINE__`
shift can produce. That reconciliation was done **by hand** and lived in a commit message.

It is now in the instrument, with four properties worth naming:

- **Deltas are reconciled against the source.** `--expect-delta` takes the lines added; every
  observed delta must be one of them.
- **A SET, not a value.** `__LINE__` is per-file, so a change touching two headers shifts each
  file's immediates by a different amount and produces two legitimate deltas. All three pairs here
  move both headers, so a single expected value would have reported a pure line shift as a real
  change. This was not defensive generality -- it was wrong before the generalization.
- **Identical disassembly plus an expected shift REFUSES.** If the caller says 27 lines were added
  and nothing differs, the two objects are not the pair the caller thinks they are. This is the
  branch that catches the defect from chain156, where a flag variable holding `-S -o -` made the
  check diff two empty files and print NEUTRAL.
- **Classifier/parser disagreement REFUSES.** The classifier's `[#$]?` is optional and the
  reconciler's is not, so `mov w2, 100` is an immediate move the parser cannot read. Rather than
  skipping it -- which would quietly shrink the denominator -- it fails closed.

Ten fixtures, each built to falsify one branch, all firing correctly: A/A identical, identical
against a nonzero expectation, all-shifted with a matching and a non-matching expectation, mixed
deltas against a set that covers them and one that does not, a real instruction change, differing
instruction counts, the unparsable immediate, and a malformed set.

**Two instrument bugs found while building it, both in my own probes rather than the code:**
`tar --wildcards` is GNU-only, so bsdtar errored, `2>/dev/null` swallowed it, and the resulting
`HOIST=0` for all four tarballs read as "the constant is absent" rather than "tar failed" --
including for mr9, which is named after it. Then zsh does not word-split unquoted parameter
expansions, so passing two paths in one variable made tar look for a single file with a space in
its name. Both were caught only because the answer was impossible on its face; neither would have
been caught by a plausible one. And a third, in the new code: BSD sed has no `\|` any more than it
has `\+`, so a single alternating expression matched nothing on the mac while working on the linux
host, and the reconciler reported every difference as unparsable. Same family as the `\b` trap.

### Queued

`rw_s_attrib2.sh` on redwood, behind heldout, waiting on the stage lock. Part 1 is the three
neutrality pairs plus the A/A control, with each tarball's constant proven present through the
preprocessor first so a verdict cannot be vacuous. Part 2 is the placement / code-presence /
admission-test attribution for redwood's width-1 deficit -- `c0pad` (identical source at a
build path one character longer), `mrf64` (kernel and dispatch compiled in, float32's row count
constexpr 0 so the branch folds away), and `bandmr`.

That third arm is the one the hoist was built to fix, and the hoist failed by 9.0% and 5.1% at
these widths. So if part 2 selects the admission test, the mechanism is open and the fix was aimed
at the wrong instruction; if it selects placement or code presence, the reload story was never
right and the hoist's failure is explained rather than mysterious.

The waiter blocks on the lock file rather than on a process name. stage_lock.sh refuses rather
than waits by design, so something must do the waiting, and every earlier queue defect here came
from a waiter keyed on the previous stage's process name. Verified detached: PPID 1, SigIgn
ending in 7 so SIGHUP is ignored, own session with no controlling terminal. The check that found
those properties initially read the wrong process -- `pgrep -f` matched the `zsh -c` wrapper whose
command line contains the script name, which is the pattern-matches-itself trap, in the
verification of a fix for the pile-up it was written to avoid.

## chain159 -- a peer's defect report finds the same shape here, with its sign reversed

The sparse-kernel-bench session reported one of its own: a corpus build finished with 2807
matrices and zero failures while producing zero MoE routing matrices, because the extraction hook
matched no module and an empty capture was not counted as a failure. Its note was that a stage
which cannot run looks exactly like a stage that had nothing to do, and that anything aggregating
over a glob or a capture is worth checking. That is the same class this project keeps producing,
so I tested for it rather than reasoning about it.

**All six live analyzers already refuse a wholly empty input directory.** That case was fixed
earlier in the sequence. The defect is one level in: not the whole input missing, but **one
subgroup missing while the aggregate looks healthy** -- which is exactly the shape the peer hit.

Constructed by taking a real 63-matrix dataset and removing all of one build's rows at one width:

    an_band2.py, k=3 stripped from bandmr
      before:  3 | 0.9958  1.1023  nan  | FAILED: differs from bandmr
      after:   3 | 0.9958  1.1023  nan  | n=60/60/0 | REFUSE: bandmr has no readings at this width

**The interesting part is the sign.** The familiar version of this defect is absent data producing
a false PASS. Here it produced a false **FAILURE** -- a verdict asserting that `band2mr` differs
from `bandmr` at a width where `bandmr` had no readings at all. Both directions have one cause, a
verdict computed from a value that does not exist, but the failing direction is the more dangerous
one to leave in place: a fabricated finding gets acted on, and the `nan` sitting beside it in the
table does not travel into the summary that quotes the verdict string.

Two fixes, and one thing that was already right:

- `an_band2.py` now names, per width, which arms its prediction actually reads, refuses when any
  of them has zero readings, and prints `n=` per arm. On intact data every verdict is unchanged,
  which is the check that the fix did not buy safety with accuracy.
- `an_attrib.py` did guard the nan, but with `continue` -- so a width that could not be judged was
  **dropped from the verdict table**, where it reads as a width that was never part of the
  analysis. Quieter than a wrong verdict and no better. It now prints the row and names what is
  missing. Fired on an input whose candidate has no readings at width 1.
- `an_attrib.py`'s absent-arm guard was already correct and still fires: width 4 reads "cannot
  attribute: mrf64 absent from this stage" rather than treating an absent arm as a flat one.

**The printed denominators immediately paid for themselves.** `n=60/60/60` on a dataset whose
header says 63 matrices -- three contribute no readings at any width, which was true before and
invisible before.

Fifteen analyzers construct a geomean that returns `nan` for an empty list. Only `an_band2.py`
rendered a HELD/FAILED string from one, which is why it was the one that manufactured a claim; the
others print `--` or refuse. The general lesson is narrower than "handle nan": a nan is safe in a
DISPLAY and unsafe in a VERDICT, and the two are worth separating deliberately rather than
hardening every site equally.

## chain160 -- the UNSWITCH constant is not emission-neutral on Zen4, and the windows are rejected on both hosts

Three results landed together: MKT's part 1 before its part 2 refused, and redwood's heldout.

### The three x86 neutrality verdicts, under Zen4 instruction selection

    A/A control   mr9 built twice   NEUTRAL, 231253 instructions, identical disassembly
    mr6 -> mr7    RAGGED+MINDEG     NEUTRAL, 20 immediates, every delta +44 = spmm.h lines added
    mr7 -> mr8    UNSWITCH          NOT NEUTRAL, 231254 -> 231253
    mr8 -> mr9    HOIST             NEUTRAL, 20 immediates, every delta +27

**The hoist's claim now holds on x86**, which is what it was owed -- and the reconciliation is
exact on both ISAs: 20 immediates, single delta, equal to the 27 lines added to `spmm.h`. The
RAGGED+MINDEG claim holds too.

**`SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_UNSWITCH` at default 0 emits one instruction fewer on Zen4.** Commit
`eddf47a` says "Off by default and emission-neutral there: 164596 instructions either way" --
and 164596 is the **ARM** count. So that claim was ARM-only and the second ISA falsifies it. One
instruction in 231254 is not a performance claim; it falsifies a stated one, which is the part
that matters. The instrument stops at differing counts by design and cannot say which instruction,
so the resubmission diffs the two disassemblies with context and reports the mnemonic histogram.

Note which way the A/A control cuts here: it was NEUTRAL with **identical** disassembly, so the
231254 -> 231253 difference cannot be build noise on this host.

### MKT's part 2 refused, and the refusal was right

`mrbuild.sh` admits the `c0pad` placement control only if its `.text` has the same size and a
different digest from `c0` -- identical source at a build path one character longer, so only
layout can differ. On MKT it came out **byte-identical**, so there is no control, and it refused
rather than report a flat placement arm that was really a second copy of `c0`.

That is a host difference, not a defect: `c0pad` is admitted on redwood, where chain142 has its
numbers. Two consequences, and neither costs the experiment:
1. **The placement question is redwood-only** -- which is where it matters, since the width-1
   deficit that motivates it is redwood's and MKT clears its floor there (chain158).
2. **On MKT, arm-vs-arm numbers carry no unmeasured layout term from path length**, because path
   length provably does not reach `.text` there. Worth having established rather than assumed.

Resubmitted as 17304145 with `c0 c0b mrf64 bandmr`, four builds over four passes so each leads
once. `mrf64` is the arm carrying MKT's question and it does not need `c0pad`.

### The degree windows are now rejected on two hosts

redwood's held-out corpus, 43 matrices, 3600 corpus rows per build. `bandmr` with no window is
best or inside the floor at every width, exactly as MKT found:

    k | c0b floor | bandmr           | mdlo             | rag2             | ragmd
    1 | 1.0310    | 0.9916 lose 6/40 | 0.9858 lose 5/40 | 0.9906 lose 1/40 | 1.0164 lose 2/40
    2 | 1.0076    | 0.9785 lose12/40 | 0.9584 lose16/40 | 0.9636 lose13/40 | 0.9453 lose13/40
    3 | 1.0101    | 1.1022 lose 1/40 | 1.0832 lose 3/40 | 1.0774 lose 4/40 | 1.0675 lose 4/40
    4 | 0.9992    | 0.9898 lose 2/40 | 0.9826 lose 7/40 | 0.9913 lose 0/40 | 0.9877 lose 4/40
    8 | 1.0089    | 1.1169 lose 1/40 | 1.1243 lose 1/40 | 1.0886 lose 1/40 | 1.0825 lose 1/40

The gate fires exactly as specified on this host too -- every gated build matches its ungated
sibling on every admitted cell -- and **the refusal is what costs**: refused cells read 0.8102 and
0.8031 at width 2 and 0.8616 to 0.8982 at width 3, so refusing is 10-20% slower rather than
neutral. Same conclusion as MKT, reached from a different corpus.

**A limit of this dataset, stated because the table invites the wrong reading.** The A/A floor at
width 1 is **1.0310** -- the same code against itself is 3.1% off unity. Every width-1 number
above sits inside that, `ragmd`'s 1.0164 included. Width 1 is **not resolvable on this corpus**,
so nothing here bears on the width-1 deficit either way.

### One new mechanism signal, and it is the first thing to partly address the width-2 population

The worst held-out cells are all width 2 at high degree, and `bandmr` is badly hurt on them --
`TSOPF_FS_b300` at 0.712, `gupta2` 0.779, `symbol_modality` 0.804, four TSOPF cells below 0.87.
The windows do not rescue them in aggregate, but `rag2` is **consistently better than `bandmr` on
exactly these cells**: 0.869 against 0.712, 0.867 against 0.779, 0.914 against 0.830.

So the trade is now visible: `rag2` spreads bandmr's concentrated damage rather than removing it,
which is why its geomean is worse (0.9636 against 0.9785) while its worst cells are much better.
That is not a ship. It is the first evidence that the width-2 high-degree population is
*addressable* by a raggedness test rather than being intrinsic to the band, and it says the thing
to look for is a test that keeps rag2's behaviour on the tail without paying for it in the middle
-- which is a different search than any of the four arms so far attempted.

### chain160 amendment -- what the one instruction actually is

Part 0 of the resubmission named it, and it weakens the claim I recorded above. The mnemonic
histogram for mr7 -> mr8:

    mov    53021 -> 53020  (-1)
    nop      578 ->   577  (-1)
    nopw     832 ->   833  (+1)

Net minus one. And every difference in the diff's visible portion is a `call` target moving by
exactly `0x10` -- functions relocated 16 bytes, not code changed. `nop` -> `nopw` is the assembler
padding to an alignment boundary with one wider no-op instead of two narrower ones, which is why
the instruction count falls with nothing semantic behind it.

So "NOT NEUTRAL" as stated above is **too strong a reading of its own evidence**. Two hypotheses
remain and the histogram cannot separate them:

- **byte-different, semantically identical** -- the `mov` is a materialized constant the compiler
  common-subexpression-eliminated in one build and not the other, because every `__LINE__` below
  the insertion shifted by 28 and two of them coincidentally became equal, or stopped being. On
  this reading the object is a relocation of the same code and the commit's *behavioural* claim
  stands even though its instruction count does not.
- **a real difference in emitted work** -- that would be the finding.

`17304209` decides it by classifying every differing line rather than the first forty, with the
unclassified count as the verdict: zero unclassified means the first hypothesis. It is compile-free,
reuses the disassemblies part 0 left on node-local scratch, and carries `afterany` on the timing
job so it cannot co-schedule onto it. It also copies them to `/matx`, so the question never needs
that node again.

What survives regardless: `eddf47a`'s "164596 instructions either way" is an ARM count presented
without its ISA, and the Zen4 count is 231254/231253. A number quoted in a commit message with no
host attached is the defect whatever the classification says, because nothing re-derives it.

## chain161 -- the exact-width kernel's unroll is wrong at widths 2 and 3, and it is a lead rather than a result

`exunroll` finished on redwood and had no analyzer, so `an_exunroll.py` was written for it, reusing
`an_band2.py`'s ingestion verbatim -- the non-finite refusal, the floor calibration, the
rep-imbalance split -- rather than re-deriving any of it.

60 matrices, five builds, five passes, balanced rotation. float32 geomean against `c0`, above 1
meaning faster than the shipped default:

    k | c0b floor    exu1          exu8          dgu0
    1 | 0.9987       0.9143        0.8619        1.0034
    2 | 1.0018       1.0497        0.9452        0.9907
    3 | 0.9998       1.0839        0.9265        0.9729

**Removing the unroll entirely is 5.0% faster at width 2 and 8.4% faster at width 3.** The shipped
depth is right at width 1 -- `exu1` loses 8.6% there -- and a deeper unroll (`exu8`) is worse at
every width. So the default is tuned for width 1 and is carrying that tuning into widths 2 and 3
where it costs.

By mean-degree band the effect is much larger and it reverses:

    k=2 | <4 0.9957 | 4-20 1.1947 | 20-128 0.9468 | >=128 0.7305
    k=3 | <4 0.9893 | 4-20 1.1879 | 20-128 1.0303 | >=128 0.8339

**19.5% at degree 4-20 and minus 27% at degree above 128.** That is the largest unexploited
per-width effect this sequence has found, and it is in the BASELINE kernel rather than in any
candidate -- it does not depend on the band or the multi-row question at all.

### Why it does not ship, and what it means for the width-2 story

On the standing goal, which is a cell count against MKL, `exu1` is a **net loss**:

    build   k=1    k=2    k=3
    c0      0/60   1/60   2/60
    exu1    5/60   5/60   5/60

Five cells below MKL where the default has zero, one and two. The concentrated high-degree damage
is exactly what crosses cells, so the geomean improves while the thing being optimized gets worse.
Same shape as `rag2` in chain160: spread the win, concentrate the loss, lose the count.

**It does change the width-2 diagnosis.** The premise behind four rejected arms was that narrowing
the band makes width 2 leave the exact kernel, and the exact kernel was treated as the thing worth
keeping. At degree 4-20 it is 19.5% short of a trivially available variant. So part of what has
been booked as bandmr's width-2 regression is a weak baseline at mid degree, and the two need
separating before another arm is spent on the departure.

But not at high degree, and that matters: `bandmr`'s width-2 regression population is
high-degree -- `TSOPF_FS_b300` at 150, `TSOPF_RS_b678_c2` at 246, the `lhr` family -- and `exu1`
is 27% WORSE there. So this is a different population, not the same problem seen twice, and a
blanket unroll change cannot address bandmr's deficit.

### Three reasons this is a lead and not a result

1. **There is no inertness control.** The stage measured widths 1, 2 and 3 only -- the widths the
   exact kernel owns under the default band of 3. Nothing was measured at a width the constants
   provably cannot reach, so there is no evidence they do not reach code they do not name. The
   analyzer refuses P4 rather than reporting it flat, which is the correct outcome and also means
   the stage cannot support a claim on its own.
2. **No GCN guardrail was measured.** `an_exunroll.py` says so on its own output rather than
   leaving a reader to assume it passed.
3. **One host.** redwood only.

So the follow-up is a proper stage: widths 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 with 8 as the inertness control, both
dtypes, the GCN widths, and both hosts. The interesting arm is not `exu1` -- it is a
degree-conditioned unroll, which is what the bands say should exist. The obvious hazard is that
unroll depth is a compile-time constant, so conditioning it at runtime means two instantiations,
and a second instantiation is precisely what sank `unsw`. Whether that cost is real here is
measurable and unmeasured: `unsw` duplicated the whole worker body, and an unroll variant
duplicates a much smaller one.

## chain162 -- the two hosts have DIFFERENT mechanisms, and that explains everything chain157 could not

Both attribution stages finished. Together they close the mechanism question that has been open
since chain151, and they do it by direct attribution rather than by inference from a failed fix.

### redwood: the cost is the per-row admission branch

    k | placement(c0pad)      presence(mrf64)       candidate(bandmr)     | reads as
    1 | 0.9951 past-floor 1   0.9920 past-floor 3   0.9711 past-floor 29  | THE PER-ROW BRANCH
    4 | 0.9995 past-floor 0   0.9972 past-floor 2   0.9895 past-floor 23  | THE PER-ROW BRANCH

Placement is flat. Code presence is nearly flat. Only the candidate moves, and it moves on half
the corpus. The `c0pad` arm is what makes this readable: identical source at a build path one
character longer, so a layout term would have shown up there and did not.

### MKT: at width 4 the cost is the code merely being PRESENT

    k | c0b floor            presence(mrf64)        candidate(bandmr)
    1 | 0.9956 past-floor 0  0.9800 past-floor 5    0.9994 past-floor 1
    4 | 0.9962 past-floor 0  0.9772 past-floor 15   0.9822 past-floor 8

Width 1 is flat for the candidate -- 0.9994 against a 0.9956 floor, one cell past floor of 42 --
which is chain158's host asymmetry confirmed on a third dataset. But at **width 4, `mrf64` is
worse than the candidate itself**: 0.9772 against 0.9822, with 15 cells past their own floor
against 8. `mrf64` has the per-row admission test **folded away at compile time** -- float32's
constexpr row count is 0 -- and only the unexecutable float64 instantiation present. So on Zen4,
compiling in code that float32 never runs costs 2.3% at width 4.

### Which resolves chain157 completely

The two hosts do not have one deficit measured twice. They have **two different dominant
mechanisms**, and every previously confusing result follows:

- `unsw` unswitches the admission test out of the row loop. On redwood that is exactly the cost,
  so it gains. It also **instantiates the worker body twice**. On MKT code presence is itself
  expensive, so the duplication costs there and not on redwood.
- Hence chain157's finding: the low-degree gain replicates on both hosts (both remove the branch)
  while the high-degree cost is 0.977-0.987 on MKT and 0.998-1.002 on redwood. chain151's
  explanation was right **about MKT** and wrong to generalise.
- And the hoist's failure stops being mysterious: it removed a per-row *reload of A1_pos*, not the
  *branch*. attrib2 says the branch is the cost. The hoist was aimed at the wrong instruction, and
  chain156 inferred that from its failure -- this measures it directly.

The work-scaling probe agrees and adds a split: `mrf64` reads **DISPATCH** on both hosts (kernel
time's interval includes 1, the wrapper's excludes it) while `bandmr` reads **KERNEL** on both. One
limit worth stating -- the probe stacks two copies of the matrix vertically, doubling rows and
nonzeros together, so "KERNEL" here means "scales with the matrix", not "per nonzero specifically",
and it cannot separate a per-row branch from per-nonzero work.

### What this makes actionable

`unsw`'s gain and `unsw`'s cost are now **separately priced**, which they never were before. The
gain is branch removal, worth ~2% at low degree on two hosts. The cost is the second instantiation,
and `mrf64` prices exactly that in isolation at 2.3% on MKT at width 4. So the question is no
longer "does unsw work" -- it is whether the branch can be unswitched **without** duplicating the
whole worker body. Hoisting only the multi-row-eligible inner loop, or branching once outside the
row loop over two *small* bodies rather than two full workers, would take the gain without the
thing that is measured to cost. That is a different arm from any of the five attempted.

### chain160's amendment was wrong, and instruction count is a bad instrument

The classification jobs ran on both hosts and overturn what I recorded. Adding
`SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_UNSWITCH` at default 0:

    host      differing instructions   of total    count delta
    MKT       ~34,335                  231,254     -1
    redwood   2,582                    163,194     -2

**15% of MKT's instructions differ while the count differs by one.** My amendment read the
mnemonic histogram as "one mov plus padding" -- but a histogram cannot see register renaming
(`mov %ebx,%r9d` -> `mov %r11d,%r9d` is still a `mov`) and my classifier did not recognise
`lea 0x...(%rip)` displacement shifts as the same benign relocation as a branch target, so
they landed in "unclassified" and drove an H2 verdict.

What the differences actually are: RIP-relative displacements shifting by exactly `0x10`, branch
and call targets shifting, register reallocation on redwood, and immediate moves whose deltas are
`0x1922 -> 0x193e` = 6434 -> 6462 = **+28 exactly**, the lines added to `spmm.h`. Nothing yet
indicates different *work*, but "byte-different" is now established at a scale I had dismissed.

Two lessons. **Instruction count is a near-useless proxy for emission neutrality** -- it moved by
one while 15% of the object changed. And the fact that HOIST and RAGGED+MINDEG produced exactly
**20** differing instructions on both hosts, against these numbers, is what makes those two
verdicts strong: the instrument does discriminate, by three orders of magnitude.

The behavioural question is still open and instruction counting cannot close it. The right
instrument is the clock: time mr7-at-default against mr8-at-default and see whether the churn is
worth anything. That is the next stage, and it is cheap.

## chain163 -- the unroll follow-up is launched, and check-then-submit is racy

`unroll2` runs the same design on both hosts from a shared body, `unroll2_body.sh`, sourced by a
thin per-host wrapper -- so the two hosts run one design rather than two that agree today. It
fixes all three of the reasons chain161 was a lead rather than a result:

- **Widths 4 and 8 are added as the inertness control.** The exact-width kernel provably cannot
  reach them under the default band of 3. These are the readings that can *void* the stage: an
  unroll constant that moves width 8 is touching the generic path, and every chain161 number
  would be confounded. chain161 measured only widths 1, 2 and 3 -- every width the kernel under
  test owns -- so it had no such control by construction.
- **The GCN guardrail is measured**, at the widths a two-layer GCN calls. Width 3 is inside the
  band, so this is a gate and not an accompaniment.
- **Both hosts.**

The correctness grid also straddles every plausible unroll factor -- row counts 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8,
9, 15, 16, 17, 64, 257 -- because an unroll constant is exactly the change that is right on
average and wrong on the remainder.

### A co-tenancy near-miss, and the protocol was the defect

`unroll2` was submitted to MKT at 20:38 and landed on `mkt1` beside a peer session's
bandwidth-heavy job that had started at 20:36. My error: MKT was genuinely free when they
submitted, and I then went straight to `sbatch` without re-reading the queue. Caught it at 5
seconds, while still compiling, so nothing was contaminated; cancelled and resubmitted as
`17306323` with `--dependency=afterany` on their job.

**The lesson is not "check more carefully".** Check-then-submit is racy: the gap between reading
`squeue` and `sbatch` landing is unbounded, and no amount of care closes it. A Slurm dependency has
no such gap. So the rule now is to never submit a timing job to MKT bare -- always compute the
dependency from whatever is running or pending and pass it, *even when the queue looks empty*,
because an empty dependency is a no-op and costs nothing.

This is the same shape as several defects in this file: a guarantee that depends on someone
remembering, replaced by one the system cannot get wrong. The stage lock on redwood is the same
idea, and the reason redwood was unaffected.

One asymmetry worth recording: a dependency protects *my* numbers from someone else's job, not
theirs from mine. Mutual protection needs both parties to use it, or an outright agreement.

### chain163 amendment -- the dependency rule as stated would deadlock

The rule recorded above -- "compute the dependency from whatever is running or pending" -- is
**wrong as written**, and the peer session caught it before it cost anything. `afterany` is
satisfied when a job *terminates*. Bobby's four `JobHeldUser` jobs on `mkt` are PENDING and may
stay so indefinitely, so depending on them does not delay a job, it **deadlocks it forever**.

The current submission is unaffected because its dependency was a single hand-picked job id, but
the general rule needed fixing before it was used. Held jobs must be excluded by **reason**, not by
state -- `squeue -p mkt -h -o "%i|%T|%r|%j"` and drop `JobHeld*`. Jobs pending on `Dependency` must
NOT be dropped: such a job will eventually run and co-tenant, so it has to be waited for. That is
the one case where the naive answer is right, which is what makes the distinction easy to get
backwards.

`scratchpad/sbatch_after.sh` implements it and was fired against the live queue rather than
reasoned about: it keeps `17306323:17306296` and drops all four held jobs. That set is exactly what
the peer's independently written helper computes, which is the closest thing to a cross-check
available for a rule with no test corpus.

Worth naming the shape, because it is the third instance in this sequence: **a safety mechanism
whose failure mode is worse than the hazard it prevents.** Co-tenancy costs one contaminated run;
a deadlocked dependency costs every run until someone notices the job never started -- and a job
stuck in PENDING looks exactly like a job politely waiting its turn.

## chain164 -- every degree band in this file is blind to locality, and that is testable

A peer session reported that its block-amplification statistic is a **pure function of row
lengths**, with the consequence that two structurally different generators came out bit-identical
in every column of its results table -- identical constant row length, mean per-row column span
3900 against 575. Its note was that any statistic reducing a matrix to a row-length profile is
silent about locality by construction.

**That applies directly here.** Every banded conclusion in this file bands on `deg = nnz/rows`,
and the harness records `rows, nnz, deg` and nothing else. All three are pure row-length
statistics. So the axis is blind to locality in precisely the way described -- and SpMM is
bandwidth-bound, which makes locality the thing that ought to drive these effects.

The specific claim at stake is chain161's unroll reversal: `exu1` reads **1.1947 at degree 4-20 and
0.7305 above degree 128** at width 2. That is currently attributed to degree because degree is the
only axis measured. If locality correlates with degree across this corpus -- and on a corpus that
is largely DLMC pruned-ResNet blocks plus SuiteSparse, there is no reason to assume it does not --
the attribution is **unfalsified rather than established**, and a degree-gated fix would be gating
on a proxy for the wrong thing.

This is not a claim that the attribution is wrong. It is a claim that nothing so far distinguishes
the two, and the distinction is cheap to make.

`locfeat.py` computes per-matrix locality for both measured corpora and is queued on redwood behind
`unroll2`. Three things about how:

- **It imports production's `_locality_ratio` rather than reimplementing it.** That function is
  simultaneously the analytic tile-j gate and a learned-model feature, so a harness with its own
  version would be measuring a second definition that agrees today and drifts silently later. The
  npz-to-CSR load *is* replicated from `mrgate.py`, deliberately -- that is deserialization, not
  policy, and the distinction is the whole point.
- **It refuses a locality outside [0,1]** rather than writing it. The proxy's precondition is
  column-sorted CSR; a value that cannot be what it claims means the precondition failed, and
  since position within a band decides a verdict later, a bad value is worse than a missing one.
- **It waits for the stage lock** even though it is cheap and CPU-light, because it loads every
  matrix in the corpus from disk and that I/O beside a bandwidth-bound timing run is the exact
  perturbation this file keeps warning about. Locality is a property of the matrix rather than the
  machine, so it runs on one host and its output joins to both.

A follow-up that costs nothing later: `mrgate.py` should record locality alongside `deg` so this
join is never needed again. Not done now -- both hosts are executing that file in a loop, and
editing a harness mid-run is its own defect.

## chain165 -- "the node was idle" was an assumption on both hosts; now it is a record on one

A peer session pointed out that the A/A control measures the noise floor of the instrument and
**cannot tell you the node was idle**. That gap matters more than it sounds: a co-tenant present
for a whole run does not add visible noise, it *inflates the A/A floor*, and the real effect then
reads as inside the floor. The failure mode is a **false negative**, which is the kind that does
not announce itself.

The right instrument differs by host, and the difference is not cosmetic.

### MKT: ask the scheduler, and it is retroactive and free

Slurm knows what it placed and when, so there is nothing to sample and nothing to miss.
`scratchpad/cotenancy.sh <jobid>` reads the job's own window out of accounting and returns every
other job whose window overlapped it **on the same node**.

**Validated on both a positive and a negative control before being trusted**, because a detector
with only one is not tested:

    17306306  (cancelled for landing beside skb-amp)  -> CO-TENANT FOUND: skb-amp, 16 cpus,
                                                          20:36:25 -> 20:45:21 vs mine 20:39:13 -> 20:39:29
    17304145  (attrib2b, believed exclusive)          -> CLEAN

Then run over every MKT job behind a recorded conclusion in this file:

    17287573  unsw          00:41 -> 02:39   CLEAN
    17290869  windows       03:06 -> 05:19   CLEAN
    17295447  hoist         09:06 -> 11:04   CLEAN
    17299344  neutrality    14:24 -> 14:32   CLEAN
    17304145  attribution   17:39 -> 18:51   CLEAN

So chain151, chain154, chain156, chain160 and chain162's MKT halves are **certified**
co-tenant-free rather than believed to be. That is a real upgrade in what those numbers mean, and
it cost one query.

### redwood: no scheduler, so the record has to be built, and it starts now

redwood has no Slurm and **nine logged-in tmux sessions across three users**, so exclusivity there
has rested on a single `top` snapshot taken once today. `scratchpad/rw_loadsample.sh` samples
`/proc/loadavg` and any non-self process above 10% CPU once a minute, nice'd to 19.

Two properties it needed:
- **It terminates on its own**, when the stage it was named for stops holding the stage lock, or at
  a hard deadline. A sampler that outlives its subject is the stale-poller defect this project has
  hit repeatedly, and it decides via the same lock file every other waiter here reads, so it cannot
  outlive its subject by a *different* rule.
- **Its co-tenant count is a floor, not a measurement.** `ps` `%cpu` is a lifetime average, so it
  understates a process that just started. Better to say so than to report the number as exact.

First samples during `unroll2`: load 16.98 and 12.08 of 32 cpus, own processes at ~1700%, **zero
other-user processes above 10%**. So redwood is currently ours.

**The honest gap: every redwood run already recorded in this file has no exclusivity record.**
band2, unsw, heldout, exunroll and attrib2 all completed before sampling existed, and the first 19
minutes of `unroll2` are unsampled too. Nothing suggests they were contended -- the one snapshot
taken mid-session showed only our own load -- but "nothing suggests" is not evidence, and on the
host with three users and no scheduler it is the weaker claim of the two hosts, which is the
opposite of how it has been treated.

### chain165 amendment -- the accounting is complete, and mkt1 is shared more widely than assumed

The peer session asked the right question about the tool before relying on it: does `sacct -a`
actually return every user here, or does it degrade silently into returning only your own jobs? On
a cluster that restricts accounting the two are indistinguishable -- every verdict reads CLEAN.

**Checked: unrestricted.** 186 distinct users and 32,941 records since Sep 5. So the CLEAN verdicts
above are complete lists rather than floors.

**And a correction to something I asserted one message earlier.** I said mkt co-tenancy could only
come from within this account, because the `mkt` partition's only user is `bobbyy`. That is true of
the partition and false of the machine: **`mkt1` serves both `mkt` and `mkt-interactive`**, and
three users have run on it since Sep 1 -- `azeinali`, `bobbyy`, `usman25`, the latter via
interactive jobs. So coordinating with the peer session is **necessary but not sufficient** for
mkt1 exclusivity.

`cotenancy.sh` was already node-scoped rather than partition- or account-scoped, which is the only
reason it is sound. A query written the way I had just described the problem -- scoped to the `mkt`
partition, or filtered to this account -- would have missed a real co-tenant while looking
identical. Direct recheck of all five measurement windows for foreign-user jobs on mkt1: **zero in
every window.**

**The live cross-user control was inconclusive and I nearly recorded it as a pass.** Running the
tool on another user's job returned CLEAN -- but that means "nothing overlapped that window", not
"the filter can see foreign users", and this cluster has never actually produced a foreign-user
overlap on mkt1 to test against. So the tool now takes `COTENANCY_SELFTEST=<table>` and was fired
on a constructed input:

    foreign user on the same node       -> FOUND (both the foreign job and a same-account sibling)
    foreign user on a DIFFERENT node    -> CLEAN (mkt2 correctly ignored)
    empty table                         -> CLEAN, not an error

That is the difference between "no evidence of contamination" and "an instrument demonstrated to
detect contamination". The same distinction the neutrality tool needed, and the same fix: an input
the live system cannot produce has to be constructed.

## chain166 -- why a contaminated pass cannot be dropped, and the manifest-versus-bulk distinction

A peer asked whether a 22 GB sequential read off mkt1's `/scr`, streamed over ssh, would perturb
`unroll2`. The answer is worth recording because the reasoning is not the obvious one.

**Throughput is not the issue, and their own number shows it.** 22 GB in 15-30 minutes is 12-24
MB/s -- about 0.02% of mkt1's memory bandwidth, three orders of magnitude below the effect being
resolved. The risks that do *not* scale with throughput are LLC pollution from DMA writes and
page-cache churn, and on EPYC 9334 the narrow widths this stage measures are specifically an
L2-miss/L3-hit band, which is where cache pollution would land. Small, but pointed at the right
place.

**What actually decides it is that a contaminated pass cannot be excised.** The rotation is five
passes over five builds with each build leading exactly once, because the lead build in a group
reads systematically fast -- an earlier job in this sequence had four builds over six groups and
both once-leading arms came out 0.5-1.2% slow **on identical source**, which is the size of the
effect at stake. So if a transfer overlapped two of five passes, discarding them would not leave
three clean passes; it would leave an **unbalanced rotation carrying a bias the same size as the
signal**. The only remedy is rerunning the whole stage.

That is a general property of interleaved-rotation designs and it cuts against the usual instinct:
robustness to a bad pass is exactly what the balanced rotation trades away for cancellation of the
lead-build bias. Worth knowing before assuming a contaminated subset can be dropped.

**The alternative offered is the more useful half.** Rather than copying 37 GB of derived data off
node-local scratch, transfer the **manifests and a per-file digest list** -- kilobytes, no
meaningful I/O, safe to run beside a live measurement. That is the difference between "we can
regenerate this" and "we can prove the regenerated copy is the same corpus". Without digests a
post-rebuild corpus is unverifiable and any comparison spanning the rebuild is quietly invalid; with
them the bulk data becomes genuinely re-derivable rather than nominally so. Same distinction as
reproducible-versus-idempotent: idempotent is the weaker property and the one that looks identical.

## chain167 -- five analyzers pooled two populations, and it inverted chain161's ship verdict

A peer session described a stratified sampler that sorted and strided and so silently dropped
whichever category sorted last -- invisible in the output because every count looked reasonable.
Checking for the same class here found `mkkeys_split.py` clean (it draws with
`rng.choice(replace=False)`, not a stride) and then found something worse one level up.

**`mkkeys_split.py` splits the corpus at nnz >= 1e6 and says in its own docstring why: "Both groups
are reported separately and neither is dropped; the point of the split is that pooling them dilutes
a kernel effect into a floor."** Control matrices take about 22us per call against a per-call floor
of about 22us, so their time is mostly floor. Of seven analyzers, **only `an_ship.py` ever read
`groups.txt`.** `an_attrib`, `an_band2`, `an_heldout`, `an_unsw`, `an_resid` and `an_exunroll` all
pooled -- so every geomean behind chains 151, 154, 157, 158, 160 and 162 was diluted.

**The direction of the bias is what makes this serious.** Dilution pulls every ratio toward 1. So
an effect reported as real is real-or-larger -- harmless. An arm reported as **FLAT** may simply
have been diluted below tolerance, which is a **false negative**. And `an_attrib`'s three-way
verdict turns on exactly that reading -- "placement flat, presence nearly flat, candidate moves" --
so pooling could have manufactured the verdict it reported.

### chain161 was understated by more than double, and its ship verdict was the wrong population

float32, `exu1` against `c0`, redwood:

    k | TARGET (37)   pooled (60)   CONTROL (23)
    1 | 0.9368        0.9143        0.8792
    2 | 1.1145        1.0497        0.9532
    3 | 1.1465        1.0839        0.9902

The two groups move in **opposite directions**, which is the whole reason the split exists. On the
matrices where the kernel is most of the call, removing the unroll is **+11.5% and +14.7%**, not
the +5.0% and +8.4% recorded. By degree, target group: **1.2215 at degree 4-20 width 2** and
**1.2079 at width 3**, on 26 matrices.

**And the ship verdict inverts.** chain161 said `exu1` puts 5 of 60 cells below MKL against the
default's 1, so the geomean improved while the goal got worse. Split:

    below MKL, exu1   TARGET 1/37, 1/37, 1/37     CONTROL 4/23, 4/23, 4/23
    below MKL, c0     TARGET 0/37, 0/37, 0/37     CONTROL 0/23, 1/23, 2/23

**80% of the damage was control-group cells** -- matrices whose call is mostly per-call floor. On
the group that can express a kernel effect it is one new cell per width against a 22% gain on 26 of
37 matrices. That is a completely different trade from "five cells for five percent".

**The stated blocker is also one matrix.** chain161 reported -27% above degree 128 as the reason a
blanket change cannot ship. In the target group that band has **n=1** (0.5581); the -27% was
carried by the control group's n=5. So the population claimed to block this is a single matrix in
the group that matters, and the real target-group loss is at **degree 20-128 width 1** (0.7865,
n=9) -- a different band than the one recorded.

### chain162 survives, and sharpens

    redwood TARGET | placement 0.9987 pf 0 | presence 0.9957 pf 0  | candidate 0.9738 pf 19/37
                   | placement 0.9995 pf 0 | presence 0.9948 pf 1  | candidate 0.9870 pf 17/37
    MKT     TARGET | (no c0pad)            | presence 0.9629 pf 14/18 (k=4) | candidate 0.9769 pf 5

On the target group placement and presence are **cleaner** than pooled (past-floor 0 rather than 1
and 3), so "the per-row branch" is better supported, not worse. MKT's width-4 finding strengthens:
code presence costs **3.7%** and is past-floor on **14 of 18** target matrices, against the
candidate's 0.9769 on 5. And MKT width 1 reads 1.0051 past-floor 0 -- the host asymmetry is cleaner
still.

**An unplanned cross-validation.** The work-scaling probe independently classified `mrf64`'s cost as
DISPATCH rather than KERNEL. A per-call cost should therefore be *larger* in the floor-dominated
group, and it is: redwood `mrf64` reads 0.9860 in control against 0.9957 in target. Two instruments
built for different questions agree on the mechanism.

The remaining analyzers still pool. That is a known defect now rather than an unknown one, and the
priority is `an_unsw` and `an_heldout`, whose conclusions include flat readings.

## chain168 -- chain157's revision survives the split, and width 4 is worse than recorded

The documentation session raised the sharpest possible objection to chain167's own finding: chain157

denomination rather than avoiding it.

Re-scored on the split. This stage has no `groups.txt`, so the split is **derived** at the same
pre-registered `nnz >= 1e6` and labelled as derived, because a derived split and a read one are not

    k | A/A floor (target) | TARGET        | control       | pooled (recorded) | verdict
    1 | 0.9984 (n=10)      | 0.9940 (n=10) | 0.9952 (n=12) | 0.9947 (n=22)     | inside floor
    2 | 1.0057 (n=10)      | 0.9954 (n=10) | 1.0044 (n=12) | 1.0003 (n=22)     | inside floor
    3 | 1.0008 (n=10)      | 0.9983 (n=10) | 1.0103 (n=12) | 1.0048 (n=22)     | inside floor
    4 | 0.9972 (n=10)      | 0.9805 (n=10) | 0.9932 (n=12) | 0.9874 (n=22)     | BEYOND floor, SLOWER

Two caveats on the line rather than in a footnote: the target group at degree >= 20 is **n=10**, so

**And my own re-score table printed ratios with no floor beside them on the first attempt** -- a

### A correction accepted

## chain169 -- my floor-constant caveat named the wrong widths, and unifying the constant flipped two verdicts

The documentation session could not reconstruct my own caveat from my own table, and was right not
to be able to. I wrote that the tolerance is floored at the constant "at widths 1 and 8". Computed
from the printed target-group floors under the analyzer's actual rule, `max(0.010, |1-floor|*2)`:

    k | floor    spread*2  tol      binds       |1-cand|
    1 | 0.9984   0.0032    0.0100   CONSTANT    0.0060
    2 | 1.0057   0.0114    0.0114   spread      0.0046
    3 | 1.0008   0.0016    0.0100   CONSTANT    0.0017
    4 | 0.9972   0.0056    0.0100   CONSTANT    0.0195
    8 | 1.0089   0.0178    0.0178   spread      0.0044

**The constant binds on {1, 3, 4}, not {1, 8}.** Width 8 has the widest measured spread of all
five, so I named the single cell where the constant is *least* relevant. Their two alternative
explanations -- that the tolerance is not the doubled form, or that the deciding floor is not the
printed column -- are both false: it is the doubled form and it does read the printed column, so
the table and the verdict rest on the same numbers. The error was mine in naming the widths, which
is the smaller of the two possibilities and the one that needed checking to establish.

Width 4's marker is worth noting: the constant binds there, but the candidate is 0.0195 away --
nearly twice the tolerance -- so that verdict holds under any rule in the range.

### And the check found something the caveat was hiding

`an_unsw.py` carried **two different tolerance minimums**: `max(0.010, ...)` in the re-score table I
added and `max(0.015, ...)` in the pre-existing per-band table. The same question -- is this cell at
its floor -- answered against different floors depending on which table you read. I introduced the
second one next to the first without noticing.

Unified to a single `TOL_FLOOR = 0.010`, defined once with its rationale: the constant exists only
so an implausibly tight A/A spread cannot manufacture a significant-looking difference, it is not
the gate (the gate is `|1-floor|*2`, and CLAUDE.md forbids a fixed ratio as the gate itself), and
0.010 sits about 3x above the tightest A/A spread observed on these hosts (0.16%, doubled 0.32%).
0.010 rather than 0.015 because **the looser value makes a FLAT reading easier to obtain**, and a
false flat is the failure this sequence keeps meeting.

**Tightening it flipped two of twenty band cells, both HELD to FAILED:**

    k=3, degree >=128   P3 HELD "unsw == bandmr"  ->  FAILED: 0.9752 vs 0.9899, apart by 0.0147
    k=4, degree 20-128  P1 HELD "unsw at floor"   ->  FAILED: 1.0148 outside 0.010

The first is the substantive one: a **1.5% high-degree cost at width 3 that the looser constant was
absorbing**, which is the same direction as MKT's high-degree penalty and had been reading as
agreement. The second is a failed prediction rather than a regression -- unsw is *faster* than the
floor there. Five further lines changed only because the constant's value is printed in the message
text.

**chain168's conclusion is unaffected**: the aggregate re-score used 0.010 on both sides, so widths
1/2/3/8 sitting inside their floor at degree >= 20 does not depend on this change. What changes is
one per-band cell, in the direction of unsw costing more rather than less.

Two lessons worth separating. A tolerance floor is defensible and a *second* tolerance floor in the
same file is not -- and the straddle band between two such constants is precisely where a marginal
arm lands. And where the constant binds rather than the measurement, the output now says so on the
line, because a verdict that rests partly on a chosen number should not require recomputing the
rule to discover that.

## chain170 -- the width-3 high-degree cost is a control-group artefact, and the top band has no target population

The documentation session asked whether the per-degree-band table splits by population, because if
it pools then the newly-flipped width-3 cell is a diluted figure and -- by the direction rule --
a diluted *cost* is a floor rather than an estimate, so the target-group number could be worse.
That would make the host asymmetry a difference of degree rather than of kind and drop the
loop-split arm's expected value.

**It pooled.** `series()` took a `pop` argument but the band table called it without one, so it
defaulted to pooled. Now split. And the answer runs the other way.

**The `>=128` band has n=1 in the target group** (against n=5 in control), at every width. So the
cell that flipped cannot be given a target-group figure at all, and the table now refuses rather
than printing one:

    band    | target | control
    <4      |      1 |       5
    4-20    |     26 |       6
    20-128  |      9 |       7
    >=128   |      1 |       5

A `MIN_POP = 3` refusal replaces the geomean wherever a population is too small to be a rate. The
point is not the threshold but that **a single matrix must not be printed wearing a percentage** --
the previous output would have rounded it into a rate indistinguishable from the n=26 cells.

So the pooled 0.9752 at width 3 and degree >= 128 is **five sixths control-group matrices**, whose
call is mostly per-call floor. In the two target bands that are actually populations, width 3 reads:

    k=3, 4-20   (n=26) | bandmr 1.1961 | unsw 1.2035 | P3 HELD: unsw == bandmr
    k=3, 20-128 (n=9)  | bandmr 1.1393 | unsw 1.1359 | P3 HELD: unsw == bandmr

**No duplication tax at width 3 in either real target band.** The refinement being worried about
does not survive the split; it was a control-group effect, which is consistent with `mrf64` reading
DISPATCH rather than KERNEL -- a per-call cost belongs in the floor-dominated group.

So "the duplication tax is absent on redwood" stands for the target group, the host asymmetry
remains a difference of kind, and the loop-split arm keeps its expected value.

**And the width-4 blocker localizes.** The only target-group failure at the two-host width:

    k=4, 20-128 (n=9) | bandmr 1.0081 | unsw 0.9881 | P4 FAILED: unsw WORSE than bandmr

About 2% at degree 20-128 on nine matrices. That is the whole of the two-host cost, in one band, and
it is now specific enough to design against rather than a width-level aggregate.

Worth noting what the split did to width 1: `unsw` fails P1 in both target bands (0.9875 at 4-20,
0.9800 at 20-128, both outside the floor) while still being better than `bandmr` there (0.9728,
0.9835). A failed prediction and an improvement at the same time -- which is why "P1 FAILED" must
not be read as "the arm is worse".

## chain171 -- two summary reversals in one review, and the fix is to emit the comparison

The documentation session caught my own width-1 wording in the trap I had just warned them about.
I wrote that `unsw` fails P1 in both target bands "while still being better than `bandmr` there
(0.9728, 0.9835)". Their reading and their pairing are both correct:

    band    n    bandmr   unsw     unsw vs bandmr
    4-20    26   0.9728   0.9875   +1.52%  clears tol
    20-128   9   0.9835   0.9800   -0.36%  inside tol

**Better in one band and 0.36% behind in the other.** Inside tolerance, so it changes nothing about
