the arm -- and it is exactly the shape I had flagged one message earlier: a summary line that
reverses one of the cells it summarises.

**That is the second such reversal in this review.** The first named the wrong widths for the bound
tolerance ({1,8} for {1,3,4}); this one reversed a direction. Both were caught by a reader
recomputing from my own printed columns, which is the wrong place for that work to happen -- and
both survived my writing them down, so proofreading is not the fix.

The fix is the same one that worked for the tolerance marker: **emit the comparison instead of
narrating it.** The band table now carries a `CAND vs bandmr` column giving the signed percentage
and whether it clears the tolerance. A column that states the direction cannot be summarised
backwards, and the reader no longer has to divide two other columns to check a claim.

This is the third instance of one pattern worth naming plainly: where a conclusion is derived from
the output by a human step, that step is where the errors are. The `[constant]`/`[A/A spread]`
marker, the `MIN_POP` refusal, and now the direction column all move a derivation out of prose and
into the tool.

**And it paid for itself immediately** -- though less dramatically than I first wrote it. With the
column present, one cell reads as a gain: float64, width 2, degree 20-128, `unsw +2.78% clears
tol` -- `unsw` at 1.0178 against `bandmr` at 0.9903 on nine matrices.

I recorded that as a finding nobody had looked at. It is not. **chain157 already states it in
aggregate** -- "on float64 redwood is neutral-to-faster, including 19 of 22 at 1.0218 for width 2"
-- same statistic, same direction, same host, fourteen sections earlier. The effect was not unread.
What the column added is the **per-band target-group version that clears its own tolerance**, which
is the form a claim has to take here before it counts: 19-of-22 at 1.0218 is a pooled count over a
corpus whose control half is mostly per-call floor, and it carries no tolerance. The aggregate
existed; the measurement did not.

That distinction is the whole reason for the split and the tolerance column, so it is worth not
blurring: promoting an aggregate to a measurement is a real step, and it is a smaller one than
discovering the effect.

**What the arm's ledger now says**, all of it on the target group: a ~2% two-host low-degree
float32 gain; a ~2% float32 cost at width 4, localised to degree 20-128 on nine matrices; and a
~2.8% float64 gain at width 2 on those same nine matrices in that same band. The float32 cost and
the float64 gain share a degree band and a population but differ in width and dtype, so I am
recording that as a **coincidence of position, not a mechanism** -- I have no account that predicts
both. Worth flagging because the float64 half of this work has been treated throughout as a
smaller-signed echo of float32, and this cell does not fit that: it moves the other way.

### The other session's own finding, accepted

They recorded their error rather than only the correction, and it is the more useful half:
they flagged the pooling correctly and then inferred the wrong *direction* from it. "Dilution
understates a cost" presumes the target group has a population to dilute. At n=1 the pooled figure
is not a diluted target number -- it is a control number wearing a pooled label, and no reasoning
about direction recovers a measurement that was never taken. That generalises past this file: the
direction rule is a statement about mixtures, and it says nothing when one component is empty.

## chain172 -- the unroll lead confirms on both hosts and dies as a blanket constant, and the corpus split I added concentrates what it un-diluted

`unroll2` finished on both hosts: 50 CSVs each, five builds over five passes, balanced rotation,
61 matrices on redwood and 42 on MKT. It answers chain161 and produces four separate defects in the
analysis it was analysed with. Taking the defects first, because two of them change other chains.

### The GCN guardrail was measured on both hosts and never reported

`an_exunroll.py` ingested `sg_*.csv` into a `"gcn"` group at line 77 and then read that group in
exactly one place: a test for whether to print `NO GCN GUARDRAIL IN THIS STAGE`. There was no GCN
table. So while the stage measured nothing the warning fired and said so; the moment the stage DID
measure the guardrail, the warning fell silent and **nothing took its place**. Arriving data turned
the honest warning off without turning any reporting on.

That is the worst shape a guard can take, and it is worse than the ones already recorded in this
file, because the failure is invisible in exactly the runs that matter. A blank where four
predictions print green reads as a fifth pass. The rule that catches the class: **a guard's silence
has to mean the thing was CHECKED, never just that its input showed up.** The absence warning and
the table are now one decision in one place -- if the table has no rows, that is what prints.

### The pre-registered inertness check was over two widths and only one was tested

`unroll2_body.sh` registers P1 as "widths 4 and 8 are FLAT", and calls it the reading that can void
the stage. The analyzer tested width 8. Widths 4 and 8 are both outside the exact-width band --
`SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI` is 3 and all three arms live inside `if (exact_width && ...)` -- so both
are controls and half the control was never read.

The untested half is the half that fails. Width 4, target group:

    host      c0b floor   exu1      exu8      dgu0
    redwood   1.0008      0.9989    1.0003    0.9989     all flat
    MKT       1.0110      0.9701    1.0042    0.9658     exu1 and dgu0 MOVE

Testing one width of a two-width control and printing "flat" is the same defect as the guardrail
above, wearing different clothes. The numbering disagreed too -- the harness pre-registers P1/P2/P3/
P4 and the analyzer printed its own P2/P3/P3/P4 against different content, so "P4 passed" meant
different things in the two files. Both are fixed; the labels now follow the pre-registration.

### The split I introduced in chain167 fixed dilution by concentrating the corpus

chain167 split every corpus at `nnz >= 1e6` because pooling diluted the kernel effect. It does. It
also concentrates, and nothing said so:

    stage group     matrices   families   biggest family
    MKT   target    18          5         uni_chimera_i1_A x14  (78%)
    rw    target    37         22         uni_chimera_i1_A x14  (38%)

That is not this stage's corpus, it is **every stage's**: `attrib2bmkt`, `band2mkt`, `f64lay`,
`hoistmkt`, `hv`, `mkthi1`, `mktprobe`, `shipmkt`, `unswmkt` and `unroll2mkt` all read 18 matrices
in 5 families, 78% one generated family; every redwood stage reads 37 in 22. Only the held-out
stages escape (5% and 10%). So a per-matrix target geomean on MKT counts one synthetic family
fourteen times, and I have been reporting those as the trustworthy half of the split.

Two consequences, which must not be conflated:

- **Within a degree band the concentration is harmless here.** At degree 4-20 `exu1` reads 1.2147
  per-matrix and 1.2004 per-family on redwood (11 families), 1.1438 and 1.1827 on MKT (3). The
  non-chimera matrices move the same way, so the band effect is not a family artefact.
- **The aggregate is not harmless**, because the family sits entirely in ONE band. 14 of redwood's
  26 matrices at degree 4-20 are chimera and the 20-128 band has 9, so a per-matrix aggregate
  over-weights the band where `exu1` wins against the band where it loses. Family-weighting
  redwood's width-2 aggregate takes it from **1.1088 to 1.0358**.

chain171's cell is unaffected and worth saying so explicitly: its band is degree 20-128 on
`unswrw`, n=9 in **9 distinct families**. The chimera family is entirely inside 4-20.

`an_exunroll.py` now prints the composition and a per-family table beside the per-matrix one, so the
reweighting a careful reader would do by hand is in the output. Three families is a thin basis and
the column says `fam=3` rather than leaving it to be noticed.

### What the stage actually found: the effect is real, two-host, and `exu1` still cannot ship

chain161's lead reproduces on its own host across two independent stages and confirms on a second.
By fine degree band, `exu1` against `c0`, all matrices:

    band      redwood  k=1     k=2     k=3    | MKT  k=1     k=2     k=3
    8-16      n=27     1.0135  1.2069  1.1990 | n=19 1.0059  1.1538  1.1082
    16-32     n=14     0.8412  0.9908  1.0879 | n=2  0.9943  0.9963  1.0306
    128-512   n=5      0.7231  0.7879  0.8497 | n=4  0.9435  1.0058  1.0189

**The effect is not "widths 2-3" and not "degree 4-20". It is mean degree 8-16 at widths 2 and 3**,
worth 11-21% on both hosts, and it is gone by 16-32. redwood's high-degree collapse does not
replicate on MKT, so the loss that made chain161 refuse to ship is single-host; the gain is not.

And then `exu1` fails P1 on MKT at every width outside the band, in one direction:

    corpus width 4   0.9701      GCN k=6    0.9857
    corpus width 8   0.9923      GCN k=7    0.9830
                                 GCN k=16   0.9518

Five widths, two different workload sets, one sign, 1-5%. redwood is flat on all five (0.9964 to
1.0053). None of those widths executes the code `exu1` changes. `exu8`, which changes MORE code in
the same kernel, is inert on all of them -- so it is not code volume; the two arms that move are
the two that SHRINK the exact kernel, which reads as alignment rather than mechanism, and MKT's own
A/A floor is widest exactly at width 4 (1.0110, the largest in its table).

**This retires chain162's `mrf64` reading from curiosity to supported.** That was one arm, one
width, one stage, and I recorded it as "on Zen4, compiling in code that float32 never runs costs
2.3% at width 4". Here the same host charges an unrelated constant 1-5% across five widths while the
other host charges nothing. Same host, same direction, different mechanism entirely.

It also kills the arm. GCN k=16 is the real hidden dimension, not a probe width, and 0.9518 is a
4.8% regression on the workload the library is for. The standing gate is that a regression is a
finding to report, not a shape to tune around, and it does not matter that the mechanism is
probably layout: the binary is slower there. `exu1` does not ship.

### The arm that can ship was already in the tree

`spmm.h` line 4128 does not use a fixed unroll. It reduces one by mean degree:

    while (exact_unroll > 1 && mean_deg < (long)exact_unroll * narrowk_exact_degunroll_mult)
      exact_unroll >>= 1;

with `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_DEGUNROLL_MULT` shipping at 1. Starting from 4 that gives unroll 4 to
every matrix of mean degree 4 or more -- so the 8-16 band, where two hosts agree the right depth is
1, is handed 4. **The mechanism the measurement asks for already ships; its threshold is wrong.**
The multiplier has never been swept.

    MULT       unroll 1    unroll 2    unroll 4
    1 (ships)  deg < 2     2-4         >= 4
    2          deg < 4     4-8         >= 8
    8          deg < 16    16-32       >= 32
    16         deg < 32    32-64       >= 64

`MULT` is a `long` compared at runtime, not a template parameter, so no kernel's code changes shape
and the out-of-band widths have nothing to align differently -- which is the entire reason to prefer
it to `exu1`, and P1 tests it rather than assuming it. `dgm2` is a graded control: at MULT=2 the
8-16 band still gets unroll 4, so it must NOT move that band.

Launched on both hosts as `dgmult` (redwood pid 1650248, MKT job 17308803, submitted through the
dependency rule with the four held jobs excluded by reason). Five predictions, P1 being the
discriminating one: if a pure threshold change also moves MKT's out-of-band widths, the layout
attribution above is wrong and the cost belongs to something the arms share.

### One more thing about `exu1`, recorded because it nearly went unnoticed

The env hook for this constant accepts `0`, `2`, `4` and `8` and refuses everything else. `exu1`
sets it to **1** through a compile-time define, which bypasses that validation entirely. The value
turns out to be meaningful and the correctness grid passes on it at every width and row count in the
straddle. But a build-defines arm can reach configurations the runtime hook is written to reject,
and no part of the three-build path checks that the value it is measuring is one the code admits.

## chain173 -- the held-out stage's GCN guardrail was never printed either, and the loop-split arm is built

Two pieces of work, one prompted by the other.

### The same defect, in the analyzer whose conclusion is still live

chain172 found `an_exunroll.py` ingesting a GCN guardrail group and reading it only to decide
whether to print an absence warning. That is a class of defect, not an incident, so I audited every
analyzer that ingests `s[hg]_*.csv` for it:

    an_band2.py      2 mentions, 1 consuming   -- computes a real guardrail
    an_unsw.py       2 mentions, 1 consuming   -- computes a real guardrail
    an_dgmult.py     6 mentions, 3 consuming   -- table + verdict (written in chain172)
    an_exunroll.py   6 mentions, 3 consuming   -- fixed in chain172
    an_heldout.py    1 mention,  0 consuming   -- INGESTED AND NEVER READ

`an_heldout.py` is worse than the one already fixed: it has no absence warning either, so the
held-out stage's GCN guardrail was collected on **both hosts**, across four arms and 24 cells each,
and reported nowhere at all. Nothing in its output ever mentioned a guardrail, so there was not
even a blank to notice.

Printed, using `an_unsw.py`'s worst-cell-against-its-own-floor form:

    redwood                                            MKT
    bandmr  pubmed   f64 k=7   0.9589 (floor 0.9850)   bandmr  none of 24 beyond its spread
    mdlo    pubmed   f64 k=7   0.9617 (floor 0.9850)   mdlo    none of 24 beyond its spread
    rag2    cora     f64 k=16  0.9831 (floor 0.9961)   rag2    none of 24 beyond its spread
    ragmd   citeseer f32 k=3   0.9825 (floor 1.0073)   ragmd   citeseer f32 k=16  0.9435

**It does not establish a regression, and the reason is in the shape of the flags.** `bandmr` and
`mdlo` flag the *identical* cell at nearly the same ratio against the same floor. Two different arms
regressing one cell alike is a cell whose own same-code floor is understated, not two independent
regressions -- and 4 of 4 arms flagging *something* says the same more weakly. On the second host
three of the four are clean. No cell is flagged on both hosts, so by this project's own rule nothing
here is confirmed.

So the honest reading is narrow and it is still worth having: **the held-out stage's per-cell
guardrail threshold is too tight on redwood**, `pubmed float64 k=7` is a cell to re-measure, and
`ragmd` -- already rejected on aggregate -- is the only arm flagged on both hosts, at two different
widths.

Both cautions are now emitted rather than narrated: the worst-of-24 line says it is a multiple
comparison and points at re-measurement instead of a verdict, and the shared-cell case prints its
own diagnosis. The reason to emit the caution rather than suppress the finding until it is
significant is that suppressing it is exactly what left the guardrail unprinted.

### The loop-split arm, built

The arm chain162 identified and chain168-171 did not get to: unswitch the multi-row admission test
out of the **row loop** rather than templating the entire worker.
`SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_LOOPSPLIT`, default 0.

`multirow_ok` is a `const bool` fixed before the parallel region, so the row loop can be entered
through a compile-time tag once per **claim** -- a claim is a chunk of rows, so on the short-row
matrices where the branch costs most this is one test against thousands. The worker's workspace
setup, its work-stealing claim loop and its zero-slice drain stay single-bodied, which is strictly
less duplication than UNSWITCH for the same branch removal.

Two constants that differ only in the default build, which is the whole trick: `MR_ROWS_LIVE` gates
whether the multi-row block is in the instantiation at all, `MR_PRETESTED` whether `multirow_ok`
has already been tested. With the split off they are `true` and `false`, so
`if constexpr (MR_LIVE && true)` and `(false || multirow_ok)` restore the shipped condition exactly.

The `#if` surrounds only the lambda's opening and closing lines; the loop header and its 500-line
body are **shared text, not duplicated source**. Two reasons, both learned here: UNSWITCH measured a
forwarding lambda at 14 instructions of 164596 with its own constant off, so a default-off mechanism
cannot afford to wrap anything; and two `#if` arms holding the same 500 lines drift apart silently,
which is worse than either cost.

Checked before it is measured:

- **Control flow survives the wrap.** Every `break` in the body is switch-local and every `continue`
  targets the row loop; there is no `return`, no `goto`, and no `break` aimed at the enclosing claim
  loop.
- **Default emission is neutral**, proven rather than asserted: 20 differing instructions of
  169165, all bare immediate moves, every delta exactly 41 -- which reconciles against the source as
  31 lines inserted above the row loop plus 10 below it, with all ten of `spmm.h`'s `TORCH_CHECK`
  macros sitting below both. The A/A control at equal-length build paths reports identical
  disassembly on the same pair, so the instrument was working.
- **Correctness**: 576 cases over both dtypes, twelve row counts straddling every plausible unroll
  factor, three densities and eight widths. Zero mismatches.

**What is NOT checked: the split path has never been compiled.** It is guarded on `__AVX2__`
because the multi-row kernel is, and the only ARM host cannot build it. An x86 compile and
correctness run come before any timing, and both x86 hosts are currently running `dgmult`.

## chain174 -- the row split's NO-GO names a testable mechanism, and the answer to three data points is to count them

Prepared while `dgmult` runs, not yet executed. Recording the reasoning because it touches a closed
verdict and the framing matters.

The width-2 high-degree regression (`connectus` 0.602, `TSOPF_FS_b300` 0.712, two-host) is the
oldest open ship blocker here, and the mechanism built for exactly it -- the row-split partition --
is in the tree and off. I went looking for whether its threshold had ever been swept, expecting to
find it unmeasured. It is thoroughly measured: the verdict is NO-GO, arm-variant across hosts, with
float64 gaining 8.8% on MKT and losing 9.0% on redwood on the same cells with the same code. That
is a sound rejection and this does not reopen it.

What it does take up is one sentence of the verdict:

> A gate that admitted connectus and excluded nw14 would be worth having, and I could not find one
> that was a mechanism rather than a fit to three matrices.

The verdict then names the separating quantity: the typical length of the rows the split is **not**
splitting, against the segment width. `connectus` averages 1971 nonzeros over its other 511 rows and
wins on both x86 hosts; `nw14` averages 11305 over its other 72 and loses on both. The mechanism
that implies is specific -- a split helps only when a segment is comparable to or wider than a
typical unsplit row, because otherwise it replaces work the kernel already does at its most
efficient with units an order of magnitude shorter. On those two matrices the ratio is 0.90 against
6.4, a sevenfold separation.

**That is a stated mechanism, and it was refused for having three data points. The answer to three
data points is not to fit them more carefully -- it is to find out how many points exist.** So the
next step is a count, not a measurement: `splitcensus.py` walks the corpus, calls production's own
`scorch_spmm_row_imbalance` and `scorch_spmm_seg_width` rather than restating either (ops.cpp
exports both for precisely this reason, and its comment notes the imbalance probe is "easy to get
almost right" because it is the longest run of equal-nonzero cuts landing in one row, not max degree
over mean), and reports where every gate-firing matrix sits on the ratio.

It is structural -- indptr only, no timing -- so it cannot be confounded and does not need a quiet
host. `maxdeg` is computed by a direct scan, which production deliberately avoids; that is a census
quantity rather than a policy, and the per-call cost production is avoiding does not exist offline.

**Pre-registered before any of it runs**, so what follows is a test and not a fit:

- Fewer than 5 matrices on each side of ratio = 2, *excluding the three the verdict rested on*, and
  there is no population. The NO-GO stands unchallenged, and reporting that is the outcome rather
  than a reason to lower the bar.
- With a population, the timed stage predicts a GAIN below 1 and a LOSS above 3, with 1 to 3
  unclaimed. A rule that predicts correctly on matrices it was not derived from is a mechanism; the
  same rule fitted to `connectus` and `nw14` is what the verdict correctly refused.

Both verdict branches were exercised on constructed inputs before the real corpus was touched, and
the analyzer refuses an empty census rather than reporting a clean nothing.

## chain175 -- the threshold retune works: `dgm8` takes all of `exu1`'s gain and none of its cost

`dgmult` finished on both hosts, 50 CSVs each, five builds over five passes, balanced rotation,
equal row counts per build. **The arm the mechanism pointed at is confirmed on both hosts and it is
the one that could ship.**

### P2: the gain, in the band, on two hosts

Mean degree 8-16, widths 2 and 3, target group, against `c0`:

    host      k   dgm2 (control)   dgm8              dgm16             floor    % of exu1 (dgm8)
    redwood   2   0.9955  n=22     1.2186            1.2181            0.9958   106%
    redwood   3   1.0036  n=22     1.2061            1.1936            0.9979   104%
    MKT       2   1.0058  n=16     1.1708            1.1787            0.9987   111%
    MKT       3   1.0024  n=16     1.0999            1.1037            0.9995    92%

**A pure threshold change recovers 92-111% of what `exu1` got by changing the depth outright.** The
mechanism was read correctly: the shipped ladder gives the 8-16 band an unroll of 4 and the band
wants 1, and moving the threshold is enough.

**P5 held on both hosts**, which is what makes that attributable. `dgm2` cannot reach the 8-16 band
by construction -- at MULT=2 the band still gets unroll 4 -- and it reads inside the floor in all
four cells. So the arms act through the threshold and not through something they happen to correlate
with. (P5 is also now a two-sided test; it was written one-sided, and a `dgm2` moving the band
*down* 10% would have printed "held, does not reach this band".)

### P1 and the GCN guardrail: both separate `dgm8` from `dgm16`, and both vindicate the prediction

chain172's attribution said `exu1`'s out-of-band cost on MKT was alignment, and predicted that a
runtime `long` compared per call would not pay it. Confirmed:

    MKT, width 4 (outside the exact-width band)     exu1 0.9701      dgm8 1.0089 (floor 1.0043)
    MKT, GCN k=6 / k=7 / k=16                       exu1 0.9857/0.9830/0.9518    dgm8 0.9902/0.9964/0.9986

`dgm8` passes P1 at both control widths on both hosts and passes the GCN guardrail on both hosts at
all four widths. `exu1` failed three MKT GCN widths including k=16, the real hidden dimension.

**`dgm16` is out, on two independent signals.** It moves out-of-band on MKT at width 4 (1.0202) and
width 8 (1.0126) -- faster, but P1 says a threshold cannot reach those widths -- and it regresses
GCN k=16 on MKT at 0.9889 past a 0.010 tolerance. It buys nothing over `dgm8` in the band.

One label in the guardrail was wrong and is fixed: all three arms gain 2-7% at GCN k=3, and the
analyzer called that "an arm reaching code it does not name". cora, citeseer and pubmed have mean
degree 4.90, 3.74 and 5.50, and these arms change the unroll for exactly those degrees, so the gain
is **on-mechanism** -- it is the guardrail's good news, not a confound, and the note read as the
opposite.

### The standing goal: the cell count, stated honestly

MKT target group, cells below MKL:

    build    k=1     k=2      k=3      k=4     k=8
    c0       1/18    18/18    18/18    3/18    2/18
    dgm8     1/18     2/18     3/18    1/18    2/18

Sixteen cells at width 2 and fifteen at width 3. **The honest form: three distinct families**, since
14 of MKT's 18 target matrices are `uni_chimera_i1_A`. The two that are not are `G_n_pin_pout`
(degree 10.0, 117.6 -> 98.7 us against MKL's 106.6) and `n4c6-b10` (degree 11.0, 141.1 -> 113.2
against 118.5) -- both in the 8-16 band, as the mechanism requires. What still loses is `connectus`
and `relat8`, both far outside the band, both untouched by this arm because its threshold cannot
fire there. `connectus` is chain174's question, not this one.

redwood recovered **zero** cells, and that is not a failure: `c0` already loses 0 of 37 at widths 1
and 2 there. Its gain shows up as raw speed instead, 1.22x.

### The inertness check took three versions and my own hand-check was wrong twice

Worth recording because the wrong answers were the comforting ones.

Above mean degree 4*MULT the ladder keeps the unroll at 4, so the arm runs `c0`'s code and any
difference is the instrument. Getting that comparison right took three attempts:

1. **Min/max ranges.** An outlier statistic over 36 cells that says nothing about whether any
   single cell moved. It reported "the arm exceeds its own A/A spread" for all three arms.
2. **The arm left inside its own control set.** `o > max(vs)` then compared a value against a range
   containing it, so it could never be true: **the check answered "0 of 36 outside, INERT" on any
   input whatsoever.** Same family as a guard credited for its neighbour's refusal, and worse,
   because the vacuous answer is the reassuring one.
3. **Calibrated.** Above degree 64 all five builds are code-identical, so their spread is a pure
   instrument reading -- 1.28x on one 20-microsecond cell. Under the null the arm and its controls
   are exchangeable, so the chance the arm is the min or max is 2/(controls+1); accumulating that
   gives the count to expect, and the count is a sum of Bernoulli trials so its sd comes free.

    host      arm     n    extreme   null expects
    redwood   dgm2    36   15        16 +- 3.0     INERT
    redwood   dgm8    36   18        16 +- 3.0     INERT
    redwood   dgm16   21    9         8 +- 2.2     INERT
    MKT       dgm2    42    8        18 +- 3.2     INERT
    MKT       dgm8    42   10        18 +- 3.2     INERT
    MKT       dgm16   33   13        13 +- 2.8     INERT

All six inside one sd. That also resolves P3's flag: `dgm8` read -3.29% in the >=128 band on
redwood (n=5, control group) and the worst individual cell is 0.8602 on a 20-microsecond matrix
where five code-identical builds span 1.28x. It is noise, and the null says so rather than my saying
so.

**My two hand-checks were both wrong**, in ways the tool then caught. The first pooled the `ours`,
`oursb` and `mkl` readings into one median because the scratch script had no `arm` filter. The
second truncated matrix names to 24 characters, so I read a different matrix's row and concluded the
opposite. Both are arguments for emitting the derivation rather than doing it at the prompt -- the
same point as chain171, arrived at from the other direction.

### What is still missing before this could ship

**float64 is unmeasured.** `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_DEGUNROLL_MULT` is not dtype-gated, so flipping its
default changes float64 as well, and this stage ran float32 only. The policy comment's own ladder
was derived from an x86 **float64** width-1 sweep (+12.4% at degree 2-4, -15.7% at 4-8, +4.8% above
8), so float64 is not a formality here -- it is the dtype the constant was first reasoned about.
That measurement comes next, on the same corpus and rotation.

## chain176 -- float64 contradicts float32 and the two x86 hosts disagree in sign, so the constant splits by dtype

`dgm64` finished on both hosts, same corpus, same rotation, same arms as the float32 stage. **It
contradicts float32, and the contradiction is not noise.** Target group, mean degree 8-16:

    band 8-16          float32                        float64
    redwood   k=2      1.2186   k=3  1.2061           1.0712   k=3  1.0458
    MKT       k=2      1.1708   k=3  1.0999           0.9603   k=3  0.8819

float32 is a two-host gain of 10-22%. **float64 is +7.1%/+4.6% on one x86 host and -4.0%/-11.8% on
the other**, with floors of 1.0034/1.0082 and 0.9863/1.0036. Opposite signs, same code, same
matrices, both x86-64 with AVX2.

**It is attributable to the threshold, which is what makes it a finding rather than a puzzle.**
`dgm2` cannot reach the 8-16 band -- at MULT=2 a matrix of mean degree 8-16 still gets unroll 4 --
and it reads inside the floor in all four float64 cells on both hosts (1.0029, 0.9958, 1.0015,
0.9980). So the arms act through the threshold and the two hosts genuinely disagree about what
depth that band wants in float64.

There is a plausible mechanism and I am not claiming it: float64 halves the lanes per vector, so a
row of degree 8-16 offers half as many vector iterations, and the deeper unroll's independent
accumulator chains matter more. That predicts the *direction* of MKT's loss and says nothing about
why redwood gains, so it is half an explanation.

**float64 also regresses the GCN guardrail at k=7 on BOTH hosts** -- 0.9871 on redwood and 0.9891
on MKT, past tolerances of 0.010 and 0.011. Two hosts agreeing is this project's confirmation
standard, so unlike the single-cell flags in chain173 that one counts.

### The response is a per-dtype constant, and the precedent is in the same header

Committed as `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_DEGUNROLL_MULT_F32` and `_F64`, both defaulting to the shared
`SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_DEGUNROLL_MULT`, which stays at 1. Same construction as
`SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32`/`_F64` and `SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32`/`_F64` -- and the header already
said why, about the four neighbouring vector constants: *"Two of them also disagree across hosts,
which no single expression in bytes can say."* This is a third.

**Not host-gated, deliberately.** Nothing the compiler knows separates these two machines; they
differ in microarchitecture, cache hierarchy and pool shape, all invisible at compile time. A gate
on something the compiler cannot see is a build flag someone has to remember. Leaving float64 at 1
makes it bit-identical to what ships today, which is a stronger guarantee than any host predicate.

Proven rather than asserted: 20 differing instructions of 169165 against `HEAD`, all bare immediate
moves, every delta exactly 5 -- the lines added above `spmm.h`'s ten `TORCH_CHECK` macros, with
`scorch_policy.h` contributing none because it has no line-sensitive macros at all. A/A control at
equal-length build paths reports identical disassembly. Correctness 432 cases, 0 mismatches.

### The analyzer was float32 in twelve places, so it would have skipped every verdict

`an_dgmult.py` had `"float32"` written into twelve conditions. Run on a float64-only stage it
printed every aggregate table and then **silently skipped all five predictions, the GCN guardrail
verdict, the band tests and the inertness check.** Tables with no verdicts reads as "nothing
wrong" -- the third instance this week of the same shape, after the guardrail that was collected
and never reported and the two-width control tested at one width.

Fixed with an explicit `PDT`, announced on its own line, and a **refusal** when the requested dtype
is absent: "a verdict block that silently skips is indistinguishable from one that passed." The
float32 verdicts are unchanged after the edit, which is the check that the parameterisation did not
quietly alter what it had already concluded.

One cross-dtype trap caught in the same pass. The band table reports each arm as a percentage of
`exu1`'s gain, and `exu1` was measured on **float32 only** -- `unroll2` ran that dtype. On the
float64 stage that column would have divided a float64 reading by a float32 baseline and labelled
it a fraction. It is now withheld, printing "exu1 float64 unmeasured" instead of a number.

### Still open: ARM is affected, and it is being measured rather than assumed

The multiplier is not ISA-gated and the exact-width kernel compiles on NEON. Flipping `MULT_F32` to
8 changes ARM emission in **exactly four instructions**, all of them the ladder's own comparison
immediates -- `cmp #0x3 -> #0x1f` and `cmp #0x2 -> #0x10`, the thresholds moving from 4 and 2 to 32
and 16 -- and nothing else. So the define reaches ARM, and the neighbouring constant has form:
`SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI_F32` 3 -> 1 is a two-host x86 win that regresses ARM to 0.7229 and ships
x86-gated for exactly that reason.

So `MULT_F32=8` cannot ship globally on a two-x86-host result. Running now on the M5 -- the only
NEON host, so this is a single-host reading by construction -- over **the same 34 matrices pulled
from redwood's cache**, 27 in the mean-degree 8-16 band where the arm fires and 7 at degree >= 64
where the ladder provably cannot, as the inertness control. Same matrices rather than a local
substitute, so the ARM number lines up against redwood's 1.2186 and MKT's 1.1708 instead of being
a third corpus nobody can compare.

Two things already passed there: the two no-define trees at equal-length paths emit **identical
disassembly**, so the ARM A/A floor is measuring the machine and not the build; and both candidates
are correct over 360 cases each.

One label in that stage must not be misread: `mrgate.py`'s third arm is `torch.sparse.mm`, recorded
in the CSV as `mkl`. **On ARM that is not MKL** -- there is none on this machine -- it is torch's own
fallback, and its column cannot be compared against the x86 stages' MKL numbers. The ARM question
is arm-vs-arm, so nothing depends on it.

## chain177 -- the row split's firing set is SIX matrices, and my census restated the gate the code warns about restating

chain174 asked a counting question: the row-split NO-GO named a discriminator and refused it for
having three data points, so how many points exist? Answered, and the first answer was wrong by a
factor of 290.

### The mistake, which the source had already written down

My census decided "does the gate fire" as `imbalance >= 2`. **That is one term of the gate.** The
shipped rule also carries `SCORCH_SPMM_SPLIT_MIN_NNZ` (150000) and `SCORCH_SPMM_SPLIT_MIN_DEGREE`
(256). So the first run reported **1745 firing matrices of 8384**, and `spmm.h` says exactly why not
to do that, in the comment directly above the gate call:

> One call, because the gate lives in one place: `scorch_spmm_split_seg` answers "how wide a segment,
> or leave the rows whole" and is the same function a harness or a test asks. **Splitting this rule
> into a copy here and a copy in the harness is how a firing set ended up with two firing matrices in
> its inert group and reversed the sign of its own conclusion.**

I had read that comment, quoted its neighbour in chain174's write-up as the reason to call
production rather than restate it, and then restated it anyway -- one term of it, which is the form
that looks like calling production. `scorch_spmm_split_seg` is exported for this and returns a
positive segment width exactly when the split would run.

Two consequences worth keeping. Calling *some* of a production rule is not a weaker version of
calling it, it is a different rule -- and it is harder to spot than an outright reimplementation,
because the names match. And a census against a **default** build would have returned zero
everywhere, since `MIN_IMBALANCE` ships at 0 and 0 disables the mechanism; the corrected census
therefore refuses an all-zero result rather than reporting an empty population, and that refusal
was fired on a default build before the real run.

### The answer

With production's own gate, built at `MIN_IMBALANCE=2`, over all 8407 cached matrices:

    matrix     rows    nnz       deg       imb  ceiling  other_deg/seg   prior result
    rail582     582    402290     691.22    2    45.1     0.862          never measured
    connectus   512   1127525    2202.20    7     9.4     0.895          WON on both x86 hosts
    rail516     516    315412     611.26    2    40.4     0.970          never measured
    us04        163    297538    1825.39    2    25.6     3.038          never measured
    nw14         73    904910   12396.03    6     9.9     6.398          LOST on both x86 hosts
    kl02         71    212536    2993.46    2    27.8     7.053          LOST

**Six matrices, in a corpus of 8384.** 23 were unreadable and are reported as refused, not skipped.

Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions.

**The discriminator separates the three measured matrices perfectly.** connectus at 0.895 won;
nw14 at 6.398 and kl02 at 7.053 lost. There is no overlap and the gap is a factor of seven, which
is what the NO-GO observed with two matrices and is now three.

**And the pre-registered bar cannot be met, because it asks for more matrices than exist.**
chain174 registered "5 new matrices on each side of ratio = 2 or there is no population". The three
never-measured matrices are `rail582` (0.862) and `rail516` (0.970) below, and `us04` (3.038) above
-- 2 and 1. The analyzer prints NO POPULATION and that is the pre-registration working as intended.

But the reason it fails is not the reason the bar was written. I set 5-per-side expecting a corpus
of candidates and got a universe of six, of which three are already spent. **A bar that demands
more data than the population contains is not a standard, it is an impossibility**, and reporting
"no population" without saying that would imply more data could settle it. More data cannot: this
is every matrix in 8400 that fires the rule.

What is actually available is a **3-matrix out-of-sample test covering half the firing set**, with
the prediction registered in advance and the mechanism stated a priori. Two-and-one can **refute**
the discriminator -- if `us04` gains or either `rail` loses, the rule is dead -- but it cannot
establish it. That asymmetry is the honest description, and it is worth stating rather than
converting into either a green light or a dead end.

### And it would not revive the split anyway

Worth saying plainly, because a discriminator that separates connectus from nw14 addresses the
*second* of the NO-GO's two reasons. The first was **arm-variance across hosts on float64** -- MKT
gaining 8.8% against a 1.0004 floor where redwood lost 9.0% against 0.9956, on the same cells with
the same code. A rule that excludes nw14 and kl02 leaves connectus as the firing set, and it is
possible that the float64 disagreement was an artifact of pooling three matrices -- but the
per-matrix float64 breakdown is not in this document and no split-stage CSVs are in the ledger, so
that is a hypothesis I cannot test for free and am not going to assert. **The NO-GO stands**, on the
ground it was decided on.

The census is the contribution here: the number that was missing, which is six.

## chain178 -- the arm that was measured is not the arm that ships, and proving it took fixing the instrument

`dgm8` was chosen on `-DSCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_DEGUNROLL_MULT=8`, the **shared** macro, which moves
both dtypes. chain176 then established that float64 disagrees in sign across the two x86 hosts and
regresses GCN k=7 on both, so what ships is the **float32** macro alone behind an AVX2+FMA gate.
Those are different objects, and the number 1.2186 belongs to the first one.

The gate is committed as `28762af`. What follows is what it took to be able to say that.

### The gate fires, and a presence count could not have told me

The first check I ran was worthless and it is worth recording why, because it looked like evidence.
I grepped the built object for the ladder's comparison immediates and got `24 cmp $0x10`,
`2 cmp $0x1f`, `615 cmp $0x1`, `248 cmp $0x3`. The 31 and 16 are the MULT=8 thresholds, so the
presence reads as confirmation -- but `cmp $0x1` occurs **615 times** in that object for entirely
unrelated reasons, so its presence proves nothing and its absence was never expected. A check whose
negative outcome was never possible is the "check passed == nothing to check" shape.

What settles it is three builds and a digest:

    default build (the gate)                       700d8b5dfb7c9c79  1536048 bytes
    same tree, -D..._MULT_F32=8 forced             700d8b5dfb7c9c79  1536048   <- byte-identical
    same tree, -D..._MULT_F32=1 forced             e7ec77af15775bda  1537272   <- differs

Byte-identity on the first pair is the proof the `#ifndef` resolved to 8; the inequality is the
proof the value reaches code. And a fourth build with **both** per-dtype macros forced to 8 is
byte-identical to the shared-macro build (`40b3eca08fe85306`), which is what shows the two macros
are consumed independently rather than one shadowing the other.

### The instrument was wrong, and it was wrong in the direction that costs a run

The float64 exclusion needs float64 emission to be untouched. `symneutral.py` compares two objects
symbol by symbol, normalising `0x`-prefixed hex and `<sym+0x..>` branch targets. Asking it whether
a float32-only define touches float64 code returned **9 of 23 float64 SpMM symbols changed**, at
identical instruction counts.

Identical count with a changed digest is the tell, and the differences were all of this form:

    < call   310c3 <spmm_csr_double_v2_core(...)+0x43>
    > call   310d3 <spmm_csr_double_v2_core(...)+0x43>

The **within-symbol offsets are identical** (`+0x43`, `+0x61`, `+0x66`); only the absolute address
moved, by 0x10, because unrelated code above it changed size. objdump writes a destination as a
*bare* hex token, which carries no `0x` prefix, so the normaliser never saw it. Fix is a lookahead
so only a hex token objdump follows with `<` is treated as an address:

    ADDR = re.compile(r"\b[0-9a-f]{4,}\b(?=\s*<)")

After the fix: **23 of 23 float64 symbols identical**. The verdict inverted, and the wrong verdict
was the one that would have sent a float64 timing stage after a null. Re-running the detector's
controls mattered as much as the fix -- byte-identical objects read neutral on every needle, and
the pair that must still differ kept 4 changed float32 symbols while shedding 24 address-noise ones.

### A runtime `long` comparison does change code shape at -O3

The sweep's own DEF entry stated its safety argument in these words: "MULT is a `long` compared at
runtime, so no kernel's code changes shape and the out-of-band widths exu1 regressed on MKT have
nothing to layout differently." **That is false.** Holding the tree fixed and moving only the
float32 macro:

    scorch_spmm_row_narrow_exact<float,4,2>      out-of-line at MULT=8, INLINED at MULT=1
    scorch_spmm_row_narrow_exact<float,6,2>      inlined     at MULT=8, out-of-line at MULT=1
    spmm_csr_v2_core<float, false>               6334 vs 6401 instructions

Fifteen of the eighteen width/unroll combinations are out-of-line either way, and exactly one
unroll-2 instantiation trades places. The constant feeds the inliner's budget. Semantically the
same eighteen kernels; not the same object -- so the sweep's number does not transfer, and the
shipped configuration has to be timed as itself.

This also retro-explains chain175's loose end. `exu1` regressed **out-of-band** widths on MKT
(0.9701 at width 4, 4.8% at GCN k=16) and the session attributed that to alignment rather than
mechanism without a mechanism to name. This is the mechanism: an unroll constant that cannot reach
width 4 arithmetically can still move width 4's code, because it moves what the inliner does with
the whole translation unit.

### Scope, bounded from the source rather than assumed

The performance convention names GCN, autoencoder and attention, and only GCN was measured. It
turns out the other two cannot be reached, and the bound is exact:

- `spmm.h:4091` sets `exact_width` only when `B1_size <= exact_hi_`, and `exact_hi_` is
  `SCORCH_NARROWK_EXACT_HI`, which **ships at 3**. The ladder at `spmm.h:4124` sits inside
  `if (exact_width && ...)`. So the constant is unreachable at k >= 4.
- The only two call sites of `scorch_spmm_row_narrow_exact` are both inside `spmm_csr_v2_core`.
  `spmm_csr_linear_fused_float` -- the AE path -- does not call it.

AE and attention run at widths in the hundreds, so they are out of scope by construction, and
widths 4 and 8 in this stage are the empirical check of exactly that claim.

**And an inherited comment in the analyzer had this backwards.** It said GCN widths 3, 6 and 7 all
sit inside the band, citing `exact_cap_` = 7. But `exact_cap_` is the *instantiation* cap -- the
widths a template exists for -- and it only ever clamps `exact_hi_` **down**: `if (exact_hi_ >
exact_cap_) exact_hi_ = exact_cap_` turns 3 into 3. The band is widths 1-3. That inverts how the
guardrail table reads: only k=3 is in scope, and a movement at k=6, 7 or 16 is a confound rather
than news.

### C5: the stage proves it is timing the ship, per host, before it times anything

Every number about a build is a claim about a binary, so the stage's first act is to build the
**gated tree with no defines** -- literally what ships -- and require it to be disassembly-identical
to the `gate` arm it is about to time. Three details make it real rather than decorative: it builds
at the same path string the other arms used (`$R/wk`), it greps the gated default out of the
extracted header so a stage handed the pre-gate tree twice cannot pass for the wrong reason, and
it exits non-zero rather than continuing.

    redwood   NEUTRAL: 163100 instructions, identical disassembly
    MKT       NEUTRAL: 231236 instructions, identical disassembly

**It also proves the ISA predicate holds on each host, for free.** If `__AVX2__ && __FMA__` were
not defined, the gated tree's default would resolve F32 to 1 and differ from the forced-8 arm, so
C5 would fail. It passed on both, so the gate demonstrably fires on redwood and on Zen4 -- which is
a stronger statement than the three-build digest, and automatic.

ARM is the other half: pre-gate against gated on the M5 gives identical disassembly over 169165
instructions, so the exclusion is byte-proven and not argued.

### The analyzer's own C5 guard passed a failing proof

Worth recording because it is a one-character class of bug in a check written to be strict. The
guard was `if "NEUTRAL" not in _c5`. `neutral_disasm.sh`'s failure line is
**"NOT NEUTRAL: instruction counts differ"**, which *contains* the substring the guard looks for,
so a c5.txt reporting a real emission difference read as a pass. Anchoring on the line's first
token and refusing `NOT NEUTRAL` and `REFUSE` by name fixes it; all four possible file contents
(fail / refuse / empty / pass) now discriminate.

Two more guard defects in the same block, both found by testing them rather than reading them. The
freshness check answered for the content check when the file was fresh-but-failing, leaving the
content path untested -- so content is now checked first. And the freshness direction is the
non-obvious one: C5 runs *before* the timing loop, so in a coherent run c5.txt is **older** than
every CSV, and a c5.txt *newer* than the CSVs means stale timings from an earlier run in a reused
directory.

### MKT confirms the shipped object. redwood went down mid-stage, so this is half a claim

`c0` is the pre-gate default, `c0b` the same source again as the A/A floor, `gate` the shipped
constant -- and C5 proved on this host that `gate` is disassembly-identical to what the committed
tree builds by default (231236 instructions). Six passes, three builds, rotation balanced.

**C1, the claim.** float32, target group, mean degree 8-16:

              gate     per-family   floor    tol     fraction of the sweep arm
    k=2      1.1490    1.1901 fam=3  0.9978   0.010   87%
    k=3      1.0874    1.0902 fam=3  1.0071   0.014   87%

87% of a number produced by a different object is the right kind of answer: the same sign, well
outside the floor, and slightly short -- which is what the instantiation trade predicts and why
this stage was run instead of inheriting 1.1708.

**And the cell count, which is what the standing goal is measured on.** Below-MKL cells, target
group, float32:

    build     k=1     k=2     k=3     k=4     k=8
    c0        1/18    18/18   18/18   1/18    3/18
    c0b       1/18    18/18   14/18   1/18    2/18
    gate      1/18     2/18    3/18   2/18    2/18

In the effect band alone (degree 8-16, 16 of the 18) it is **16/16 -> 0/16 at k=2 and 16/16 ->
1/16 at k=3**. The A/A floor has to be read alongside it: at k=3 identical code moves 4 cells on
its own (18 -> 14), because those matrices sit at parity, so k=3 is honestly "the gate moves 15
where the control moves 4". At k=2 the control moves none and the gate moves 16.

**C2, the out-of-band control the blanket arm failed.** k=4 reads 0.9821 against a 0.9890 floor
(tolerance 0.022) and k=8 reads 0.9928 against 1.0016. Inside, both. This is the width where
`exu1` read 0.9701 and lost its case.

**C4, the GCN guardrail.** Clean at all four widths, and k=3 is 1.0812 -- faster, on-mechanism:
cora, citeseer and pubmed have mean degree 4.90, 3.74 and 5.50, which a multiplier of 8 gives
unroll 1. k=6, 7 and 16 sit outside the band and read 1.0082, 1.0114, 1.0120.

**C3 fails, and one matrix is the entire reason.** float64 k=2 reads 1.0126 against a 1.0%
tolerance -- a GAIN, on a dtype whose 23 SpMM symbols are byte-identical between the two builds.
Leave-one-out puts all of it on `connectus`:

    all 18 target matrices              1.0126
    minus connectus                     1.0064   (floor 0.9964, n=17)

`connectus` is 512 rows holding 1127525 nonzeros -- mean degree 2202 -- and it is the matrix
family that holds a tenth of itself in one row, so the whole-row partition is a scheduling coin
flip. Its readings are **bimodal**, two modes about 10% apart, and the mode is drawn once per run
and then applies to every width in that run:

    connectus float32 k=4, ms by pass    p1      p2      p3      p4      p5      p6
      c0                                0.1333  0.1467  0.1462  0.1337  0.1328  0.1332
      c0b                               0.1318  0.1469  0.1331  0.1323  0.1343  0.1335
      gate                              0.1459  0.1330  0.1476  0.1464  0.1327  0.1464

Every build reaches both modes; `gate`'s minimum is below `c0`'s; p5 has all three builds low.
`gate` drew the high mode in 4 of 6 runs against 3 of 12 for the other two, which is Fisher
p ~ 0.13 -- suggestive of nothing. The effective sample is 6 runs per build, not 30 cells, because
one draw covers all five widths, and that is also why the ratio is nearly constant across k=1..8
including the widths the constant cannot reach.

So C3's failure is not a float64 regression. **It is the tolerance being too tight for a corpus
containing a matrix whose own spread is 15%**, and the reason the tolerance did not notice is worth
recording: the floor is `2 * |1 - c0b/c0|` computed from MEDIANS, so it inherits exactly the
blindness to bimodality described below. C1 is immune by construction -- it is judged in the
degree 8-16 band and connectus sits at 2202.

### The inertness check was wrong twice more, in opposite directions

The per-cell null reported `connectus` k=2 at 0.9048 "where the code-identical builds span 1.01x",
which reads as a 9-sigma regression. **1.01x is the span of two MEDIANS.** The raw readings of the
same two builds span 1.12x. A median is the right statistic for the cell and the wrong one for its
spread, so the span now comes from raw readings.

Then I widened the outside-the-null ENVELOPE to raw readings as well, which looked like the same
fix and destroyed the check: it read **0 of 42 outside where the null expects 28**, because a
median of six runs is far less variable than a single run and essentially always sits inside a raw
envelope. That is the vacuous-and-reassuring answer for the third time in this comparison's
history. Exchangeability is a statement about LIKE QUANTITIES -- the arm's median against each
control's median -- so the envelope stays on medians and only the reported span is raw. Restored,
it reads 28 of 42 against a null of 28 +- 3.1.

### What is missing

**redwood became unreachable at some point after 06:10, and the run's fate is UNKNOWN.** MKT is
therefore the only x86 host with a verdict, and the house standard is two. Nothing ships on one
host.

The first version of this paragraph said "unreachable from 06:10, at 5 of 54 CSVs", which claims
more than was observed and in the direction that reads as a lost run. What was actually seen:
redwood answered at 06:08 with 4 CSVs and at 06:10 with 5, and the next attempt was at 10:14 and
failed. **The outage began somewhere in that four-hour window and nobody watched it start.** At the
measured pace -- about 6 minutes per build-pass, three builds per pass, six passes -- the stage was
due to finish around 07:47, so the likeliest case is that it COMPLETED and all 54 CSVs plus c5.txt
are sitting on /scratch, unreachable rather than lost.

Reachability, from two vantages with different networks and healthy egress:

    myth54   171.64.15.19    ICMP 100% loss   tcp/22 timeout
    sc       10.79.12.70     ICMP 100% loss   tcp/22 timeout   (reaches myth:22 fine)

The failure mode is a TIMEOUT and not a refusal, so nothing answers at the IP layer -- this is not
sshd dying on a live host. Traceroute cannot narrow it further because campus filters the probes:
hop 1 is already `*`. From outside, a powered-off host and a host firewalled off at its own subnet
edge are indistinguishable, and that limit is worth stating rather than resolving by guess.

A watcher is waiting and will distinguish the cases that matter once the host answers: the driver
still running (wait), the driver gone with 54 CSVs (pull and analyse), or the driver gone with fewer
(relaunch, and do NOT analyse the partial CSVs as a whole run).

## chain179 -- the loop split is rejected for the thing it was built for, and pays off somewhere nobody proposed

The multi-row loop split has been built, compiled and correctness-checked since chain173 and had
never been put on a clock. MKT, four builds over eight passes, redwood down.

**The stage needed four builds and the reason is the finding that nearly wasn't.**
`SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS` is **0** on this branch, and a zero row count folds `multirow_ok` and
the whole dispatch out of the instantiation. So `-DLOOPSPLIT=1` alone is **inert here**: a two-build
stage would have measured a dormant switch and reported a clean null, which reads as "the split
does not help" and is in fact "the split was never compiled in". Multi-row therefore has to be on
in both arms, making the reference `mrf2` and not `c0`:

    c0 / c0b   tip default                                    the A/A floor
    mrf2       -DSCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2              the reference
    mrf2ls     the same plus -DSCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_LOOPSPLIT=1

L3 was pre-registered to catch exactly that failure, and it passed loudly -- multi-row moved at all
four firing widths on the target group, by a lot: **1.1925 / 1.1910 / 1.3377 / 1.2241** at k=5, 6,
8, 16 against floors within 0.5%. So the precondition is live and L1 is falsifiable.

**L1, the claim, is NOT SUPPORTED.** Hoisting the per-row `multirow_ok` test out of the row loop:

    k=5   0.9902     k=6   0.9926     k=8   1.0046     k=16  1.0133
                     (floors 0.9989 / 1.0016 / 1.0053 / 0.9985, tol 0.010-0.011)

Three of four inside the floor, one at +1.3%. A test that runs once per row and is loop-invariant
turns out to cost about nothing -- the branch predictor gets it right every time, which is what a
`const bool` fixed before the parallel region should produce.

### The half of the mechanism I mis-specified

L2 was pre-registered as an INERTNESS control: widths 2 and 4 cannot reach multi-row, since
`exact_width` claims 1-3 and `SCORCH_SPMM_HALFVEC_F32=1` excludes width 4 by name, so a move there
would mean the arm was touching code it does not name. **That reasoning was wrong, and the code says
so in its own comment:** under the split those calls take the `false_type` instantiation, where
`if constexpr (MR_LIVE && MR_ROWS_LIVE)` *deletes* the multi-row block rather than predicting it
away -- "the false arm compiles the block away entirely". Widths 1-4 are therefore **in scope**, and
they are the half of the split's mechanism nobody proposed it for.

    k=4   1.0921    17 of 18 target matrices more than 1% faster, 0 slower
    k=2   0.9800     0 of 18 faster, 15 of 18 more than 1% slower

Both are broad rather than a cell or two. The single k=4 exception is `connectus`, whose own
c0-against-c0b floor reads 1.0998 on that width -- the bimodal wide-row matrix from chain178, noise
by its own control. So: **the dead multi-row block was costing width 4 about 9%**, and width 4 is
precisely the width the multi-row dispatch refuses on purpose. In a shipped-with-multi-row
configuration, the half-vector width pays to carry code it never executes.

Width 2 goes the other way by 2%, consistently, and runs the exact-width kernel rather than the
register block.

**L4, the GCN guardrail, fails.** This guardrail is on-mechanism here, unlike the unroll ladder's:
k=6, 7 and 16 are all inside the firing range 5..32, and k=3 is inside the dead-block-removal case.

    k=3   0.9830      k=6   0.9867      k=7   0.9893      k=16  0.9977
                      (floors within 0.7%, tol 0.010-0.013)

Three of four regress, 1.1 to 1.7 percent, on real citation graphs at real layer widths.

### Verdict, and what one host can decide

**Rejected as it stands, on two independent grounds**: the claim it was built for is not supported,
and it regresses the GCN guardrail at three of four widths. One host is enough for that -- a single
host can kill an arm, it just cannot ship one -- so redwood is not needed to close this.

What survives is a lead, not a result: **the dead-block cost at width 4 is worth ~9% and is
mechanically explained.** The right change is narrower than this arm -- remove the multi-row block
from instantiations where `multirow_ok` is provably false, without restructuring the row loop that
the exact-width path and the 5-7 widths share, which is where all of this arm's costs sit. That is
a different patch and it needs its own stage.

And the whole question is conditional: **multi-row does not ship on this branch.** Everything above
describes a configuration that only exists if `MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2` ships first, which is its own
open arm with its own history. Worth stating because L3's 1.19-1.34 is the largest number in this
chain and it belongs to multi-row, not to the split.

### Three analyzer defects, all of which flattered the arm

- **L1 read "HOLDS -- faster at 1 of 4 firing widths."** The pre-registration named widths 5, 6, 8
  AND 16; one of four is not the claim holding, and that line is exactly what gets quoted as "the
  split is faster". Now requires all four and reports NOT SUPPORTED otherwise.
- **L2's mis-specification** turned the split's own mechanism into a confound verdict, which would
  have voided L1 for the wrong reason and buried the 9% finding as noise. Re-specified as a
  two-sided finding that does not gate L1.
- **The GCN table labelled k=3 "outside; a move here is a confound"**, which was the same error one
  layer down. Widths below 5 are in scope through the dead-block removal.

## chain180 -- the dead block does cost the widths it cannot serve, and it still does not explain why multi-row was rejected

chain179 ended with a lead nobody had proposed: with multi-row compiled in, *removing* the dead
multi-row block was worth about 9% at width 4 -- a width the multi-row dispatch refuses on purpose.
The obvious next thought is that this is what killed multi-row in the first place: chain131 rejected
`MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2` on a width-2 regression, and if merely *carrying* the block taxes the widths
below 5, then multi-row's cost is a code-layout artefact rather than anything the kernel does, and
the arm deserves reopening with the block excised.

This stage tests that. MKT, four builds over eight passes, redwood still down.

**Isolating presence from behaviour needs a build where the block exists and cannot run.**
That is what the fourth build is:

    c0 / c0b   tip default                                              the A/A floor
    mrf2       -DSCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_ROWS_F32=2                        the reference
    mrdead     the same, plus -DSCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_MINNNZ=4e18L       present, unreachable

`MINNNZ` is a runtime `nnz >=` threshold, so setting it past any real matrix disables multi-row
*without* letting `if constexpr` fold the block away. If the compiler had proved the branch dead
anyway and deleted it, the whole stage would be measuring `c0` twice under another name.

**D1, the precondition, holds: the block survived.**

    instructions: c0 250637    mrf2 255838    mrdead 255694
    mrdead is -0.056% of mrf2's count, and +2.018% of c0's

`mrdead` carries essentially all of `mrf2`'s extra code (it is 144 instructions short of it, and
5057 instructions above `c0`), which is the fact the whole stage rests on. Per-symbol, 126 of 127
matched symbols are byte-identical between `mrf2` and `mrdead` and exactly one changed. Correctness:
624 cases each for `mrf2` and `mrdead`, 0 mismatches. `.text` digests distinct for all three configs.

**D2, the suppression, holds.** Where `mrf2` moves 19-34%, `mrdead` reproduces -11% to +3% of that
move -- i.e. none of it, in both directions:

    k=5   mrf2 1.2022   mrdead 0.9884   floor 1.0009
    k=6   mrf2 1.1972   mrdead 0.9790   floor 1.0035
    k=8   mrf2 1.3430   mrdead 0.9923   floor 1.0054
    k=16  mrf2 1.2256   mrdead 1.0061   floor 1.0119

So the runtime threshold really did turn the kernel off. Note the residual: at k=5 and k=6 `mrdead`
is 1.2% and 2.1% *below* `c0`, outside a 1.0% floor -- the presence cost showing up at firing widths
too, where it is normally hidden by the 20% the kernel wins back.

**D3, the question, splits.** At the widths multi-row cannot fire, is the cost still there with the
block merely present? Fraction is `(1 - mrdead) / (1 - mrf2)`, so 1.0 means presence explains all of
it and 0.0 means none:

    k=4   mrf2 0.9867   mrdead 0.9819   floor 1.0032   tol 0.010   fraction 1.36   PRESENCE
    k=2   mrf2 0.9977   mrdead 0.9953   floor 1.0201   tol 0.040   fraction 2.04   UNRESOLVABLE

**Width 4 answers yes.** The block costs that width without ever executing, and `mrdead` is if
anything slightly worse than `mrf2` there (fraction above 1), consistent with pure code layout --
`mrdead`'s extra live threshold compare buys nothing back. Taken with the firing-width residuals,
**a 1-2% presence cost is real at k=4, 5 and 6.**

**Width 2 does not answer at all, and width 2 is the whole reason the stage exists.** `mrf2` reads
0.9977 there against an A/A floor of 1.0201 -- the floor is *three times looser than the effect
being attributed*, so there is no cost at width 2 to assign to either mechanism. chain179's 0.9800
at k=2 did not reproduce here.

The looseness is *led* by one matrix but not caused by it. Leave-one-out on the k=2 floor:

    full floor (18 target matrices)          1.0201    tol 0.040
    without connectus (own ratio 1.0984)     1.0157    tol 0.031
    next three worst are the chimera family, each ~1.03; dropping any one leaves 1.019

So even with the single worst contributor removed, the floor is 1.6% against an effect of 0.23%,
and dropping a matrix for reading badly on its own control is not something to do anyway. Width 2
is unresolvable on this corpus, full stop.

The k=4 verdict survives the same test, which is the reason to trust it: dropping connectus there
moves the floor from 1.0032 to 0.9982, tolerance unchanged at the 0.010 minimum, while `mrf2` and
`mrdead` sit at 0.9867 and 0.9819. **PRESENCE at k=4 is not connectus.**

**D5, GCN, reported.** k=3 is presence-only, k=6/7/16 are in the firing range.

    k=3   mrf2 0.9957   mrdead 0.9948   floor 0.9949
    k=6   mrf2 1.0427   mrdead 0.9916   floor 1.0010
    k=7   mrf2 1.0370   mrdead 0.9946   floor 0.9994
    k=16  mrf2 1.0612   mrdead 0.9979   floor 0.9993

Multi-row is worth 3.7-6.1% on the citation graphs at layer widths 6-16, and `mrdead` gives it all
back, which is D2 again on a different corpus.

### Verdict

**The presence cost is confirmed and it is not an explanation for chain131.** Both halves matter.
A block that is compiled in but never entered costs 1-2% at k=4, 5 and 6, which is a real and
slightly surprising result -- it is the instruction-cache and layout tax of code that never runs.
But chain131 rejected multi-row on width 2, and width 2 is where this stage has no resolving power.
So **re-opening multi-row on a presence theory is not supported by this run.** The next thing width
2 needs is its own measurement with a floor tighter than the effect, not another mechanism stage.

The `~9% at width 4` from chain179 also shrinks on re-measurement to ~1.3-1.8% at that width
(`mrf2` 0.9867, `mrdead` 0.9819 against a 1.0032 floor, versus chain179's 1.0921 for removing the
block). Those are different comparisons -- chain179 measured *removing* the block via the loop
split, this stage measures *disabling* it at runtime -- but the gap is large enough that the width-4
opportunity should be sized by the excision patch itself, not quoted from either stage.

### Four analyzer mis-specifications, each of which would have been read as a result

- **D2 demanded that `mrdead` sit inside the A/A floor**, which conflates "the kernel didn't fire"
  with "the block costs nothing". `mrdead` is 1-2% below `c0` at firing widths *because of the very
  presence cost the stage is measuring*, so the check would have declared the stage void for showing
  its own finding. Re-specified as "reproduces less than 25% of `mrf2`'s move".
- **Width 2 was labelled BEHAVIOURAL while `mrf2` was itself flat there.** With no effect to
  explain, a fraction near 2.0 is a ratio of two noise readings and means nothing. Added
  UNRESOLVABLE, gated on `abs(1 - mrf2) > tol`.
- **The final ANSWER invoked chain131 -- a width-2 result -- while width 2 was unresolvable.** The
  conclusion is now gated on width 2 actually resolving, which is why it reads "neither explained
  nor overturned" instead of "explained".
- **A guard checked the wrong entry.** A `sed`-derived copy left `grep -q "\[mrf2ls\]"` under a
  `[mrdead]` error message, and since `mrf2ls` *is* present in the build table, it would have passed
  for the wrong reason on every run. Fixed, then verified by confirming it refuses on its own input.
  Same edit had duplicated `[mrf2]`; the two lines were identical, so one was deleted.

### And one instrument gap

D1's per-symbol block reported "126 identical, 1 changed" but **never named the changed symbol** --
the call site piped `symneutral.py` through `tail -n 3`, which drops the `CHANGED  n -> m insns
<symbol>` line the script does emit. The identity of that one symbol is the most informative line in
the proof (if it is `spmm_csr_v2_core<float,...>` the story is layout; if it is something else the
story is different), and it was thrown away by the harness rather than missing from the tool. Now
filtered on `CHANGED|ONLY IN ONE|symbols matched|VERDICT` instead of truncated. The surrounding
`if [ -f "$SYMNEUTRAL" ]` also skipped silently when absent; made loud.

### chain180 addendum: the "remove the dead block" lead is a layout lottery, not a mechanism

Written after reading the dispatch rather than after another run, because it changes what the lead
is worth and would otherwise be re-derived wrongly.

`spmm.h:4641` guards the block with `if constexpr (MR_LIVE && MR_ROWS_LIVE)`, and `MR_ROWS_LIVE` is
only ever `false` when `SCORCH_SPMM_MULTIROW_LOOPSPLIT` is on -- the caller at 5082-5089 dispatches
on the runtime `multirow_ok` into a `std::true_type` / `std::false_type` pair. **So the loop split
IS the excision mechanism; there is no separate narrower patch to write.** "Remove the block where
`multirow_ok` is provably false" and "restructure the row loop" are the same switch, which means
chain179 did not reject a bundle it could be un-bundled from.

That also relocates chain179's costs. At the GCN widths 6, 7 and 16 `multirow_ok` is *true*, so the
`true_type` instantiation runs -- it still contains the block, and the only differences are that
`MR_PRETESTED` skips the per-row test and that the row loop now exists in two instantiations.
chain179 established the per-row test is free (that was L1, and it is why L1 was NOT SUPPORTED). So
the 1.1-1.7% GCN regression at firing widths is not the hoist and not the excision: it is the cost
of the loop existing twice.

And the excision's own sign is not consistent. Every one of these is a width where multi-row cannot
fire, so all three are pure excision effects:

    k=4        +9.2%   (chain179)
    k=2        -2.0%   (chain179)
    GCN k=3    -1.7%   (chain179)

Helps one, hurts two, all in the same "cannot fire" class. Nothing about instruction-cache pressure
or removed code predicts a sign flip between widths 2, 3 and 4 that all take the same excision.
What does predict it is layout: which instantiations the inliner keeps, where the branch targets
land, how the loops pack. chain178 already established that a *runtime `long` comparison* changes
code shape at -O3, trading one unroll-2 instantiation between inlined and out-of-line. This is the
same phenomenon a layer up.

**So the lead is weaker than chain180 recorded it.** Not "the dead block costs width 4 about 9%,
go and take it", but "removing the block moves widths 2, 3 and 4 by -2 to +9 percent with no
predictable sign, and the +9 at width 4 is one draw from that distribution." Tuning on it would be
overfitting to a layout draw, which is exactly what the performance convention in CLAUDE.md
forbids. If it is worth pursuing at all, the stage is a **duplication-only control** -- build with
the split on but the `false_type` arm still containing the block, so both instantiations are
behaviourally identical and only the duplication differs. If GCN still regresses there, the cost is
duplication and the excision half can never pay at a firing width.

## chain181 -- width 2 cannot be judged by comparing builds, and that is the answer

MKT job 17324491, four builds over 24 passes, 2h21m, redwood still down. Every precondition passed:
split byte-identical to chain180's, mrbuild's five build checks confirmed present rather than
re-implemented, instruction counts reproducing chain180's exactly (c0 250637 / mrf2 255838 /
mrdead 255694), 56 correctness cases per candidate with 0 mismatches, and the rotation's balance
checked rather than assumed.

**The stage was reframed before it ran, and the reason is worth stating.** chain180 asked "is there
a width-2 cost" and could not answer. Measured from chain180's own passes, the per-matrix paired
spread at width 2 is 3.39%, of which only 1.46% is within-process, against an effect of 0.23%. An
exact sign test needs ~200 paired passes per matrix for 0.35 power at 0.5%: detection was never
buyable. So this stage asks the question the decision turns on -- is the width-2 cost small enough
that it cannot justify blocking 19-34% at widths 5..32 -- as an **equivalence test at a
pre-registered +/-1% margin**, with the CI from a bootstrap over matrices.

Three design changes, each from measurement rather than preference:

- **24 passes = every permutation of the four builds exactly once.** chain180's cyclic rotation
  balanced each build's lead count but never varied *who ran before whom*: `c0b` ran immediately
  after `c0` in every pass where it did not lead. 4! = 24 balances position (6 each) and all 12
  ordered adjacent pairs (6 each). The harness generates the permutations and then checks both
  counts, because a rotation believed to be balanced is how the fixed predecessor survived.
- **The reference is both identical-source builds**, `sqrt(c0 * c0b)` per pass, so the reference
  carries half the process noise a single build would and a symmetric split between them cancels.
- **The estimator is chosen at width 4 and applied unlooked-at.** `ours/MKL` cancels between-process
  state; on chain180's data it tightened width 2 from 1.0149 to 1.0031 and *loosened* width 4 from
  1.0034 to 1.0088. Choosing per width on that basis is selecting the estimator on the outcome. At
  the control width here `raw` wins outright -- A/A bias **0.006%** against `vsmkl`'s 0.675% -- so
  `raw` is what the verdict uses.

**The redesign worked, and width 4 is the proof.** The A/A floor there is **1.0001 [0.9974,
1.0026]** -- two byte-identical builds agreeing to 0.01% with a 0.26% half-width, against
chain180's 1.0032. N2, the power control, holds: mrf2 reads **-0.96% [-1.54%, -0.27%]** at width 4,
reproducing chain180's presence cost with a CI clear of parity.

### And then width 2 refused, for a reason that is the result

    width 2, target group, estimator raw
      c0/c0b   1.0080  [1.0051, 1.0107]   +0.80%     <-- IDENTICAL .text
      mrf2     0.9803  [0.9746, 0.9875]   -1.97%
      mrdead   0.9837  [0.9772, 0.9902]   -1.63%

The A/A arm -- two builds mrbuild proved have identical `.text` -- differs by **+0.80% with a CI
that excludes parity**. The pre-registered gate says an equivalence verdict is void if an
identical-source pair cannot itself be shown equivalent at the margin, so no answer is given. That
gate was written before the run and it caught exactly what it was for.

Four diagnostics locate it, and it is not any of the usual suspects:

- **Not an ordering effect.** If it were warmup or position, reversing the order would reverse the
  sign. It does not: c0/c0b reads +0.66% in the passes where c0 ran first and **+1.02%** in the
  passes where c0b ran first. Positive both ways.
- **Not a few matrices.** 17 of 18 have c0 slower, up to +1.76% (`relat8`, `uni_chimera_i1_A_08/09`).
- **Not within-process arm order.** `ours` against `oursb` -- same code, same process -- reads
  +0.15% / -0.39% / +0.07% / -0.51% across the four builds at width 2, and +/-0.09% at width 4. So
  width 2 carries a half-percent-scale artefact per build object that does not average away, and
  width 4 does not.
- **It moves the answer by the whole margin.** mrf2 against c0 reads 0.9826, against c0b 0.9732,
  against their geometric mean 0.9803 -- a **0.97% spread from nothing but which identical-code
  build is the reference.** At width 4 that spread is 0.51%.

**So the finding is about the instrument, and it is more useful than either verdict would have
been: on this corpus at float32 width 2, the identity of the build object is worth about 0.8% even
when `.text` is byte-identical.** (Scope corrected by chain182 below, which ran the same four
builds and the same 24 permutations at the same width on a *different* corpus and got an A/A floor
of 0.9989 [0.9971, 1.0018]. The artefact belongs to the `nnz >= 1e6` group -- the chimera family
and connectus -- not to width 2. As first written this sentence claimed the width, which was too
broad.) The `.text` is the same; what differs is everything around it -- the object lives
at `$R/c0` versus `$R/c0b`, so the containing ELF, and therefore the mapped layout of code that at
width 2 is short enough to be alignment- and ITLB-sensitive, is not the same. chain178 already
established that a runtime `long` comparison reshapes code at -O3; this is the same class one level
out, and it is consistent across stages: chain180's paired A/A read +1.49% at width 2, same sign.

**On this corpus, no build-versus-build comparison can resolve width 2 to better than about a
percent.** (chain182 shows that qualifier matters: on chain131's own population the same
comparison resolves to 0.23%.) That is the real reason chain131's width-2 rejection of multi-row
had not settled here -- chain131, chain179
and chain180 were all build-versus-build comparisons at a width where build identity alone is worth
most of the effect they were measuring.

### What the numbers say anyway, stated as evidence and not as a verdict

mrf2 reads **-1.97% [-2.54%, -1.25%]** at width 2 and mrdead **-1.63%**, so mrdead reproduces 83%
of the cost: if the cost is real it is mostly **presence**, the block being compiled in, rather than
the kernel executing. GCN k=3 leans the same way (mrf2 -0.82 to -1.60%, mrdead -0.15 to +0.50%,
A/A -0.02 to -0.87%).

That pooled number is roughly 2.5x the demonstrated build-identity artefact, so a width-2 cost of
about a percent and a half is the most probable reading. What it is **not** is a reproduction of
chain131 -- see the amendment immediately below, which is the more important result of this stage.

### Amendment: this corpus was never chain131's, and chain131's worst matrix reverses sign

Two conflations, caught by going back to chain131's own table rather than to its conclusion.

**First, chain179's -2.0% at width 2 is a different quantity from chain181's -1.97%.** chain179's
arm was `mrf2ls` against `mrf2`, so its number is what the loop split costs *given multi-row is
already on*. chain181 compares `mrf2` against the default, which is what chain131 measured. The two
values being within 0.03 of each other is a coincidence, and reading it as a reproduction was wrong.

**Second, and this is the substantive one: chain131 did not reject multi-row on a small pooled
effect. It rejected it on a coherent regression POPULATION** -- long-tailed degree distributions at
width 2, on both hosts: connectus 0.602 / 0.817, lp_osa_14 0.852, cari 0.850, lhr34c/lhr71/lhr71c
0.820 / 0.834 / 0.845, com-Amazon 0.885, relat8 0.905, as-caida_G_08x 0.934. Those are 10-40%
regressions on named matrices, not a 2% average.

Only **two of those nine** matrices are in chain181's target group, and one of them reverses:

    matrix       chain131          chain181 mrf2 at width 2   its own A/A
    connectus    0.817 (MKT)       1.0289  = +2.89% FASTER    1.0008
    relat8       0.905 (MKT)       0.9677  = -3.23% slower    1.0176
    the other seven                not in this corpus at all

**connectus was the anchor of chain131's rejection and it now reads faster, on a tight floor.**
relat8 keeps the sign at a third of the magnitude, but against a 1.76% A/A floor of its own, so it
is marginal by its own control. `com-Amazon` is in the control group, which this stage does not
judge; the remaining six are absent.

So the honest status is not "corroborated" and not "overturned": **chain131's ground is largely
UNTESTED, and its single worst matrix does not reproduce.** The corpus is why. chain181 inherited
chain180's `nnz >= 1e6` target group, which was chosen to make a big-matrix presence effect
visible, while chain131's finding was about *long-tailed degree distributions at small-to-mid
size*. Three stages in a row have been measuring a width-2 question on a corpus that excludes most
of the population the question is about.

**That, and not another estimator, is the next stage: run this design on chain131's own regression
population.** It is cheap -- those matrices are small -- and it is the only corpus on which the
verdict means anything. The single-object instrument described below is still needed to get inside
a percent, but on the right corpus the effects were 10-40%, which is far above the 0.8%
