**The definitive compiler check, which neither of us named:** `readelf -p .comment <obj>`. ELF
objects carry the producer string in `.comment` — `GCC: (GNU) x.y.z` — so the answer is in the
objects themselves and needs no build log. One read per object, at seal time, alongside `size -A`.

**Convergence: `size -A` alone settles the sign, and the mechanism hunt is conditional on its
answer.** The audit retracted its own cold-partitioning account with local evidence, which I
re-ran and confirm with one amendment. On `src/scorch_ops.cpython-311-darwin.so`: the mangled
prefix `spmm_csr_v2_coreIfLb0E` selects 6 symbols, 3 of them `.omp_outlined` and **0 of them
`.cold`**. So a substring selector on the mangled prefix does capture the outlined family, which
means under a 12-symbol group selected that way, redistribution into `.cold` or `._omp_fn.N` moves
code *within* the group and cannot change the total — and a −11155 group sum means code left the
group. The amendment: `.cold` symbols on `spmm`-matching names are **4**, not 0 — but they belong
to `SpmmCsrPlan::run`, the `SpmmCsrPlan` constructor and a pybind11 `class_<SpmmCsrPlan>` helper,
i.e. the plan layer, not the kernel. The conclusion holds: this build put no cold partition on
`spmm_csr_v2_core`. Clang and GCC differ here, so it is local evidence, not a redwood fact.

What survives of that exchange is narrower and was still worth the instrument change: `core` is
multi-symbol and the dispatch is not in the function's own symbol, so a single-symbol size is the
wrong quantity whatever the selector was.

**The reordering.** Two mechanisms do survive a substring selector — the function being inlined
into its callers in one arm and emitted out-of-line in another (its code moving to symbols with no
prefix at all), and GCC's `-fipa-icf`, on by default from `-O2`, folding identical functions and
leaving an alias whose bytes leave a group total with nothing leaving the object. The second is a
live candidate precisely because these arms' dead-code elimination makes surviving bodies converge.
Both have cheap signatures in the same unfiltered dump: for the first, whether the unsuffixed symbol
exists in all five arms and whether the *callers* differ in size; for the second, two names at one
address. A jump table moving to `.rodata` as switch cases fold is real but is tens to hundreds of
bytes and should be excluded explicitly rather than left open.

But none of that is needed first, because **the whole-object `.text` total answers the question
independent of every selector, alias and outlining decision**. If code merely moved between
symbols, the total is unchanged; if it left, the total drops. `size -A` reports every section, so
the one escape — code moving between sections rather than out of the object — is covered in the
same read. So the pass is: `size -A` first and the verdict comes from it; the mechanism hunt runs
only if the answer is "moved", and then it is looking for which of the two survivors did it.

Locally, for calibration of the signature: 54 addresses in that object carry more than one symbol,
3 of them in the `spmm` family, including `.cold.1` and `.cold.2` of `SpmmCsrPlan::run` at the same
address — so two-names-at-one-address is common enough that it needs the *sizes* read alongside it
rather than being treated as folding on sight.

**The folding-signature count, with units, because neither 1 nor 3 was right as stated.** Two
counts were being compared across different objects. Measured properly on the local object, in one
pass so the definitions cannot drift: **2** shared addresses carry at least one `spmm`-matching
symbol, **3** `spmm` symbols sit at a shared address, and **both** of those addresses are mixed
`spmm`/non-`spmm`. The mixed part is the one that matters for identical-code folding, since a
kernel folded against a non-kernel function is still folded and a count filtered to kernel names
first would miss exactly those. (My earlier 3 also came from a `grep -F -f` over address strings,
which can match an address as a substring of a longer one — same number, weaker derivation.)

The clusters themselves make the sizes mandatory rather than advisable. `0x9f694` holds 6 symbols,
2 of them `spmm` — the `.cold.1`/`.cold.2` pair of `SpmmCsrPlan::run`. `0x9f814` holds **31
symbols**, 1 of them `spmm`. Thirty-one names at one address is not thirty-one folded functions;
it is almost certainly a set of zero-size cold stubs placed at the same offset. Mach-O carries no
`st_size` here so the local object cannot tell those apart, which is the whole point: **two names
at one address is not a folding signature without the sizes.** On ELF at seal time
`nm --print-size` supplies `st_size` and the question resolves. Also the unstated dependency, the
second thing the missing selector gates: an alias carrying a size makes a naive group sum
double-count and an alias with `st_size` 0 makes it undercount, so identical-code folding's effect
on that 12-symbol figure has a sign nobody recorded.

**Case sensitivity, for the record.** The 4-versus-0 disagreement on `.cold` symbols was
`grep -c 'spmm'` against `grep -ci 'spmm'`: the class is `SpmmCsrPlan`, so a case-sensitive filter
against a mangled name misses it. A one-character-wide instance of the filtered census, and worth
naming because a reported 0 is the shape that stops further looking.

**The all-cold finding is right for the two `spmm` clusters and wrong as a general claim, and the
difference matters for the check.** Confirmed 37 of 37: every symbol at `0x9f694` (6) and `0x9f814`
(31) is `.cold`-suffixed, so those are cold labels collapsing onto one section offset because the
functions have no cold blocks, not folded bodies. But object-wide the rate is not 37 of 37. Of
**54** colliding addresses, **20** are all-cold and **34 are not**, and the not-all-cold ones are
genuine identical-code folds:

- `0x67bc8` — `std::__sort5<_ClassicAlgPolicy, spmspm_csr<float>(…)>` and the same instantiated
  through `spmspm_csr<int>(…)`, two distinct template instantiations at one address.
- `0x492d8` — four `unordered_map` / `unordered_set` / `unordered_multimap` helpers from pybind11's
  type registry at one address.

So identical-code folding is **live in this build and does fold kernel template instantiations**.
The naive signature is not useless, it is contaminated: the all-cold clusters are the false
positives and they are separable by inspection in the same pass. **The check is collisions where
not every member is `.cold`, plus `st_size`** — two conditions, both available from one
`nm --print-size` read on ELF.

And the filter lesson recurs a third time, on my own filter: `spmspm_csr` does not contain the
substring `spmm`, so the folded kernel instantiation above was invisible to every count either of
us ran tonight. Three instances in one exchange, all the same defect and each with a different
width — case (`spmm` versus `Spmm`), substring (`grep -F -f` over address strings matching a
longer address), and vocabulary (`spmm` missing `spmspm`). **The ICF check at seal time filters by
nothing**: it enumerates every colliding address, drops the all-cold clusters, and reads the sizes.

**Scope correction to the entry above, and it is the largest one in this exchange: the local object
cannot contain the code the five arms differ in.** `nm` on `src/scorch_ops.cpython-311-darwin.so`
matches **`regblock` 0 times and `gather` 0 times**. That is the direct proof — the whole dispatch
at `:4861-5100` sits inside `#if defined(__AVX2__) && defined(__FMA__)` (`:4861`), which is false
on ARM, so `SCORCH_RB`, the deep switch, `:5026` and every symbol the arms vary are absent from
that object. `regtile` matching 3 is the NEON path, a different kernel family.

The measurements in the two entries above all stand as measurements — the 6-symbol split of
`spmm_csr_v2_core<float, false>`, the 37-of-37 all-cold clusters, the 54 collisions, the folded
`__sort5` instantiations. The lambdas at `:4480`/`:4483` and the OpenMP regions at `:5289`/`:5302`
are outside the AVX2 guard and genuinely present. What does **not** stand is reading any of it as
an observation of the code path under study, and the previous entry presented the folding finding
without restating that limit.

What survives, stated at its real strength: identical-code folding demonstrably folds kernel
template instantiations in a real build of this source, and the mechanism is code-shape-driven, so
it transfers in kind to redwood's objects. The **flag** does not transfer — clang has no
`-fipa-icf`, so what folded those two `__sort5` instantiations here is ld64 coalescing or LLVM
function merging. GCC's `-fipa-icf` is the analogue and is on from `-O2`, so the expectation for
redwood is sound, but the local object demonstrates the phenomenon and not the flag.

**The vocabulary gap, measured.** On this object `spmm` matches 182 symbols against 240 for
`spmm|spmspm|spmv|sddmm|ttm|regblock|regtile|gather` — 58 missed, composed of 38 `spmspm`, 12
`spmv`, 5 `sddmm` and 3 `regtile`. Non-cold collisions reaching the narrow filter: **0**. Reaching
the broad one: **6**. So the narrow filter finds no kernel-family folding candidates at all where
the broad one finds six. (The audit's absolute counts run 57 higher for both filters — 239 and 297
— with the identical 58 gap and identical composition, so one of us is scanning a superset of the
symbol table; it changes nothing here because the seal-time pass depends on no absolute count.)

**So the filter defect has a fourth axis, and it is the worst of them.** Case (`spmm` versus
`Spmm`), substring (`grep -F -f` over address strings matching inside a longer address), vocabulary
(`spmm` missing `spmspm`), and now **target** — a filter that matched correctly, against an object
that could not contain the answer. The first three return a wrong number; the fourth returns a
right number about the wrong thing, which is the failure that survives review. This is
"hosts compile different kernels" in its most direct form: redwood is AVX2, the M5 is NEON, and an
AVX2-only region cannot be studied on the NEON object however carefully the symbols are counted.

**The 57 resolved, and it inverts the earlier lesson.** Same tool, same target — `/usr/bin/nm`
(llvm-nm) on `/Users/bobby/scorch-beat-mkl/src/scorch_ops.cpython-311-darwin.so`, 1029360 bytes,
Sep 8 23:15. The difference is **case sensitivity**: `nm -jU | grep -c spmm` gives 182 and
`grep -ci spmm` gives 239, difference exactly 57, and the extra lines are `SpmmCsrPlan` (123
occurrences) and `SpmmPlanKind` (2). Not a tool difference, not a target difference — the audit's
three hypotheses (external-only, duplicate names, the other object in `/Users/bobby/scorch`) were
each correctly eliminated, and the answer was a fourth thing neither of us tested.

The inversion is the part worth keeping. Earlier in this same exchange, case-insensitivity was the
**fix** — `grep -c 'spmm'` returned 0 `.cold` symbols where `grep -ci` found the 4 on
`SpmmCsrPlan`. Here case-insensitivity is the **over-match**, because `SpmmCsrPlan` is the plan and
pybind11 dispatch layer, not a kernel, so for a kernel-family census the case-sensitive 182 is the
number you actually want. Both counts are correct for their own filter and neither is correct
without it. So the rule is not "always use `-i`" — it is **print the tool and the target beside
every number**, which is the same discipline as the target axis one level down: state what was
measured, not only what was found. Two sessions quoted 239 and 182 at each other six times tonight
without either naming its command, and the only reason the gap surfaced is that it was suspiciously
exact.

**Correction to the line above: it mixed three units, inside the entry that fixed a count by naming
its flag.** "The extra lines are `SpmmCsrPlan` (123 occurrences) and `SpmmPlanKind` (2)" is wrong
three ways. Measured with units labelled, `/usr/bin/nm` (llvm-nm) on the same object:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| symbols matching `spmm`, case-sensitive | 182 |
| symbols matching `spmm`, case-insensitive | 239 |
| symbols matching `Spmm` | **58**, not 57 |
| symbols matching both `Spmm` and `spmm` | 1 |
| `SpmmCsrPlan` symbols | **57** |
| `SpmmCsrPlan` occurrences, mangled stream | 57 |
| `SpmmCsrPlan` occurrences, demangled stream | **123** |
| `SpmmPlanKind` symbols | **3**, not 2 |

The slips: occurrences read as symbols, the *demangled* stream's count reported for the mangled
one, and 2 where the object holds 3. The last two have the same cause — the line was produced by a
pipeline that pre-filtered with `grep -v spmm` and then demangled, so the third `SpmmPlanKind`
symbol was the dual-case one and had already been removed. That symbol is
`scorch_native::spmm_plan_kind_from_name(...)`, lowercase in the function name and capital in the
`SpmmPlanKind` return type, which is also why the capital-`Spmm` set overshoots the gap by exactly
one: 58 − 1 = 57.

So the closing rule needs one more clause than it had. The flag is part of the target, **and so is
the stream**: `nm -jU` and `nm -jU | c++filt` are different targets, and the same `grep -o` returns
57 against one and 123 against the other. Naming the tool and the object is not sufficient if the
pipeline transforms the text in between, and a count of matches is not a count of symbols.

## chain201: depth pays at the level, and the pre-registered gradient test REFUTES the mechanism

Sealed at `~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/chain201-deepwindows-redwood`, digest
`d1f16d9d7064869a7f19c2c05143d2a6507ba75c21f830728eb883c21f35c02a`, 63 files, `shasum -c` clean,
analyzer COMPLETE. 50 files, 10 passes, 0 readings refused at ingestion, 161 matrices in 7 degree
bands, widths 4/8/12/16/20/24/32. Estimator `medmed`, chosen at k=8 where no arm fires.

**P3a HOLDS — the design's premise is now measured rather than assumed.** All three sibling pairs
sit inside the identical-source floor at both inert widths, so a firing-arm-over-inert-sibling
ratio carries no layout term by construction. The two floors:

| inert width | identical-source (build) | within-process | layout share |
|---|---|---|---|
| k=8 | ±1.01% | ±0.36% | 0.66% of the build floor |
| k=4 | ±0.29% | ±0.32% | 0.00% |

Against chain199's ±0.35–0.65% within-process and ±0.52–0.78% build: k=8's build floor is looser
than chain199's, k=4's is tighter, and both within-process floors sit at or below chain199's range.

**The size verdict is `cannot resolve`, exactly as pre-registered.** −0.047% per KB at k=8 and
−0.100% at k=4, whole-range effects 0.09% and 0.19%, both inside their widths' floors, over the
three within-window pairs spanning 1932 bytes. The analyzer's own gate declined to name a
direction. So the size covariate question that consumed the night changes no verdict.

**P3b — depth wins at the level at every firing width**, against an inert sibling:

| arm | width | nvec | over sibling | floor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dp2 | 12 | 2 | **+6.3%** [1.0546, 1.0718] | ±1.31% |
| dp2 | 16 | 2 | **+6.1%** [1.0520, 1.0699] | ±0.40% |
| dp3 | 20 | 3 | +1.6% [1.0095, 1.0230] | ±0.73% |
| dp3 | 24 | 3 | **+5.0%** [1.0402, 1.0613] | ±1.41% |
| dp4 | 32 | 4 | +2.3% [1.0124, 1.0330] | ±0.40% |

P3c holds too: the inert pair agrees at every firing width, so no width's diagonal is placement.

**P3d — the gradient inverts, which was pre-registered as a refutation.** The reading was written
one-directional before the data existed: falling with the vector count fails the mechanism whatever
the size sign; rising is consistent with it but not conclusive.

| width | nvec | gradient (deg≥64 minus deg<16) | vs bars | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 2 | **+5.63 pts** | 1.35 global / 0.91 local, CIs disjoint | SURVIVES |
| 16 | 2 | +2.71 pts | CIs overlap | not established |
| 20 | 3 | −1.10 pts | inside | not established |
| 24 | 3 | −0.95 pts | inside | not established |
| 32 | 4 | **−6.92 pts** | 1.35 global / 0.14 local, CIs disjoint | SURVIVES |

Both surviving cells clear both bars with disjoint band confidence intervals, and they have
**opposite signs**. At nvec 2 the high-degree bands gain most (d64-256 +10.4%, d>256 +8.6%); at
nvec 4 they lose — `dp4 over dp2` at deg≥64 reads 0.9836 [0.9702, 0.9949], a confidence interval
entirely below parity. **The degree structure of the gain is not the mechanism's.** chain199's
+1.90-point gradient at one vector count was never evidence for it, and this stage was built to
find that out.

**Nothing ships, on the stage's own pre-registered standard.** P3b required every degree band
faster than the inert sibling, because a gain in some bands and a loss in others is a rule fitted
to a degree regime. That holds for **1 of 5** firing widths (dp2 at k=16) and fails for the other
four.

**A regression to report rather than tune around.** At nvec 4, high-degree matrices are slower with
the deep kernel: pooled deg≥64 reads 0.9836 with the interval excluding parity, and per band
d64-256 is 0.9850 [0.9670, 1.0019] and d>256 is 0.9824 [0.9612, 0.9984]. The per-band floors there
are wide enough (±0.78%, ±2.21%) that the analyzer calls them indeterminate, but the pooled
gradient clears both bars, so the direction is established even where the level is not.

**P4 passes and is the one clean result for shipping:** no arm is slower than the shipped object at
any width beyond that width's own floor, including the five widths each arm cannot reach.

**P5 — and the apparent MKL gain is entirely a layout artefact at a width where nothing fires.**

| arm | behind MKL | at k=4 | excluding k=4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| c0 | 40 / 1127 | 15 / 161 | 25 |
| c0b | 37 / 1127 | 15 / 161 | 22 |
| dp2 | 31 / 1127 | 9 / 161 | 22 |
| dp3 | 34 / 1127 | 9 / 161 | 25 |
| dp4 | 32 / 1127 | 9 / 161 | 23 |

The identical-source pair spans 22–25 outside k=4 and the three deep arms span 22–25 — the same
range, so the effect there is null. The whole 6-to-9 cell difference sits at k=4, where **no arm
can fire**, and it agrees with the +2.0–2.3% speed artefact P3a measured at that width. Reading the
pooled 40 → 31 as depth buying nine cells would have been wrong, and it is only visible because P5
is reported by width and ungated.

**chain199's k=4 artefact replicated.** The pre-registered expectation was 1.023, measured on a
different chain; the three arms read 1.0212, 1.0233 and 1.0199 — off by −0.2%, +0.0% and −0.3%.

### The object census, which settles the sign puzzle and the compiler in one read

`size -A`, `nm --print-size --defined-only` with the selector written down
(`grep spmm_csr_v2_coreIfLb0`, the `<float,false>` instantiation, 6 symbols), and
`readelf -p .comment`, on the five arms:

| arm | `.text` | `.text.unlikely` | group (6 syms) | Δ`.text` | Δgroup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| c0 | 715033 | 0 | 35238 | — | — |
| c0b | 715033 | 0 | 35238 | 0 | 0 |
| dp2 | 713801 | 0 | 24579 | −1232 | −10659 |
| dp3 | 713977 | 0 | 25003 | −1056 | −10235 |
| dp4 | **715785** | 0 | 25639 | **+752** | −9599 |

**The verdict is `moved`, not `left`.** `.text` is flat to within ±1232 bytes while the symbol
group moves ~10 KB, so roughly 90% of the group delta is code relocating to symbols outside the
group and the object's total code is nearly unchanged. Three further readings:

- **The compiler is GCC 11.4.0** (Ubuntu 22.04), from `.comment`. So GCC's suffix naming and
  `-fipa-icf` apply and clang's machine outliner does not. `readelf -p .comment` answered in one
  read what no build log recorded.
- **`.text.unlikely` is 0 in every arm.** Cold partitioning contributes nothing here, so that
  mechanism is dead on redwood as well as locally — a prediction that could have gone either way
  given the two compilers differ.
- **dp4's `.text` is larger than `c0`'s by 752 bytes**, which is the sign the ~3.5 KB deep-body
  estimate predicted for a window arm and the opposite of the −11155 that started the puzzle. The
  net code change across all five arms is within ±1.2 KB.
- The unsuffixed symbol count is **3 in every arm**, so the function is not inlined away in any of
  them: inlining-into-callers is not the mechanism either.

And the selector is now recorded, which resolves the discrepancy it was gating: this 6-symbol sum
over the `<float,false>` instantiation gives 35238 for `c0`, where the earlier census's 12-symbol
figure was 62183 — a broader selector spanning more than one instantiation. Its Δ of 11155 and this
one's 10659 are the same effect measured over different symbol sets, which is why the number was
unquotable without its selector.

### The −10659 has a destination, and the sign puzzle is closed

Two corrections first, both to the entry above.

**Retracted: "dp4's `.text` is larger than c0's by 752, the sign the ~3.5 KB deep-body estimate
predicted."** That holds for `dp4` alone. `dp2` is −1232 and `dp3` is −1056, the opposite sign, so
two of three arms contradict it. All three sit within ±1232 of `c0`: flat and non-monotone. `.text`
confirms **no net change** and cannot confirm a deep body of any size, because a flat total cannot
separate a body arriving from plain-body elimination offsetting it. A prediction two arms
contradict is not a prediction that survived.

**P5's null is stronger than reported, and the statistic is estimator-fragile.** An independent
re-derivation from the raw CSVs under a different estimator — per-key median over the ten passes,
then counting `ours_ms > mkl_ms` — gives c0 41, c0b 45, dp2 32, dp3 35, dp4 35; at k=4, 16/16 for
the identical-source pair against 9–10 for the deep arms; excluding k=4, **25 and 29** for the
identical-source pair. My own numbers had c0b at 22, so the ranges merely coincided; under that
estimator the build-to-build spread is 4 cells and **strictly exceeds** the 3-cell c0-to-dp2
difference. Same conclusion, no room left in it. And c0b reading 22 under one estimator and 29
under another — a 7-cell swing on identical data, in the arm that carries the null — is itself the
finding: **threshold counts near parity are decided by the estimator**, so excluding k=4 is
necessary and not sufficient, and the statistic cannot resolve 3 cells either way.

**Now the destination.** `nm --print-size` diffed per symbol over the `spmm` family, `c0` against
`dp2`, with no name filter narrower than the family:

| Δ bytes | c0 | dp2 | symbol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **−10659** | 27850 | 17191 | `spmm_csr_v2_core<float,false>::'lambda'(int,int)::operator()(int,int) const` |
| −1354 | 1354 | 0 | `scorch_spmm_row_narrow_exact<float,6,8>` |
| −1045 | 1045 | 0 | `scorch_spmm_row_narrow_exact<float,6,2>` |
| −671 | 671 | 0 | `scorch_spmm_row_regblock<float,2,false,scorch_simd<float>>` |
| −611 | 611 | 0 | `scorch_spmm_row_regblock<float,2,true,…>.constprop.0` |
| +1367 | 0 | 1367 | `scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32<5>` |
| +1266 | 0 | 1266 | `scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32<2>` |
| +1190 | 0 | 1190 | `scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32<4>` |
| +1357 | 0 | 1357 | `scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32_ms<1,4>` |
| +1131 | 0 | 1131 | `scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32_ms<1,8>` |
| +1113 | 0 | 1113 | `scorch_spmm_row_regtile_partial<double,6,false>` |

**The entire −10659 is one symbol: the OpenMP worker lambda's `operator()`, which is where the
dispatch lives.** And the gainers are row kernels that are **absent from `c0` entirely** and
present in `dp2` — inlined into the lambda in one arm and emitted out of line in the other. So the
mechanism is inlining redistribution inside the worker lambda: the deep body's arrival changed the
inliner's budget and pushed a set of gather and regtile kernels out of line, while some
`narrow_exact` and `regblock` bodies went the other way. `.text` flat to ±1232 and the whole `spmm`
family flat to ±1349 (`c0` 280116, `dp2` 278893, `dp3` 278767, `dp4` 280588) are the same fact
measured two ways.

Three things this settles. The mechanism is **redistribution**, as the audit originally proposed,
though by neither the route it named (cold partitioning — `.text.unlikely` is 0 everywhere) nor the
one it proposed next (the `regblock` template — that sums to 5108 in `c0` against 3826 in `dp2`,
which *deepens* the deficit rather than filling it). The destination symbols carry **no
`spmm_csr_v2_core` prefix at all**, so every selector defined from that instantiation excluded them
by construction — which is why a count was unquotable without its selector, one last time. And
`dp2` losing `NV=2` is now visible at the byte level: `regblock<float,2,false>` at 671 bytes and
`regblock<float,2,true>.constprop.0` at 611 both go to zero, with a `.constprop` clone present
exactly as GCC's naming predicted.

**The accounting closes, and the gainers are one switch statement.** The top-ten listing above does
not close on its own — its rows sum to −5871 against a family delta of −1223, so it was a
magnitude ranking and not a balance sheet. Every symbol, no truncation:

| | n | sum |
|---|---|---|
| losers | 8 | −16329 |
| gainers | 12 | +15106 |
| unchanged | 226 | — |
| **net** | | **−1223**, the family delta exactly |

And the twelve gainers are not a scatter. They are `scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32<2,3,4,5,6,7,8>`,
`scorch_spmm_row_gather_f32_ms<1,2>`, `<1,4>`, `<1,8>`, `scorch_spmm_row_regtile_partial<double,
6,false>`, and a 45-byte pybind11 helper — that is, **the complete set of `SCORCH_RG(KK)` and
`SCORCH_RGS(KK,SS)` instantiations from the switch at `:5010-5025`**, moving from inlined into the
worker lambda in `c0` to out-of-line in `dp2`. `gather_f32<1>` is the one arm that does not move.

Which lands on the same few lines twice: that switch is the block opened at `:4996`, whose
`default: SCORCH_RB(1)` at `:5026` is the answer to the `NV=1` reachability question earlier in
this document. The code that relocated and the code that settled the reachability asymmetry are the
same statement — an independent coherence check on both readings.

**The defect, stated better than I stated it.** I wrote that the destination carries no
`spmm_csr_v2_core` prefix, so every selector defined from that instantiation excluded it. True but
misleading: the **donor** does carry the prefix, was inside the group, and the group reported its
loss correctly to the byte. The selector was not blind to the effect — it was blind to **one side
of it**. When the underlying quantity is conserved, a view that captures only the donor turns
redistribution into apparent loss, and no better prefix repairs it, because the gainers live in a
different namespace by nature. The repair is to measure the conserved total, which `size -A` did on
the first read. That is the general form of every filter defect in this document: the question is
not whether the filter is correct but whether it spans both sides of whatever is conserved.

Three corrections to the mechanism as it was first proposed, from its own author, recorded because
the pattern of which parts survived is the useful part. The **mechanism** was right — an inlining
budget in the worker lambda, and the lambda is exactly the symbol that lost the 10.6 KB. **Which
bodies moved** was wrong: the plain `regblock` bodies were named, and `regblock` is a net loser at
5108 against 3826, so the later candidate was wrong in the opposite direction from the earlier one.
And **why the census missed them** was wrong in the way that matters: the claim was that those
symbols persist either way and so are invisible to a census. They do not persist — they are absent
from `c0` and appear in `dp2`. The census missed them because they were never named, not because
they were always there.

**The exchange is 96% conserved, which is why the donor-side number was arbitrary rather than
merely imprecise.** Gross movement is 16329 + 15106 = **31435 bytes across 20 symbols** for a net
of −1223, so net over gross is **3.9%**, and 226 of 246 symbols do not move at all. The range of
answers available to a one-sided selector therefore spans −16329 to +15106 — a 31 KB window — and
the group's −10659 was one draw from it. When that much of the movement cancels, a partial view's
**sign and magnitude are not approximations of the truth; they are arbitrary**. That is the number
to put in front of the rule, and the concentration (20 of 246 moving) is what made the balance
sheet tractable at all.

**The single non-mover: the direction survives, the test does not exist.** `gather_f32<1>` is the
one arm of the switch absent from the gainer list, and the proposed reading was that an inlining
budget evicts expensive bodies first and keeps the cheapest — falsifiable, it was argued, because
`gather_f32<1>` should then be well under the movers' 1113-byte floor. Measured: **`gather_f32<1>`
has zero symbols in either object**, and so does every other `gather_f32<K>` in `c0`:

| arm | `gather_f32<K>` symbols |
|---|---|
| `c0` | none, for any K |
| `dp2` | K2=1266 K3=1537 K4=1190 K5=1367 K6=1521 K7=1581 K8=1594 |

So the cleaner statement is that in `c0` the **entire** gather switch is inlined into the worker
lambda, and in `dp2` seven of its eight arms are emitted out of line while K=1 stays inlined. The
budget story's direction holds — the arm never evicted is the narrowest, one column and scalar —
but the specific test proposed cannot be run, because K=1's body size is *unobservable* when it has
no symbol. That is the `regblock_deep` fact for the third time in this document: **absence of a
symbol is not a measurement of size**, so a prediction about the size of an inlined body is not
falsifiable by `nm`. What is observable and consistent: every evicted arm is at least 1190 bytes,
and the sizes are not monotone in K (K4 is the smallest mover at 1190, not K2), so "cheapest stays"
is supported in direction and not established in form.

The coherence with `:5026` is correspondingly tighter than stated above. The movers are not merely
the arms of the switch whose `default:` answered the `NV=1` question — they are **every arm of that
switch except the one the source singles out**. `narrowk_gather` is initialised
`(B1_size == 1) ? 1 : 0` at `:4351`, and the half-vector guard's comment at `:4886` says `B1_size
>= 2` keeps k=1 with the gather kernel that owns it. The case the source treats specially is the
case the compiler treats specially, arrived at independently.

**Further correction, and the K=1 case is closed as unidentifiable rather than weak.** "Supported
in direction, not established in form" was still one step too strong. The design has **no
contrast**: outcome is *constant* across every measurable case — all seven observable arms were
evicted — and the single case with the other outcome has no measurement. So relating body size to
retention has **zero usable comparisons**, not a weak one, and the non-monotonicity note (K4 the
smallest mover at 1190, K3 out of order) does not bear on it, because seven cases sharing one
outcome carry no ordering information about retention. This is the same non-identifiability as the
five-point size association earlier in this document, in a smaller frame: the contrast that would
carry the information is exactly the one that cannot be measured.

And the retained-versus-removed distinction is itself unobservable, which gives three stories where
I had one. Zero symbols for `gather_f32<1>` is consistent with all of:

1. **inlined because cheap** — the inlining-budget story;
2. **inlined because its call site differs** — `narrowk_gather` is initialised
   `(B1_size == 1) ? 1 : 0` at `:4351`, and the comment at `:4880-4883` states that float k=1 "is
   instantiated but only routed when asked for separately, because the nonzero-axis gather kernel
   owns it";
3. **eliminated as provably unreachable** — if `case 1:` is dead under that routing, it is removed
   rather than inlined.

All three produce no symbol and the symbol table separates none of them. So K=1's behaviour is not
evidence for the inlining budget in either direction, and the budget stays supported by what is
actually observable: **10659 bytes left the lambda and 15106 appeared as out-of-line callees, in
the arm that added code to it.** By the standard this document has been applying all night — ask
whether the quantity can distinguish the candidates before spending a read — three explanations
predicting the same observation makes this not worth measuring rather than worth measuring
carefully. Closed.

---

## chain202: the reading order and the bars, recorded before the data and with the peek disclosed

The stage is 7 arms x 14 passes over 89 keys x 3 widths, one binary called with seven different
`nthreads_override` values, finishing about 11:03. `ov24` and `ov24b` are the same object with the
same argument, so the negative control is a floor by construction and the k=4 layout artefact that
spoiled chain201's cell count cannot exist here.

**The peek, stated first because it changes what this section is worth.** To exercise two new
analyzer blocks I ran them on the 22 complete files available at 3 of 14 passes, which printed all
seven arms' behind-MKL counts. So this is not a blind pre-registration. What protects the bars from
it is that they are *derived by the analyzer from the sealed data* rather than chosen by me: the
A/A bar is `ov24` against `ov24b` at the full pass count, and the estimator bar is the two
estimators' disagreement count on the arm in question. Neither is a number I can set.

**The reading order, unchanged from before the peek.** The estimator-spread line must be nonzero
first — a zero disagreement count beside a zero spread means the check did not fire and says
nothing. Then the seal. Then the NULL group under both estimators as the floor. Nothing from ADOPT
or CAPONLY until that floor is in.

**Two bars, and a count claim must clear both.** They are different quantities. P3a bounds a
*ratio*; the cell count is a sum of threshold crossings, so cells sitting near the 1.01 boundary
move it with no timing difference large enough to appear in P3a.

At 3 passes the A/A bar reads 1 cell (ratio-of-medians) and 0 (median-of-ratios), against 3 and 4
at 2 passes. Both are computed from the same data, which is the point: an A/A spread shrinks with
pass count, so a bar taken at 2 passes and applied at 14 is too loose in a known direction, making
the gate over-strict and hiding real effects rather than admitting false ones.

**But the shrinkage cannot be read off the 2-pass row, and this corrects the paragraph above as
first written.** The rotation balances position and ordered-pair over all 14 passes, so a 2-pass
subset is unbalanced *by construction* -- 7 positions against 2 passes leaves 35 of 49 arm-position
cells never used -- and the 3/4-to-1/0 move therefore conflates sample size with rotation balance.
The clean comparison is available for free and was verified against `orders_named.txt` rather than
assumed: **each half of the rotation is position-balanced**, every arm-position cell used exactly
once with none unused, so halves-against-whole isolates sample size with position balance held
fixed.

**The construction, corrected twice.** My first description said the halves are not cyclic shifts,
which is true only in the dimension I tested: rows 1-7 are not positional rotations of row 1, and
that test does return False. But they *are* exact cyclic shifts of the arm labels. On chain202's own
`orders_named.txt` there is a single symbol permutation sigma with row(i+1) = sigma(row(i))
elementwise throughout each half, and sigma is a full 7-cycle in the natural ascending arm order --
`ovp -> ov2 -> ov4 -> ov8 -> ov16 -> ov24 -> ov24b -> ovp`. So each half is a cyclic Latin square
generated by a group action on symbols rather than on positions, and my "reached some other way"
was wrong. The distinction earns its keep, but it earns it for *two* of the three balance
properties and not the third, and running them together was a second overreach:

| property | warrant |
|---|---|
| position balance per half | **structural** — any full 7-cycle on symbols gives a Latin square |
| pair balance over all 14 | **structural given the reversal** — reversing inverts every pair, so `c_d(h2) = 7 - c_d(h1)` and every class totals 7 |
| pair balance *within* a half | **not structural** — base-dependent |

Enumerating the family (base[0] fixed to 0 without loss, 720 bases) gives **420 at the 21-at-3 /
21-at-4 optimum, 294 at max deviation 1.5, and 6 at 2.5** — and those 6 are exactly the arithmetic
progressions mod 7, `base[j] = j*m`, which includes **ascending arm order**. So the obvious
"simplification" of the base is the worst case in the family.

Half 2's base is half 1's base exactly reversed -- cycle indices `[0,1,6,2,5,3,4]` against
`[4,3,5,2,6,1,0]`, a match at shift 0 -- and that reversal is the mechanism for the perfect 14-pass
pair balance, because reversing the base inverts every pair's order so the two halves cancel.

**And the ordered-pair caveat is a parity obstruction, not an imperfection.** 7 rows x C(7,2) = 147
pair-observations spread over 7 x 6 = 42 ordered pairs is 3.5 each, which is not an integer, so **no**
7-row design over 7 arms can be pair-balanced. The observed 21-at-3 and 21-at-4 is therefore the
optimal split, not an approximation of a better one that exists. Halves-against-whole is the *best
available* isolation rather than merely better than the 2-pass row; stated that way so a later
session does not go looking for the smarter subset. That the most-even split is the optimum rests
on the enumeration — 0.5 is the minimum achievable max deviation over all 720 bases — and not on
defining optimal as most-even, which would assume the conclusion.

**The hazard, and why the check moved into the analyzer.** With an ascending base the rotation keeps
position balance and keeps the perfect 42-at-7, while per-half `c_d` collapses from `[4,3,4,3,4,3]`
to `[6,5,4,3,2,1]`. Reproduced: every other line the analysis prints still passes. That is the
failure mode this whole line of work keeps turning up — a degradation that leaves the printed
evidence intact — so the property is now *computed* by `an_c202.py` from `orders_named.txt` rather
than stated in a comment and checked in a shell. The analyzer recovers the generator from
consecutive rows instead of assuming one, reports `c_d` beside the verdict, and says explicitly
that the shrinkage reading is unverified when the orders file is absent. Exercised on four inputs:
the real order (OPTIMAL both halves), an ascending base (DEGRADED at 2.5), a mid-range base
(DEGRADED at 1.5), and a missing file.

**Two preconditions, and the second is not implied by the first.** Recovering the generator
establishes that *some* single permutation maps each row to the next; it does not establish that
the permutation is a full 7-cycle, and `c_d` needs one, because the classes `d = (b-a) mod 7`
presuppose a single cyclic order over all seven arms. A permutation of cycle type (4,3) maps every
row to the next just as consistently as a 7-cycle -- verified -- so without a separate orbit-length
gate `c_d` would be six plausible numbers indexed against a labeling that does not exist. The gate
is exact for a reason needing no enumeration: among 7 points a single orbit of length 7 *is* the
whole set, so `orbit(x) == 7` for any one x iff sigma is a full 7-cycle.

The orbit gate and the position check overlap in coverage while testing different things, and both
are load-bearing. Of all 5040 permutations of 7 points only the 720 full 7-cycles give a Latin
square -- 0 across all fourteen other cycle types, for a random base as well as an ascending one --
so position balance happens to be an exact detector for the same condition. Deleting either because
"the other covers it" reopens the hole, and the analyzer now says so in place.

**Both derived pair-balance lines are theorems of the reversal, so neither is a check.** This
supersedes the paragraph below, which treated the per-class complement as the version that can
fail. Reversing the base commutes with applying sigma elementwise, so half 2's row i is exactly
half 1's row i reversed, and each of the seven row-*pairs* contributes exactly 1 to every ordered
pair's precedence — total 7, **for any generator and any base, with no property of sigma entering**.
Verified over all 5040 permutations of 7 points, 0 deviating. The per-class version is equally
implied: under the reversal `c_d(h2) = c_(7-d)(h1)`, and `c_d + c_(7-d) = 7` holds for all 720
bases, so the complement is `[7]*6` necessarily.

Their only discriminating power is against a *broken* reversal, and there they are equally
probabilistic — **95.0% each** over 556 full-cycle trials with an unrelated second base. So the
deterministic check is the row-wise reversal itself, `half2 row i == reverse(half1 row i)`, at 556
of 556, and it is the exact property the proof uses. That check is now in the analyzer; the other
two print labelled `(IMPLIED by the reversal, not an independent check)`, because reported as
passing checks they invite a reader to count them as independent corroboration of a design property
when they are consequences of the construction.

One correction to my own measurement in passing: a first pass put the per-class detection rate at
13.8%, which was a denominator error — the loop count was used instead of the number of trials
actually tested, and only 14.3% of random permutations of 7 points are full cycles (720 of 5040).

**The reduction: of eight lines about the rotation, exactly three can fail.**

| | line | status |
|---|---|---|
| check 1 | the generator is a full 7-cycle | can fail |
| check 2 | the row-wise reversal, `h2[i] == reverse(h1[i])` | can fail, detects 100% |
| check 3 | per-half base optimality, `c_d in {3,4}` | can fail, 300 of 720 bases |
| corollary | position balance / Latin square | from check 1 |
| corollary | class uniformity | from check 1 |
| corollary | within-half complement `c_d + c_(7-d) = 7` | holds for every base |
| corollary | across-half per-class complement | from check 2 |
| corollary | pooled 42-at-7 | from check 2 |

The pooled and per-class detectors are not two tests of equal power but **the same test**: over
4000 broken-reversal trials the agreement table is 3803 both-fail / 197 both-pass, with **zero
disagreements**. Equal rates alone would not have established that.

**And a retraction of my own, one layer up.** I had written that the position check was "load-bearing
and not a duplicate" of the orbit gate. That was true only on the premise that the gate was missing.
With the gate present the two are logically **equivalent** — all 720 full cycles give a Latin square
and none of the other 4320 do — so position balance cannot fail independently. It is still printed,
because it states the property the halves comparison needs in the design's own terms, but as a
corollary. The analyzer now prints the three-and-five split explicitly and ends with the test that
generated it: a line is a check only if an input exists that makes it fail.

**Pooled pair balance is the weaker statement, so it is reported per class.** The (4,3) design uses
only 25 of 49 arm-position cells and is thoroughly broken, yet its pooled precedence still reads a
flat `[7]`. A wrong-but-symmetric design gives a flat pooled count. What actually shows the reversal
did its job is the per-class complement, `c_d(first) + c_d(second)`, which reads `[7,7,7,7,7,7]` on
the real order. The severity note is also printed per failure class: a base-choice failure downgrades
the halves comparison to suggestive, while a generator or position failure voids it, and leading
with the base explanation when no base failed would send a reader to inspect something intact. The bar table prints all 14, both halves, and the 2-pass row relabelled UNBALANCED, and
the shrinkage prose appears only when halves were actually printed. The halves also disagree with
each other by however much a 7-pass bar varies, which is the uncertainty on the bar itself.

**Completeness is checked against a DECLARED row count, not a modal one.** 89 keys x 3 widths x 3
inner arms + 1 header = 802, each factor read from the file that declares it (`keys.txt`, the `KS=`
line in the stage body, the `ARMS` list in the timing harness). A modal guard was the first version
and it has a defect that matters: the mode is a majority statistic, so a stage that died early
enough for *every* file to be short makes the truncated length the mode and passes the whole run.
Twenty-one files uniformly cut to 442 rows give the modal guard zero disagreements and the declared
guard twenty-one refusals. The observed mode is still printed, beside the declared count, as the
evidence the derivation is right rather than as the thing being trusted.

The truncation test is only the negative control, and chain201 supplies the positive one: 50 files
at 3382 lines, 0 at any other length, 50 of 50 writer lines reporting 3381, and `keys.txt` at 161
giving 161 x 3 x 7 + 1 = 3382. Design, writer, and length agree at the declared value, 50 for 50.
A guard needs both halves; this one had only the refusing half until that was checked.

Two details only visible in the writer: the timing harness legitimately drops rows on a calibration
or timing failure and prints a `SKIP` line for each, so a declared count alone would refuse an
honest short file — the seal branches on the SKIP count, currently zero, which makes every shortfall
a truncation unambiguously. That zero is reported as *unexercised* rather than credited as a passed
check: the drop paths emitted nothing in the nearest archived run either, so zero is equally
consistent with no failures and with the path not firing in practice, and the count cannot separate
them. The seal verifies that comparison against chain201's sealed log rather than asserting it. And the harness prints `wrote <path> (801 rows)` as its last act, so the
log carries the writer's accounting while the length check carries the file's. Those fail in
opposite directions — truncated after the writer finished, versus killed before its final print —
and requiring both closes each other's blind spot.

**One statistic was zero by construction and is fixed at the source.** The estimator-spread median
read exactly 0 on chain201's data because 294 of 534 cell-arms had a single reading, and at one pass
ratio-of-medians and median-of-ratios are identical by algebra. Above half the sample contributing a
structural zero does not dilute a median, it defines it. The spread now runs over cells with at
least two passes and prints the excluded count beside itself.

### Metamorphic relations, and the analyzer defect they found

Every guard in this line of work compares a number against a reference — a floor, a declared count,
a conserved total — and the one failure mode that repeatedly got through is a plausible number
computed from a wrong base, which is *defined* by there being no reference to compare against. A
metamorphic relation replaces the reference with an invariance: transform the input so the answer
cannot change, run the same code, require the answer not to change. It needs no second
implementation, no known answer, and no known-good corpus.

Three relations now run in the seal (`meta_c202.py`, ~13s against 3.2s for one analysis):

- **scale** — multiply every `ms` by a constant. Every ratio statistic must be invariant. Catches a
  normalization applied twice, not at all, or to one arm only.
- **reorder** — shuffle CSV rows within each file. Every pooled statistic must be invariant. Catches
  accidental position dependence in a reduction, which is the family the timing rotation exists to
  defend against and which was otherwise unguarded on the analysis side.
- **swap** — exchange the two A/A arms' labels, with `--ship`/`--aa` passed swapped so the roles
  follow the data. Their counts must exchange and no other arm's may move. This tests the
  *estimator* the way an A/A pair tests the machine.

**They found a real defect on the first run.** `boot()` drew resample *indices* into `xs`, so with
the seed fixed the CI was a function of the order `xs` arrived in rather than of its multiset — and
that order came from a group list built by iterating a dict, so it moved with CSV row order.
Demonstrated directly: the same nine ratios in three orders, same seed, gave `[1.0872, 1.2456]`,
`[1.0869, 1.2490]` and `[1.0877, 1.2483]`. The point estimate was bit-identical throughout, which
is why nothing else caught it — a geomean is order-independent and a percentile is not. Fixed by
sorting inside `boot`, after which all three relations hold.

**And a second finding that the fix does not remove.** At small n a bootstrap percentile is a coarse
function of the resamples, so it moves under *any* perturbation. Measured over 40 seeds on nine
scattered ratios, the CI bounds span 0.0061 (lower) and 0.0076 (upper) — noise in the third decimal
behind four printed digits, and larger than some floors quoted here. The pre-registered `nboot` is
deliberately **not** changed, since lowering the Monte-Carlo error mid-flight would make these
numbers incomparable with chain201's at the same setting. Instead the analyzer now prints the
bootstrap's own resampling spread beside each floor, with the standing rule attached: a verdict
within that spread of a floor boundary has not cleared it. On the full-population floor at n=89 the
spread is ~0.001, so the main floors are stable; it is the small subgroups where it binds.

**Conservation, and the sourcing of `attempted` decides whether it is a check at all.** `attempted
= tested + skipped` now prints beside every behind-MKL count, and `pair()` records the same
decomposition for the n behind every CI. The first version took `attempted` from `len(T[arm])` — a
count of the rows present — which makes the identity a tautology: a key absent from the CSV never
becomes an iteration, so the identity holds at the smaller number and reports nothing. Confirmed by
deleting one key's rows, after which the line read `264 = 264 + 0` rather than failing. It is now
sourced from the **declared** count, 89 keys from `keys.txt` x 3 widths = 267, and the counted form
survives only as a fallback that says in the output that it cannot detect a missing cell. Same
printed number, opposite epistemic status — the modal-versus-declared distinction from the file
level, one level down.

**And the declared form catches what the 802-row guard structurally cannot.** A row count is a
cardinality test, and 801 data rows are equally consistent with the correct 801 distinct
`(key, width, inner-arm)` triples and with one triple duplicated plus another missing — the
exchange preserves the cardinality exactly. Constructed and measured: duplicating one key's rows
and deleting another's leaves the file at exactly 801 rows while distinct triples fall to 792 and
distinct keys to 88. The run is then silently short one matrix and double-weighting another with
every row-level guard passing. So the seal now also counts distinct triples per file, and the
analyzer reconciles distinct cells per arm against the declared 267. That arithmetic is the same at
both levels — 89 x 3 = 267 and 267 x 3 = 801 — which is exactly why the two guards look
interchangeable and are not. On this sourcing the conservation line is not display discipline; it is
the completeness check row counting cannot perform, and it belongs with the other checks.

**The reproducibility-versus-accuracy distinction on the bootstrap fix.** The order defect measured
0.0008 on the lower bound and 0.0034 on the upper, while the same estimator's seed-to-seed spread
at that n is 0.0061 and 0.0076 — so the defect sat *inside* the resampling noise, 2.2 to 7.6 times
smaller. Fixing it bought reproducibility, which is a precondition for everything else, and **not**
accuracy: the interval is no better afterwards and the limiting error is `nboot`. Stated because
"we found and fixed a defect in the bootstrap CI" otherwise reads as the CI being good to the digits
shown. Relatedly, the resampling spread now prints as a fraction of the CI width it came from —
measured at 4.7% of width at n=9 and 5.8% at n=89, comparable, while the absolute figures differ
sevenfold — so the absolute number cannot travel to a subgroup with different dispersion.

**The honest limit.** A metamorphic relation cannot catch an error invariant under its own
transformation — a wrong-but-symmetric estimator passes renaming perfectly. So this is a detector
for one class: indexing, labeling, ordering, normalization. That happens to be the class that
produced both of the wrong-base errors in this review cycle, which is what makes it worth the lines.

### What constrains the corpus, and where the chain is actually open

Two sessions computing 267 from the same `keys.txt`, `KS=` line and `ARMS` list is **not** two
independent determinations of the count. It is two implementations of one specification: it catches
a transcription slip or an off-by-one in either loop, and cannot catch anything wrong with those
three files, because both sides inherit whatever they say. Worth having under that name and not the
stronger one.

**chain202's total is declared by a literal, which is stronger than the resolve guard suggests.**
`chain202_body.sh` P0 contains `if len(keys) != 89: sys.exit("REFUSE: %d keys, not chain200's 89")`.
So a short or padded key list fails closed before anything runs. The `resolvecheck.py` invocation
below it passes `--expect-keys "$(grep -c . "$R/keys.txt")"` — the line count of the file it is
checking — so that guard is exact for *resolution* failures and structurally vacuous for *list
completeness*, exactly as the declared-versus-counted rule predicts. But it is not load-bearing for
completeness here, because the literal above it already closes that.

**The open layer is composition, not total, and it is quantifiable.** Of the 89 keys, **49 are
pinned by name** through the cells-subset rule — every confirmed-cell key must appear in the corpus
— and the remaining **40 are constrained only by the count**. No key is named explicitly in
chain202's P0. So a substitution of those 40 passes every check the stage makes. The key list is
`/scratch/bobbyy/c198_keys.txt`, 89 lines, shared by chains 198, 199, 200 and 202, with no
generator for it present on the machine; its composition is not reconciled against anything.

**And the two stages protect different things, neither protecting both.** chain201 has the
distributional guard — seven degree bands, refusing if any holds fewer than 15 matrices — and no
literal total, so its 161 keys could have been cut to the 105 floor with every P0 refusal passing.
chain202 has the literal total and **no band rule at all** (`grep -c band` on its body is 0), so a
biased drop of the kind that emptied a degree band on MKT would not be caught by composition here,
only by the total. The right stage has both.

**Correction: "reconciled against nothing" is false, and the composition reconciles.** Three
earlier ledgers on this machine hold the same 89-key list — chain198 (as `c198_keys.txt`), chain199
and chain200 (as `keys.txt`) — and all three digest identically to chain202's under a pinned
collation. The seal now performs that reconciliation and prints MATCHES for each. That is real
independence: different stages, different seals, different times, where two sessions computing 267
from one `keys.txt` had none. It does not close the layer above the list — nothing constrains what
the 89 keys *should* be — but it removes substitution-since-chain198 from the open set.

**And the digest I first recorded was wrong, for the reason this section is about.** I wrote
`6199541616c836e3…`, taken from an unpinned `sort` over ssh. redwood's non-interactive shell carries
`LANG=en_US.UTF-8`, and these keys are full of `_` and `-` — exactly the characters whose collation
differs between C and UTF-8. The same byte-identical file digests to
`07c545b95be6548252a1b6dd7faed3287a3ab761c41e4c145a2d96c0d7394239` under `LC_ALL=C`, which is the
figure every sealed copy agrees on. The orders genuinely differ, first at `ss/adder_dcop_16` against
`ss/Andrianov/ins2`, and neither `sort` errors. **A digest of a sorted list is a digest of the
order, so an unpinned sort makes it environment-dependent rather than a property of the set.** The
correct digest is the one above; the raw file is `d9184eb95ff6eb6b…`.

The alternative reading of that mismatch was a substitution finding, not a formatting note, and it
was resolved before the seal rather than after. `c202/keys.txt` is byte-identical to
`c198_keys.txt`, verified with `cmp`.

**Every sort in the seal is now `LC_ALL=C`, and the second reason matters more than the first.**
Beyond the digest, `sort -u` decides *uniqueness* by collation rather than by bytes, so under a
locale where two byte-distinct strings compare equal it merges them — and the distinct-cell guard
counts with `sort -u`. That would undercount silently: a spurious refusal, or worse, masking the
exact duplicate the guard exists to find. Measured on the live data the counts agree at 801 either
way, so this is a hazard that is not currently firing rather than a defect that was; recorded as
such.

### Nine of twenty-two `SHA256SUMS` manifests are CRC-32, and the check that reads them as verified

Classified by content rather than by filename, the ledger tree under
`~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/` holds 22 files named `SHA256SUMS`:

| attestation | manifests | attested lines |
|---|---|---|
| genuine SHA-256 | 13 | 777 |
| `cksum` output (CRC-32 + byte count) | 9 | 2346 |

The nine are `chain185-w1fix-mkt` (76), `chain185-w1fix-redwood` (72), `chain187-w1unroll-mkt`
(73), `chain187-w1unroll-redwood` (78), `chain188-w1ship-redwood` (67), `chain189-tsweep-mkt` (12),
`fixtures/` (661), `harnesses/` (184), and the **top-level milestone manifest** (1123). The
transition is clean at chain190 — every chain from there on is genuine, including 191–201.

So three quarters of the attested lines in this tree carry a 32-bit error-detecting code under a
filename claiming a cryptographic hash. CRC-32 detects accidental truncation; it does not resist
substitution, where a collision is cheap to construct. For those nine, "sealed" means "not
accidentally corrupted", not "not replaced". **This is reported, not repaired** — regenerating a
historical attestation would destroy the only record of what was actually attested at the time, and
that is not a call to make silently.

**The check that reads them as verified.** `shasum -a 256 -c` on a `cksum` manifest exits 1 with
`no properly formatted SHA checksum lines found`. That message contains **zero `FAILED` tokens and
zero `OK` tokens.** A driver that greps for `FAILED` and treats its absence as a pass therefore
reads a CRC-32 manifest as fully verified — loud to a human reading stderr, silent to the check.
The seal's own form counted non-OK lines instead, which did refuse, but only because `shasum`
emits that error into the captured stream; had it exited quietly the count would have been zero and
the check would have passed vacuously. It now requires the **OK count to equal the manifest's line
count**, which cannot pass on an empty or unparsed result. Verified in both directions: chain189
reads 0 of 12 and refuses, chain201 reads 62 of 62 and passes.

**And the locale hazard, with two claims tested rather than reasoned.** The `comm`/`join` mismatch
is real and reproducible: with the corpus and target key lists both `LC_ALL=C`-sorted, `comm -23`
under the ambient locale reports 22 keys unique to the target where `LC_ALL=C comm` and a Python
set difference both report 0. **But `comm` warns** — `file 1 is not in sorted order`, 107 bytes on
stderr. The wrong number arrived with a warning attached that nothing was reading, so the rule is
"route stderr where a check can see it", not "these tools fail quietly".

What is *not* real here is `sort -u` merging byte-distinct strings. Eight inputs forming four pairs
differing only by `_` or `-` give 8 distinct under both `en_US.UTF-8` and C, on GNU coreutils 8.32
and macOS BSD sort, and the real object's demangled symbol list gives 525 distinct either way.
Collation changes order, not uniqueness. `LC_ALL=C` is still pinned on every sort in the seal, but
for the digest reason rather than the merging one.

## chain202: the override ladder. Verdict NO at all three widths, and the control fails at two of them

Sealed at `chain202-adoptladder-redwood`, 113 files, manifest
`2e16dba596a1dcc73aaab1387ff06308398fcfc115458778b01fbc7379e0fede`, 112 of 112 lines verifying.
Stage finished 11:03:10 against an 11:03:09 prediction. 98 of 98 files at exactly 802 rows and 801
distinct `(key, k, arm)` triples; writer accounting 98 of 98; corpus digest matching chain198/199/200;
metamorphic relations 0 of 3 violated. One object, `98f8eb8670b1060e`, single build with
`defines=''`, so every arm is that binary called with a different `nthreads_override` and no layout
artefact is possible.

**The pre-registered verdict is NO at every width.** `ok_r` requires the ADOPT group's CI lower
bound to exceed `1.0 + floor`, and over the whole ADOPT population it does not: k=2 reads 0.9945
[0.9057, 1.0803], k=4 reads 1.0160 [0.9348, 1.0963], k=32 reads 0.8531 [0.7770, 0.9375]. At k=4 —
the one width whose control holds — that is a `no/YES`, which the pre-registration reads as
*chain200 was measuring the pool*: 24 workers existing rather than being used, which belongs to the
caller and not to this kernel. **Nothing ships.**

**Correction: the control fails at ALL THREE widths, and my predicate was the reason it looked
like two.** `inside()` tested whether a CI *overlaps* the floor band — failure-to-reject, not
evidence of absence — so it passes on imprecision. At k=4 it passed a NULL worst-arm CI of
[0.9405, 0.9996], **8.4x wider than the ±0.35% band it was judged against and excluding parity
outright**. A control that a sufficiently wide CI always passes is not a control. Replaced with
three outcomes — `effect` (CI excludes parity), `nopower` (CI contains parity but is wider than the
band), `flat` (CI contained in the band, the only pass) — after which the verdict line reads
`NO (nopower,effect)` at k=2, `NO (nopower,effect)` at k=4 and `NO (effect,effect)` at k=32.
CAPONLY also fails at k=2 and k=4, having been passed by the same overlap test. This is the
equivalence-versus-detection error that this project has a standing note about, made in the one
place it decides a control.

One limit of the corrected test, stated because it bounds what a pass could ever have meant:
containment is **not achievable at n = 24–29 on this data for any pair**, including the
same-argument A/A. So `nopower` is the honest outcome rather than a near-miss, and no margin at this
n could have certified the control. The load-bearing statistic is therefore parity exclusion, for
which the A/A pair is the positive control — and `ov24`/`ov24b` **never excludes parity at any
width**, while 11 of 21, 6 of 21 and 17 of 21 of the other pairs do.

**The artefact grows strongly with width, and it reaches the pair the gain is measured across.**
On NULL cells, where every arm delivers one worker, `ov16`/`ovp` — the pair carrying the whole k=4
gain — reads −0.22% [0.9940, 1.0029] at k=2, **+1.65% [0.9968, 1.0532]** at k=4, and **+7.22%
[1.0168, 1.1471]** at k=32, the last excluding parity. At k=4 that neither demonstrates an artefact
nor rules one out below +5.3%, against a +6-cell gain — so the k=4 result is unattributable for
want of control power, not because an artefact is proven. `ov16`/`ov24` at k=4 does exclude parity
at +2.19%, reproducing the checker's +2.08% independently. The earlier "0.5–0.7% at resolved 1" was
the k=2 end of a range reaching six times that.

**So nothing at any width is attributable, and the pre-registered NO is the only thing standing.**
The mechanism claim is unaffected and now better measured: a positive override declines into a
private-team launch, so the argument moves more than the worker count, across a six-fold width
dependence.

The original sealed capture is kept unmodified at `c202_analysis.txt` with the corrected read
alongside it as `c202_analysis_corrected.txt` and a `CORRECTION.txt` stating what changed —
re-sealed at 116 files, 115 of 115 verifying, manifest
`5e0e7daf79db12228c474727c60df18fa7e58daae94f3186d560f1d9e0fa2046`. Replacing the original would
have destroyed the record of a defect found within the hour, which is the same reason the nine
CRC-32 manifests were reported rather than regenerated.

**The negative control fails at k=2 and k=32, and the failure is localized.** NULL is the group
where every arm resolves to the same team, so every arm must be flat. The headline `ov24/ovp` pair
is inside the floor at all three widths, but the control is over *every* arm and the worst arm is
outside it: k=2 `ov24/ov4` reads 0.9954 [0.9933, 0.9974] against a ±0.23% floor, and k=32
`ov24/ov16` reads 0.9578 [0.9163, 0.9906] against ±0.51%. Only k=4 is clean.

P4 localizes it exactly. Grouped by resolved count rather than by arm, at resolved **1** — where
every arm runs a single worker — the arms still differ: at k=2, `ov16` 1.0006, `ov8` 1.0024, `ov24`
1.0000, `ov24b` 0.9991, `ov2` 0.9980, `ov4` 0.9954, `ovp` 0.9809. Several carry disjoint CIs. **At
the same resolved team count, different override arguments give different times**, so something
other than the team is moving. The mechanism is already documented: a positive override is not a
hard cap — it declines into a private-team launch — so the argument changes more than the worker
count. That was known qualitatively and is now measured at 0.5–0.7%.

**The ladder itself is monotone in the resolved team and saturates at 16.** At k=2, against 24
workers as the reference: 2 workers read 0.4070 (2.46x slower), 4 read 0.6623 (1.51x), 8 read 0.9264
(1.08x), 16 read 1.0221 and 24 read 1.0000, both inside the floor. So worker count is the mechanism
on the population, and everything above 16 is flat. k=4 reproduces it: 0.4047, 0.6679, 0.9637,
1.0273, 1.0000.

**The A/A timing floor is clean at all three widths** — 0.9994 [0.9953, 1.0041], 1.0012 [0.9978,
1.0053], 1.0016 [0.9959, 1.0086]. Worth recording that at 3 passes the k=2 A/A had read 0.9874
[0.9790, 0.9961], a 1.3% control failure with a CI excluding parity, which resolved entirely by 14
passes. A control failure on partial data is not a control failure.

### The cell count, which is the scoreboard, and why it still does not ship

| arm | behind MKL of 267 (rom / mor) | k=2 | k=4 | k=32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ov16` | **23 / 23** | 8 | 11 | 4 |
| `ovp` (the default) | 28 / 27 | 8 | 17 | 3 |
| `ov8` | 30 / 28 | 12 | 13 | 5 |
| `ov24` | 35 / 33 | 12 | 20 | 3 |
| `ov24b` | 37 / 35 | 11 | 23 | 3 |
| `ov4` | 78 / 77 | 42 | 30 | 6 |
| `ov2` | 131 / 129 | 55 | 43 | 33 |

The A/A bar at 14 passes is 2 cells under both estimators, and `ov16` carries zero estimator
disagreement (23/23), so pooled 28 -> 23 looks like it clears. **It does not, for two reasons found
by the independent reading, and the second is the stronger.**

First, per width the gain is entirely at k=4 — 6 cells under both estimators against that width's
own A/A bar of 3 (`ov24` 20 vs `ov24b` 23) — and it **costs 1 cell at k=32 under ratio-of-medians
and 2 under median-of-ratios, against a k=32 A/A bar of 0.** A regression against a zero bar is a
finding, not a shape to tune around.

Second, **the estimator gap is unstable between arms that are identical by construction**: at the
1.00 threshold `ov24` reads 41 / 35, a ratio-of-medians-minus-median-of-ratios gap of **+6**, while
`ov24b` reads 40 / 40, a gap of **0**. Same object, same argument. So the zero-estimator-disagreement
figure I cited for `ov16` carries no information.

**Both of the paragraphs above are wrong as written, and the corrections came from splitting on the
balanced halves.** They are kept rather than deleted because the errors are the instructive part.

*The threshold mismatch.* I wrote that the median-of-ratios A/A bar is "5 cells, not 2" and
concluded `ov16` does not clear. The 5 is a bar computed at the `> 1.00` threshold; the gain it was
compared against is at `> 1.01`, the analyzer's pre-registered value. At the pre-registered
threshold the between-arm bar is **2** and the gain clears in **all six realisations** — rom +5/+3/+7
against bars 2/2/1, mor +4/+5/+7 against bars 2/2/4, over all 14 passes and each balanced half. At
`> 1.00` it clears in five of six, the exception being all-14 median-of-ratios at +5 against a bar
of 5. So the conflation was mine, between a bar at one margin and a gain at another.

*The two statistics are also not the same quantity.* The within-arm estimator gap asks how much the
*estimator choice* moves one arm's count; the between-arm count difference asks how much two
identical arms differ *under one estimator*. The first is a caution about reading a gap as evidence;
it does not license using it as the second. The measured between-arm median-of-ratios bar is 2 over
all 14 passes, ranging 1 to 4 across halves.

*And the k=32 regression changes sign.* Across the balanced halves it reads −1, −1, 0 under
ratio-of-medians and −2, −2, **+1** under median-of-ratios, while the bar it is measured against
takes both 0 and 1. A 1-to-2 cell cost against a bar with that much of its own variation is inside
it, so "a regression against a zero bar" does not hold here — the zero was a single draw, and the
halves being position-balanced is what makes that demonstrable rather than a fished subset.

**What actually blocks shipping, after those two arguments are struck.** The pre-registered verdict
is NO at all three widths and decides on its own terms. The control fails at two of three widths.
And the effect lives at exactly one width: k=2 is **+0 in all six realisations**, k=32 is
sign-unstable, and k=4 carries everything at +6/+4/+7 (rom) and +6/+7/+6 (mor) against bars of
3/0/3 and 3/2/4. A gain at one of three widths with another null and the third sign-unstable is a
width-specific effect, which is the overfitting case this project's performance convention exists to
refuse — not a pooled margin problem. A thread cap at 16 does not ship, for those three reasons and
not for the two I first gave.

The bar also did not tighten with pass count: 2/2 over all 14 passes against 2/2 and 1/4 on the two
balanced halves. So fourteen passes bought essentially nothing on the cell-count statistic, which
is the second number that says whether the first one was worth collecting.

**And the confirmed board cells move the other way from the population, which is reported and not
gated.** Within ADOPT, restricted to the confirmed cells, the ambient policy is *faster* than
forcing 24 workers: 15.4% at k=2 (n=9, floor ±3.87%) and 26.6% at k=4 (n=8, floor ±4.81%), both
CIs excluding parity. At k=32 the ADOPT population reverses decisively the other way — forcing 24 is
faster, `ovp` slower by 14.7% — but that width's control is dirty, so it is not interpretable. The
pre-registration put the verdict on the population, so these subgroup readings are recorded as
observations, not as a result; they are also the small-n regime where the bootstrap's own resampling
noise runs 4-6% of the CI width.

CAPONLY is flat at all three widths (1.0082, 1.0121, 0.9993, all inside their floors), so the second
lever stays where it was: read in P4 by resolved count, not here.

### The override is declined on 36-44% of cells, and the null is the tightest of fifteen pairs

Two findings from the independent reading, both reproduced here from the sealed CSVs.

**`resolved` is not `override`, and the decline is deterministic.** `resolved` takes a single value
across all 14 passes in **1869 of 1869** `(build, key, k)` cells, so this is structure and not noise.
Declined cells of 267: `ov16` 117, `ov8` 111, `ov2` 106, `ov4` 106, `ov24` 95, `ov24b` 95. Two
distinct declines exist — **82 cells deliver 1 worker in every override arm** regardless of the
request, and **24 cells deliver 32**, above the pool of 24, so on those a request for *2* workers
delivers *32*. Any monotone-in-thread-count claim must therefore be stated over delivered counts.
P4 already is — its rows are grouped by resolved count, with the arm named only as the route, so
the ladder above stands as written — but the requested-count reading of an arm name does not.

**And the dedicated null is the most agreeable of the fifteen override-arm pairs, by a factor of
three.** On the 82 cells where every override arm delivers the same count, so no thread-count effect
can exist, the maximum per-cell deviation runs: `ov24`/`ov24b` **0.0278**, then 0.0896, 0.1139,
0.1515, … up to `ov16`/`ov2` at 0.8336, with a median across the fifteen of **0.2223**. That is
expected rather than anomalous — `ov24`/`ov24b` is the only pair passing the *same* argument, and a
positive override declines into a private-team launch, so every other pair traverses a different
dispatch route even where the delivered count is identical. But the consequence is real: **the A/A
pair bounds measurement noise at identical argument, and does not bound the artefact between two
arms passing different arguments.** Using it as the bar for a `ov16`-versus-`ovp` *ratio* would
understate the artefact by roughly an order of magnitude.

That objection applies to the ratio statistic and not to the cell count, which is a different
quantity: on the same 82 cells every override arm reads **5 of 82** behind MKL and `ovp` reads 4, so
the count bar on that population is 0 to 1 cell. The ratio spread over those cells runs 0.028 to
0.834 while the count is near-constant — which is the check that the 82 carry no effect, and the
reason the count comparison survives a bar the ratio comparison does not.

One caveat to keep with the 82: `resolved = 1` in two arms does not prove identical execution, since
the route that declines a request for 2 differs from the one declining a request for 24 and the
timing includes it. So that spread bounds arm-identity artefact rather than being a pure noise
floor — an upper bound on artefact, which is what makes it the right bar and the wrong name.

**The two pipelines agree exactly on the counts once the threshold convention is matched.** The
independent reading used `> 1.00` where this analysis uses `> 1.01`; at `> 1.00` all seven arms
reproduce to the cell — `ovp` 30/31, `ov2` 132/131, `ov4` 79/79, `ov8` 32/31, `ov16` 27/26, `ov24`
41/35, `ov24b` 40/40. Two independently written pipelines over one sealed dataset, agreeing on every

### Correction 2: the control's *reachability*, and the same defect in the printing function

The overlap-for-equivalence fix in the previous section left three things wrong. None of them moves
the verdict — NO at all three widths, nothing attributable, no thread cap ships — and all three
were found by a second independently written reading disagreeing with a number.

**Containment was asserted to be unreachable and is reachable at the narrowest width.** The fix's
comment said containment — the only passing outcome — was unachievable at n = 24–29 for any pair
including the same-argument pair. Measured over all 21 arm pairs it is **2 of 21 contained at k=2**
in that width's ±0.23% band (3 of 21 against a fixed ±0.35%), and **0 of 21 at k=4 and k=32 in both
bands**. So `nopower` at k=2 is a shortfall of power for that particular pair, while at the two
wider widths no design at this n could have certified the control and parity exclusion is the
load-bearing statistic. The analysis now prints the count per width beside the verdict instead of
asserting it, with the consequence of a zero spelled out.

**The A/A pair's own containment must not be read at all.** The band is `max(|lo−1|, |hi−1|)` of
that pair's CI, so its containment in it holds by construction up to two asymmetries — the
reciprocal, since a band is symmetric in ratio space and a reciprocal is not, and the seed offset
the floor is computed under. At k=2 those two suffice to flip its verdict, at a margin of 4e-5.

**`row()` had the identical overlap defect and the fix had not reached it.** Every printed row's
label came from `else: "inside the floor"`, so a CI that excludes parity printed as quiet. Of the 45
rows so labelled, **only 12 are contained in their band; 24 contain parity while being wider than
it; 9 exclude parity** — among them the k=32 control row itself, `ov24/ovp` n=24 **1.0267 [1.0026,
1.0568]**, a 2.7% difference on cells where no argument can change the team. The verdict block had
already used the fixed predicate, so the capture contradicted its own verdict line rather than
reaching a wrong one. Labels are now FASTER / SLOWER / `under floor, EXCLUDES parity` / `flat,
contained in band` / `no power (contains parity)`.

**The parity-exclusion count is not seed-stable, and neither is the count of stable pairs.**
Reported as 11 / 6 / 17 of 21 at k=2 / 4 / 32; at k=32 that is 16 over 9 seeds and **15 over 25**.
The ratio list per pair is fixed and only the resample draw changes, so the statistic to read is the
margin by which the pinned seed's CI clears parity against the seed-to-seed spread of the bound
deciding it. Exactly one pair per width sits inside its own resampling noise:

| width | boundary pair | CI at the pinned seed | margin | seed spread |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| k=2  | `ov24b`/`ov16` | 1.0021 [1.0001, 1.0039] | +0.00007 | 0.00018 |
| k=4  | `ovp`/`ov4`    | 0.9961 [0.9908, 0.9999] | +0.00006 | 0.00013 |
| k=32 | `ov4`/`ov16`   | 0.9814 [0.9598, 0.9998] | +0.00019 | 0.00099 |

Which is why the two pipelines differed by **exactly one pair at all three widths**: not a
convention difference, one pair per width whose side of the boundary the resample picks.

**What none of it touches: the positive control holds.** The boundary pair is never the
same-argument pair. `ov24b`/`ov24` contains parity at every width and every seed tried (25 of 25
non-exclusions at k=32, margin −0.00147). So the arm-identity artefact lives between *different*
arguments, not between two spellings of one, and it grows six-fold with width — **0.75% → 2.11% →
4.35%** — which supersedes the earlier pooled "0.5–0.7%" quoted from the narrowest width alone.

**And the seal reported "2 checked" for three metamorphic relations**, having counted a phrase only
the two text-diff relations emit; the authoritative `0 of 3 relations violated` was correct

| width | pair | paired convention | medians convention |
|---|---|---|---|
| k=2 | `ov24b`/`ov16` | 200/200 deterministic | 0/200 deterministic |
| k=4 | `ovp`/`ov4` | 200/200 deterministic | 200/200 deterministic |

They are right at k=2 and k=4 and my original diagnosis was wrong there. At k=32 they are not: 25
draws cannot distinguish a rate of 0.965 from 1.000, since **0.965²⁵ = 0.41** — a clean sweep is the
single most likely outcome. Both terms are live at k=32, only the convention at the narrower two.
The general point: a determinism claim needs enough draws to exclude a high rate.

**My bound-versus-centre claim is withdrawn, and the weaker replacement needs a refinement too.**
Measured against the bound that actually decides each verdict — nearest parity, so the lower bound
above it and the upper below:

| width | centre gap | deciding-bound gap | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| k=2 | 0.000488 | 0.000549 (lower) | 1.1x |
| k=4 | 0.001339 | 0.000968 (upper) | **0.7x — the centre overstates** |
| k=32 | 0.000126 | 0.001048 (upper) | 8.3x |

So "at least as large at every width" does not hold either. The accurate form is weaker than both:

conclusion drawing on it is unaffected, needing only that reseeding cannot certify a
parity-exclusion count, which the table establishes alone.
