chain203's construction is measurably better at the interim point: **21 of 42 ordered pairs at
chain202's halfway mark against 77 of 110 at chain203's** — 50.0% versus 70.0%, and 77 rather than
the 55 that a design covering each unordered pair once would give. Pass 11 of chain203 is therefore
a stronger interim read than pass 7 of chain202 would have been.

### The format scanner was blind to the commonest member of its own defect class

Adding the landed-balance check, a `%` operator ended up on the wrong `print`: one string carried an
orphaned `%d` and printed it literally, and the next received operands it could not use and raised
`TypeError`. `fmtcheck.py` — which exists for exactly this class — reported **0 format defects**,
because its mirror check looked only for `%%` in a never-formatted string and a bare `%d` sailed
through.

It now flags any conversion in a string no `%` operator ever touches, with two narrowings so that
prose *about* formats is not flagged: the space flag is excluded (the flag set `[-+ #0]*` admits a
space, so "0% at 2400" and "17.2% reading" parse as conversions), and a spec named inside backticks
is an explicit opt-out — which makes the fix at a flagged prose site "backtick the spec", better
writing as well as a quieter scanner. A string bound to a name that is `%`-formatted elsewhere is
skipped, since its conversion is used, just not at the assignment.

Then the test that should have come first: the exact edit that defeated the scanner was rebuilt as a
mutant, and the widened scanner catches it at the right line. **A scanner never shown to fail on its
own defect class is the same vacuous guard as a metamorphic relation that holds because the
transform is a no-op** — the third instance of that shape here, after the value-sorted permutation
and the stale mutant copies.

### Two rotation tables can both be balanced, and one of them is the wrong chain's

The ledger holds chain202's *named* table and chain203's *indexed* table under parallel names, and
chain203's named table exists only on redwood:

| file | shape | sha256 | chain |
|---|---|---|---|
| `orders_named.txt` (ledger) | 14 × 7 | `0c6ba41bf200e006` | chain202 |
| `orders_idx11x22.txt` (ledger, and redwood) | 22 × 11 | `0a74b3f908f5a0c2` | chain203 |
| `c203/orders_named.txt` (redwood only) | 22 × 11 | `5097fd2d3a719ef3` | chain203 |

**Both ledger tables are balanced**, so a check asking "is this rotation table balanced?" answers
yes on either, and pointing `--orders` at the wrong one during a chain203 analysis certifies
chain202's schedule for chain203's data. That is a passing check describing the wrong chain — the
same shape as a stale mutant, with a different artefact.

The `--orders` path now refuses before computing any balance, on three discriminators, because any
one of them can be satisfied by accident: the row width against the run's arm count, the table's
**arm set** against the run's, and rows all being the same width. The arm set is the only one that
catches a same-shape table under a different arm labelling, so it has its own fabricated input — a
table of the right width with one wrong label.

**And the generator that produced the table had a relative write path.** `mkorders11.py` wrote to
`orders_idx11x22.txt` in the current directory, so invoking it from a ledger directory would have
overwritten sealed evidence in place. The generator is deterministic, so an accidental in-place
regeneration changes only the mtime and **`SHA256SUMS` still verifies** — a mutation of sealed
evidence that passes every integrity check in use. It only causes damage if the output ever moves,
under a different Python or a different iteration order, and then it causes it silently. It now
requires `--out PATH`, absolutises it, and refuses a path that already exists.

Running it under `--out` also settles the provenance question: its output is **byte-identical** to
the sealed table, `0a74b3f908f5a0c2`. That matters for one specific claim rather than for validity —
the 77-of-110 adjacency gain is a *causal* claim about the construction, and a hand-edited table
would have left the property true and the attribution unsupported. Two facts from the generator's
own output belong in prose rather than in a script's stdout: exact precedence balance is
**impossible**, since 605/110 = 5.5 is not an integer, so 55-at-5 / 55-at-6 is an optimum and not a
missed target; and **0 of 4000 random bases** met the reversal-paired-difference condition, with
only 19.4% of those reaching the precedence optimum — so the construction is not reachable by
sampling, and the two conditions are independent.

### A shared scratch directory that one script rebuilds is a race that reports as a data defect

Running the check census while the battery was running produced two failures that looked like
neither. The census rebuilds its work directory from scratch and the spike test rebuilds its case
directory per case, so each removed a directory the other was reading. The symptoms were
`REFUSE: missing arm: ov2 or ov2b absent` — a corpus with five of eleven arms — and a check
reporting `DID NOT FIRE: no summary line`. One reads as a broken corpus and the other as a broken
check; neither reads as a collision, and the reader cannot tell from inside.

Fixed structurally rather than by discipline: the spike case directory is now per-process, and the
census takes an exclusive lock on its work directory and refuses if another census holds it, naming
the scripts that depend on its subdirectory names. The work directory itself cannot be made
per-process, because those names are the interface between four scripts. Same family as the stale
mutant copies and a stale ledger snapshot, except the artefact is destroyed rather than outdated.

### A named rotation table cannot be identified by its shape, and balance is relabelling-invariant

Refusing a table of the wrong width with the wrong arm set turned out to pin the table's *shape
and labels*, not its identity. One index table mapped through different arm orders yields
different named tables with **identical width, identical arm set and identical balance**; only the
content digest separates them:

| mapping | position-balanced | predecessor-balanced | pairs | content digest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| harness `$ARMS` | yes | yes | 110/110 | `7ae1273bc3bc90fd` |
| `sorted()` | yes | yes | 110/110 | `51beadb47afbcb32` |
| three shuffles | yes | yes | 110/110 | three more distinct digests |

The mechanism is in the harness: it maps the index table to names through its `$ARMS` string, so any
reordering of that string — grouping the duplicate arms differently, alphabetising it, inserting a
rung — produces a different named table that passes every shape and label check.

**So the index table is the right input, not merely the tidier one: the questions asked of the
table do not depend on the mapping, so the input should not carry one.** `--orders` now requires the
digit form and accepts a named table only against an asserted `--orders-sha256` that must match —
printing a digest lets a reader check, asserting it stops the analysis.

**And the invariance that makes this work is narrower than it looks.** Position and predecessor
balance are invariant to relabelling, verified on this table under five mappings: identical balance
at every prefix, five distinct digests. Every *per-arm* statement is not. On the 9-row prefix all
**11 of 11** arms have a different position histogram under `sorted()` than under the harness's
order, with mean positions differing by up to 0.66. The analyzer had been mapping through
`sorted()` and getting the right answer for the right reason without saying so — which would have
become wrong the moment the report answered the obvious next question, "not balanced *how?*", with
a per-arm breakdown. It now takes `--arms`, checks its set against the run's, and when it is absent
prints in the output that no per-arm figure may be derived.

**One truncation case survives all of it.** An 11-row cut of the 22-row table is itself
position-balanced, so it passes width, arm set and both balance tests. The only thing that catches
it is a landed pass with no row in the table — a refusal added for the wrong-table case that turns
out to be load-bearing for this one too.

### The pattern: a check built for the partial case cannot be validated on the complete one

Three defects here share a shape, and the shape is a testing-strategy conclusion rather than three
anecdotes:

| defect | inert while | live when |
|---|---|---|
| CV computed on a hardcoded 6 passes | every arm had ≥ 6 passes | the pass count differs from 6 |
| override compared against the corpus-wide maximum pool | pool is 24 on every row | the pool varies per cell |
| positions mapped through `sorted()` | the rotation is complete, where symmetry gives every arm the same histogram under any mapping | the prefix is partial |

Each was added to serve a partial or interim read. Each is invisible on the complete artefact the
suite normally runs against, and a test written on that artefact passes. **The fixture for a
partial-case check has to be partial** — a complete fixture is evidence about the wrong regime.

### Four ways a verification artefact goes wrong, and none of them fails a test

| variant | what happens | how it reports |
|---|---|---|
| stale | the artefact is older than its subject | reports *passing*, tests nothing |
| destroyed | the artefact is removed under a reader | reports a data defect one layer below the cause |
| duplicated | the artefact is copied beside its source | never errors, only agrees |
| degenerate | many artefacts satisfy the check | passes while describing the wrong object |

All four occurred in this one session: stale mutant copies on `/tmp`, a work directory rebuilt under
a concurrent reader, regenerated copies of a sealed rotation table sitting in a scratch directory,
and the named rotation table. **None of them produces a failing test.** So the detector cannot be
the suite — it is an inventory of which bytes were read, which is why naming the artefact and its
digest beside each number did more work here than any assertion added. The duplicated case has the
cheapest mitigation: rename the copy so its name carries its provenance (`MY_REGEN_…`) rather than
deleting it, since deleting also destroys the evidence that the check was run.

### The third rotation question: did the run execute the table?

Three separate questions, and only two were being asked:

| question | answered by |
|---|---|
| which bytes the table holds | the digest |
| whether the design is sound | the balance check |
| whether the run executed it | nothing |

The third is not implied by the first two. A digest-verified, fully balanced table can sit beside a
run that ordered its arms some other way — a different file read, a different arm list mapped
through, a reorder inside a pass — and every check described above passes. It is the degenerate
case one level up: the artefact is right and its relationship to the data is unverified.

The evidence is in the run log, and the first version of this check read the wrong line of it. The
harness prints each completed pass with a bracketed arm order:

    pass p9 of 22 done 17:13:44  [ov16b ov24 ov24b ov2 ov8b ovp ov4b ov16 ov4 ov8 ov2b]

**That bracket is an echo of the plan, not an observation.** The body does
`ORD=$(sed -n "${P}p" "$ORDERS")`, then `for A in $ORD`, then `echo "... [$ORD]"` — so comparing
the table against the bracket cannot fail by construction. It is the vacuous-guard shape again: a
check that reports a match it could not have missed.

The comparison is still worth making for two non-circular reasons. The log carries arm **names**
while the table carries **indices**, so it confirms which arm list the harness mapped through —
which makes `--arms` checkable rather than merely declared, and only
`ovp ov2 ov2b ov4 ov4b ov8 ov8b ov16 ov16b ov24 ov24b` reproduces the log while `sorted()` fails on
every pass. And the bracket comes from the run, so a *different* `$ORDERS` file than the one being
analyzed is detected.

**The non-circular record is the `wrote` sequence.** Inside the loop each arm emits
`wrote .../sh_<arm>_float32_p<N>.csv` as its subprocess finishes, so that sequence is an
observation where the bracket is a plan. The arms run sequentially, so completion order is
execution order — were they to overlap this comparison would need to change rather than be
trusted. `passlog_c203.py` now compares all three records:

    totals over 9 passes: table==bracket 9, bracket==observed 9, table==observed 9
    passes whose observed arm count != 11: none

Firing inputs, one per claim the check makes:

| input | result |
|---|---|
| two `wrote` lines of one pass swapped, bracket untouched | `bracket==observed` falls to 8, refuses |
| one `wrote` line deleted | refuses: an incomplete record is not a wrong order |
| the wrong arm order | refuses on every pass |
| an empty log | refuses rather than reporting "0 of 0 match" |

The first is exactly the case the bracket comparison is structurally blind to, and the third row
matters for its own reason: comparing a short observed list against a full table row would report a
*wrong order* where the truth is an *incomplete record*.

**Run retroactively on chain202, whose log is on the same host: 14 of 14, table == bracket ==
observed, no pass with an arm count other than 7.** So chain202 was designed balanced and executed
as declared, established from an observation rather than an echo, on the chain whose verdict is in
circulation. chain203's log exists only on redwood at the time of writing, so the same retroactive
check needs it sealed with the ledger after the last pass.

### An interim band read is not authorised, and the analyzer now says so

A position-balanced prefix is free of position bias. That is a statement about rotation and not a
licence to read bands there: an extra look is an extra look however clean its schedule, and
amendment 3 puts the bands at the completed rotation.

The price was measured on chain202's own duplicate-arm A/A pair, with each look centred on its own
estimand so both are exact size tests and every rejection is multiplicity:

| group | n | look 1 (7 passes) | look 2 (14 passes) | either | inflation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NULL k=2 | 29 | 0.066 | 0.054 | 0.100 | 1.85× |
| NULL k=32 | 24 | 0.166 | 0.098 | 0.224 | 2.29× |
| ADOPT k=2 | 31 | 0.068 | 0.124 | 0.182 | 1.47× |
| ADOPT k=32 | 25 | 0.066 | 0.070 | 0.116 | 1.66× |

**Two looks cost 1.47× to 2.29× the single-look false-positive rate** — modest rather than
catastrophic, because the looks share their first passes and all their cells and are therefore
strongly correlated, which is the same mechanism that limits it. It is not free, and it lands on
the stage whose entire purpose is a null control.

The inflation *ratio* is the robust part of that table; the absolute levels are approximate,
because the centring uses the same cells it then resamples from. A first attempt at the same number
centred the population on the 14-pass statistic and ran a 7-pass look against it — a different
functional, so uncentred — and produced a **12.09× "inflation" that was entirely a bias term.**
That is why the ratio rather than the level is the reportable quantity.

A separate observation from the same table deserves following up after the completed run: the
**single-look rates read 0.054 to 0.124 against a nominal 0.05**, which would make the final bands
somewhat anti-conservative before any multiplicity is added. That needs a cleaner construction than
the one that produced it, and it is queued rather than acted on.

So with `--orders` given and fewer passes landed than the table declares, `an_c203.py` refuses the
band stages, naming amendment 3 and the measured price. **Deliberately with no override flag:** an
interim read requires an amendment, and an amendment is a change to the pre-registration followed by
a change to this code — a flag would be the licence the scope confusion already granted once.
Stage 1, the partition, the refusal paths and everything else whose answer comes from `resolved` or
from filenames rather than from `ms` are read at any prefix, which is why reading the partition at
six passes was sound.

## The bootstrap percentile interval's realised level, and what it does and does not change

The bands in this document are 95% bootstrap percentile intervals on a geometric mean over cells.
That nominal 95% is an assumption, and at the group sizes this design actually produces — 24 to 64
cells — it is wrong in a measurable direction. Two independent constructions agree that the
intervals are anti-conservative.

**Measured on chain203's own A/A pairs**, with the null imposed on the generating distribution (the
pool of per-cell pass-paired log-ratios is centred once, before any replicate draws from it, so the
estimand is exactly 0 and every exclusion is a false positive), 4000 replicates per row, Monte
Carlo standard error 0.003:

| pool | n | non-coverage | against nominal |
|---|---|---|---|
| pooled across widths and arms | 24 | 0.092 | 1.8× |
| pooled | 29 | 0.085 | 1.7× |
| pooled | 40 | 0.082 | 1.6× |
| pooled | 64 | 0.080 | 1.6× |

Pooling across widths and arms describes no row the design reads, though. Done per (rung, group,
width) on each population's own residuals and at each group's own n, 34 populations were large
enough to characterise and **none of the 34 reads below nominal**, spanning 0.056 to 0.131 — 1.1× to
2.6×. The spread is the finding: a control row and an effect row at the same width and the same n
draw from different populations and need different corrections, so no single widening constant is
available.

Read per row that claim would be too strong. At 4000 replicates the bottom of the span carries a
standard error of 0.0036, so 0.056 sits 1.65 standard errors above 0.050 and is not individually
distinguishable from nominal. Read as a set it is far stronger than the per-row version. Under a
true null each population reads at or above nominal with probability about one half, so all 34
doing so has probability 5.8e-11 if they are independent; collapsing the three widths to 11
effective units gives 4.9e-4, and a deliberately conservative six effective units still gives
1.6e-2. **The joint claim is decisive where the individual rows are not** — the same repair the
chain202 control rows needed further down, arrived at from the other direction.

An independent construction on chain202's data reaches 0.147 at k=32 where this one tops out at
0.131, and that is not two measurements conflicting. The partitions differ: this table's groups are
each rung's cells resolving equal to, above and below ambient, while the other uses the
pre-registered null / cap-only / adopt partition, on a different corpus. Different definitions of
the same cells, so the ceilings are not the same quantity.

**Discreteness is not the cause, measured rather than assumed.** The empirical arm resamples a pool
of discrete atoms while a normal comparison arm draws from a continuous distribution, so a two-arm
comparison charges any granularity cost to the tail. Expected ties in a draw of n is about
C(n,2)/atoms: 0.21 at n=24 on the 1335-cell pool, and 1.03 on a 267-cell one. A third arm — a
normal discretised to the same atom count, resampled identically — reads within Monte Carlo error
of the smooth normal at both granularities (−0.007 to +0.009 at 1335 atoms, −0.008 to +0.000 at
267). A peer independently falsified the same hypothesis from the other side, discretising a
lognormal to 267 atoms and finding the method's behaviour unchanged. So the tail attribution
survives: +0.014 to +0.029 against a moment-matched normal.

**Three standard interval methods were measured and none reaches nominal at these sizes**: the
percentile interval at 1.4× to 2.6×, bootstrap-t at 0.101 to 0.131, and BCa *worse* than percentile
on this data, up to 0.167 — which is not explained by the acceleration estimate's stability, the
bias term's stability, or pool granularity, all three of which were measured and none of which
accounts for it. The cause of BCa's behaviour here is unknown and is recorded as unknown. A level
calibration against the A/A pair is therefore the remaining option **by elimination**, not by
preference.

### What this does not license: a direction

An earlier draft of this analysis argued that the effect is biased toward a false NO, because a
narrow interval is less likely to contain parity and a control passes by containing parity. Both
halves of that are true and the conclusion does not follow, because it assumes every row is equally
affected. Per population they are not: null groups span 0.066 to 0.131 and effect groups 0.075 to
0.123, overlapping almost completely. Both error rates are inflated, neither uniformly, and reading
a net direction off one pooled figure is choosing the estimator to suit the question. **The claim is
withdrawn.**

### chain202's NO is not weakened by this

chain202's verdict rested on its NULL control failing at all three widths, and the obvious worry is
that an anti-conservative interval manufactured exactly that. It did not, and the quantity that
settles it is the **joint** probability rather than an expected count.

The three control rows are the same matrices at three widths in the same passes on the same host,
so they are not obviously independent, and under strong positive dependence three failures out of
three would stop being surprising. Measured rather than assumed, by resampling matrix keys — a key
carries its residual at every width, so whatever cross-width correlation exists is reproduced
without being modelled — the correlations are +0.002 to +0.140 in one construction and −0.168 to
+0.221 in an independent one, two of three negative there. **The three rows are effectively
independent**: at 40000 replicates the observed all-three rate is 0.0006 against an independent
product of 0.000646, a dependence factor of 1.0×.

So under a true null the interval alone produces three control rows failing about **6 in 10000 times
— roughly one run in 1700**. chain202 observed it. The interval defect accounts for a negligible
part of that failure and the control failure is real, which leaves chain202's NO standing on the
same ground it was written on.

One construction detail worth keeping: the first version of the joint measurement averaged the five
duplicate pairs' residuals per key, leaving a pool of exactly 24 atoms drawn at n=24, and its own
built-in validation caught it — the k=2 marginal read 0.123 where the per-population measurement on
the same cells reads 0.076, a 15 standard-error disagreement. A pool no larger than the draw is far
coarser than the pool that estimates the same population's shape, and coarseness inflates
non-coverage on its own. Requiring the marginals of a joint construction to reproduce the
independently measured per-row rates is what made that visible.

### What the design already absorbs, and what it does not

**First, the size of the defect expressed as what it would change.** Everything above is a ratio of
exclusion *rates*, and a rate ratio is not a width ratio. The widening a realised rate implies is
the ratio of normal quantiles, z(0.975)/z(1-a/2):

| realised non-coverage | as a rate ratio | implied widening |
|---|---|---|
| 0.056 | 1.1x | +2.6% |
| 0.076 | 1.5x | +10.5% |
| 0.092 | 1.8x | +16.3% |
| 0.131 | 2.6x | +29.8% |
| 0.147 | 2.9x | +35.2% |

So the whole measured span of the defect is **a 3% to 35% widening of a band**, not a factor of 2.6
in anything a reader would act on. That bounds the damage without waiting for the calibrated re-run,
and it is the figure that belongs beside the rate.

**Second, it does not shrink both sides alike, and an earlier draft of this section said it did.**
The operative bar for chain203 is each rung's own X/Xb pair on the same group the effect is computed
on, so bar and effect are produced by the same bootstrap at the same n on the same population. That
much holds. But an excursion is |centre − 1| + halfwidth, and a width correction scales the
halfwidth while leaving the centre alone, so the two sides scale differently whenever their
centre-to-halfwidth ratios differ. Writing the effect as |c_e| + f·h_e and the bar as |c_b| + f·h_b,
the derivative of their ratio in f has the sign of h_e|c_b| − h_b|c_e|: **the effect-to-bar ratio
rises with widening exactly when the bar is the more centre-dominated side, and falls when the
effect is.** Both directions occur by construction, so no single sign statement covers the table.

The derivative is the useful form because it is independent of the widening factor: the direction is
the same for every f, which a single evaluation at one f could not establish. As an illustration, on
the **three rows** where amendment 3's structure already exists in chain202 — bar ov24/ov24b against
effect ov24/ovp, both on the adopt group, same cells, same n, pass-paired over 14 passes — the
effect-to-bar excursion ratio moves from 3.04 to 3.55 at k=2, 3.55 to 3.81 at k=4, and 19.99 *down*
to 16.70 at k=32 under a +30% widening. Both directions, by −16% to +17%, **flipping nothing**: none
of those three rows comes within 3× of its bar. Three rows at the one rung, not the verdict table.

The fixed bars carried from chain202 do not share the cancellation at all, because they were measured
at chain202's group sizes and are applied at chain203's — 31 against 29 at k=2 and k=4, 40 against 26
at k=32. The measurement that would settle the whole question is a re-run of the verdict table with a
calibrated level applied to **both** the bar and the effect, counting how many verdicts move; queued
for the completed passes.

### The general residue

Across both constructions, synthetic populations matched to the real residuals on standard
deviation, skew, kurtosis, and in one case on the tie rate exactly, all behaved differently from the
real pool on this statistic. **A moment-matched synthetic population is not a substitute for the
real one when validating an interval method** — which is an assumption both of these constructions
rest on, and the reason neither is offered as more than a measurement of the real pool.

Two limits on all of the above. The replicates draw cells i.i.d., which ignores the pass-level
averaging the multi-pass design exists to provide, so the real correction may be smaller. And the
intersection used for the joint rate is 24 keys, so k=2 and k=4 are evaluated at n=24 rather than
their true n=29; that moves the independent product from about 0.0007 to about 0.0005, the same
order either way.

**No change was made to the analyzer's interval.** This is a finding about the instrument's realised
level, recorded with the numbers, and `cover_level_c203.py` re-runs on the completed data. Tuning
the interval on a partial prefix to a single construction's constant is the overfitting the
pre-registered bootstrap floor was added to avoid.

## The measured object is not the local tree, and three claims that follow from that

### The local working tree's thread policy differs from the pinned tarball

`scorch_c199.tgz` is the object every chain from 199 onward measures, and the harness verifies three
of its defines. It does not verify the rest, and the rest differ from `/Users/bobby/scorch`:

| | pinned tarball | local working tree |
|---|---|---|
| `scorch_nthreads` signature | takes a `rows_per_thread` parameter | does not |
| `SCORCH_SPMM_ROWS_PER_THREAD` | **1** | absent |
| `SCORCH_SPMM_CEIL_ROWBIND` / `_MAXROWS` / `_NT_CAP_PHYS` | present | absent |

So **any derivation about the measurement from local source is unsound**, and one was made: a peer
read the composition-adoption clause as source text in a local working tree, this document read
`ov24/LOWER = ∅` from redwood data, and the two were combined into "the redwood binary implements
that clause as written". That conclusion compared a *different* source against the built binary and
**is withdrawn**. Both halves named the wrong object — the peer was reading
`scorch-beat-mkl/src/scorch/csrc/scorch_policy.h`, last modified the previous day, and does not hold
the tarball at all.

The general form is worth keeping, because it is a failure mode specific to a two-party check. The
joint claim was "source read by one party plus data measured by the other equals build-matches-
source", and it fails if *either* half names the wrong artefact — while **looking stronger than
either half alone**, which is what made it persuasive. Two sessions cross-checking is not
independence when one is reading a different artefact than the other is measuring. The theorem itself is unaffected — `SCORCH_SPMM_NT_CAP (-2L)` and
`SCORCH_GRAIN_SPMM 150000` are both confirmed in the tarball, and the harness checks them on every
run — but the build-versus-source check it was said to supply does not exist.

### The selector between capping and adopting is row-axis capacity, not density

The 13 cells that follow `min(request, ambient)` exactly are the cappers with ambient above 1. An
earlier attempt here proposed nonzeros-per-row as the selector, because within each ambient stratum
the separation is clean — at ambient = 4 the two capping cells read 2993 nnz/row against adopters at
1.00 to 90.85, and so on at every stratum. **That hypothesis is false.** Corpus-wide, 3 identity
cells sit at or above the cappers' minimum density (the densest adopter reads 2202 against the
cappers' minimum of 1287), so the within-stratum separation was an artefact of the stratified view.
Rows alone does not separate them either — the ranges overlap.

Read from the pinned source rather than inferred, `scorch_nthreads` is
`min(rows / SCORCH_ROWS_PER_THREAD, work / grain)` clamped to `[nfloor, num_procs]`, and the
adoption clause bounds the override by the same row proxy: `cand = min(override, rows/16, num_procs)`
applied with `max` against the policy count. So the quantity that decides is the **row-axis parallel
capacity**, and these are few-row products:

| matrix | rows | rows/16 | ambient observed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kl02` | 71 | 4 | 4 |
| `bibd_15_7` | 105 | 6 | 6 |
| `bibd_17_8` | 136 | 8 | 8 |
| `us04` | 163 | 10 | 10 |
| `nw14` | 73 | 4 | **6** |
| `bibd_19_9` | 171 | 10 | **22** |

That table takes one width per matrix, which flatters it. **Across all 13 capping cells the row
proxy predicts the observed count on 7 of 13**, and it cannot do better in principle, because
`rows/16` is width-independent and the observed count is not:

| matrix | rows/16 | ambient at k=2, 4, 32 |
|---|---|---|
| `bibd_15_7` | 6 | 6, 6, **14** |
| `kl02` | 4 | 4, 4, **22** |
| `nw14` | 4 | **6**, **12**, 24 |
| `bibd_19_9` | 10 | **22**, 24, 24 |

Adding the width-dependent term makes it *worse*, not better: `min(rows/16, work/grain)` matches on
**2 of 13**, because in 11 of the 13 the observed count is *above* that minimum. So the two terms of
`scorch_nthreads` do not produce these counts — a third mechanism raises nearly all of them, and the
pinned source's row-bound ceiling block is it. Its comment states the rule "takes a few-row product
from 4 workers to 22" and names `kl02` and `nw14` at 71 and 73 rows as the targets; **`kl02` at k=32
reads exactly 4 → 22.** That is the documented transition observed on the measured host.

As a *separator* rather than a predictor the row proxy is strong: all 13 cappers fall in [4, 10] and
**147 of 148 adopters sit above 10**, against nonzeros-per-row's three overlaps. The single boundary
case settles the question though, and it settles it against the row proxy: the lone adopter at 10 is
**`us04` at k=32**, and `us04` at k=2 and k=4 is one of the 13 cappers. Same matrix, same row proxy,
both behaviours, width deciding — which is the width-dependence the table above shows, in its
sharpest form. The selector is not the row proxy alone, and it is not density; it is the ceiling
block, whose gate is the thing to read next.

### The different-argument centre shift does not reproduce under the geomean

A peer reads the ambient = 24 stratum as a different-argument, same-delivery pair — ambient delivers
24 and so does ov24 — and reports the defect as a centre shift rather than a width deficit, with both
different-argument centres below parity and the same-argument pair above it. On the same 61 cells and
the same per-cell pass-paired ratios, that split is **statistic-dependent**:

| pair | kind | geomean centre | median centre |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ovp/ov24` | different argument | 0.99507 | 0.99314 |
| `ovp/ov24b` | different argument | 0.99787 | 0.99295 |
| `ov24b/ov24` | same argument | 0.99815 | 1.00126 |

Under the **median** the pattern is exactly as described: both different-argument pairs sit about
0.7% below parity and the same-argument pair 0.13% above it. Under the **geomean** it vanishes — all
three sit below parity and the same-argument pair is the closest to it. The analyzer's bands use the
geomean, so under the statistic the verdicts are actually computed with, the recommendation to
rebuild each per-rung bar from a different-argument pair does not follow from this data. The
magnitudes also differ: 0.7% here against the 1.1% and 1.8% reported, and halfwidths of 0.008 to
0.011 against 0.017.

**A five-digit coincidence, resolved: both labellings were correct.** This document briefly argued
that a peer's same-argument row must be computing a different pair, because its centre 1.00496
matched the reciprocal of this document's `ovp/ov24` geomean to five digits, and a centre is a
deterministic function of the data and the pair. The peer ran the same argument back, since the
value also matches their `ov24b/ov24`. **Both accusations were wrong, and the argument itself was
invalid: a centre is deterministic in the data, the pair, AND the estimator.** Two different
nestings were in use, so "same value implies same pair" does not follow.

Settled by running the peer's nesting — geomean over cells within a pass, then median over passes —
on this document's own code and data:

| pair | peer reported | reproduced here |
|---|---|---|
| `ov24/ovp` | 0.989375 | 0.989375 |
| `ov24/ov24b` | 1.004962 | 1.004962 |
| `ov24b/ov24` | 0.995064 | 0.995064 |
| `ovp/ov24` | 1.010740 | 1.010740 |

Four of four to six digits, so the peer's labels are right and so are the ones here; the match was a
genuine coincidence across two estimators. A cross-implementation digit match is a labelling
discriminator **only under a fixed estimator**, and reporting the estimator alongside is what makes
it one.

**And it exposed a defect in the nesting used here: it is not reciprocal-invariant.**
`1/(ovp/ov24)` reads 1.004955 while `ov24/ovp` reads 1.005032. Taking a per-cell median over an
*even* number of passes averages the two middle values, and the mean of a set is not the reciprocal
of the mean of its reciprocals. The peer's nesting takes a geomean within each pass, which is
exactly reciprocal, and reads reciprocal to six digits. For a quantity that is a *ratio*, that is an
argument for their nesting independent of anything about centres — and it is the kind of defect that
never shows up until the same pair is computed both ways round.

### Which moved, the pass set or the estimator

An earlier claim here called a timing-shape agreement a "code-level reproduction". That was too
strong: the same ledger and the same estimand should be bit-identical and were not. The pass set is
identical — 14 passes in the ledger — so the estimator moved. Three nestings of the same data:

| nesting | ov2 | ov4 | ov8 | ov16 | ov24 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| median over passes, then median over cells | 1.01 | 0.99 | 0.94 | 0.78 | 1.49 |
| geomean over cells of the per-cell median | 1.04 | 1.17 | 1.07 | 0.87 | 1.45 |
| median of all cell-pass ratios pooled | 1.01 | 1.04 | 0.96 | 0.80 | 1.51 |
| the peer's reading | 1.01 | 1.00 | 0.94 | 0.77 | 1.44 |

So the right label is **two estimators over the same data**, which is the weaker but more useful
statement: the agreement is the deliberate convention variance this work relies on, not a
reproduction. The dip at ov16 survives all three nestings (0.78, 0.87, 0.80), which is the part of
the shape that does not depend on the choice.

## The per-cell reduction is not reciprocal-invariant, and the fix is a pre-registration change

`an_c203.py`'s pre-registered `how='paired'` reduces each cell with `statistics.median` over the
per-pass **ratios**. At an even shared-pass count — 22 is, and 14 was — a median averages the two
middle values, and the arithmetic mean of a set is not the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of its
reciprocals. So a band's point estimate depends on which arm is the numerator, by an amount the
output never states, and a reader comparing a band against its reciprocal elsewhere finds a
disagreement that is arithmetic rather than physical.

Measured with `recip_c203.py`, which reports |1/(num/den) − (den/num)| for every pair:

| data | worst aggregate reciprocal gap | worst per-cell gap |
|---|---|---|
| chain202 ledger, 14 shared passes | 1.5e-4 | 0.0067 |
| chain203 snapshot, 6 shared passes | 2.0e-3 | 0.0658 |

The two rows differ by 13× because of the pass count, not the data — see the sweep below.

**The 88%-of-a-margin figure is a 6-pass artefact and must not be carried to the read point.** The
defect is exactly **zero at odd pass counts** — a median over an odd count is a single element, and
reciprocating reverses the order so that element maps to its own reciprocal — and it decays with the
count at even ones. Swept over prefixes of chain202's 14 passes, with the log-space form beside it:

| passes | parity | registered | log-space |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | even | 1.2e-2 | 1.1e-16 |
| 4 | even | 2.5e-3 | 2.2e-16 |
| 6 | even | 1.8e-3 | 2.2e-16 |
| 8 | even | 4.7e-4 | 2.2e-16 |
| 10 | even | 3.2e-4 | 1.1e-16 |
| 12 | even | 1.7e-4 | 2.2e-16 |
| 14 | even | 1.5e-4 | 2.2e-16 |
| any odd | odd | ~1e-16 | ~1e-16 |

So at 6 passes the gap is 1.8e-3 — reproducing the snapshot figure on independent data — and by 14 it
is 1.5e-4, about **6% of the smallest margin rather than 88%**. chain203 will be read at 22, which is
even, so the defect is live there but smaller again; the figure Bobby should see is the one measured
at 22, and `recip_c203.py --sweep` prints it with the parity of the count beside it. **Without the
parity stated a later reader finds the battery reporting ~1e-16 at an odd prefix and concludes the
defect was imagined.**

**The decay is not monotone, and the claim that it was came from a max over a moving argmax.** An
earlier draft of this section reported 0 rises in 6 steps. That sequence was the *maximum* gap over
seven arm pairs, and its argmax changes at every prefix — `ovp/ov2` at n=2, `ov24b/ov24` at n=4,
`ovp/ov2` at n=6, `ovp/ov24` at n=8 and 10, `ovp/ov4` at n=12, `ov24b/ov24` at n=14 — so the
"sequence" compared a quantity that changes identity between the points being compared. A max over
several decaying sequences can rise while every member falls, and can fall while members rise.

Per pair, seven pairs over the seven even prefixes:

| pair | rises |
|---|---|
| `ovp/ov2` | 1 of 6 |
| `ovp/ov4` | 0 of 6 |
| `ovp/ov8` | 0 of 6 |
| `ovp/ov16` | 1 of 6 |
| `ovp/ov24` | 0 of 6 |
| `ovp/ov24b` | 1 of 6 |
| `ov24b/ov24` | 1 of 6 |
| **total** | **4 of 42 steps, 4 of 7 pairs rise at least once** |

So the decay is **not** monotone on this reduction either, and a peer reaches the same verdict on
theirs at 11 of 42. **The agreement is binary and not a shared rate**: 4 of 42 against 11 of 42 is
nearly 3× apart, consistent with the two reductions themselves differing by about 3× at six passes,
so "the reductions agree" means they agree on *non-monotone* and not that they behave alike.

Both sessions had published a one-line monotonicity verdict read off a max over pairs, and **the two
failures are not mirror images.** One max rose at 2 of 6 steps where members rose at 11 of 42 —
invalid instrument, correct conclusion. The other, this document's, fell at 0 of 6 where members rose
at 4 of 42 — invalid instrument, **wrong published conclusion**. Only one of the two changed a
verdict, and the other is the more dangerous kind to leave in place: an invalid instrument that
happens to agree with the truth emits nothing that flags it. That asymmetry is the argument for
printing the member rows rather than only the summary, which is what both sides changed. It cannot be extrapolated: the gap is set by the spread of whichever two values happen to
land in the middle, which no trend predicts. A peer independently found
the same defect in their own nesting, smaller by 5× to 140× depending on the pair, and confirmed the
mechanism quantitatively: for one pair the two middle values are 0.98863959 and 0.99011021, and the
arithmetic-versus-harmonic gap that spread predicts, `(d/2x)²`, is 5.52e-7 against an observed
5.58e-7. So the defect is understood to 1%, not merely plausible.

**The exact fix is one line: take the same order statistic in log space.** `exp(median(log r))`
rather than `median(r)`. Negating every log reverses the order and negates the mean of the two middle
values exactly, so it is reciprocal-invariant at every pass count — measured at 0 to 2e-16 across
every pair on both datasets, against 1e-4 to 2e-3 for the pre-registered form. It also *matches the
aggregation already in use*: cells are combined with a geometric mean, which is a mean in log space,
so an arithmetic reduction inside a geometric aggregation is the inconsistency. Centres move by less
than the gap removed — 0.98937490 to 0.98937463 on the peer's pair.

**It has not been adopted, and that is deliberate.** The pre-registration names the paired median.
Replacing it is an amendment however principled the replacement, and amendment 2 already set the
precedent that a rival reduction is *printed beside* the registered one rather than substituted for
it. So `recip_c203.py` measures the defect and its size, runs in the verification battery, and the
verdict quantity is untouched. **Adopting the log-space reduction is a pre-registration decision and
is Bobby's to make, not a peer review's and not this document's.** The case for it: it changes no
number materially, it removes an invisible direction convention, and it makes every reciprocal pair
in this document self-consistent. The case against: it is a change to a registered estimator made
while a measurement is in flight — and, on the sweep above, the defect it removes is worth about 6%
of the smallest margin at 14 passes and less at 22, which is a smaller stake than an earlier draft
of this section implied.

### Two readings that look identical and are not

The ceiling-block confirmation above couples a data reading with a source reading — `kl02` at 71
rows reading ambient 22 at k=32, against the pinned tarball's comment naming `kl02` and `nw14` as
that block's targets. That is **structurally the same claim** as the build-versus-source check
withdrawn earlier in this section, and the only difference is which artefact was opened: the
withdrawn one read a local working tree, this one read `scorch_c199.tgz` itself, extracted on the
host that ran the measurement. A peer confirms the data half independently on chain202 and reports
the source half as unverified from their side, since they do not hold the tarball. Stated here so a
later reader can tell the two apart without re-deriving which file each rested on.

### A note on the structural counts in this section

Every structural figure here — 148 identity cells, 24 saturated, 82 declined, 13 cappers, 87
distinct problems — was computed from a **6-pass snapshot** of chain203's directory, because
`resolved` is single-valued in all 267 cells across all 11 arms (0 multi-valued), which makes those
counts pass-count independent by construction. They will be re-confirmed against the completed 22
passes rather than recomputed, and a disagreement would mean the policy moved mid-run.

### Two namespaces in one CSV, overlapping

chain203's `slice` column holds `ov1`..`ov22` and its `build` column holds `ovp`, `ov2`, `ov2b`, …
so **`ov2` and `ov4` are simultaneously pass labels and arm names in the same file**, and `ov8` and
`ov16` join them as the run lengthens. Confirmed on both chains' data.

It is inert in `an_c203.py` today, and inert *by accident* rather than by design: the two namespaces
sit at different levels of one dict (`T[build][cell][slice]`) and are never looked up against each
other, and the landed-pass set is derived from filenames rather than labels. Any code that filters
across the two — a `startswith`, a set intersection, a dict keyed by "the label or the arm" —
silently returns the wrong rows.

The live label set is read from the **first data row of each file** rather than by copying the
directory, because `slice` and `build` are constant within a file — verified 0 exceptions in 66
files here and independently 0 in 98 on the chain202 ledger. That makes the check a few hundred
bytes per file instead of 29MB next to a live measurement. **The constancy check belongs inside the
extraction, not before it:** a resume, a retry or a concatenation that put two slices in one file
would make row 1 correct for the row and wrong for the file, and nothing in the output would say
so.

The second hazard is ordering, and **it is already active.** An earlier draft of this paragraph said
it was "hidden by the run's length — at chain203's six labels the lexical and numeric orders agree".
That was read off the six-pass snapshot, one paragraph after this document warned against carrying
snapshot figures forward. Read from the live directory instead, the labels are `ov1`..`ov13` and the
orders diverge:

| labels present | lexical order agrees? | first six by string order |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | yes | ov1 ov2 ov3 ov4 ov5 ov6 |
| 9 | yes | ov1 ov2 ov3 ov4 ov5 ov6 |
| 10 | **no** | ov1 ov10 ov2 ov3 ov4 ov5 |
| 13 (live) | **no** | ov1 ov10 ov11 ov12 ov13 ov2 |
| 22 (final) | **no** | ov1 ov10 ov11 ov12 ov13 ov14 |

**Divergence began at pass 10**, some hours before the paragraph claiming otherwise was written.

The collision count grows too, and an earlier version of this sentence gave the wrong onset for the
last one — it said `ov16` joins at twenty-two, which is where it was *observed*, not where it
*arrives*. The schedule is not a table but a rule: **an arm named `ovN` starts colliding at pass
N**, because the label for pass N is the string `ovN`.

| passes | collisions |
|---|---|
| 2 | `ov2` |
| 4 | `ov2` `ov4` |
| 8 | `ov2` `ov4` `ov8` |
| **16** | `ov2` `ov4` `ov8` `ov16` |
| 22 | unchanged since 16 — four |

So at the completed 22 there are four, and there have been four since pass 16. Stating the onset as
a rule rather than a row is what makes the next two points visible at all — and the error being in
the *commit* while the correct figure was in a message is the wrong way round, since the commit is
what outlives the exchange.

**The hazard is bounded at five and saturates there.** The rule partitions the eleven arms: only
those whose name is `ov` followed by digits can ever match a pass label, and the rest are immune for
a reason that cannot change — no pass label carries a `b` suffix and there is no pass `p`.

| | arms |
|---|---|
| can ever collide | `ov2` `ov4` `ov8` `ov16` `ov24` — **5** |
| structurally immune | `ovp` `ov2b` `ov4b` `ov8b` `ov16b` `ov24b` — 6 |

"Grows with the run" and "grows to five and stops" are different risk profiles, and an onset rule
with no ceiling attached invites the first reading.

**And the severity at run end is set by the rotation's design parameter, not by the labels.**
Position balance requires the pass count to be a multiple of the arm count, so the reachable run
lengths are multiples of 11:

| balanced halves | passes | collisions |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 11 | 3 |
| 2 | **22** | **4** ← this run |
| 3 | 33 | 5 |
| 4 | 44 | 5 (saturated) |

So `ov24` escapes only because the design chose two halves rather than three. A future chain adding
a third half for tighter bands would **pick up the fifth collision as a side effect of a decision
made about statistics** — nobody choosing "33 passes for a narrower interval" would think they were
touching a label namespace. That coupling is invisible in any table of observations; it needs the
rule. So "inert because the run is short" is gone and only one guarantee remains.

That guarantee is now **audited rather than argued.** Every site in `an_c203.py` that touches a pass
label, all fourteen of them:

- ingestion uses the label as a **dict key** (`T[build][cell][slice][arm]`) — order-irrelevant;
- the pass count is `len({...})` over a set — order-irrelevant;
- `PASSES_LANDED` / `PASSES_PARTIAL` are **integers parsed from filenames**, not labels, and sorted
  numerically;
- the shared-pass set in `ratios_keyed` is a **membership** test, and the `sorted()` beside it sorts
  the resulting *ratios*, not the labels;
- the CV pass iterates a dict without ordering it.

No code path orders or slices the label set, and none looks a label up against an arm name. That is
a stronger statement than "the landed-pass set comes from filenames", and it is the reason the
hazard is inert at thirteen labels as well as at six.

Reported by `labels_c203.py` in the verification battery rather than as a refusal inside the
analyzer. The analyzer is the instrument for a measurement in flight, its battery is green, and the
hazard is audited-inert — adding a refusal to a frozen instrument for an inert hazard trades a real
regression risk against no present benefit. Both findings are a rename away from being impossible.

## The census audited one file, and the battery had grown past it

`checks_c203.py` reports 73 checks with 0 untested, and that number did not move when the
verification battery grew from thirteen stages to fifteen. A peer asked which of three things that
meant. It is the third: **the census enumerates checks of `an_c203.py` and nothing else**, so a new
battery stage was never going to change it.

The question found what the constant total was hiding. A static scan of the eleven diagnostic
scripts — the ones that audit the analyzer — says they carry **23 refusals between them, of which
exactly one had ever been demonstrated to fire.** "Beside every check, an input that makes it fail"
was being applied to the instrument and to none of the things measuring it, including the two
scripts written that evening *because* defects had just been found.

`checks2_c203.py` is that census for the rest, and it now runs in the battery:

| | |
|---|---|
| refusals in source, across 11 scripts | **23** |
| FIRES | **13** |
| DID NOT FIRE | 0 |
| **UNTESTED** | **10** (was 22) |

The inventory is **scanned from source** rather than listed, so a guard added later appears as
UNTESTED instead of vanishing from the denominator. The ten that remain are almost all of one
shape — "the analyzer refused, so I could not measure" in `spike`, `swapcells`, `meta` and `cond`,
plus two corpus-thinness guards in `jointfail` — and they are reported rather than quietly dropped.

Three defects in the census itself, found while building it, each the class it exists to catch:

- **It reported 8 firing refusals and 23 untested in the same run.** Rows were keyed on a
  hand-written label while the inventory was keyed on scanned source text, so the two sets never
  intersected and the report described an object other than the one it measured. Fixed by having
  each row name a substring of the *source* refusal it targets, with an assertion that the target
  matches **exactly one** inventory entry — which immediately caught a mistyped target rather than
  letting it mark nothing.
- **One row read DID NOT FIRE because the test was wrong, not the guard.** `passlog`'s "holds no
  rows" is about the rotation *table*; the input supplied an empty *log*. The input had been built
  from the message's wording rather than from the code path above it.
- **An input built for one refusal reached an earlier one** — an empty log with two arms tripped
  the table-width check first. The same preemption hazard that hid four checks in the analyzer's
  census, in the census of the censuses.

### The census of the censuses closes: 23 of 23, and the 23 is measured

The previous section left the second census reporting **13 of 23 refusals fired and 10 untested**,
and left the 23 itself resting on a regex over source text. Both are now closed.

**Is 23 the right denominator?** A regex can only miss, never invent, so its count is a lower
bound. An AST pass over the same eleven files classifies *every* exit path rather than the ones
matching a pattern:

```
34 exit paths = 23 refusals + 8 exit-status calls + 3 usage messages + 0 unclassified
 0 raise statements, so sys.exit is the only route a refusal can take
 regex 23 vs AST 23 -- AGREE
```

The zero on `raise` is what makes the enumeration exhaustive rather than merely a second opinion:
had any file refused by exception, a `sys.exit`-only scan would be incomplete by construction and
no amount of agreement on the sites it *does* see would show it.

The first version of this cross-check was wrong, in the direction that condemns the thing it
validates. It tested `isinstance(arg, ast.Constant)` for the message, but `sys.exit("REFUSE: %s"
% x)` is a **BinOp** whose `.left` holds the literal — so every *formatted* refusal was
classified invisible, which is precisely the set the regex does see. It reported "scanner 23, AST
34, difference 11" and would have filed a correct scanner as defective. **When a new validator
disagrees with an established subject, suspect the validator: it is the newer code.** The audit
now runs on four inputs built to defeat it — a single-quoted refusal the regex cannot see, a
computed exit message, a refusal via `raise`, and a duplicate key — and each fires on its own
branch.

**The ten untested.** All ten lived in scripts that *drive* the analyzer rather than parse its
output, so no fixture built from data could reach them: they fire when the analyzer misbehaves,
and the analyzer does not misbehave. A wrapper wired to exactly one collaborator cannot
demonstrate its own guards. Four wrappers now take the analyzer path from `C203_ANALYZER`,
matching the `--analyzer` flag `meta_c203.py` already had, and the ten are reached by:

| refusal | input that fires it |
|---|---|
| `spike` / `swapcells` / `meta` "the analyzer refused" | a stub analyzer that exits 1 |
| `nbootstab` "analyzer exit %d" | the same stub |
| `swapcells` "no estimate rows parsed" | a stub exiting 0 with no estimate rows |
| `cond` "the instrumented copy does not reproduce" | an analyzer reporting its own line count — instrumentation inserts lines, so it cannot reproduce itself under instrumentation |
| `meta` "relation(s) VIOLATED" | the `scale` mutant `metafire_c203.py` already builds |
| `meta` "declared but produced no verdict" | a mutant of *meta*, one relation's bookkeeping suppressed — the guard watches meta's own conservation, so only a mutation of meta can reach it |
| `jointfail` ×2 (two thinness guards) | subsetted corpora |

The two `jointfail` fixtures are the ones that needed care. Both guards are thinness guards with
the same threshold, so the second fixture must keep the common-key count *above* the first guard's
limit or the first refusal preempts it and the row records a firing that never happened. It holds
24 common keys against a threshold of 15, and fires the second guard on residual coverage instead.

**A bookkeeping defect the fix exposed.** Tested-ness is keyed on `(script, key)`, where `key` was
the refusal's literal text up to its first format conversion. `jointfail`'s two guards both begin
`only %d`, so both keyed to `only` — firing either would have marked both tested and **removed a
genuinely untested refusal from the denominator**, which is the single number this census exists
to report. The key now collapses conversions (`%d` → `%`) instead of truncating at the first one,
and key uniqueness is asserted, with the assertion exercised on a colliding pair.

```
23 refusals in source across 11 scripts: 23 FIRES, 0 DID NOT FIRE, 0 UNTESTED
```

### Two defects in the completion script, both found by the same question

`final_c203.sh` was written before the data landed so the invocation would not be reconstructed
from memory next to a result. Re-reading it against the live machine found two steps that would
have run and produced something plausible.

**The execution record was read from a stale local mirror.** The script's own header states the
principle — "two reads of one file are one reading, so the digest has to come from the run's
filesystem" — and applies it to the rotation table via `--orders-sha256`, but the `wrote`
sequence, the *only* record in the set that observes what executed rather than echoing the
schedule back, was read from `/tmp/c203_rw.log`. Nothing keeps that file current. At 19:12 it was
**19264 bytes on redwood against 16195 locally, 88 minutes behind**. Earlier the same evening I
had read progress from that mirror and announced a 3.4× slowdown that the host's file mtimes
disproved, so this is the second time one stale copy produced a confident wrong statement. The
step now takes the digest on redwood *before* copying and compares it after: a truncated transfer
refuses, and so does a log still being appended to, which is the correct treatment of a run that
has not finished.

**The corpus-distinctness digest could not run at all.** It pointed at
`/scratch/bobbyy/suitesparse`, which does not exist, and on failure did `|| echo "(cache absent
locally; run on redwood)"` — so a step the script itself calls "an input to every effective n"
could be absent while the bands printed underneath it. Worse, `patdigest_c203.py` only accepted
`.mtx`/`.mtx.gz`, and the corpus the harness actually timed is scipy `.npz` under the
group-qualified cache that `mrgate_ov.py` was given as `--cache`. There are 2513 Matrix Market
files on the host, under `ss_extra` — but digesting those answers a different question, namely
whether two SuiteSparse matrices are equal, not whether the two things this run timed are. The
reader now loads the `.npz` the run read, all **10 of 10 keys resolve** (`ss/case9/case9_A_02.npz`,
`ss/Meszaros/aa3/aa3.npz`, …), the cache layout being the same group-qualified one that silently
dropped 50 keys on MKT, and the fetch derives its key list from `GROUPS` via `--keys` rather than
repeating it.

The reader is normalised so Matrix Market and scipy give the **same** digest for the same matrix
— 0-based indices, one fixed value format — because otherwise a cross-format comparison reports
"different" for every key and the disagreement is the encoding. Checked on a matrix stored both
ways: pattern and value digests agree; changing one value moves the value digest and not the
pattern; adding one entry moves the pattern.

The digest itself is still deferred until chain203 finishes, for the reason the script already
gave: reading those matrices off the filesystem the harness is timing against is the perturbation.
Only the mechanics were exercised here, on a non-matrix file.

### The battery's log was abridging away the verdicts it exists to record

The battery prints each stage's output through `tail`, so a long stage contributes only its last
lines. That is deliberate — the detail tables are long. It silently assumes every stage puts its
conclusion last, and two did not.

Moving the AST audit ahead of the census report, so the census total would survive abridgement,
pushed the audit's own verdict out the other side: the log then carried "23 FIRES, 0 UNTESTED"
without the line establishing that 23 is the right denominator. One end of a truncation fixed,
the other broken, and caught only by grepping the log rather than reading the exit code — the
stage was green throughout.

Asking the question of every stage found the second: **`cond` logged 14 lines against a 14-line
window, and all 14 were detail.** It computes a summary — how many condition operands were
instrumented, how many went both ways, and how many of the one-way ones sit in a guard rather
than a selector, which is the number that belongs beside the "no MC/DC" disclaimer — and then
prints the list of one-way operands *after* it. So the battery log contained no statement of what
the condition-coverage stage concluded, and had not since the stage was added. `recip` also hit
its window exactly but puts its verdict last, so it loses only detail; a third apparent hit was
my own parser absorbing the trailing exit-code table.

Two changes, at the level of the class rather than the instance:

- `cond` prints detail first and its verdict last, the convention that makes abridging safe for
  any stage, present or future. Raising one stage's window would have fixed one stage.
- `stage()` now announces abridgement: `[abridged: N lines produced, last T shown]`. A reader
  cannot otherwise distinguish an abridged stage from a short one, and neither could I.

The census stage is exempted from abridging entirely, because that stage *is* the completeness
claim: its per-refusal rows, the audit, and the total are all load-bearing.

### The battery's exit-code table could only ever print zero

Making abridgement visible required rewriting `stage()`, and the rewrite changed a number that
was not supposed to move. The old form was:

```bash
echo "### $n"; "$@" 2>&1 | tail -${TAIL:-14}
NAME+=("$n"); RC+=("${PIPESTATUS[0]}")
```

`NAME+=("$n")` is a command, and every command resets `PIPESTATUS`. So `RC` recorded the exit
status of an array append. Reduced to two lines: `false | cat` followed by that exact sequence
records 0, and recorded directly it records 1. **The table was structurally incapable of
reporting a failure**, and "all sixteen stages exit 0" had been a statement about array appends
for as long as the battery had existed.

Capturing the status properly turned one stage red on the next run, and it was a real one.
`nbootstab` had been measuring nothing. The battery invoked it as `nbootstab_c203.py "$LIVE"`,
but the sweep is built for the clean fixture — its partition string and its `--min-passes 12`
both describe the fixture — while the local live snapshot holds **six** passes against a run
that is at fifteen. The analyzer refused on the first call, the stage printed a table header
with no rows under it, and the exit-code table reported success. Run on its designed input it
sweeps three values over 83 rows: **4 unstable (5%) at nboot=150, 2 (2%) at 600, 0 at 2400**,
with a bound spread of 0.0115 at 150 that matches the figure in the script's own docstring.

Two corrections to that, both caught before they reached a conclusion:

- The analyzer *does* refuse below the pre-registered nboot — `an_c203.py:82` — but only when
  `--fixture` is absent. `nbootstab` passes it, which is how the sweep is permitted to run at
  all. A first reading of this called the refusal imaginary.
- The 5% does not contradict the 7% quoted as the pre-registration's justification. That 7% was
  measured on chain203's **first six passes** (`an_c203.py:73`); 5% is the same sweep on the
  fixture. Pointing the battery at the fixture silently changed which corpus the number
  describes, so the completion script now runs the sweep again against the finished 22-pass
  rotation, and the justification quotes each figure with the corpus it came from.

That is the third instance today of one root cause: **a local copy of remote state that nothing
keeps current.** The run log was 88 minutes behind, the corpus-cache path did not exist, and the
live snapshot is nine passes stale. Only the first was visible as staleness; the other two
presented as a passing stage and a plausible number.

The table now ends in `BATTERY PASS -- 16 of 16 stages exited 0` and the script exits nonzero
otherwise, so "green" is a claim the battery makes rather than one a reader assembles from rows.

### Fail closed on the pass count, and a positive control for the status column

Three claims tonight were built on a local snapshot holding six passes while the run had landed
fifteen, and each was caught by someone writing a sentence about it. A sentence does not survive
the next reader. One stage caught it mechanically instead — `nbootstab`, and only by accident of
carrying a required pass count of its own, which is what surfaced the whole family.

`snapshot_c203.py` gives that property to every stage that reads the corpus, at two levels:

- `stamp()` — unconditional. Each stage names the rotation its numbers came from.
- `require()` — fails closed at a minimum **the caller names**. These diagnostic stages have no
  intrinsic minimum; the requirement belongs to the claim being made, not to the code, so a
  default here would have been a fabricated number. `final_c203.sh` names 22 for all four, and
  the battery names none, which is what separates a self-test from a result.

All four refuse against the six-pass copy at `--min-passes 22` and run clean with no minimum.

**The fix re-created the blind spot it was closing.** Moving the refusal into a shared helper
made it invisible to a per-file scan of the four scripts that reach it — the exact class this
census exists to find, produced by the act of removing a duplicate. `snapshot_c203.py` is now a
census member: **24 refusals across 12 scripts, 24 FIRES, 0 UNTESTED, regex 24 == AST 24.**

**And the stamp was printed first, so abridgement cut it.** The line whose whole purpose is to
stop a six-pass number being read as a twenty-two-pass number was the line the log threw away —
the third time in one evening that abridging ate the thing qualifying a number, and this time
the victim was written two hours after the first two were found. It now re-prints at exit,
beside the numbers it qualifies, and is not registered on the refusal path.

**A positive control for the exit column.** A status line that can only report success is not a
status line. `rc-control` is a stage that exits 3 on purpose and must read 3; if it ever reads 0
the column is broken again and no other row on it means anything. `stage()` gained an expected
exit code, so a stage whose passing case is a refusal can say so instead of being excused in
prose. The table now ends:

```
  rc-control   exit 3   as expected
BATTERY PASS -- 17 of 17 stages matched their expected exit code
```

Two defects surfaced while writing those. The scanner regex had become two copies, the
inventory's and the cross-check's — the drift a cross-check exists to detect, sitting inside the
cross-check. And a prefix assignment to a shell *function* persists after it returns, so
`TAIL=24 stage x` was setting the abridgement window for every later stage that did not set its
own; nothing has been misread by it, only because every stage after the first happens to set one.

The cross-check also has its own positive control now, which it needed more than most: a
disagreeing cross-check is read as indicting the original, so a defective one does not merely
fail to confirm — it manufactures a defect in a working instrument, which is what the first
version of the AST audit nearly did. Two deliberately broken scanners run against the real
sources, one under-counting (11 files disagree) and one over-counting (2), and both are caught.

### Correction: the `TAIL` leak does not exist

The previous section reports that a prefix assignment to a shell function persists after the
function returns, so `TAIL=24 stage x` was setting the abridgement window for every later stage
that did not set its own. **That is wrong.** It was asserted from recollection of shell semantics
and never tested.

Tested: in bash 3.2.57, which is the shell this battery runs under, `TAIL=26 f` does not persist
past `f`. The behaviour is real only under `set -o posix`, which the battery never enables. The
battery's own log agrees — of **13 abridged stages, 0 used a window other than their own declared
one**, and **10 stages carry no `TAIL` and follow one that sets it**, every one of them using the
default 14. The follow-up explanation offered at the time, that nothing had been misread because
every later stage happens to set its own window, was wrong in the same breath: ten do not.

The `unset TAIL WANT_RC` added alongside is harmless and defensible under POSIX mode, but it
fixed nothing, and the three abridgement incidents are **one design weakness, not one bug with a
known fix**. An attempt to collapse them to a single root cause would have been wrong.

### The consumer set, derived rather than grepped

"All four snapshot consumers refuse at `--min-passes 22`" — four came from grepping the battery
for stages passed `$LIVE`. That is a pattern match with precisely the completeness problem the
AST pass had closed for refusals an hour earlier, and it is the wrong tool for the same reason.

`readers_c203.py` counts every call that opens the corpus, by any route, and classifies each:

```
41 scripts read the corpus; 18 belong to this chain. Of those, 5 are protected
against reporting a number from the wrong rotation -- 4 through the shared helper
and 1 by a pass-count guard of its own; the rest cannot go stale (3 read a sealed
directory, 3 construct a corpus, 6 build and read back their own fixture).
```

The one with its own guard is `an_c203.py`, whose `--min-passes` produced the "6 passes, below
the 12" refusal that surfaced this entire family. An intermediate hand count of five was also a
guess that happened to land: `an_c200` and `an_c202` carry the same guard but belong to earlier
chains, so ordering the classifier by mechanism before era counted them as protected consumers of
a corpus they will never read. Era has to be decided first.

`UNCLASSIFIED` is a refusal rather than a shrug, and the scan root is an argument — wired to its
own directory the census could only ever report the clean case, which is the defect it exists to
detect, one level up. It carries a guard, so it is a census member: **25 refusals across 13
scripts, 25 FIRES, 0 UNTESTED, regex 25 == AST 25.**

**Coverage and protection are different numbers.** 25 of 25 refusals firing says every guard
works. It says nothing about whether a reader calls one: a consumer that forgets `--min-passes`
is unprotected by a guard the census scores as fully tested. Both are printed, with a line saying
so, because the battery deliberately names no minimum for its own stages and `final_c203.sh`
names 22 — the guard is inert by design in one caller and binding in the other.

### The thirteen cleared readers, and a clearance that was false

Thirteen of the eighteen in-chain corpus readers were cleared with one sentence — "the rest
cannot go stale" — which is many items under one reason with no per-item evidence, the shape
this census exists to break up. Checking each reason found two problems.

**The "sealed" clearance was false.** Three scripts were cleared as reading a sealed directory.
There is **no manifest naming that directory and it is writable**; a parent `SHA256SUMS` exists
and does not cover it. So "sealed" was a claim about today's state, and unverified even as that.
The clearance that survives is weaker and purely code-level: they never open *this* chain's
snapshot, so no number of theirs can carry this chain's rotation. Immutability is not
established, the census says so, and the check runs rather than being assumed.

**A second clearance rested on nothing.** The fixture class accepted `"W = "` and `"def d("` as
evidence — predicates that match almost any script — and one of six was classified on those
alone. That one, `fixture_c203.py`, reads one corpus and *writes* another, reporting no
measurement at all. **A clearance is only as good as the narrowest predicate that granted it.**
The classes are now printed with counts and a code-versus-state column:

```
 5 PROTECTED    4 call the pass-count helper; 1 carries its own --min-passes
13 CLEARED      8 code        create a corpus directory; report no measurement
                1 code        builds a fixture under a known root and reads it back
                3 code+STATE  hardcoded to another chain's directory -- seal check above
                1 code        is the pass-count helper; reading the corpus is its job
```

### Every scanner takes its root as an argument

Caught four times in this project: three harnesses that hardcoded a ledger path, and the reader
census above, which wired to its own directory could only ever have reported the clean case. A
family with four instances earns a check. `scanroot_c203.py` reports **0 violations with its
positive control CAUGHT** — a refusing scanner with a fixed root is detected, so the zero is
evidence rather than a property of the check.

Reaching that took three narrowings: 16 hits, then 8, then 4, nearly all false positives from
function parameters and locals derived from them. A check with that false-positive rate gets
switched off, which is worse than not having one. The scope that survives is precise — a script
that *can refuse*, whose root is a module-level string literal it does not itself create. A
script with no refusal makes no "clean" claim for a fixed root to falsely certify, and a root the
script creates is its own scratch area.

The first version recursed without bound and had to be killed: the positive control re-runs the
script, and the child ran its own control. **A self-invoking check needs a base case** — obvious
in a recursive function, easy to miss when the recursion is a subprocess.

### The cross-check condemned the scanner it was built to confirm

`scanroot_c203.py` contains `sys.exit("REFUSE` twice as **data** — once as a search pattern, once
inside a fixture it generates. The text scan counted 3 refusals; the parse counts the 1 that
exists. On eleven files the two agreed, which is what made the scan look adequate; the twelfth
file it had never seen was enough to separate them.

**The inventory is now AST-derived.** The text scan is kept as a reported cross-check that names
where it over-counts, and over-counting is no longer fatal while under-counting still is — the
parse only counts a literal in `sys.exit` position, where the scan counts the text anywhere. The
two scanner controls were updated to watch the channel each defect now travels on, which the
earlier pair stopped doing the moment the classification changed.

**26 refusals across 14 scripts, 26 FIRES, 0 DID NOT FIRE, 0 UNTESTED. Battery 19 of 19.**

### The scanner-root check caught 0 of its 4 real instances

The previous section reported `scanroot_c203.py` at 0 violations with its positive control
caught, after three narrowings from 16 hits to 8 to 4. A synthetic fixture is a weak control for
a defect with real instances on disk, so the check was run against them.

**They exist and they are identifiable.** `COMPILER_IR_REFACTOR_HANDOFF.md` records *"four
harnesses' hardcoded ledger paths are now overridable — the fourth time that defect has been
caught here"*, and names the tree: `strategy_emission.py`, `legality_reach.py`,
`strategy_correctness.py`, `two_phase_probe.py`. `CLAUDE.md` line 197 still says the defect "has
been caught three times", so **the count in CLAUDE.md is stale** and any search anchored on it
under-counts. All four were fixed by making the path `os.environ.get(...)` overridable, so
reverting that fix reconstructs the historical defect exactly — a control set of real code
rather than a fixture.

**Against that set the check caught 0 of 4.** Three independent mechanisms, each a narrowing
made when the check knew one fewer shape of the defect than exists:

| narrowing | what it assumed | what every real instance does |
|---|---|---|
| root must be `ast.Constant` | a bare string literal | `os.path.expanduser("...")`, a `Call` |
| consumer must be `glob`/`walk`/`listdir` | a *scan* root | `sys.path.insert` — a *dependency* root |
| "can refuse" = text `sys.exit("REFUSE` | one spelling of refusal | `raise SystemExit` |

A fourth surfaced while fixing: a gate requiring at least one scan-or-inline root dropped
`strategy_emission`, whose hardcoded ledger is *only* a module-level binding used further down.
The refusal-spelling one is the worst of them — the census audit two sections above exists partly
to test the `raise` route, and the text match went in anyway.

The synthetic fixture was strictly easier than every real instance, which is exactly why it kept
firing through all three narrowings. **A control that survives a narrowing only licenses it if
the control is at least as hard as the thing being narrowed away.**

Now **4 of 4 caught reverted, 0 of 4 flagged in their fixed form**, both directions, with the
real instances as the standing control and the synthetic used only if the ledger is absent from
the host. The predicate is a non-overridable path fixed at import — literal, `expanduser`, or
`join` of those — that is absolute or home-relative and not under a scratch directory, in a
script that can refuse, bound at module level and used, or passed inline to a path-consuming
call.

**It then found two real hits in our own tree**: `cond_c203.py`'s chain202 ledger root and
`readers_c203.py`'s `SEALED` prefix. Both now take the same `os.environ.get` override the four
historical fixes used. Our tree is clean under the repaired check, which it was not under the
check that passed.

### Correction to the citation, and `ast.Constant` as one predicate rather than two incidents

**The citation above is wrong.** The previous section says
`COMPILER_IR_REFACTOR_HANDOFF.md` "records four harnesses' hardcoded ledger paths ... and names
the tree". Checked:

| name | HANDOFF | DESIGN | PHASE6_REVIEW |
|---|---|---|---|
| strategy_emission | 0 | 0 | 3 |
| legality_reach | 0 | 0 | 2 |
| strategy_correctness | 0 | 0 | 4 |
| two_phase_probe | 0 | 0 | 6 |

The *count* sentence is in the handoff, at line 32655. The *names* are only in the PHASE6
review — which is the right source anyway, being the definitive numbered document while the
handoff is an append-only slice log. And the names did not come from either: I obtained them by
listing the harness directory. One artefact was credited with two jobs, one of which was mine.

**`ast.Constant` bit twice tonight, in two independent scripts, and it is one predicate.** The
AST cross-check's first version tested `isinstance(arg, ast.Constant)` for a refusal message and
would have condemned a correct scanner; `scanroot`'s parse accepted only `ast.Constant` for a
path and missed all four real instances. `ast.Constant` matches a **literal**, and real code
builds paths and messages with `os.path.expanduser`, `os.path.join`, f-strings or `%`. So an AST
predicate over a path or a diagnostic string that keys on `Constant` matches the toy case and
misses the realistic one — and the toy case is usually the fixture, which is the mechanism by
which a synthetic control keeps firing while the check is broken. **Match the node that produces
a string, not the node that is one.**

### One definition of "what counts as a refusal"

Three times in one evening, one census held knowledge another census's predicate lacked: the
analyzer census's demonstrated refusing inputs were what the diagnostic census needed; the
refusal census's parse was what the reader census needed; and the exit-path classifier knew
about `raise SystemExit` while the scanner-root check's private copy tested only for the text
`sys.exit("REFUSE` — which is why that check excluded all four of its real instances before
examining a single path. Every one of those is a predicate implemented twice and diverging, the
same root cause as the scanner regex having become two copies.
