`refusal_c203.py` now holds the classifier and both censuses import it. It is a census member
from the start despite carrying no guard of its own: the denominator has to track a shared
module **before** a guard lands in it, which is the order the pass-count helper taught the hard
way. A member contributing zero is the correct reading, and the total is unchanged at 26 across
15 scripts.

"What counts as a root" and "what counts as a reader" are still duplicated. Unifying them is
right and is not being done immediately before the completed read has to run.

### Which repair was load-bearing, measured rather than read

`4 of 4 caught / 0 of 4 flagged` proves the repaired check works and says nothing about which of
its three repairs mattered. Worse, the refusal pre-filter ran first and excluded all four
instances before either other predicate saw a path — so two of the three were diagnosed by
reading the code. A decomposition that adds up is not a mechanism.

The ablation reverts one repair at a time against the four real instances:

| ablation | reverts | caught |
|---|---|---|
| refusal test | parse-based `can_refuse` → the original text match | 0 of 4 |
| path parse | `expanduser`/`join` accepted → `ast.Constant` only | 0 of 4 |
| consumer set | `sys.path.insert` accepted → scanning calls only | 1 of 4 |

**All three are load-bearing.** With the pre-filter fixed, the `Constant`-only parse alone still
hides all four, so each is independently sufficient. That is the evidence the earlier claim
lacked, and it could as easily have gone the other way.

**Writing it produced the same defect it exists to prevent.** In the battery the ablation
reported *"0 of 3 repairs are load-bearing"*, the opposite of the standalone run. The
shared-predicate refactor two commits earlier had given `scanroot` a `from refusal_c203 import
can_refuse`, and the ablation writes its mutant to a temp directory where that import fails.
Every variant crashed, the baseline caught 0 of 4, and nothing could score below zero. **A
measurement whose failure mode is indistinguishable from its null result** — the `PIPESTATUS`
shape, one level up, and it passed once before an unrelated refactor moved a dependency under
it. It now puts the source directory on the path and refuses when the baseline scores below the
full control set, because "the baseline is broken" and "no repair matters" print the same thing
otherwise.

**And one of its guards was unreachable by construction.** Any target that fails to anchor also
catches nothing, so the broken-baseline guard always preempted the no-op guard. Anchors are now
checked before the baseline is measured, which is the right order regardless: a mis-anchored
ablation is a property of the definitions, a broken baseline is a property of the control set.
The census reported this correctly by naming which refusal fired instead of the intended one.

### The control set is not fully reproducible from the repo

The four instances are named in `COMPILER_IR_REFACTOR_PHASE6_REVIEW.md` — except that
`legality_reach` appears there twice and both times as the prefix of an **output artefact**
(`legality_reach_base.json`, `legality_reach_repin.json`), never as the harness. Three of the
four are named as harness files; the fourth is only inferable. The check now reads the names
from the review, lists the directory, and reports the difference standingly: *1 harness holds an
overridable ledger path but is not named in the review.*

I nearly deleted that finding. The first reaction was "a predicate matching one spelling again",
and widening the match to bare stems would have counted the JSON artefacts as naming the harness
and silently agreed the control set was complete. **Widening a predicate because it reports
something inconvenient removes the report, not the cause.**

**Battery 20 of 20; 29 refusals across 16 scripts, 29 FIRES, 0 UNTESTED.**

### Six harnesses, two override mechanisms, and a detector that knew one

Chasing a filename in the review turned up that the harness directory holds **six** scripts with
a ledger path, not four. Two of them — `result_write_boundary_probe.py` and
`result_write_reach.py` — have no `os.environ.get` at all, which briefly looked like two unfixed
instances of the defect. They are not: the path is an argparse `--harness` **default**, equally
overridable, just by flag rather than by environment. There are no live instances.

The real finding is about the detector. It keyed on `os.environ.get` and therefore saw **4 of
the 6**. **A detector that knows one spelling of the *fix* under-reports the population it is
reconciling** — the same one-spelling problem as matching `\w+\.py`, now on the other side of
the comparison, and the third time tonight a text predicate has been narrower than the thing it
names. Both mechanisms are reported now.

Also checked: `strategy_correctness_reach.py` is named in the review but does not exist on disk,
so it is a review-only name and not a fifth instance.

### Consolidation moves a risk, it does not remove one

A shared predicate module was the fix for three divergence defects, and it is what broke the
ablation: the ablation copies a script out of its directory and runs it elsewhere, where the
sibling import does not resolve. The general statement is not "shared modules are risky" but
**consolidation converts a divergence risk into a dependency risk, and anything that relocates,
copies or sandboxes a file pays it.**

That is the second cost of consolidation found here. The first was that removing a duplicate
also removes the per-file evidence a guard is present, which is why a shared module joins the
census the moment it exists rather than when it acquires a guard. Both costs are real, both are
now guarded, and the divergence was still worth fixing — three defects against one.

### Two families, named

**A measurement whose failure mode is indistinguishable from its null result.** Six instances:
the exit table that could only print 0; `shasum -c` on a CRC-32 manifest printing zero OK and
zero FAILED; a driver refusing on its first call and printing a bare header; a census
denominator fixed by construction; an ablation whose broken baseline made every variant score
"not load-bearing"; and, already in the tracked record from earlier work, a suite runner that
aborted before measuring and reported success. An absent check is visible — a check that runs,
passes, and cannot fail is *more* reassuring than none. **The null result has to be
distinguishable by construction**, which is what the failing-on-purpose stage, the
not-vacuous count, and the baseline refusal each supply.

**Preemption: a guard made unreachable by a guard in front of it.** Four instances — an input
built for one refusal reaching an earlier one; the broken-baseline guard preempting the no-op
guard; the refusal pre-filter short-circuiting the path predicates it was measured beside; four
checks hidden behind earlier ones in the analyzer census. Standing form: order guards so the
cheapest-to-satisfy precondition is verified first, and assert **which** refusal fired.

### The fixes were not applied to every copy

The harness population is not one directory. There are **17 harness directories** in the cache
and the named scripts exist in several milestones each, so reconciling against the current one
cannot see a stale copy in an earlier one — and a stale copy carries the original defect, is
never run again, and nothing points at it. `strategy_correctness_reach.py`, which the previous
section called a review-only name, is on disk in three other milestones; that conclusion was
drawn from looking in one place.

A file-level test — the file contains a ledger literal *and* contains `os.environ.get`,
`argparse` or `sys.argv` *somewhere* — clears all 45 files that hold a ledger path. It is
necessary and not sufficient, because it never establishes that the **specific** literal is the
overridable one. The per-literal version walks each path constant outward and asks whether that
constant is a default of an override construct:

```
17 harness dirs, 155 .py files scanned, 47 ledger literals
11 files hold a literal that sits inside no override at all
```

`workspace-confound/harness/suppress_probe.py` holds three, and uses `sys.argv` elsewhere in the
file, which is exactly how the co-occurrence test clears it:

```python
REACH = os.path.expanduser("~/.cache/scorch-codex/two-pass-position/harness")
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.expanduser(".../workspace-confound/worktrees/base-5113e0c/src"))
TREE  = os.path.expanduser(".../workspace-confound/worktrees/base-5113e0c")
```

So "caught four times" counts **fixes applied to four specific files**, not the absence of the
defect from the tree. These are historical ledger artefacts under `SHA256SUMS` and are not being
edited — the finding is about what the record means, not a repair to make.

My own predicate needed the same correction twice over on the way: it first matched any string
containing `scorch-codex`, so a docstring *explaining* where the ledger lives counted as a
hardcoded path, 2 of the first 15 hits. **A literal that mentions a thing is not a use of it** —
the mention-versus-use error for the third time tonight, this time in the predicate written to
avoid it.

**The symmetry, which is the general lesson.** A reconciliation compares two sets, and a
one-spelling predicate on either side biases it in a different direction: on the *fix* side it
under-reports the fixed population and manufactures apparent violations; on the *name* side it
under-reports the named population and manufactures apparent gaps. Both of tonight's errors —
keying on `os.environ.get`, requiring `\w+\.py` — are that. Enumerate by the thing that cannot
be spelled two ways: the literal path on one side, the file on disk on the other.

### Correction: 11 files hold the literal, 1 defeats the rule

The previous section's headline — "11 harness files still carry a hardcoded ledger path" — is
true as a literal count and wrong as a statement about the rule. The rule is *"harnesses take a
tree root as `$1`"*, and stratifying the 11 against that:

| | |
|---|---|
| read `sys.argv` and hardcode only where **sibling harness code** lives | 10 |
| never read `sys.argv`, pin the measured tree, and **forge** `sys.argv` | 1 |

Ten of them take their tree root correctly. What they hardcode is the location of a sibling
harness module they import — brittleness of exactly the kind the shared-predicate module
inflicted on the ablation tonight, not a harness measuring the wrong tree. Counting them under
the same heading over-states the rule's defect by ten.

**The one real instance is worse than a literal.**
`workspace-confound/harness/suppress_probe.py` is the only file of the eleven that never reads
`sys.argv` — it has zero reads and **two writes**:

```python
TREE = os.path.expanduser("~/.cache/scorch-codex/workspace-confound/worktrees/base-5113e0c")
sys.argv = ["strategy_correctness_reach.py", TREE, "/dev/null", "5113e0c"]
import strategy_correctness_reach as SCR
```

It pins the measured tree to one worktree at one SHA, imports scorch from that tree, and then
synthesises `sys.argv` to feed the constant into `strategy_correctness_reach` — one of the four
harnesses this defect was historically caught and repaired in. **The repair is present, its
signature is honoured, and the caller satisfies the `$1` contract with a constant.** No count of
literals surfaces that, and it is the only site where "this harness cannot be pointed at a
different tree" is actually true.

So the numbers that mean something: fixes applied to **4** files; files presently defeating the
`$1` contract, **1**; files holding a ledger literal in a use the rule does not forbid, **10**.
These are sealed artefacts under `SHA256SUMS` and are not being edited. The forward rule is the
deliverable: **a harness that invokes another harness passes its own `$1` through, and never
synthesises one.**

**Two limits of the scan, stated rather than left implicit.** `decision-survey/harness/
interaction.py` has an unterminated string literal and cannot be parsed — it is reported as
`UNPARSEABLE`, a named outcome, not as clear; 1 of 155 files is unscanned. And
`probe_missing_cell.py` builds its ledger path component-wise, `Path.home() / ".cache" /
"scorch-codex" / ...`, which resolves to the identical hardcoded location while containing no
separator. A predicate keyed on path-shaped literals is **evadable by construction** by a `/`
operator chain, with no intent to evade required.

**And the discriminator I used to stratify contained the same error a fourth time.** Keying
"takes a tree root" on the presence of `sys.argv` would have cleared `suppress_probe.py`, which
mentions it more often than any other file in the set — every mention a **write**. Read versus
write is mention versus use again, inside the predicate written to stratify the predicate
written to avoid mention-versus-use.

### Correction to the correction: the literal scan was the wrong instrument

Three things in the section above are wrong, and fixing them replaces the whole approach.

**1. "Zero reads and two writes" is false as written.** `suppress_probe.py` has three
`sys.argv` nodes, and one of them is a Load — `_ARGV = sys.argv` at line 33, the save half of
a save-and-restore. The true statement is narrower and stronger: **zero subscript reads of
`sys.argv`, one Load, two Stores.** Reading a positional argument is the rule's requirement;
saving the list object is not.

**2. The benign column is 11, not 10.** The count excluded `decision-survey/harness/
probe_missing_cell.py` from *both* columns — it appeared only in the paragraph naming the
evasion that hid it. It is benign (`root = Path(sys.argv[1]).expanduser().resolve()`, which is
the rule itself) and it hardcodes only two sibling milestones' harness directories. **11 benign
+ 1 violating = 12.** Beside a count, the count of what the count could not see.

**3. "0 positional reads" separates the 12 because it was built on the 12.** Run over all 154
parseable harness files it flags **8**, of which 1 is real:

| discriminator | flags, corpus-wide | real | controls proving it can clear |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 subscript reads of `sys.argv` | 8 | 1 | 0 |
| Stores a `sys.argv` built from constants | **1** | 1 | **3** |

**The positive control is the finding.** `frontier_untaught_control.py`, present identically in
two milestones, also forges `sys.argv` — and is correct:

```python
parser.add_argument("tree"); parser.add_argument("out"); parser.add_argument("commit")
assert_tree(args.tree, args.commit, role="frontier-untaught-control")
sys.argv = [os.path.abspath(args.harness), "--out", os.path.abspath(args.out)]
runpy.run_path(os.path.abspath(args.harness), run_name="__main__")
```

It takes a tree root as `$1`, asserts its provenance, and builds the forged argv **out of its
own arguments**. Forging is not the defect; forging from constants is. Without this file the
second discriminator is unvalidated — a test that flags one file and has never cleared
anything is indistinguishable from a test that flags that file for the wrong reason.

**So the right test is not about ledger literals at all.** The defect is *"synthesises an argv
instead of passing its own through"*, and an AST test for exactly that finds **one site,
`workspace-confound/harness/suppress_probe.py:35`**, across the whole corpus. It needs no
path-shaped-literal predicate, so the component-wise `Path.home() / ...` construction that
evades the literal scan **cannot evade it** — a synthesised argv is synthesised however its
strings were spelled. The literal scan's blind spot, reported honestly two sections ago as a
limit, turns out not to be a limit of the finding but a reason the literal was never the right
thing to scan for.

One residual, stated because it bit twice: my first version of this detector also flagged
`suppress_probe.py:38`, the *restore* `sys.argv = _ARGV`, because a name bound from a bare
`sys.argv` Load was not recognised as carrying the process's real input. Same Load-versus-
subscript distinction as defect 1, one layer down, in the instrument written to fix it.

### The predicate in the previous section had the wrong quantifier

The test committed above asks whether **any** element of the forged `sys.argv` derives from
the file's own inputs. `sys.argv[0]` is the program name and no callee reads it as data, so
splicing it in front of three constants launders the entire list. This clears it:

```python
_SAVE = sys.argv
TREE = os.path.expanduser("~/.cache/scorch-codex/workspace-confound/worktrees/base-5113e0c")
sys.argv = _SAVE[:1] + [TREE, "/dev/null", "5113e0c"]
```

Same defect, same hardcoded tree, cleared. Verified against the committed code, not argued:
**CLEARED**.

The rule is positional. Element 0 is the program name and carries nothing; **at least one of
slots 1..n must derive from this file's own inputs.** "At least one" rather than "all", because
an option *name* like `"--out"` is part of the call protocol rather than data, and requiring
every slot to be tainted flags the one correct forger in the corpus. With that quantifier:

| input | verdict |
|---|---|
| `suppress_probe.py:35`, the real defect | FLAG — slots 1..3 all constant |
| the slot-0 mutant above | FLAG — slots 1..3 all constant |
| `frontier_untaught_control.py:129`, the correct forger | CLEAR — slot 2 carries input |
| `suppress_probe.py:38`, the restore `sys.argv = _ARGV` | UNDETERMINED |

The restore is benign but its length is not statically resolvable, so it reports
**UNDETERMINED rather than CLEAR** — fail closed. Corpus verdict is unchanged in substance:
one flagged site, and now a constructed defect that the previous version missed is caught.

**The shape of the error is the point.** The residual recorded one section above — failing to
recognise a bare `sys.argv` Load as carrying input — did not get fixed. It moved. Recognising
the Load made the instrument over-credit the list that Load appears in: a false negative on
recognition became a false positive on quantifier, same Load-versus-subscript distinction,
same instrument, one layer up.

**Two structural gaps, sized rather than asserted.** The predicate matches a Store whose target
is the whole `sys.argv`. Two other spellings of the same handoff exist, and both detectors were
first proven to fire on constructed instances before their corpus counts were believed:

| spelling | detector fires on fixture | instances in corpus |
|---|---|---|
| `sys.argv[1] = TREE` / `sys.argv[1:] = [...]` | yes, 2 of 2 | **0** |
| `sys.argv.insert/append/extend` | yes, 2 of 2 | **0** |

**One route the predicate cannot see at all, stated as an open limit.** A harness can hand a
constant tree to another harness without touching `argv` — `subprocess.run([sys.executable,
other, "/hardcoded/tree"])`, `runpy.run_path`, `exec`. There are **51** such invocation sites
in these files. This is not hypothetical and not a corner: the correct precedent above,
`frontier_untaught_control.py`, dispatches through `runpy.run_path`, so it is the live
mechanism in this corpus and an `argv`-shaped predicate is silent on it by construction. A
crude taint pass over those 51 leaves 22, but that number has demonstrated false positives —
the taint does not cross function parameters, and of 10 sampled, 4 carry a parameter name into
the call. **So there is no count for this route, only its size.** Recorded as unmeasured rather
than as zero.

### No quantifier can decide this, because the property belongs to the callee

Three caller-local tests were tried and each was cleared by a mutant one slot over:

| test | defeated by |
|---|---|
| any element derives from input | prefixing `sys.argv[:1]` — slot 0 launders the list |
| every slot 1..n derives from input | flags the corpus's one correct forger (slot 1 is `"--out"`) |
| at least one of slots 1..n | pin slot 1, pass `args.out` in slot 3 |

The third is verified, not conceded: `sys.argv = [abspath(args.harness), TREE, "--out",
abspath(args.out)]` returns **CLEAR** from the committed predicate with the tree pinned.

They fail for one reason. **Which slot is a tree is a fact about the callee**, and no
quantifier over the caller's list can recover it. Each fix moved the exemption one position
and the hole reopened next to it.

**The corpus states the contract, so it is readable.** `tree_provenance.assert_tree(tree,
commit, role=...)` is called by 61 files, and the callee's own source says which slot feeds it:

```python
TREE = os.path.abspath(sys.argv[1])                      # strategy_correctness_reach.py
PROVENANCE = [assert_tree(TREE, sys.argv[3], role="tree")]
```

So: resolve the callee, read the argv index its tree argument comes from, and require **that
one slot** of the caller's forged argv to derive from the caller's own inputs. Unresolvable
callee gives UNDETERMINED, never CLEAR.

| input | verdict | reason |
|---|---|---|
| `suppress_probe.py:35` | **FLAG** | callee reads its tree from `argv[1]`; caller's slot 1 is a constant |
| frontier-shaped mutant, bound to that callee | **FLAG** | same, and slot 3 carrying input no longer launders it |
| same shape with slot 1 carrying `args.tree` | CLEAR | slot 1 derives from own input |
| `frontier_untaught_control.py:129` ×2 | CLEAR | callee `frontier_ext2.py` reads **no** tree from argv |
| `suppress_probe.py:38`, the restore | UNDETERMINED | caller's slot not statically present |

**And the mutant's own defect-hood turns out to be callee-dependent, which is the whole
point.** Paired with its own default callee, `frontier_ext2.py`, the pinned tree sits in a slot
that callee never reads — `frontier_ext2.py` takes only `--out`, and the real control conveys
its tree by `sys.path.insert(0, join(tree, "src"))` rather than by argument. The same source
text is a defect against one callee and inert against another. A caller-local test cannot be
merely imprecise about that; it is answering a different question.

Corpus verdict is unchanged: **one flagged site.** What changed is that the reason is now the
contract it violates rather than a property of its own syntax, and the test survives a mutant
that defeated all three previous versions.

**Its limits, since it has them.** The callee must be resolvable statically — by an `import`, a
`runpy.run_path` literal, an argparse default, or the forged `argv[0]` — and must be in the
corpus. All four caller sites here resolve; a caller that computes its callee's path would
report UNDETERMINED. The `subprocess`/`runpy`/`exec` route carrying a constant tree **without
touching argv** (51 invocation sites, no reliable count of violations) is still not covered by
any of this, and is still recorded as unmeasured rather than zero.

### The option form, and where 61 comes from

**A callee can take its tree as an option, and the test collapsed that into "no tree".**
`tree_slot` returned two outcomes — an argv index, or nothing — so a callee taking `--tree`
reached the same CLEAR branch as a callee taking no tree at all. A forged
`sys.argv = [prog, "--tree", TREE, "--out", args.out]` would then read as the legitimate
clearance that `frontier_untaught_control.py` earns. Fourth instance of the same laundering,
now through the option/positional distinction rather than through a slot.

The contract is now three-way — positional index, option name, or none — and the option branch
checks the element *after* the flag:

| fixture | verdict |
|---|---|
| forge `["tilefix_differential.py", "--tree", TREE, "--out", args.out]` | **FLAG** — value after `--tree` is a constant |
| same with `os.path.abspath(args.tree)` | CLEAR — derives from own input |

Real corpus unchanged: **one flagged site.**

One detail differs from how this was reported to me, and it makes the hole slightly worse.
`blocker1-tilefix/harness/tilefix_differential.py:99` declares
`add_argument("--tree", required=True, help="worktree root to measure")` but **never calls
`assert_tree`**. So the branch was being reached by a file that plainly takes a tree *and* has
no provenance assert at all. The detector now recognises an argument named `tree` as a tree
contract independently of `assert_tree`, which is why it fires here.

**Where the 61 comes from, since it is load-bearing and should be re-derivable.** Population:
155 files in the 17 `*/harness` directories.

| reading | count |
|---|---|
| text `assert_tree(` appears anywhere | 62 |
| **AST: ≥1 call to a function named exactly `assert_tree`** | **61** |
| contains `def assert_tree` | 9 |
| definer files that *also* call it | 9 |

The 62 and the 61 differ by exactly one file: `decision-survey/harness/probe_missing_cell.py`
defines and calls **`_assert_tree`**, and the substring `assert_tree(` matches inside it.
Mention versus use for the fourth time in this thread, now as substring-versus-identifier.

Two corollaries. Subtracting the 9 definer files to get "genuine callers" removes 9 real
callers, because **all 9 define and call**. And the single unparseable file contains no
`assert_tree` at all, so it does not move this count — that was worth checking rather than
assuming, since it moves several others.

### "UNPARSEABLE" names a pair, not a file

`decision-survey/harness/interaction.py` was reported above as UNPARSEABLE, 1 of 155
unscanned. That is a property of the pair (file, interpreter):

| interpreter | result |
|---|---|
| Python 3.9.6 (system) | SyntaxError — EOL while scanning string literal |
| Python 3.11.15 (the `scorch` env, which CLAUDE.md requires) | SyntaxError line 457 |
| **Python 3.12.13** | **parses** |

```python
f"         the control cell is {'clean' if control_clean else 'NOT clean -- '
                                'the apparatus is suspect'}."
```

The replacement field spans two physical lines. PEP 701 legalised that in 3.12; under 3.11 an
f-string expression cannot contain a newline. So the honest disposition was right — a named
outcome rather than a silent clearance — but the label needed its interpreter printed beside
it, the same way a count needs its population.

**Re-run under 3.12, every number is unchanged:**

| | 3.11 | 3.12 |
|---|---|---|
| files scanned / UNPARSEABLE | 154 / 1 | **155 / 0** |
| substring `assert_tree(` | 62 | 62 |
| AST calls to `assert_tree` | 61 | 61 |
| `def assert_tree` | 9 | 9 |
| forged-argv verdicts | 1 FLAG, 2 CLEAR, 1 UNDETERMINED | identical |

The coverage gap closes to zero and moves nothing. Worth running rather than assuming: the
gap was reported as a limit precisely because an unscanned file could have held anything.

**The implication is larger than the scanner, and is not mine to resolve.** The file cannot be
compiled by the interpreter this project pins — `python3.11 interaction.py` fails before
executing a line, and the `scorch` env is 3.11.15. Whatever produced `decision-survey`'s
results therefore ran a ≥3.12 interpreter. That is a question for whoever sealed that
milestone, recorded here because it would otherwise only be found by accident. No claim is
made about the milestone's provenance.

### The population was a directory-name convention, and the test decides 3 of 18 sites

Every count above rests on "155 files in the 17 `*/harness` directories". That is a naming
convention, not a definition of the corpus. Walking all **40,577** `.py` files under the cache
for a `sys.argv = ` Store:

| where | files |
|---|---|
| inside `*/harness/` | **3** |
| outside `*/harness/`, not a repo copy | **14** |
| inside `*/worktrees/` (whole-repo copies, correctly excluded) | 0 |

The 14 are unmistakably harness scripts by name and role — `run_clean_harness.py` ×3,
`census_exact_tip.py` ×4, `run_clean_capture.py`, `run_exact_audit.py`, `gate_arm.py`,
`compare_exact_emitter_latency.py`, three `capture_*_latency_activation.py` — living in
`correctness-sweeps/scripts/`, `correctness-sweeps/census54/`, `schedule-audit/`, `gating/`,
and milestone roots. So **"exactly one flagged site" was computed over 3 of 17 argv-forging
files**, and the denominator was never established.

**Running the callee-contract test on the other 14 decides nothing at all:**

| | sites | FLAG | CLEAR | UNDETERMINED |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| inside `*/harness/` | 3 | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| outside | 15 | 0 | 0 | **15** |

Not one of the fifteen resolves. The reason is more basic than the splat: **the callee is not
in the corpus**, because the corpus was defined as `*/harness/*.py`. `benchmark_compiler_ir.py`
is named explicitly by three of them and is not in it.

The shapes, which is where the instrument's limits show:

| shape | count | example |
|---|---|---|
| starred splat | 8 | `[str(source), *sys.argv[1:]]` |
| all-constant | 3 | `['benchmark_compiler_ir.py', 'latency', '--warmup', '1', ...]` |
| mixed | 4 | `[sys.argv[0], '--output', str(temporary_output)]` |

Eight use a splat, so **the slot count is not statically resolvable and an index-based contract
test must return UNDETERMINED even with the callee in hand** — including
`[str(source), *sys.argv[1:]]`, which is exactly the pass-through idiom named as the correct
form two sections ago. The test would refuse to certify the thing it was built to prefer.

**So the instrument's decisiveness was a property of the population, not of the instrument** —
the same overfitting shape as the discriminator it replaced, one level up. On the 155 it read
1 FLAG / 2 CLEAR / 1 UNDETERMINED; on the 18 real forging sites it reads 1 / 2 / 16.

**What stands and what does not.** The flagged site stands: `suppress_probe.py:35` forges a
constant tree into a callee that reads `argv[1]` as its tree root, and both those facts are
read from the two files' own sources. What does not stand is the implied completeness — the
headline should be **one flagged site among the 3 of 17 argv-forging files the population
contained, with 14 files and 15 sites unexamined**, 8 of them not decidable by an index test
at all. No claim is made that any of the 14 is a violation; three of them are all-constant
forges of the same syntactic shape as the one flagged, and whether that matters turns on a
callee outside the scanned set.

## chain203: the rung-wise ladder, completed rotation, sealed

22 passes × 11 arms landed on redwood at 22:14:26; 242 files, 89 matrices, 3 widths, 0 readings
refused at ingestion. The rotation is balanced as declared and as landed (110 of 110 pairs), and
21 of 21 completed passes ran in exactly the row the orders table declares — confirmed from the
writer's `wrote` sequence, which is an observation, not from the bracket, which is an echo of
`$ORDERS` and could not have disagreed.

**One positive finding out of 45 (width, rung, group) rows.**

| width | rung | group | n | ambient/X | band | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **32** | **ov24** | **HIGHER** | **25** | **1.1806 [1.0768, 1.2949]** | 0.0044 | **X FASTER by 18.1%** |
| 2 | ov24 | HIGHER | 31 | 1.0110 [0.9314, 1.1093] | 0.0126 | no power |
| 4 | ov24 | HIGHER | 31 | 0.9901 [0.9234, 1.0716] | 0.0067 | no power |

The k=32 `ov24/HIGHER` group is **set-identical to chain202's ADOPT group** (digest
`1ec8352efdd15bc6`), so this is the composition-adoption clause raising the team above ambient,
not the cap. At override == pool the cap cannot bind, which is why the LOWER group is empty at
all three widths — a theorem given `override == pool`, and a theorem about *this host*, whose
pool is 24.

**Everything the cap does is negative, monotonically in how hard it caps.** On the LOWER groups,
where the override clips the team below ambient:

| rung | k=2 | k=4 | k=32 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ov2 | −162.2% | −168.6% | −187.3% |
| ov4 | −60.4% | −63.6% | −71.7% |
| ov8 | −12.0% | −8.4% | −9.0% |
| ov16 | no power | no power | no power |

So the ladder reads: **capping below the pool is harmful and the harm scales with the cap;
raising above ambient is worth +18.1%, and only at k=32.** The width dependence is the part
that needs a second host before it is a claim about the kernel rather than about redwood.

**Three caveats attached to the 18.1%, none of which is a reason to discard it.**
Percentile-interval non-coverage at these group sizes runs 0.069 to 0.090 against a nominal
0.050 — 1.4x to 1.8x — measured by an independent Monte Carlo construction on this run's own
A/A pool (n=1335, kurtosis 17.63). The finding sits at n=25, where empirical non-coverage is
0.080. Its interval `[1.0768, 1.2949]` clears parity by far more than that inflation, but the
nominal 95% is not 95%. Second, the seed-stability sweep at nboot=2400 leaves 2 of 83 rows
decided by the resampling rather than the data; **neither is this row.** Third, the
pre-registered per-cell reduction carries a reciprocal-direction gap of 9.04e-05 in aggregate,
4% of the smallest pre-registered margin — reported, not corrected, because changing a
pre-registered estimator is not this script's call.

### The seal

`chain203-rungwise-redwood`, 257 files, manifest 256 lines, **256 of 256 report OK**, manifest
digest `ca1a6cadee317690938f18cf04389f48f06ef9d9c56ee70c3c599129e54f0424`. Verified by requiring
the OK count to *equal* the manifest's line count, not by the absence of `FAILED` — nine
manifests in this tree are `cksum` output, on which `shasum -c` prints zero OK **and** zero
FAILED. Field 1 is 64 hex characters, so this one is genuinely SHA-256.

**With a negative control, because a verification that has never failed is not a verification:**
appending one byte to `c203_analysis.txt` moved the count to 255 of 256; restoring it returned
256 of 256.

Data guards, all passing on declared values rather than observed modes: 242 of 242 files
(11 arms × 22 passes); every file exactly 802 rows against 89 keys × 3 widths × 3 inner arms + 1
header, derived from the three files that declare those factors; every file 801 **distinct**
`(key,k,arm)` triples, which the row count structurally cannot check; and three-way agreement
between design, the writer's own `wrote` accounting (242 of 242 at 801), and the file lengths.
The corpus key list matches the sealed copies from chain198, chain199, chain200 and chain202;
**chain201 differs**, which is recorded rather than explained.

**Two defects in my own seal script, both caught by its positive classifier rather than by exit
status.** The analysis was first reported `UNKNOWN -- truncated or killed mid-write` when it had
completed fine: the classifier looked for chain202's `END OF ANALYSIS` marker, and `an_c203.py`
has **no unconditional terminal marker** — it prints a verdict-specific tail and leaves through
`sys.exit("REFUSE: ...")` on the other path. So "COMPLETE" here means "reached the no-refusal
tail", which coincides with end-of-main only because nothing follows it. And the metamorphic
stage reported `3 declared, 0 reported a verdict` because the seal passed a positional where
`meta_c203.py` takes `--dir`; that reading was *correct* — the relations genuinely did not run.
Fixed, it reports 3 of 3 declared relations present across 6 verdict lines, 0 VIOLATED. The
count-equality guard was replaced by a **set-of-names** comparison, because each relation runs
in two contexts and a count equality refuses a correct run while a set comparison still catches
the defect that guard exists for: a declared relation that never ran cannot appear in the output
being counted.

### Corrections to the chain203 entry, and the writer is now in the seal

**"21 of 21 completed passes" is wrong; it is 22 of 22.** The sealed log holds 22 bracket lines
and the sealed read says `22 of 22 completed passes ran in exactly the row the table declares`.
The 21 came from a **superseded first run** of the read whose output I quoted instead of the one
I sealed.

The cause is worth more than the correction. My wait fired on *"11 p22 CSVs exist"* at 22:12:37;
the runner recorded `pass p22 of 22 done` at **22:14:26**, 109 seconds later. In that window
every CSV was on disk and the run was not finished, so a read taken there saw 22 passes of data
and 21 passes of rotation evidence — and reported the smaller number without complaint. **A
completeness signal that is not one**: the file count was the wrong predicate for "the pass is
done", and the check that would have caught it silently narrowed its own denominator instead of
refusing. The fix is to wait on the runner's own completion line, not on an output count.

A second, smaller slip in the same area: I grepped `^pass p[0-9]+ of` and got **0 matches**, and
briefly took that as the log lacking the line. The line is indented. The log was right and the
anchor was wrong.

**The population phrasing overstates the width result.** "The same group at k=2 and k=4 shows no
power" reads as one set of matrices going quiet at other widths. It is not the same set — the
HIGHER rule selects different cells by width:

| width | n | members-sha256 |
|---|---|---|
| 32 | 25 | `1ec8352efdd15bc6` |
| 2 and 4 | 31 | `fa59aa79e3e262c8` |

So the claim is about **the rule's behaviour across widths, not about 25 matrices going quiet** —
a weaker statement than the phrasing implied, and one that still needs a second host.

**The mechanism is confirmed from the data rather than inferred.** On those 25 cells
`resolved[ov24]` is 24 on every one while `resolved[ovp]` spans 1..23, so the rung raises the
team above ambient everywhere on the group. A cap cannot do that.

**A third row-arm nothing reads.** Every CSV carries `ours`, `oursb`, `mkl` at 267 rows each, and
`oursb` appears **0 times** in `c203_analysis.txt`, `an_c203.py`, `meta_c203.py`,
`chain203_body.sh` and `c203_rw.log`. `mrgate_ov.py:19` says what it is — *"`oursb` is `ours`
again — identical code, identical argument — and is the noise floor"* — and line 155 binds
`{"ours": ours, "oursb": ours, ...}` to the same function object. So the run carries a free
within-invocation A/A on 64614 cell pairs that the analysis never opens.

**And the writer was not in the ledger, which is why that took reading an unsealed file.** The
seal held every CSV and no program capable of writing one: `rw_s_chain203.sh:32` points at
`/scratch/bobbyy/mrgate_ov.py` and `c203/mrbuild.sh`, both outside the sealed set. The column
semantics of the primary data were therefore not re-derivable from the artefact. Both are now
sealed, and a guard refuses a ledger without them. Re-sealed: **259 files, 258 of 258 manifest
lines OK**, digest `0ebd13f91046ae4005f6ad4df11175159fbe1942bec61959d7f38fb943d5ccb8`.

**That guard needed two fixes before it was worth having, both found by its own controls.** It
first keyed on the comma-joined header and refused a ledger that already contained the writer —
`mrgate_ov.py` emits the header through `csv.DictWriter.writeheader()`, so the joined string
appears nowhere in its source. A literal predicate against programmatically built text, the same
shape the forged-argv work hit four times. Re-keyed on column names one at a time, it still
refused: `csv` writes RFC-4180 **CRLF**, so `head -1` yields `...,batch\r` and the last column
never matched. Both were caught by a **positive** control — a directory with the writer added,
which must pass — rather than by the negative one, which passed throughout while the guard was
broken.

**The A/A pool convention, since the non-coverage figure is calibrated off it.** The pool is the
per-cell `median(log r)` kept **in log space** (mean ≈ 0), n = 1335 = 267 cells × 5 duplicate
pairs, and the kurtosis 17.63 is the raw fourth standardised moment (normal = 3). Computing the
same pool in **ratio** space, `exp(median(log r))` with mean ≈ 1, gives ≈ 16.74 — a ~5% gap that
is the space the moment is taken in, not a disagreement about the data.

### The k=32 NULL verdicts are carried by the reduction, and arm identity alone costs 2.2%

Both checks below are computed from the sealed CSVs.

**1. The saturated A/A that stage 1 named and did not measure.** Stage 1 reported 24 declined-
argument cells — 21 at k=32 — where ov2/ov4/ov8/ov16 all deliver **32** threads, and observed
that "any pair of those rungs is an A/A on these cells". It never computed them. On those 21
cells delivery is constant by construction and only the declared argument differs:

| pair | centre [lo, hi] | parity |
|---|---|---|
| ov4/ov2 | 1.0027 [0.9926, 1.0117] | contains |
| ov8/ov2 | 0.9923 [0.9841, 0.9995] | **excludes** |
| ov16/ov2 | 0.9794 [0.9501, 1.0004] | contains |
| ov8/ov4 | 0.9880 [0.9804, 0.9948] | **excludes** |
| ov16/ov4 | 0.9778 [0.9485, 0.9993] | **excludes** |
| ov16/ov8 | 0.9876 [0.9576, 1.0105] | contains |

**3 of 6 pairs exclude parity where the thread count provably cannot differ**, with deviations to
**2.2%**. This is arm identity alone — the cost of passing a different `SCORCH_SPMM_NT_CAP`
argument that the kernel then declines.

**Like-for-like, it is ~2.8x a same-argument replicate, not 3-12x.** Comparing these against the
0.0011-0.0020 X/Xb half-widths reported over all 267 cells is not like-for-like: those are
267-cell bands and these are 21-cell bands, so most of the ratio is n. On **the same 21 cells**,
the same-argument pairs read 0.9923 / 0.9999 / 1.0054 / 1.0034 — deviations to 0.8%. So arm
identity at identical delivery costs up to 2.2% against up to 0.8% for a same-argument
replicate.

A naming collision worth fixing while it is visible: "half-width" here means amendment 1's
`max(|lo-1|, |hi-1|)`, the largest deviation from parity the interval admits. Reported as
`(hi-lo)/2` the same rows read 0.0073-0.0264. Same intervals, same parity verdicts, different
numbers — which is the same question raised about the stage-4 bar, in the other direction.

**2. The k=32 NULL "X SLOWER" verdicts are a property of the reduction.**

| rung | n | gm-cells / med-pass | med-cells / med-pass | per-cell skew |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ov2 | 25 | 0.9814 | 0.9966 | −2.435 |
| ov4 | 26 | 0.9592 | 0.9988 | −2.224 |
| ov8 | 26 | 0.9526 | 0.9938 | −1.845 |
| ov16 | 25 | 0.9341 | 0.9959 | −2.016 |
| ov24 | 64 | 0.9958 | 1.0011 | −1.292 |

The published verdicts — **X SLOWER by 4.3% / 5.0% / 7.1%** at ov4 / ov8 / ov16 — read **0.1% to
0.6%** under median-over-cells. Same sign, an order of magnitude apart, and every median-reduced
deviation sits inside the 2.2% arm-identity effect measured above. The skew column is the cause:
at −1.8 to −2.4 a minority of cells with very low ratios carries the geometric mean while the
median is untouched.

**So those rows are statements about a tail, not about the typical matrix at k=32**, and the
earlier entry should not have reported them as a single number. They are reported here with both
nestings and the skew beside them.

**The headline is unaffected and should also carry a range.** The k=32 ov24/HIGHER finding reads
1.1805 under gm-cells and 1.1441 under med-cells, both bootstrapped intervals excluding parity,
all four nestings agreeing in sign, per-cell skew **+0.884** — the one group here whose skew is
positive and modest. So "**faster by 14.4% to 21.2% depending on the nesting**" is the honest
form, against an arm-identity floor of 2.2%.

### Three seals, one set of bytes — and a column documented as the floor that nothing reads

**The data did not move across the three seals.** The ledger was sealed three times in twenty
minutes as its own defects were fixed, and the manifest digest changed each time
(`5bf54a1c…` → `ca1a6cad…` → `0ebd13f9…`). The 242 CSVs are byte-identical across all three, so
every number computed against the first seal stands against the current one.

**Establishing that needed the digest convention named, which it was not.** An independent
digest-of-digests over the same 242 files gives six different answers depending on convention:

| convention | first 16 |
|---|---|
| `shasum … \| shasum` — full lines, glob order | `113531ec0ca8bf97` |
| digests only, `LC_ALL=C` sorted | `71b3c893b669bc2e` |
| digests only, glob order | `03da884f05179cd4` |
| full lines, `LC_ALL=C` sorted | `b18ad917f1073688` |
| sorted digests, no separator | `523f8645bc2b84a1` |
| `cat` of all files in sorted order | `cdb26700a4d87493` |

Two parties can hold identical bytes and report different digests, with no defect on either
side. The stage-1 membership digests **do** state their convention verbatim; a digest-of-digests
used to certify a snapshot needs the same treatment. Third naming collision in this thread,
after "half-width" and the stage-4 bar.

**And a manifest digest identifies a ledger at a moment, not a ledger.** A verifier quoting one
has evidence that it looked, not that a later citation refers to the same artefact. What
survives a re-seal is a snapshot of the data files plus a digest-of-digests over them. The
failure is silent: re-sealing does not invalidate a verifier's arithmetic, it invalidates the
verifier's claim to have checked the thing being cited. **Seal reports should carry the manifest
digest and the read time.**

**`oursb` is documented as the noise floor and no analysis reads it.** `mrgate_ov.py:19` calls it
"the noise floor"; `:155` binds `{"ours": ours, "oursb": ours, …}` to the same function object,
and the `batch` column confirms the same batch size for both against a different one for `mkl`.
It is a same-code, same-argument, same-batch replicate taken inside one invocation. In the
sealed ledger, `oursb` appears in exactly one file — `mrgate_ov.py`, the writer — and in **zero**
analysis artefacts.

No number is affected, and the analysis made the **more conservative** choice: calibrating
against the across-invocation X/Xb pairs rather than the within-invocation replicate, whose
half-widths are narrower. But two sealed statements disagree — the writer names a floor the
analysis does not use — and a reader grepping for "noise floor" lands on a column nothing
consumes. **Recorded rather than fixed:** both the writer and its live copy produced a sealed
result, and editing either next to that result is the perturbation, not the repair. The choice
is the user's — have the analysis read the column, or have the writer stop calling it the floor.

### "3 of 6 exclude parity" is a statement about intervals, not about effects

The saturated-A/A entry above reports 3 of 6 pairs excluding parity with deviations to 2.2%.
That is true and it reads as three effects. Run like-for-like against the same-argument pairs on
the same 21 cells, it is one:

| pair | kind | centre [lo, hi] | dev | parity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ov2b/ov2 | same-arg | 0.9923 [0.9794, 1.0021] | **0.77%** | contains |
| ov4b/ov4 | same-arg | 0.9999 [0.9920, 1.0082] | 0.01% | contains |
| ov8b/ov8 | same-arg | 1.0054 [0.9979, 1.0155] | 0.54% | contains |
| ov16b/ov16 | same-arg | 1.0034 [0.9896, 1.0158] | 0.34% | contains |
| ov8/ov2 | cross-arg | 0.9923 [0.9841, 0.9995] | **0.77%** | excludes |
| ov8/ov4 | cross-arg | 0.9880 [0.9804, 0.9950] | 1.20% | excludes |
| ov16/ov4 | cross-arg | 0.9778 [0.9485, 0.9993] | 2.22% | excludes |

**`ov8/ov2` and `ov2b/ov2` have the same centre — 0.9923, deviation 0.77% — and differ in verdict
only because the same-argument interval is wider.** Its exclusion is a narrower interval, not a
larger effect, and its effect size *is* the largest same-argument deviation measured on the same
cells. So:

- **ov16/ov4 at 2.22%** — 2.9x the same-argument scale, the one pair clearly above arm identity
- **ov8/ov4 at 1.20%** — 1.6x, marginal
- **ov8/ov2 at 0.77%** — at the floor, not separable from arm identity whatever its interval says

The substantive conclusion is unchanged — the declared argument moves the reading where delivered
threads provably cannot differ — but it rests on **one pair, not three**, and the floor to quote
is **0.77%**, the largest same-argument deviation on these cells, not the 2.2% maximum.

This is the rule the rest of this document applies, turned on a row it had exempted: an exclusion
is not an effect until its size is compared against a same-treatment bar on the same population.
An interval and an effect are different objects, and "excludes parity" names the first.

**The `batch` column, corrected to its stronger form.** `ours` and `oursb` are not merely
set-equal in batch size — they are **equal cell by cell, 267 of 267**, both with 249 distinct
values over min 1 / max 5948, while `mkl` has 213 distinct values over min 1 / max 1832 and
coincides with `ours` on **2 of 267** cells. So the within-invocation replicate matches on
per-cell batch as well as on code and argument, which is a stronger statement than either the
set equality or the single-cell figure it was first reported as.
