`/Users/bobby/scorch-beat-mkl/.git` is a *file* — `gitdir:
/Users/bobby/scorch/.git/worktrees/scorch-beat-mkl` — so this is a linked worktree, not a clone.
There is one `objects` directory, 377 MB, and no bundle or mirror anywhere on the machine.

| | |
|---|---|
| checkouts against that store (`git worktree list`) | **217** = 216 linked + 1 main |
| of those, living under `~/.cache/scorch-codex` | **214** |
| unpushed commits, single copy | **285 at `f715ac2`**, +1 per commit since |
| remote refs containing HEAD | 0 |
| local capacity | 39% used, 2.2 TiB free — space is not the constraint |

Losing that one directory loses the commits **and** the 214 pinned trees every ledger's
`worktrees/` entry resolves through. The sealed CSVs and manifests survive; the trees they were
measured against do not, which leaves a surviving ledger only partly re-derivable.

**And the 214 is a correction to a number this document produced an hour ago.** The first count
was **102**, taken as `~/.cache/scorch-codex/*/worktrees/*/`. That is a directory-name convention.
113 further checkouts sit under the cache with other names — `address-review-full.nOgjSc/
latency-base`, `c1-009802f/quality-base`, `c1-009802f/focused-worktree`, `emitter-5c6b26e/
full-suite/worktree`, `phase6-exit-f218c2e/latency/candidate-worktree` — carrying exactly the same
dependence on exactly the same object store.

**This is the `*/harness/*.py` defect again, three hours later, on an unrelated question.** There
the convention held 3 of 17 argv-forging files and made an instrument look decisive; here it held
102 of 214 pinned trees and made a risk look half its size. The first understated a defect count,
the second understates an exposure.

**The tell was the same both times: a count that matches a directory name rather than the thing
being counted.** `*/harness/` is where harnesses are *usually* kept; `*/worktrees/` is where
worktrees are *usually* kept. Neither is what either word means. The reliable form is to ask the
tool that owns the fact — `git worktree list` enumerates checkouts because git maintains that
list, and it cannot be fooled by a directory name.

Two smaller units differences resolved the same way, by naming the unit rather than picking a
winner: **217 vs 216** is checkouts-including-main against linked-only, and **62 vs 61** was
substring `assert_tree(` against calls to the exact identifier. Three units collisions in one
session, none of them a disagreement about the data.

**A count that its own recording invalidates.** The row above first read "unpushed commits: 285".
Committing the sentence that said so made it 286, and committing this correction makes it 287. An
unpushed-commit count written into a commit is stale the moment it lands — not because time
passed, but because **the act of recording is the thing that moves it**. Anchored to a SHA it is
a true statement that stays true: 285 at `f715ac2`.

Same family as the manifest digest identifying a ledger at a moment, with the loop closed one
turn tighter: there, re-sealing invalidated a verifier's claim to have checked the artefact;
here, writing the number down is what falsifies it. The general form is that a measurement of a
system you are inside needs the observation point named, and for a git count the observation
point is a commit.

**And the grep that justified that edit was itself truncated.** The claim above — "the document
contains three other 285s" — came from `grep -n "285\|286" | tail -5`. That grep returns **40
lines at `3b2a33d`**; I described its tail as its result. The statement happened to be right about distinct
statements and was derived from a view that could not have established it.

Counted properly, the two readings are far apart:

| reading | count |
|---|---|
| substring `285` (at `3b2a33d`) | **22** occurrences — `1.2850` ×5, `1.285` ×5, `1.2851` ×2, `4285`, `1.0285`, `0.285` |
| standalone token `285` (at `3b2a33d`) | **7** lines: 3 in this correction, 1 table value, 2 the dropped-cell counter, 1 a line distance |

So a find-and-replace on the digits would not have damaged three true statements, it would have
rewritten **fifteen measured speedup ratios** into nonsense. The `286` half of the same grep hit
`52866`, `4286`, `17286204` and `0.000286` — a row count, a matrix dimension, Slurm job IDs.

That is **substring versus token, the fourth instance tonight**, after `assert_tree(` matching
inside `_assert_tree(`, a `sys.argv[..] =` pattern matching the first `=` of `==`, and `p[0-9]+`
matching the SuiteSparse key `p6000`. It is the first of the four to appear in an *editing*
decision rather than in a census, where the cost is corrupted data rather than a wrong count. The
fix is the same every time: ask what the token **is**, not what characters it contains.

And the truncation is its own repeat — `tail -5` of a 40-line result is the same shape as the
abridged battery output that ate three verdicts earlier in this chain. A qualifier that is
discarded by the view you are reading through is indistinguishable from a qualifier that was
never there.

**This is where the recursion stops, and the stopping move is the anchor rather than a recount.**
The three counts above were measured at `3b2a33d` and are exact there. Publishing them in
`732de77` made them 45 / 32 / 10, because the passage reporting them contains the digits it
reports. This paragraph moves them again, and deliberately does not say to what.

That is the third self-invalidating count in a row, each one level further out: the unpushed
count went 285 → 286 → 287 → 288 through four acts of recording; then a count *about* the
document changed the document. Four commit subjects in `main..HEAD` carry a figure about this
file, and every one of them moved the figure it reported.

The general form was already written here — *a measurement of a system you are inside needs its
observation point named* — and the thing worth adding is that **it applies to itself, so
correcting an unanchored count by publishing a fresher one cannot terminate.** `40 lines at
`3b2a33d`` is true permanently. `40 lines` is true for exactly one commit. Anchoring is not a
tidier way of writing the number; it is the only version of the sentence that survives being
written down.

No further count of this document appears below, which is the other half of the fix: the numbers
that matter here are about **chain203's data**, and that data is sealed, byte-identical across
three seals at `113531ec0ca8bf97…` under a stated convention, and cannot be moved by anything
written about it.

### Row-level provenance is clean, and the ambient stratification is not empty

**Duplication and provenance over the sealed CSVs, a layer nobody had checked.**

| check | result |
|---|---|
| rows | 193,842 |
| distinct `(arm, pass, key, k, row-arm)` keys | **193,842** — 0 duplicated |
| two factorisations | 242 × 801 = 11 × 22 × 267 × 3 = 193,842, agree |
| `(arm, pass)` groups carrying exactly 801 rows | 242 of 242 |
| `build` column == the filename's arm | **0 violations** |
| `slice` column == `ov<pass>` | **0 violations** |

The last two are the addition: the columns that *name* the arm and the pass agree with the
filename on every row, so no file's contents can have been written under a label other than the
one it carries. Row-count and distinct-triple guards cannot see that.

**The ambient stratification of the identity population — and it has one reachable finding, not
none.** Restricting to ov24's 172 identity cells (`resolved[ov24] == 24 == its own override`) and
stratifying by what ambient resolves to gives **22 strata, n = 1 to 85**. Four clear the
pre-registered floor of 8:

| ambient | n | ambient/ov24 | CI | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **9** | **1.4469** | **[1.1523, 1.7794]** | **excludes parity — ov24 faster by 44.7%** |
| 10 | 8 | 1.0074 | [0.9173, 1.1124] | flat |
| 15 | 12 | 0.9825 | [0.9532, 1.0024] | flat |
| 24 | 85 | 1.0056 | [0.9989, 1.0127] | flat |

**That pattern is the ambient-dependence.** Where ambient picks a single thread, forcing 24 is
worth 44.7% on 9 cells above the floor; where ambient already picks 10, 15 or 24, the override is
flat. It is the headline finding seen from the other side — adoption pays exactly where ambient
under-provisions — and it is reachable at this corpus rather than void.

**Everything below the floor is void, and the reason is stronger than the floor.** Eight further
strata exclude parity at 5.3% to 21.1%, in both directions, and all are under n=8 with four at
n=2. **At n=2 the percentile bootstrap over cells has three distinct resample outcomes, so the
2.5/97.5 percentiles ARE the two per-cell centres** — verified, not argued:

| ambient | per-cell centres | CI | CI == range? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 0.7657, 0.8222 | [0.7657, 0.8222] | yes |
| 13 | 0.7814, 0.9194 | [0.7814, 0.9194] | yes |
| 16 | 0.9405, 0.9533 | [0.9405, 0.9533] | yes |
| 19 | 1.1441, 1.1507 | [1.1441, 1.1507] | yes |

So "excludes parity" there means only *both cells fell the same side of 1*, which a null does half
the time. Amendment 4's degenerate-resample regime exactly: **no effect measurable, not a small
one.**

**But "unreachable" overstates it.** 89 keys spread over 22 ambient values cannot put 8 cells in
most bins — 18 of 22 strata are unusable — yet the four that are usable include the one where the
mechanism should be largest, and it is. The honest statement is that this stratification is
**mostly unreachable and not uninformative**: its single above-floor effect is the largest
centre-stable reading in the chain — see the four qualifications below, which replace an earlier
claim here that it was *reduction-independent*.

### The population-is-a-convention defect, third instance, and the cost escalated

Three times in one session, on three unrelated questions, a population was defined by something
that merely *correlates* with the thing being counted:

| # | filter | held | actual | cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `*/harness/*.py` | 3 | **17** argv-forging files | a miscount, and an instrument that read 15-of-15 UNDETERMINED outside its own glob |
| 2 | `*/worktrees/*/` | 102 | **214** pinned git worktrees | a data-loss exposure reported at half size |
| 3 | `ambient 2..23` | 20 | **22** strata present | **a false negative on a real effect** |

The third was a literal `if a < 2 or a > 23: continue`, written because the step had been *named*
"the identity population stratified across ambient 2–23" — a range inherited from chain202's
stratum description and implemented as a hard bound without checking which ambient values this
corpus contains. The stratum carrying the largest effect sits at **ambient 1**, one below the
filter's floor.

**The escalation is the point.** The first two produced numbers a reader could re-derive. The
third produced a conclusion — *"the identity population gives no evidence of ambient-dependence"* —
that was the opposite of what the data says, from an enumeration the filter had truncated at both
ends. A miscount is recoverable; a false negative closes a question.

**And the other end of the filter hid the finding a second way.** The dropped high stratum,
ambient 24 with n=85, is the *same 85 cells* already measured under a different heading as the
different-argument null. Verified: the two cell sets are identical, and the two readings are exact
reciprocals — `ov24/ovp` 0.994462 against `ambient/ov24` 1.005569, difference **0.00e+00** under
`exp(median(log r))`. So one stratum was excluded by a range bound and another was already in hand
under another name, which is how a 22-stratum enumeration reported 20.

*(That exact zero is itself a demonstration of the reciprocity result recorded earlier: the
log-space reduction is reciprocal-invariant by construction, where the linear median is off by up
to 3.3e-05 at 22 passes.)*

**The rule, stated so it is checkable rather than agreeable: run the defining property over the
complement before believing the enumeration.** `*/harness/` is where harnesses are usually kept.
`*/worktrees/` is where worktrees are usually kept. `ambient 2..23` is where ambient usually lands.
None of the three is what the thing *is*, and in all three cases the complement was one command
away — `git worktree list`, an AST walk over the whole cache, `sorted(set(resolved[ovp]))`.

### The ambient-1 finding, qualified four ways

The section above called it "the largest reduction-independent reading in the chain". **That word
is wrong, and I had not run the check I applied to everything else.** Put through the same four
nestings as the headline:

| nesting | centre | CI | parity |
|---|---|---|---|
| gm-cells / med-pass | 1.4469 | [1.1523, 1.7794] | **excludes** |
| med-cells / med-pass | 1.4750 | [0.8498, 2.0246] | **contains** |
| gm pooled | 1.4271 | — | — |
| med pooled | 1.4727 | — | — |

**The centre is reduction-stable — 1.4271 to 1.4750, a 4.8-point spread, tighter than the
headline's 14.4–21.2%. The exclusion is not: it rests on gm-cells alone.** At n=9 a
median-over-cells has high resample variance, so the reading is that the median lacks power to
exclude parity here rather than that the effect is absent — but "reduction-independent" is the one
thing the table cannot support. Correct form: **centre reduction-stable at 1.43–1.48, exclusion
under gm-cells only.**

Three more qualifications it carries and the headline's did not:

**9 cells are 7 distinct keys** — `Pd_b`, `Pd_rhs`, `TSOPF_RS_b162_c3_b`, `TSOPF_RS_b300_c2_b`,
`adder_dcop_16`, `m3plates`, `poli`, two of them appearing at two widths. If amendment 4's floor
of 8 counts *cells*, 9 clears it; if it counts *independent problems*, 7 does not. That is
unresolved here and it decides whether this row is above the floor at all — the same
cells-versus-keys question as chain202's nine-cell group.

**It pools three widths** — 2 at k=2, 2 at k=4, **5 at k=32**. Every other band in this chain is
per-width, and the headline is itself width-dependent (14.4–21.2% at k=32 against flat elsewhere).
So this stratum is not comparable to the rows around it, and the majority of its cells are the
width where adoption is known to be largest.

**And it carries neither caveat the headline carried.** No non-coverage figure — measured
percentile non-coverage ran 0.069–0.090 with 0.080 at n=25, so at n=9 it should be at or above the
top of that range, and this row's interval is what decides it. And it is one host.

**What survives is still the finding**: 7 of 9 per-cell centres above parity, ~45% on the centre
under every reduction tried, and a real progression against the flat ambient-10/15/24 strata. It
needs the same second-host qualification as the 18.1% and one more sentence of hedging than it
was given.

*This is the mirror of the correction two sections up: a step was declared void and recomputing it
found an effect; then that effect was declared reduction-independent and running the nestings
found it was not. Both errors were self-corrections forced by a second implementation, and
neither would have surfaced from one.*

### The agreed digest convention does not survive a host change

The ledger's 242 CSVs were cross-checked against the source directory still on redwood
(`/scratch/bobbyy/c203`), a copy neither seal nor verifier had touched. **The content is
identical.** But the convention that two sessions had agreed on for certifying that — full
`shasum` lines, glob order, unsorted — reports a mismatch:

| form | local ledger | redwood source | |
|---|---|---|---|
| full lines, **glob order** | `113531ec0ca8bf97…` | `2e59154e87f2843d…` | **differ** |
| full lines, `LC_ALL=C` sorted | `b18ad917f1073688…` | `b18ad917f1073688…` | match |
| digests only, `LC_ALL=C` sorted | `71b3c893b669bc2e…` | `71b3c893b669bc2e…` | match |

The cause is collation, not content — **but see the correction below: the mechanism stated here
was wrong, and the example was not an instance of it.**

**So the unsorted form is usable for detecting a rename inside one directory on one host, and
unusable for verifying a copy against its source.** It was chosen over the sorted form *because*
it catches a rename — a real advantage — and the cost was never stated: it silently reports a
mismatch on identical bytes the moment the comparison crosses a filesystem. On a night whose
running theme was naming the convention, the convention we agreed on had an unnamed precondition:
**one host, one locale.**

The durable statement is the order-independent one. `71b3c893b669bc2e…` over content, or
`b18ad917f1073688…` over lines under a pinned sort, both of which reproduce on both hosts. And
the useful result underneath the digest argument: **the sealed ledger is byte-identical to the
data still sitting in the directory the run wrote it to**, 242 files, verified from a route that
cost nothing to reopen.

### The collation diagnosis was wrong three ways

The conclusion above survives — 242 files byte-identical, the unsorted form unusable
cross-host — but the mechanism named for it does not.

**1. The example pair is not an instance.** I wrote that macOS sorts `sh_ov16_` before
`sh_ov16b_` and redwood does the opposite, attributing it to C-vs-UTF-8. Both locales agree on
that pair here:

```
LC_ALL=C           sh_ov16_float32_p1.csv  sh_ov16b_float32_p1.csv
LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 sh_ov16_float32_p1.csv  sh_ov16b_float32_p1.csv
```

The effect is real but starts elsewhere. C and macOS-UTF-8 name order differ at **66 of 242**
positions, first at `sh_ov24_float32_p1.csv` (C) against `sh_ov2_float32_p1.csv` (UTF-8) — a
digit-versus-underscore comparison, not the `b` suffix I pointed at.

**2. It is not C versus UTF-8 at all.** Measured on this machine:

| order | digest |
|---|---|
| glob | `113531ec0ca8bf97` |
| `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8` name sort | `113531ec0ca8bf97` — identical to glob |
| `LC_ALL=C` name sort | `9c3c1221d68ef6df` |
| redwood's glob | `2e59154e87f2843d` |

macOS glob order **is** macOS UTF-8 order, and redwood's is a **third** order reproducible from
neither. Both hosts run the same nominal locale (`en_US.UTF-8`), so the split is **glibc versus
Darwin collation for one locale name**, not C versus UTF-8. That is a worse problem than the one
I described: the locale string matching is no guarantee, and `LC_ALL=C` — the usual fix — gives
an order matching *neither* host's glob.

**3. The form I recommended carries the same kind of unnamed precondition I was complaining
about.** `b18ad917…` survives the crossing for a specific reason: sorting full `shasum` lines
sorts by the **digest**, which is hex and collates identically everywhere; the filename is only
trailing text. So it is portable **only while no two files share a digest** — a tie breaks on the
filename and collation re-enters. Measured here: **242 lines, 242 distinct digests, 0 duplicates**,
so it holds for this corpus. That number belongs beside the digest or the guarantee is untested.

**One figure, since reconciled — see below.** I measure 66 of 242 positions differing between C
and macOS-UTF-8 against an independent 44. Both describe the same permutation under different
operations.

**What to carry**, with the conditions attached rather than implied:

- `71b3c893b669bc2e…` — digests only, `LC_ALL=C` sorted. Content identity, order-independent,
  portable unconditionally. Blind to renames.
- `b18ad917f1073688…` — full lines, `LC_ALL=C` sorted. Keeps filenames in scope and portable
  **given 242 of 242 distinct digests**, which must be stated with it.
- `113531ec0ca8bf97…` — full lines, glob order. Same-host rename detection only. Not a
  cross-host check, and not reproducible from a locale name.

### 66 and 44 are the same permutation under two operations

The 44 came from `diff <(… LC_ALL=C sort) <(… en_US.UTF-8 sort) | grep -c '^[<>]'` — 22 `<` lines
plus 22 `>` lines. That counts **diff's minimal edit script**, not positional disagreement, and it
was reported as "positions differing". Both numbers are correct measurements of one block move,
and the arithmetic closes:

| | |
|---|---|
| positions at a different index | **66**, one contiguous run, 0-based 44..109 |
| `sh_ov2_*` names, shift | 22 names, **−44** |
| `sh_ov24_*` and `sh_ov24b_*`, shift | 44 names, **+22** |
| names that do not move | 176 |
| 22 moved + 44 displaced | = **66** positions |
| lines diff needs to describe that block move | 22 + 22 = **44** |

*(The independent report attributed the +22 group to `sh_ov24_*`/`sh_ov2b_*`; measured, it is
`sh_ov24_*` and `sh_ov24b_*`. `sh_ov2b_*` does not move. The counts and the arithmetic are
unaffected — in ASCII `'4' < '_' < 'b'`, so C puts both ov24 groups ahead of `sh_ov2_` while
leaving `sh_ov2b_` behind it.)*

**Report 66, and say which operation produced it.** The two diverge exactly when a *block* moves,
and a block move is what a collation change does to sorted filenames — so this discrepancy is
systematic for the whole class of question, not a one-off.

**And 44 is reachable three independent ways in this data**, which is how a mislabelled figure
survives cross-checking: diff's edit lines (22+22), the displaced-name count (44), and the 0-based
index of the first divergence (44). That third one lands on `C[44] = sh_ov24_float32_p1.csv`
against `UTF8[44] = sh_ov2_float32_p1.csv` — independently confirming the corrected example above,
and by coincidence rather than by derivation. Three routes to one number is a reason to go back to
the command that produced it rather than accept whichever derivation matches.

**The general form, which is the durable part.** Two mislabelled predicates surfaced within
minutes of each other: a loose substring reported as an anchored trailer check, and an edit
distance reported as a positional count. They fail in *opposite* directions — the first
manufactured a violation, the second understated a real effect by a third — so direction is not
the lesson. **The label has to name the operation, not the intent: when reporting a count over a
population, state the operation that produced it in the same breath as the number.**

**The permutation is monolithic at the arm-block level**, which is a stronger statement than the
shift table and explains why diff needs only 44 lines. Full census, 22 files per arm:

| shift | groups |
|---|---|
| **−44** | `sh_ov2` |
| **+22** | `sh_ov24`, `sh_ov24b` |
| 0 | `sh_ov2b`, `sh_ov4`, `sh_ov4b`, `sh_ov8`, `sh_ov8b`, `sh_ov16`, `sh_ov16b`, `sh_ovp` |

**Every group carries one shift — no group splits.** So all 22 passes of an arm move together and
this is one block of 22 crossing a block of 44, not 66 independent reorderings. The block order
follows the ASCII account exactly: C gives `ov24 ov24b ov2 ov2b`, macOS-UTF-8 gives
`ov2 ov24 ov24b ov2b`, with `'4'=52 < '_'=95 < 'b'=98`.

*(One correction to the census as it was reported to me: it said "exactly 2 of 11 groups move"
while its own table listed three nonzero shifts. Measured, **3 of 11 arm groups move** — `ov2`,
`ov24`, `ov24b`. My own first restatement of that was loose too: I called them "2 contiguous
blocks that swap", which implies two separate regions. They are **one contiguous run** — C block
order is `ov16 ov16b | ov24 ov24b ov2 | ov2b ov4 ov4b ov8 ov8b ovp`, movers at block indices 2–4 —
inside which the 22-file `ov2` block and the 44-file `ov24`+`ov24b` block exchange adjacent
halves. Exact structure: **3 groups, 1 run, 66 positions (0-based 44..109), 44 diff lines.** Fourth summary in four messages that was wrong beside correctly
measured data — the numbers were right every time and the sentence over them was not, which is
exactly what makes that failure mode credible.)*

### Three ways a digest or a freshness check reads clean while measuring nothing

**1. `find` in this shell is `bfs`, and it rejects relative `-newermt` arguments.** Measured on
`~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl`, same argument, both binaries:

| `-newermt` argument | shell `find` | `/usr/bin/find` | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'7 days ago'` | **0** | **2150** | **disagree** |
| `'2026-09-07'` | 2336 | 2336 | agree |
| `'-7d'` | 0 | 0 | agree |
| `'now'` | 0 | 0 | agree |

`find` is a shell function from the session snapshot that execs with `ARGV0=bfs`. The English
relative form is the one that breaks; absolute timestamps agree exactly. **Two refinements to how
this was reported to me:** `-7d` and `now` do *not* diverge — both binaries return 0, and for
`now` that is the correct answer — so the demonstrated failure is the English-phrase form alone.
And it is **not silent**: bfs writes a pointed error to stderr and **exits 1**. Only a check that
counts stdout lines is fooled; one that tests exit status or reads stderr catches it.

The direction is still the dangerous one where it does bite — a genuine freshness null and a
rejected argument both print 0, so the null reads confirmed *and* the control meant to prove the
population non-empty also reads 0. **Two harnesses do use `-newermt`** — see the correction below; the
claim of zero was a population error.

**2. A 16- or 32-hex digest does not name its function.** On the identical input stream:

| function | first 16 |
|---|---|
| `shasum -a 256` | `113531ec0ca8bf97` |
| `md5` | `6671ab8b7d4e711e` |

Nothing about the string says which produced it. Where this would bite hardest is precisely the
cross-host collation digests above — a function mismatch there is **indistinguishable from a real
host difference**, which is the exact confusion that section was written to resolve. All three
forms re-derived under a named function: `113531ec0ca8bf97` (sha256, full lines, glob order),
`b18ad917f1073688` (sha256, full lines, `LC_ALL=C` sorted), `71b3c893b669bc2e` (sha256, digests
only, `LC_ALL=C` sorted).

**3. And a corrupted pipeline produced a well-formed digest rather than an error — mine, just
now.** Re-deriving the third form with the `awk` body written as `'{print \$1}'` inside a
double-quoted string mangled the program. `awk` errored to stderr, contributed nothing to the
pipe, and the result was **`e3b0c44298fc1c14`** — the SHA-256 of *empty input*. It is 64 valid hex
characters, it sits in a column of digests, and by inspection it is a digest. The correct value is
`71b3c893b669bc2e`.

**`e3b0c44298fc1c14…` is the value to recognise on sight.** It is what any digest of a stream that
turned out to be empty looks like: a broken filter, an empty glob, a `cd` that failed. The
analyzer already prints it legitimately, once, labelled `(the empty group)` for `ov24/LOWER n=0` —
so the same 64 characters are a correct result in one row and evidence of a broken command in
another, and only the label distinguishes them.

### Four corrections to the section above, including the fix that is not a fix

**1. `/usr/bin/find` is not the safe default. The two binaries have complementary gaps.**

Counts are over `~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl` with **no `-type` filter**, so they include
directories; the `-type f` column is given beside them because correction 4 below quotes the file
counts and a reader should not have to work out which question each answers.
`1788851438` = 2026-09-08 00:10:38 PDT, so the epoch and ISO rows agree because no file falls in
the ten minutes between them.

| `-newermt` argument | `bfs` (shell `find`) | `/usr/bin/find` | `-type f`: bfs / sys |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'7 days ago'` | 0, exit 1 | 2150, exit 0 | 0 / 2121 |
| `'@1788851438'` | 2150, exit 0 | **0, exit 1** | 2121 / 0 |
| `'2026-09-08'` (ISO) | 2150, exit 0 | 2150, exit 0 | 2121 / 2121 |

BSD `find` rejects the **epoch** form that bfs accepts. So "call `/usr/bin/find` explicitly" —
which the section above recommends — breaks the epoch form, and only the **ISO absolute** form
works under both. That is the rule to carry.

**2. "No harness of mine uses `-newermt` (0 files)" was a population error.** It is **2 of 187**,
and both are live:

```
harnesses/poll_mkt.sh:21    ssh … sc "find /matx/u/bobbyy/staging/${STAGE}_mkt.tgz -newermt '@'$T0 … | wc -l"
harnesses/poll_stage.sh:36  same form
```

I searched the scratchpad and both git worktrees and never searched
`~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/harnesses/` — the directory where this milestone's harnesses
actually live. Positive controls on that population, so the predicate is not vacuous: 187 files,
8 match `find `, 2 match `shasum`.

**The conclusion survives, for two reasons I did not state instead of the one I did.** The form is
absolute epoch, not an English phrase, and the `find` executes **inside `ssh … sc`** where it is
GNU findutils, not the local bfs. Both guards are therefore fine as written.

**But the local-failure shape is worth recording**, because `poll_mkt.sh:18-19` says what the
guard is for: *"the tarball must be NEWER than this poller, or it is a previous stage's output
under a name this stage inherited — a defect that has happened once here and reads as a complete
run."* If that `find` ever ran under BSD find, `fresh` would be 0 unconditionally and
`if [ "${fresh:-0}" = "0" ]` would take the refuse branch forever. **Fail-closed** — a stuck
poller, not a stale pull — but the guard would have stopped being a test while still reading as
one.

**3. `e3b0c44298fc1c14` appears four times, not once, and only one is labelled.** All in
`c203_analysis.txt`: bare table rows at lines 133, 148, 163 (`ov24/LOWER 0 e3b0c44298fc1c14` for
k=2/4/32) and the summary at line 176 carrying `(the empty group)`. So "only the label
distinguishes them" is true of **1 in 4** — three legitimate appearances are unlabelled entries in
a digest column, which strengthens the point rather than weakening it.

**4. My own `find` counts had an unnamed predicate — inside the section about unnamed predicates.**
I reported 2336 and 2150; the file counts are 2304 and 2121. The gap is directories, which I did
not filter or mention: **2304 files + 32 dirs = 2336**, and 2121 + 29 = 2150. Both are correct
numbers for different questions, and I published one while describing the other.

## Every manifest verifies, and none of them names the script chain203 ran

The nine manifests in `~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/` that are *named* `SHA256SUMS` and
*contain* `cksum` output — CRC-32 plus a byte count, three fields — had been recorded here as
"unverifiable by `shasum -c`". That records a property of the wrong tool. They verify with `cksum`,
and running it closes 2346 attested lines that had been reported as covered while nothing had read
them.

Verified by shelling out to `cksum`, not by reimplementing the POSIX CRC, so the check does not
restate the thing under test. **2339 of 2346 OK, 7 MISMATCH, 0 MISSING.**

The 7 are 5 distinct files, all in `harnesses/`, all grown, every mtime after its manifest's, and
the chronology reconciles exactly against the three manifest write times:

    top-level SHA256SUMS         sealed 09-08 23:17   1123 lines   1118 OK   5 MISMATCH
    harnesses/SHA256SUMS         sealed 09-09 10:41    184 lines    182 OK   2 MISMATCH
    harnesses/SHA256SUMS.sha256  sealed 09-13 11:37    186 lines    186 OK   0 MISMATCH

`fmtcheck.py` (1678→2640), `spmmstat.py` (9003→10215) and `mrbuild.sh` (32363→33621) were edited
09-09 06:08–08:16, inside the eleven-hour window between the first two seals, which is why those
three fail at top level and pass inside `harnesses/`. `mkt_attrib2b.sbatch` (10409→11584) and
`rw_s_movid.sh` (5124→6299) were edited 09-13 11:36 and fail in both. No data directory has a
single mismatch. Continued harness development, not corruption.

**The count of genuine SHA-256 manifests recorded here was 15 at 1188 lines. It is 16 at 1374.**
The sixteenth is `harnesses/SHA256SUMS.sha256`, 186 lines, verifying 186 of 186 — the file
`MANIFEST_NOTE.txt` describes as the thing that gives the directory something that verifies. It was
missed because the population was taken as "one `SHA256SUMS` per chain directory", and this manifest
matches neither half of that: it is not named `SHA256SUMS` and it is not in a chain directory. Same
shape as the three earlier population errors in this document — a count that matches where the thing
is usually found. The fix is the same one: enumerate over the tree, then look at what the net
caught. Under `spmm-beat-mkl/` that is 25 manifests, 16 + 9.

**Correction to the paragraph above, which published a number that is not what its sentence says.**
The first version of this passage read "837 manifest-named files under `~/.cache/scorch-codex`, of
which exactly 9 are `cksum` and 718 are SHA-256", offered as the result of enumerating by the
defining property. Two things are wrong with it and neither is the arithmetic, which is exact:
718 + 109 unparseable + 1 empty + 9 = 837.

First, it was a **name** net — filename contains `SUMS`, or contains `sha256`, or ends `.cksum` —
reported as a content enumeration, which is the label-the-operation defect occurring inside the
sentence prescribing the fix for the population defect. Second, and worse for a reader, 718 is not
a count of manifests and so is not parallel to the 9 it is quoted beside: **177 of the 718 are
single-line receipts** (one digest, one file: `base.so.sha256`, `activation.json.sha256`), 52 are
two or three lines, and **489 have four or more lines**. A receipt and a ledger manifest are
different objects and only the second is what "9 cksum manifests" is counting.

The peer's independent net — `SHA256SUMS*`, `*.sha256`, `*MANIFEST*`, `*cksum*`, `*sums*` — gives
819 files and 485 SHA-256, agreeing exactly on 9 `cksum`. The 233-file gap is entirely net width,
not classification: my net catches `artifact-sha256.txt` (31), `receipt-sha256.txt` (29),
`EVIDENCE_SHA256SUMS` (12), `script-sha256.txt` (8), `grid-base-SHA256SUMS` (7) and
`corpus-base-SHA256SUMS` (7), none of which match a `.sha256` suffix or a `SHA256SUMS` prefix. Both
nets under-collect, in different directions.

**And a content-only net over-collects.** Enumerating all 2437 files in the milestone tree by first
line yields 17 `cksum`-shaped files, 8 of which are not manifests at all: the `orders_idx*.txt`
pass-order tables are whitespace-separated integers, so `chain203-rungwise-redwood/orders_idx11x22.txt`
("1 2 3 5 10 4 8 11 7 9 6") satisfies "three fields, first two numeric" for a reason that has
nothing to do with checksums. 17 − 8 = 9. So neither net alone settles a population: a name net
misses members, a content net admits non-members, and the only thing that closes it is reading what
the net caught.

**Two structural points, both of which survive the arithmetic being right.**

**1. Attesting a manifest as a file says nothing about whether its claims hold.**
`harnesses/SHA256SUMS.sha256` verifies 186 of 186, and one of those 186 lines is `SHA256SUMS`
itself — the `cksum` manifest containing two false entries. Its digest is correct; the file's
contents are stale. So a directory can be 100% attested by its newest manifest while an older
manifest inside it asserts two things that are not true, and no check that verifies manifests
against files can see the difference. `MANIFEST_NOTE.txt` intended exactly this and says so; the
point is that the outer verification carries no signal about it, so the note is the only thing that
does.

**2. `MANIFEST_NOTE.txt` reached the diagnosis on 09-13 and still did not run the tool.** It names
the format precisely — "CRC-32 plus a byte count, not SHA-256" — and concludes that `shasum -a 256
-c` "was not verifying anything before these edits either; the edits did not break it." Both
sentences are true. The inference that a three-field manifest wants the three-field tool is one step
away and was not taken for two days. Knowing the format is not checking the file.

## The declined arguments are the E-core recruit firing on x86, and the inertness proof has an unnamed precondition

chain203 found, counted and named the anomaly correctly. Its `c203_analysis.txt:74-76` reports
**"DECLINED ARGUMENTS: 24 cells where the delivered count exceeds the pool, on 4 of the 5 rungs
(ov2, ov4, ov8, ov16). Delivered counts there: [32]. Identical across those rungs on every cell:
True. By width: {4: 3, 32: 21}."** Recomputed from the sealed CSVs here: 24 cells, {4: 3, 32: 21},
delivered [32], arm set identical on every cell and equal to
`{ov2, ov2b, ov4, ov4b, ov8, ov8b, ov16, ov16b}`. Every number reproduces.

**The mechanism it names is the one branch that cannot have run.** The analysis says *"The
remembered ceiling request floors the cap there, so on those cells the low rungs are
ceiling-dominated"* — that is `SCORCH_SPMM_NT_CAP_FLOOR_CEIL` raising `nt_cap` to `ceil_request`.
But `ceil_request` is only ever assigned inside a block guarded by `nnz_per_thread > 0`, and
`SCORCH_SPMM_NNZ_PER_THREAD` is **`0L`** in the object chain203 ran — verified in the tarball and
again in `/scratch/bobbyy/c203/c0/src/scorch/csrc/scorch_policy.h`. So `ceil_request` is 0 on every
call, `floor_ceil && ceil_request > nt_cap` is never true, and the ceiling explains none of the 24.
Independently: the ceiling's own conditions (`rows <= 128` and `nnz >= 192*rows`) hold on **1 of the
24** cells — `nw14`, 73 rows — so even with the branch enabled it could account for one.

**The branch that did run is the E-core recruit decline**, `scorch_policy.h` in
`scorch_spmm_nthreads`:

    if (recruit_min_work > 0 && work_true >= recruit_min_work) {
      const long pool = nthreads_override > 0 ? (long)nthreads_override
                                              : (long)omp_get_max_threads();
      if ((long)nthreads >= 2 * pool) nt_cap = 0;   // 0 means "no cap", below
    }
    if (nt_cap > 0 && (long)nthreads > nt_cap) nthreads = (int)nt_cap;

`SCORCH_SPMM_RECRUIT_MIN_WORK` is `10000000L`. So the cap is **switched off entirely** — not raised
— when the true work reaches ten million and the already-resolved count is at least twice the
declared pool, leaving whatever the earlier raise block produced, which is bounded by
`omp_get_num_procs()` = 32 on redwood.

**The attribution is exact, with the complement measured.** Sorting all 267 arm-cells of `ov2` by
`work_true = nnz*k`:

    below 10,000,000 : 243 cells, 0 declined
    at or above      : 24 cells, 24 declined

Not one cell crosses in the wrong direction, and the straddling pair is `FX_March2010` at 9,660,768
(capped to 2) against `rail516` at 10,093,184 (delivered 32) — a 4.5% gap around the constant. The
arm set follows from the same rule without adjustment: the gate `nthreads >= 2*override` with
`nthreads` = 32 is met for overrides 2, 4, 8 and 16 and not for 24, where 2·24 = 48 > 32. That is
why `ov24` shows zero, and it is a theorem about this host rather than a property of the rung.

### The same branch is on the shipped path, and its inertness argument is not general

`scorch_policy.h` says of this rule: *"it is a hybrid-pool rule that is STRUCTURALLY INERT on a
uniform one rather than a second policy… on x86 the pool is 24, the gate is at 48 and the count is
at most 32, so this condition provably cannot fire there and the cap stays unconditional — which is
the configuration every x86 number above was measured in."*

The code does not read `omp_get_max_threads()` for the pool when an override is present; it reads
the override. And **production passes one**: `ops.py` `_composition_hints` returns
`torch.get_num_threads()` as `nthreads_override` for both drop-in SpMM symbols, which
`prebuilt_kernels.py:303` hands to the kernel. So the substitution in the proof is valid exactly
while `2 * torch.get_num_threads() > omp_get_num_procs()`, and that is a precondition the comment
does not state. When a caller sets a thread count below half the affinity set, the branch fires on a
uniform pool.

Measured on both x86 hosts, resolve-only, no timing, on the same 89-matrix corpus:

    host      num_procs   torch pool   cells delivering MORE than the pool (k=32)   team
    redwood   32          24           0                                            --
    redwood   32          16           21                                           32
    redwood   32           8           21                                           32
    MKT       64          64           0                                            --
    MKT       64          16           21                                           64
    MKT       64           8           21                                           64

Same 21 cells at k=32 and 3 at k=4 on both hosts, same `work_true` threshold, and the delivered team
tracks each host's `num_procs`. The boundary on redwood is one unit wide and lands where the rule
predicts — `2*pool <= num_procs`:

    pool 15 -> 21 cells exceed    pool 17 -> 0
    pool 16 -> 21 cells exceed    pool 18 -> 0

So on a 64-CPU allocation a caller asking for 8 threads gets **64** on these matrices, an 8× excess
over the declared budget, on a pool with no E-cores to recruit.

**What is not claimed: nothing here is timed.** Whether the wider team is faster or slower at a
small pool is unmeasured, and the honest counterfactual is awkward — the only way to get the capped
count through the shipped interface is to raise the override past the gate, so the natural arm pair
is override 16 (delivers 32) against override 17 (delivers 17), a one-unit change in the argument
for a fifteen-worker change in the team. That is a chain, not an addendum. The finding is that a
documented "provably cannot fire" does fire, which is reportable on its own.

### chain200's thread sweep: five of seven arms are one treatment on 21 cells

chain200 built the same `scorch_c199.tgz` (`rw_s_chain200.sh:27`), set its arms with
`OMP_NUM_THREADS` per invocation rather than by affinity (`chain200_body.sh:162`), and its harness

which is exactly the configuration that meets the gate. Run against chain200's own build object at

    arm t1  (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1)  -> 21 of 89 cells at k=32 deliver a team of 32
    arm t2                       -> 21 cells, team 32
    arm t4                       -> 21 cells, team 32
    arm t8                       -> 21 cells, team 32
    arm t16                      -> 21 cells, team 32
    arm t24                      -> 0

So on those 21 cells **five of chain200's seven arms delivered the identical 32-worker team**, and

### Correction: most of the section above was already established, and here is the part that is not

The memory file `spmm_thread_bound_chains_dead.md` already carries a section titled "A POSITIVE
OVERRIDE IS NOT A HARD CAP, and the exception is a different launch path", and it already records:
the `SCORCH_SPMM_RECRUIT_MIN_WORK` mechanism and its `10000000L` value; that the source's inertness
argument "is sound for a caller passing the real pool and **fails for a sweep arm passing a low
override**"; the `resolved > override` detector; that chain200 crosses the threshold on **0 cells at
k=2, 3 at k=4 and 21 at k=32**; and that chain189/190 were checked from their sealed ledgers at **24
of 305 cells**, chain190 reading `{1:32, 2:32, 4:32, 8:32, 16:32, 24:24}` — five of six swept arms
collapsed onto 32 — and chain189 reading all six arms at 32. So the chain200 table above re-measures
a recorded result on chain200's own object rather than establishing a new one, and the claim that
five of its arms are one treatment was already on file for chain190 in the same form. Stated here
because presenting it as new would overstate it.

Four things today added.

**1. chain203's sealed analysis attributes its own 24 cells to a branch that cannot execute, and
that branch is one of the override's three declared roles.** The analysis says "the remembered
ceiling request floors the cap there", and the memory description likewise lists "a remembered
ceiling widening survives the cap" as the third of the override's three roles. `ceil_request` is
assigned only inside a block guarded by `nnz_per_thread > 0`, and `SCORCH_SPMM_NNZ_PER_THREAD` is
`0L` in this object — so the role is **dead code here**, and the ceiling's own conditions hold on 1
of the 24 cells anyway. The override has two live roles in this build, not three.

**2. The attribution is now exact rather than consistent.** 243 cells below `work_true` 1e7 decline
zero times; the 24 at or above decline 24 times; the straddling pair is 4.5% apart around the
constant. Knowing the threshold is crossed by 21 cells is weaker than knowing no cell crosses in the
wrong direction.

**3. The exposure is not limited to sweep arms — it reaches an ordinary caller.** The recorded
framing is "fails for a sweep arm passing a low override". But `ops.py` `_composition_hints` makes
production pass `torch.get_num_threads()` on every drop-in SpMM, so the gate is at twice *the user's
own thread setting*. Any caller who sets `torch.set_num_threads(n)` with `2n <= omp_get_num_procs()`
is in the firing configuration. Confirmed on two hosts with the boundary one unit wide — redwood
fires at 16 and not at 17, MKT delivers 64 where 8 was asked — which is the first time this has been
read as a property of the shipped interface rather than of a harness.

**4. `resolved` is the delivered worker count on these cells, which did not follow from the policy
alone.** `at::parallel_for` spawns `min(nthreads, at::get_num_threads())`, so a resolved 32 against a
pool of 8 could have meant 8 workers. It does not: `spmm.h:5288` takes `#pragma omp parallel
num_threads(nthreads)` exactly when `nthreads >= 2 * at::get_num_threads()`, the same condition the
policy declines its cap for. The decline exists so this launch gate is satisfiable — deliberate, not
an oversight. The team really is 32.

And the inertness claim is **duplicated at both launch sites**, `spmm.h:5284` for the drop-in and
`spmm.h:6409` for the fused Linear-SpMM, each arguing from "pool = every physical core"
("redwood: pool=24 = every physical core, omp_get_num_procs()=32 counts only SMT siblings,
nthreads<=32 < 2*24=48 can never trigger"). Both hold at pool 24 and both fail together below 17, so
a fix has three sites to reconcile and not one.

## One idiom, four decision points, and every inertness argument fails at the same pool

The expression

    const long pool = nthreads_override > 0 ? (long)nthreads_override
                                            : (long)omp_get_max_threads();

occurs at three separate decision points in this object, and a fourth reads
`at::get_num_threads()` for the same purpose:

    scorch_policy.h:2093   recruit decline      cap dropped when work_true >= 1e7 and nthreads >= 2*pool
    scorch_policy.h:2391   partition work gate  gate active only when pool <= SCORCH_SPMM_PARTITION_GATE_MAXTHREADS
    spmm.h:5288            drop-in launch       raw omp team when nthreads >= 2*at::get_num_threads()
    spmm.h:6415            fused launch         same condition, same team

Each is guarded by an argument that it cannot fire on x86, and each argument is stated in the same
form — substitute the physical core count for the caller's pool:

    policy.h:333   "on x86 the pool is 24, the gate is at 48 and the count is at most 32, so this
                    condition provably cannot fire there"
    policy.h:2093  "On an all-physical-cores pool no recruit is EVER at stake (x86: pool 24, gate at
                    48, count at most 32) ... structurally inert on a uniform one, not a second policy"
    policy.h:1401  "A ceiling between the two pools makes the gate PROVABLY INERT on the larger host:
                    it cannot fire at a pool of 24, so the x86 measurement stands unchanged by
                    construction rather than by a second grid agreeing"
    spmm.h:6409    "makes the recruit fire ONLY on a P-core-only-subset pool: on a non-hybrid /
                    all-physical-cores pool (e.g. x86 redwood: pool=24 = every physical core,
                    omp_get_num_procs()=32 counts only SMT siblings) nthreads<=32 < 2*24=48 can
                    never trigger"

`SCORCH_SPMM_PARTITION_GATE_MAXTHREADS` is **16**. The recruit gate is met when `2*pool <=
omp_get_num_procs()`, which on a 32-CPU host is `pool <= 16`. **The two constants land on the same
pool value**, so the measured boundary of the recruit finding above — 15 and 16 fire, 17 and 18 do
not — is simultaneously the partition gate's boundary. At a caller pool of 16 on redwood, x86
hardware runs the ARM-calibrated branch of two independent rules at once, and the pool is the only
thing that changed.

**They do not, however, act on the same products, and that is worth being exact about.** The
partition gate turns the row partition off below `MINGRAINS * GRAIN_SPMM` = 2 × 150000 = **300,000**
units of work proxy; the recruit drops the cap at or above `RECRUIT_MIN_WORK` = **10,000,000** units
of true work. At k=32 the two work measures coincide, so the regions are disjoint by a factor of 33
and no cell is touched by both. "Both rules become live at pool 16" is right; "both fire on the same
cell" is not.

**One of the two has a measured x86 sign, and it is a cost — but not at this pool.** The partition
gate's comment says of the ceiling-disabled configuration: *"0 disables the ceiling, which lets the
gate fire at any pool (that is the configuration x86 measured at 4-9% cost, and it is not what
ships)."* That measurement was taken with the gate firing **at pool 24**, which is the configuration
the ceiling exists to prevent. What happens when the gate fires at pool 16 on x86 — which is what
ships — is not measured by it. The ceiling was chosen "between the two pools", 6–12 on the M5 and 24
on redwood, so a pool of 16 is neither host's natural pool and sits in the gap the constant was
placed in.

**The source refutes chain203's ceiling attribution in its own words, 1700 lines earlier.**
`scorch_policy.h:399-403`, on flipping `SCORCH_SPMM_CEIL_CAP_POOL` to 1: *"It changes no emitted code
today: `ceil_cap_pool` is read only inside `if (nnz_per_thread > 0 && ...)`, and
SCORCH_SPMM_NNZ_PER_THREAD ships at 0, so the whole block folds away in a release build — verified
by compiling an x86_64 -O3 object before and after."* So the header states that the ceiling block is
absent from a release build, and `c203_analysis.txt:71` attributes 24 measured cells to it. The two
sentences are in the same object.

**And the recruit's calibration table has an inverted label.** `policy.h:2084-2089` introduces the
autoencoder grid as "the ratio **of pool-launch over team-launch** by work", then tabulates
`<10M 1.192, 10-20M 0.962, 20-40M 0.770, 40-80M 0.632, >80M 0.458` and concludes "the team is worth
2.18x on the largest bucket and costs 19% on the smallest". 1/0.458 = 2.183 and 1.192 − 1 = 19.2%,
so the numbers and the prose agree only if the ratio is team over pool. Read as labelled every
bucket reverses and the rule contradicts the data it cites. The threshold and the conclusion are
unaffected; the axis label is wrong.

**What this does and does not say about the sign of the recruit newly firing on x86.** The 24 cells
are at or above 1e7 by construction, so they fall on the side of the crossing where that grid found
the wide team beneficial (10–20M reads 0.962, 20–40M reads 0.770 once the label is corrected). That
grid is **ARM-only**, and the extra workers it recruited were the M5's twelve efficiency cores.
The x86 equivalent at pool 16 recruits **SMT siblings**, which share execution resources rather than
adding cores, and the separate attempt to exploit that difference — capping to physical cores — was
measured and rejected on x86 at −9 to −11% on the caller path. So the nearest evidence points the
right way and does not transfer, and the sign on x86 stays open. What does not depend on the sign is
that four inertness arguments are false in a configuration a caller can reach with one call to
`torch.set_num_threads`.

## chain204 is running on MKT, and its analysis reproduces chain203's headline before it sees new data

Job **17439864** on `mkt1`, three arms (`ovp` override −1, `ov64`, `ov64b`), 89 keys, k ∈ {2, 4, 32},
30 passes, pool pinned at 64, 24-hour wall limit.

**The analysis was validated against the sealed result before the new data existed.** `an_c204.py`
is written independently of `an_c203.py` but copies its conventions deliberately — per-cell ratio as
the median over shared passes, four reductions, bootstrap over the cell-key-sorted vector with
`statistics.quantiles(n=1000, method="inclusive")` at q[24]/q[974], membership and value digests.
Pointed at `chain203-rungwise-redwood` with `--subject ov24 --ambient ovp` it reads:

    k=32 HIGHER   n=25 cells, 550 rows
      gm-rows 1.2123   med-rows 1.1486   gm-cells 1.1806   med-cells 1.1441
      band [1.0741, 1.3115]   floor 0.44%   verdict FASTER, all four nestings agree in sign
      members 1ec8352efdd15bc6   resolved: ambient 1..23 -> subject 24

    ^ SUPERSEDED. That band and floor were computed at --nboot 400 without saying so; at the
      script's default nboot 2000, seed 204, they are [1.0748, 1.2979] and 0.42%. The four point
      estimates are unaffected. See "the band I published was computed at nboot 400" below.

chain203 published **14.4%–21.2% depending on nesting**: med-cells 1.1441 → 14.4% and gm-rows
1.2123 → 21.2% are the two ends, and gm-cells 1.1806 against its published 1.1805 differs in the
fourth decimal only. The membership digest `1ec8352efdd15bc6` is the same value chain203 recorded
for chain202's ADOPT group. Every NULL group reads inside its own floor and every LOWER group is
empty at all three widths, which is the theorem for an override equal to the pool. So a second
implementation reproduces the headline, its floor, its group membership and its null controls.

**The recruit decline is inert in chain204's allocation, and the analysis measures that rather than
arguing it.** The decline needs `resolved >= 2*pool`; with pool 64 that is 128 and the policy caps
at `omp_get_num_procs()`, which the runner refuses unless it equals 64 — the log line is `pool 64 ==
affinity == policy num_procs ceiling`. The analysis then checks the observable directly: a positive
override is the final cap unless the cap declined, so `resolved > override` on any cell *is* the
decline, and the stage-0 check refuses if any appears. Both controls run:

    ov24 / ov24b on chain203  ->  pool 24, 0 cells with resolved > override   (passes)
    ov2  / ov2b  on chain203  ->  48 arm-cells with resolved > override, rc=1 (refuses)

The 48 is arm-cells, not cells: the same 24 cells on each of the two arms. Naming that here because
48 beside chain203's published 24 would read as a disagreement.

**A defect I introduced and caught before it cost anything.** The first body skipped an arm-pass
whose CSV was merely non-empty. `mrgate_ov.py` writes its header at open, so a wall-clock kill
leaves a non-empty partial file that a resume would treat as complete and silently drop the rest of
that arm-pass. The replacement requires exactly 802 lines — verified empirically as the only
distinct line count across all 242 of chain203's CSVs, not computed as 89 × 3 × 3 + 1 — and rewrites
anything else. It was then exercised for real: the first submission was given a 12-hour limit
against a measured 8.6 minutes per arm-pass, which is 12.9 hours for 90 of them, so I cancelled my
own job 17439687 and resubmitted at 24 hours. The resumed run's first log line is `ov64 p1 is
PARTIAL (612 of 801 rows) -- rewriting`. The guard fired on its own input on its first opportunity,
which is the only reason the 612-row file is not now part of the data.

**And an attestation gap spanning both the source and the object.** `scorch_policy.h` has **0
copies and 0 manifest lines** in the spmm-beat-mkl cache; `.h` files in this milestone number
**0**, against 250 sealed `.py`/`.sh`/`.cpp`. It is not a convention — codex-wide there are 9
manifest lines naming `scorch_policy.h` — this milestone simply does not seal headers. Put beside
`.tgz` manifest lines codex-wide, which are also **0**, the consequence is that **neither the source
of the policy argument nor the object built from it is attested anywhere in this milestone.** Every
source citation in this document therefore rests either on branch HEAD or on the unattested tarball,
whose digest is now recorded here only because it was computed by hand. The two copies also differ:
branch HEAD carries about 25 lines more than the tarball somewhere between line 400 and line 1401,
so citations agree exactly up to `:399` and need +25 after it — the header at HEAD is 2475 lines and
158,658 bytes. Found by the checker session, whose positive controls on the same population
(`mrbuild.sh` 7 copies, `csrresolve.py` 4, `spmmstat.py` 6) show the predicate fires.

### Correction: the band I published was computed at nboot 400 and I did not say so

The validation band above was quoted as **[1.0741, 1.3115]** with a floor of 0.44%. Those came from
`--nboot 400`, against the script's own default of 2000, and the document stated neither the
resampling count nor the seed. The checker session could not reach 1.3115 in roughly 160 bootstrap
runs at nboot 2000, 4000 and 10000, under two percentile conventions and three resampling units,
topping out at 1.3097 — a gap of 0.005–0.008 that was systematic rather than noisy. They were right,
and the explanation is the missing parameter.

Eight seeds at each count, on the same 25 cells:

    nboot 400    lower [1.0609, 1.0839]   upper [1.2857, 1.3115]   upper spread 0.0258
    nboot 2000   lower [1.0693, 1.0804]   upper [1.2942, 1.3018]   upper spread 0.0076

**1.3115 is the maximum of the nboot-400 seed range.** A 97.5th percentile taken from 400 resamples
is an unstable statistic, I happened to publish the extreme of its seed variation, and omitting
nboot is what made it unfalsifiable rather than merely imprecise. The authoritative reading, at the
script's default nboot 2000 and seed 204:

    k=32 HIGHER  n=25, 550 rows
      gm-rows 1.2123   med-rows 1.1486   gm-cells 1.1806   med-cells 1.1441
      floor 0.42%   band [1.0748, 1.2979]   FASTER by 7.5-29.8%, all four nestings agreeing

The four point estimates are unchanged, because none of them depends on the resample — which is
also why every quantity the checker could reproduce was a non-bootstrap one. The verdict is
unchanged: the lower bound is 18× the floor and excludes parity by a wide margin. **Every band in
this document should carry its nboot and seed**; these are 2000 and 204.

**And the floor deserves its name, because four candidates are in play and they differ by 9×.** On
the same 25 cells the same-argument pair reads a point deviation of 0.05%, a band half-width of
0.42%, and an outer band edge `max(|lo-1|, |hi-1|)` of 0.42%; the ambient pair on those cells reads
0.26%/0.37%, and pooled over all 89 k=32 cells 0.23%/0.27%. "Floor 0.42%" alone does not say which.
It is **the outer band edge of the identical-argument comparison on the same cells** — the most
conservative of the four.

**A blind spot in the 802-line guard, closed.** A line count cannot distinguish a complete file from
one resumed by *appending*: 802 lines, 801 rows, 189 duplicated and 189 keys missing passes the
count and is wrong. It is unreachable through this writer — `mrgate_ov.py:122` is `open(A.csv, "w",
newline="")`, which truncates — but that makes the guard's sufficiency a property of a *different*
file, holding only until an open mode changes or two runners share a path, with no symptom either
way. Both analyses now require the right number of distinct `(key, k, arm)` triples per file: 801
for chain204, 68760 for chain205. It costs one pass and reads `[801] ; files with duplicates or a
short set: 0` across all 66 of chain203's files. Raised by the checker session.

One phrasing correction to the paragraph that introduced the 802: 89 × 3 × 3 + 1 is also 802, so the
measured anchor and the formula agree. What measuring bought was provenance, not a different number,
and it would only diverge if the runner ever wrote a different number of row-arms per cell.

### Correction to the correction: seed and nboot do not pin a bootstrap, and the band moves again

The previous section concluded that "every band in this document should carry its nboot and seed".
That is necessary and it is not sufficient, which the checker session established by obeying both
and still not reproducing the number. At seed 204, nboot 2000, the same percentile convention and
the same 25-cell vector, two implementations read **[1.0748, 1.2979]** and **[1.0729, 1.3022]**.
Neither is wrong. `random.Random(seed).randrange(n)` once per element, `random.choices(v, k=n)`,
and `np.random.default_rng(seed).integers(...)` consume one seed differently and produce different
resamples, so the two parameters make a band **auditable** — they are what let the nboot-400 story
be confirmed — without making it **reproducible by a second implementation**.

What pins it is the index matrix. The analysis now builds it in one documented call,
`np.random.default_rng(seed).integers(n, size=(nboot, n))` on numpy's PCG64, and publishes a digest
of the sorted bootstrap statistic vector beside every band, so a second implementation either lands
the same digest or can say which of seed, nboot, generator and draw order differs without guessing.
Under that resampler the headline reads:

    k=32 HIGHER  n=25   seed_for(32,"HIGHER") = 204 + 7919*32 + 31*2 = 253674   nboot 2000
      gm-rows 1.2123   med-rows 1.1486   gm-cells 1.1806   med-cells 1.1441
      floor 0.43%   band [1.0662, 1.3032]   FASTER by 6.6-30.3%, all four nestings agreeing
      bootstrap vector sha256: claim b9e5e9fb3b7998ec   floor a212aeed3033ff30

So the band has now moved three times — [1.0741, 1.3115] at nboot 400, [1.0748, 1.2979] at nboot
2000 under Python's `random`, [1.0662, 1.3032] at nboot 2000 under numpy's PCG64 — while the four
point estimates have not moved at all. That is the useful summary of the whole episode: **the
resample-dependent digits were never cross-checkable quantities and the resample-independent ones
always were.** Quote the point estimates to four figures and the band to two, or publish the digest.

**Two further corrections from the same review, both adopted.**

The floor is a bootstrap bound too, and it was drawn on its own seed here while the effect it gates
was drawn on another — which makes their ratio a reading about two seeds. chain203's convention
shares one seed per (width, group) between a band and the effect it gates precisely so the two are
drawn on the same indices; this analysis now does the same. That also resolves 0.42 against 0.44
completely: over 40 seeds the outer edge of the identical-argument pair on these 25 cells runs
**0.41%–0.45%** at nboot 2000, both of us were quoting the outer edge, and the difference was seed.
It reads 0.43% under the shared-seed numpy resampler. At a lower bound of 6.6% against 0.43% the
margin is 15× and nothing turns on the second decimal, but the floor is the quantity a verdict is
compared against, so it gets the same provenance as the effect.

And the nboot-400 range is wider than I reported: eight seeds gave an upper bound spread of 0.0258
and forty give **0.0363**, running to 1.3151. 1.3115 was the maximum of *my eight* seeds, not of the
estimator.

### Two scoping corrections, one of which contains its own counterexample

**chain196 is itself a 4584-key ours-against-MKL board.** I wrote that "every ours-against-MKL
number in this milestone since 2026-09-10 has been read on an 89-key corpus". chain196's ledger is
dated 2026-09-10 22:15, so the sentence includes the one chain that refutes it. The accurate
scoping is **chains 197 through 204** — eight consecutive chains on at most 87 distinct problems —
which is a stronger statement than the dated one, and the dated form failed the same way
`git log --since` does at the boundary second.

chain205 is still new rather than a repeat, and for a reason worth stating: `rw_s_chain196.sh:49-56`
refuses unless the tarball defines `SCORCH_SPMM_REGBLOCK_PFD 2` and `SCORCH_SPMM_ROW_PREFETCH 1`,
so its three builds are prefetch-era objects and not the `c199` tree. The affordability precedent
transfers; the numbers do not.

**And chain196's settings, which is why chain205 was restarted.** Its full-collection family ran
`--reps 4 --target-ms 6`, keeping the 13-rep 25-ms defaults only for its nine-matrix GCN family
(`chain196_body.sh:314-320`). I launched chain205 on the defaults, measured 1726 rows in 7.5 minutes
— about five hours a pass and thirty for six — and restarted it on chain196's settings at about
28 minutes a pass. The 13.5× ratio in the settings matches the 12× I measured. Precision on a
22,920-cell board comes from the number of cells rather than reps per cell (chain196 got ±0.2%
intervals on n=2010 this way), and a noisier per-cell reading *inflates* the A/A floor, which makes
the count of cells behind MKL conservative rather than generous.

**A third generation divergence, and this one has no attested copy to fall back on.** The writer
that produced chain196's eighteen full-collection CSVs and is producing chain205's is
`/scratch/bobbyy/mrgate.py`: **a55e07bf**, 8173 bytes, 136 lines, B-matrix RNG seed at line 135.
The only attested copy is `harnesses/mrgate.py`: **4d5b05e3**, 7460 bytes, 125 lines, the same RNG
seed at line **124**. Both line citations in this exchange were therefore correct for different
files 713 bytes apart, and `chain196-fullcollection-redwood/SHA256SUMS` names no `mrgate` copy at
all — it pins its body, its runner, `mrbuild.sh`, its waiter and three analysis scripts, but not the
