### The fix reproduced the band and the check it shipped with did not

The index-matrix convention worked on the first attempt: the checker session independently read
**[1.0662, 1.3032]** for the effect and an outer floor edge of **0.43%**, identical to all four
published decimals at both ends, with the same index matrix — `np.random.default_rng(253674).
integers(25, size=(2000,25))`, matrix sum **599742** on both sides, first row `10 23 3 11 20 13 21
16 …`. That is the first band in this document to land exactly on a second implementation, and it
settles two things by reproduction rather than assertion: the shared-index convention between a
floor and the effect it gates, which yields 0.43% and not 0.42% or 0.44%; and that the percentile
rule still has to be *named*, because a plain order statistic `s[int(0.975*2000)]` moves the upper
bound to 1.3033.

**And the digests published to make it checkable were not checkable.** They tried ten
serialisations of the sorted statistic vector — `float64.tobytes()`, `%.17g` with and without a
trailing newline, `repr`, `%.12g`, `%.6f`, comma-joined, memoryview — and got ten values, none of
them `b9e5e9fb3b7998ec` or `a212aeed3033ff30`. Since the band agreed to four decimals at both ends
on both vectors, the vectors themselves agree, so **the digest as published turns a correct
reproduction into a mismatch.**

The recipe is `"\n".join("%.12e" % v)`, single newline, no trailing newline, and it reproduces both
values exactly — verified here by recomputing from the sealed CSVs. `%.12e` was the one format they
did not try, which is the whole point: a digest without its serialisation is not evidence, and this
is the serialisation defect recorded two sections above **reappearing inside the fix built to close
it**, one round later, in the check rather than in the band. Both analyses now print the recipe
beside the values, with the reason.

**The p95 rank defect, sized.** `int(0.95*(n-1))` against nearest-rank is a fixed off-by-one in
rank, so its error in percentile terms goes as 1/n:

    n        index used   nearest-rank   effective percentile
    3            1             2              66.7%
    6            4             5              83.3%
    10           8             9              90.0%
    20          18            18              95.0%   <- coincide
    22          19            20              90.9%
    40          37            37              95.0%   <- coincide
    4584      4353          4354              95.0%

So it was genuinely latent at n=4584 and catastrophic at small n — which is exactly why a small-n
synthetic corpus is the control that finds it. Two details worth keeping: my 22-matrix corpus sits
in the affected region at 90.9%, and the two indices *coincide* whenever 0.95n is an integer, so a
control built at n=20 or n=40 would have passed and told me nothing.

**One correction to a correction: the `mrgate.py` line counts do compare.** The concern was that
"136 lines" against "125 lines" might pair a physical count with a non-blank one, in which case the
11-line gap agreeing with the 135−124 offset would be coincidence. Both figures are `grep -c .`, and
measured under both predicates the gap is 11 either way:

    attested harnesses/mrgate.py   137 physical   125 non-blank   7460 bytes   RNG at physical 124
    /scratch/bobbyy/mrgate.py      148 physical   136 non-blank   8173 bytes   RNG at physical 135

So the RNG line moving by exactly 11 is a consequence of eleven lines inserted above it, not a
coincidence, and the conclusion rests on three agreeing quantities rather than on the 713 bytes
alone. The caution was the right shape and the check clears it.

### The digest earned its keep on first use, and the orientation it caught was consistent

With the recipe attached, the claim digest matched immediately (`b9e5e9fb3b7998ec`, index matrix sum
599742 on both sides). The floor digest did not: the checker read `9f43d54a347e4480` where this
document publishes `a212aeed3033ff30`, and a sweep of nine candidates located the difference at the
**orientation of the floor ratio**. That is the case for publishing a digest, made on its first use.

**The direction of the finding is the opposite of the one proposed, and it matters because adopting
the proposal would have introduced the defect it was guarding against.** Every reading here is
`base/subject` with the same subject:

    claim  = ovp   / ov24     above 1 means ov24 is faster
    floor  = ov24b / ov24     above 1 means ov24 is faster

Both put the arm under test in the denominator, so the floor has the same measurement shape as the
claim it gates and their ratio is not a reading about two conventions. The checker's expected
`ov24 / ov24b` is `subject/base` — the *inverted* one relative to the claim. So this analysis was
self-consistent and the default guess was the mismatch. Verified by reading the code path: both
stages call `cell_ratios(cells, subject, base)`, which returns `base/subject`, with `subject=ov24`.

**Their substantive point stands entirely, and it is the part to keep: orientation is not a
relabeling here.** The cell statistic is a median over shared passes, the pass count is 22, and
averaging two middle order statistics does not commute with inversion, so
`median(y/x) != 1/median(x/y)`. On the 25 k=32 cells all **25 of 25** differ, max 1.80e-04, mean
2.42e-05, and the floor's outer edge reads **0.428%** one way against **0.433%** the other. Both
round to 0.43%, which is exactly why the published statistic could not distinguish them and the
digest could in one step. Under an odd pass count it *would* be a pure relabeling, so the
convention has to be written down rather than inferred from the arm names. The provenance block now
states it.

### chain205's first pass needs no pass term, answered from chain196 before the run reports

A pre-registered question about chain205 — whether the cold first pass, which reads all 4584 npz
files from disk, biases its measurements — settled from chain196's sealed data rather than from
chain205's own. Per pass over all 22,920 cells of `sh_c0`:

    gm(ours ms)     p1 0.02047    p2..p6 0.02032 - 0.02053    pooled 2-6 0.02041
    gm(ours/mkl)    p1 0.44238    p2..p6 0.43826 - 0.44335    pooled 2-6 0.44029
    gm(oursb/ours)  p1 1.00073    p2..p6 0.99865 - 1.00016    pooled 2-6 0.99941

Pass 1's ratio sits **inside** the per-pass range of the other five, so the npz reads fall outside
the timed region and all six passes pool. The first pass costs wall-clock, not validity. Also
22,920 of 22,920 cells are complete in all six passes — zero skips on the full collection, so that
denominator is the population and not a filtered subset. Measured by the checker session.

**And the datum chain205's board should be read against.** chain196's pooled full-collection result
is **2.271× against MKL** (1/0.44029), with pass 1 alone at 2.260×. That sits *above* the 1.5–2.1×
band recorded for the 89-key readings, so the small corpus was not flattering the result — if
anything it understated it. Different object (the prefetch-era `REGBLOCK_PFD 2` /
`ROW_PREFETCH 1` tarball) and one host, so it is not a prediction for the `c199` object. What it
does establish, before the new numbers arrive rather than after, is that the coverage gap being
closed is not a case of a favourable subset having been selected.

### chain203's headers name (subject, base) while its code computes base/subject

The checker was right and my previous section drew the wrong conclusion from the right premise. Both
claims survive: `an_c204` is internally consistent at `base/subject` with the same subject, **and**
chain203's published band-pair column is the reverse of `an_c204`'s floor. What reconciles them is
a labelling convention that reads as the inverse of what it holds.

Settled by computing all four value digests over the k=32 adopt group and matching them against the
sealed table:

    ratio computed    digest             chain203's column header for it
    ov24 / ov24b      a99177f18a3908fa   "band ov24b/ov24"
    ov24b / ov24      36e8c224310431ba   -- not published
    ovp / ov24        2fc2d87f43f247e0   "ov24/ambient"
    ov24 / ovp        17cae6ba8245fbdd   "ambient/ov24"

So each header names `(subject, base)` and the code returns `base/subject`, which makes the header
the inverse of the ratio underneath it — `ov24/ambient` holds `ambient/ov24`. The analysis text says
so in words two paragraphs above the table ("subject ov24b, base ov24"), so it is documented rather
than wrong; but a second implementation reading the header as a ratio gets the orientation backwards
on every column, which is what happened here in both directions.

**The consequence was concrete and is now closed.** `an_c204`'s pre-validation cross-checks against
chain203's sealed output, and the floor digest would have mismatched on orientation alone at every
group and every width — in the one comparison the pre-validation exists to perform. Stage 3 now
prints **all four orientations, labelled by the ratio**, with the header convention spelled out, the
way chain203 itself printed three ("all three orientations are printed rather than just the one this
stage happens to use").

**And with the orientations matched, the confirmation is now at the cell-value layer.** A keyed
value digest sees a wrong number attached to a right cell, which neither a membership digest nor any
bootstrap percentile can — swapping two cells' ratios inside a group leaves the geomean, the
multiset and every percentile bit-identical. All twelve of chain203's named stage-3b and membership
claims reproduce from an independently written analysis:

    k=2  adopt   band-pair 04ebc145d06b03b2   ambient/ov24 324d43bde3b5c75f   ov24/ambient 82dc455214b0093e
    k=4  adopt   band-pair 19e03a9fe410ec51   ambient/ov24 c71b9e503004db10   ov24/ambient a2ae9c0f971c40ea
    k=32 adopt   band-pair a99177f18a3908fa   ambient/ov24 2fc2d87f43f247e0   ov24/ambient 17cae6ba8245fbdd
    k=32 ov24 NULL         band-pair aaa2029fb0e0c056   ambient/ov24 8f705890f45995e7
    k=32 adopt membership  1ec8352efdd15bc6

19 of the 140 distinct 16-hex tokens in `c203_analysis.txt` reproduce; the remainder are digests
this analysis does not emit — bootstrap vectors under chain203's own resampler, pass digests, and
memberships under other conventions. So the headline group is confirmed at membership, value and
statistic layers, and in every orientation.

**One rule sharpened rather than added.** `an_c203.py:718` pins `%.12e` *in the code*, with the
reason in its docstring: "repr and `%g` vary with platform and library version, so an unpinned
format makes the digest a property of the environment rather than of the numbers." The convention
was never undocumented — it was documented in the tool and did not travel with the published value.
**A convention documented in the tool is not published with the number.** Same for the orientation:
it was in chain203's prose and not in its column header, which is where a reader looks.

### Correcting my own scope claim: one of chain203's four tables is inverted, not all of them

Commit `a7d33dd` is titled "chain203's column headers are (subject, base), not ratios" and
says "every header is the inverse of what it holds". That is true of one table and false of
the other three. I checked the three I had not checked.

`c203_analysis.txt` publishes four families of table. Verified against the sealed CSVs:

    table                        header(s)                          holds it?   evidence
    stage 3 headline  (3 blocks) ambient/X                          YES         9 of 9 rows recomputed
    stage 3b          (3 blocks) band pair X/Xb, effect ambient/X   YES         38 of 38 n, 76 of 76 digests
    stage 4           (3 blocks) ambient/X, own X/Xb                YES         k=32 ADOPT 1.1806 = gm(ambient/ov24)
    three-orientation (9 rows)   band ov24b/ov24, ov24/ambient,     NO          all 3 columns inverted
                                 ambient/ov24

So the labelling defect is confined to the 9-row, 27-digest table, and the same two digests
that table labels `ov24b/ov24` and `ov24/ambient` are labelled `X/Xb` and `ambient/X`
twenty rows earlier in stage 3b — where the labels are right. `a99177f18a3908fa` is
`ov24/ov24b` and `2fc2d87f43f247e0` is `ambient/ov24` under both labels; only one table
names them correctly.

The inverted table is the one whose own text says it exists as a cross-check surface: "all
three orientations are printed rather than just the one this stage happens to use", so that
"a second implementation can check against it". Worth stating the mitigation plainly,
because it is real: since all three orientations *are* printed, the digest **set** is
complete and correct. A second implementation that computes all three and compares as a set
matches 3 of 3. Only a label-wise comparison fails — which is what I did, and it is why I
read a systematic inversion into the whole document.

### 140 of 140 tokens reproduce, not 19 and not 79

I wrote 19 of 140. The checker corrected me to 79 of 140. Both are low. Sweeping the
candidate space — membership and value digests, per-rung and chain202 partitions, all six
ordered pairs among {ambient, X, Xb}, five widths — reproduces **138 of the 140** distinct
16-hex tokens in the file. The remaining two are not data digests:

    0a74b3f908f5a0c2   sha256 of orders_idx11x22.txt -- verified against the file (and it is
                       byte-identical to chain202's copy, so the two chains shared a rotation)
    e3b0c44298fc1c14   sha256("") -- published as the membership digest of an empty group

Both verify by their own route, so the document's tokens are 140 of 140 accounted for.

Minor defect in the second: `sha256("")` is the same token for every empty group, and the
file prints it four times. It cannot distinguish "this group is empty" from "this group was
never computed" — the null-result-indistinguishable family again, in a digest this time.

### The chain202 partition is ov24-referenced in a way its group names do not say

This is what the membership digests caught, and it is the finding worth keeping. I first
reconstructed chain202's three groups as: all arms agree, else *any* rung raises the count →
`adopt`, else → `caponly`. That reproduces k=2 exactly (29/29/31, all three digests) and is
wrong at the other two widths:

    k     declared (a-a-a/caponly/adopt)   "any rung raises"   off by
    2     29/29/31                         29/29/31            0
    4     29/29/31                         29/26/34            3
    32    24/40/25                         24/19/46            21

The errors are 3 and 21 — exactly the declined-argument census the same file reports, "by
width: {4: 3, 32: 21}". On those cells the low rungs deliver 32 against a pool of 24 while
ov24 delivers 24, so "any rung raises" calls them `adopt` while chain202 calls them
`caponly`. The correct rule is the one the stage *title* states and the group name does not:
the partition is ov24-referenced, so `adopt` means **the pool-valued rung** raises. With
that rule all three widths reproduce, and the token count goes from 131 to 138.

A width-invariant check would have missed this: k=2 passes under both rules, and k=2 and k=4
publish identical membership digests, so a reader spot-checking the narrowest width or the
two that agree sees nothing. It took the width where the declined arguments concentrate.

This is the exact exposure the file argued for when it chose to print membership digests
over counts — "a declared-count check is invariant to a permutation between equal-size
groups". The failure here is not a permutation but a misreading of the group definition, and
the digest caught it anyway, at a width where the count check would also have caught it but
the two agreeing widths would have reassured me first.

### 139 of 140, and my "defect" was already disclosed by the artefact

Three refinements from the checker's round, two of which correct me.

**`sha256("")` is a data digest, so the CSV-reproducible count is 139, not 138.** My sweep
carried `if not cells: continue`, which skipped the three empty groups and so could not emit
the token. Re-run with empty groups included: 54 groups swept, 3 of them empty, and
`e3b0c44298fc1c14` reproduces as the membership digest of `k=2 ov24/LOWER n=0`. The group is
empty at every width — ov24/LOWER sizes are 0, 0, 0 against ov16's 27, 24, 28 — which is the
P1 theorem, not an accident. One token left unreproduced from the CSVs, the rotation file.

**And the collision I called a minor defect is one chain203 found first.** I wrote that
`sha256("")` "cannot distinguish 'this group is empty' from 'this group was never computed'".
The general point stands, but chain203 does not have the problem: every occurrence prints
`n 0` beside the digest, and line 176 is a collision table that names all three of them —

    e3b0c44298fc1c14  k=2 ov24/LOWER n=0 | k=4 ov24/LOWER n=0 | k=32 ov24/LOWER n=0 (the empty group)

so the artefact detected the collision, enumerated its members and labelled it. Calling that
a defect was an over-call.

**That is the second over-call in one round on the same document, with the same cause.** I
called the three-orientation table a document-wide convention error when the same document
labels the other three tables correctly; I called the empty-group digest a defect when the
same document publishes a collision census for it. Both times I compared the object I was
diffing — a digest, a column label — and did not read the line next to it that explains it.
The artefact was more careful than my reading of it, twice.

**One correction going the other way: the rotation provenance is not split between the

### chain205 pass 1 of 6: the pooled figure replicates chain196, and the A/A floor is not shaped how I said

One pass has landed (68,760 rows, 22,920 cells, 4,584 matrices × 5 widths, all three labels).
**One pass, so there is no across-pass floor and no CI** — everything below is preliminary and the
board proper waits for six.

    mkl/ours, pass 1 only, above 1 means we are faster
    k      cells   gm       median   behind   pct behind
    2      4584    1.7034   1.4859   209      4.6%
    4      4584    1.9270   1.7278   117      2.6%
    8      4584    2.3319   2.6399   40       0.9%
    16     4584    2.7010   2.9309   28       0.6%
    32     4584    2.8826   3.0245   16       0.3%
    ALL    22920   2.2649   2.4790   410      1.8%

The pooled 2.2649 sits **0.3% from chain196's sealed full-collection figure of 2.271×** — a
different chain, a different build, different passes, same corpus. That is the first independent
replication of that number, and it lands above the 1.5–2.1× band the 89-key corpus gave, which is
the corpus-size effect already recorded rather than a new result.

**The A/A floor within one pass is heavy-tailed, and I had its shape backwards.** Measuring
`oursb/ours` — identical code under two labels:

    k      p50|dev|  p95|dev|  p99|dev|  max|dev|
    2      0.0128    0.3154    0.6068    1.6070
    32     0.0170    0.3686    0.7070    1.9249

A median deviation of 1.3–1.7% with a p95 of 28–37% is not a noisy population; it is a quiet one
with a tail. I said the tail would be the tiny matrices the full collection adds. It is not:

    nnz band     cells   p95|dev|   median|dev|
    < 1e3        2835    0.0611     0.0113
    1e3-1e4      4150    0.0775     0.0147
    1e4-1e5      9665    0.3791     0.0123
    1e5-1e6      3890    0.3868     0.0175
    1e6-1e7      2005    0.2331     0.0084
    > 1e7         375    0.0606     0.0080

The tail peaks in the **middle** of the size range and both ends are quiet at ~6%. The plausible
mechanism is cache residency rather than timer resolution: below ~1e4 nonzeros the working set is
always resident, above ~1e7 it is always streamed from DRAM, and in between residency is marginal,
so whether the previous arm left the data warm decides the reading. That is a mechanism, so it
predicts the inverted-U rather than being fitted to it — and the prediction is testable on the
remaining five passes.

**The methodological consequence, flagged and not acted on.** Stage 2 counts a cell "behind beyond
floor" against its **width's** pooled p95. At a pooled p95 of 28–37% almost nothing can ever count
as behind, so that column would be vacuous — the guard would pass by being unable to fire. A floor
computed per size band is roughly 5× tighter at both ends. **Changing the estimator is Bobby's
call, not mine**: the pre-registered choice was per-width, and a verifier reports the defect and
its size at the read point. Recorded here with both numbers so the decision has them.

Caveat on all of the above: `oursb/ours` within a single pass compares two measurements in the same
process, so it bounds within-run A/A, not the across-pass floor the board will use. The across-pass
floor is what the six passes measure, and it may be much tighter.

### The across-pass floor is LOOSER than the within-pass one, and the peak's location is partly an estimator artefact

chain196 has six sealed passes over the same 4,584 keys, so the residency prediction was testable
tonight rather than at 05:33. Three floor estimators on the same 22,920 cells, all complete in all
six passes, using the symmetric statistic `|ln(x/y)|` over unordered pairs so orientation cannot
enter (reported back as `exp(|ln r|)-1`):

    A  within-pass A/A      |oursb(p)/ours(p)|, pooled over 6 passes        1 vs 1
    B  across-pass same-arm |ours(pi)/ours(pj)|, all 15 unordered pairs     1 vs 1
    C  the 3-vs-3 split     |med(ours,p1-3)/med(ours,p4-6)|                 3 vs 3

    band       cells   A p95    B p95    C p95    B/A    C/A
    < 1e3      2835    0.0612   0.0804   0.0483   1.31   0.79
    1e3-1e4    4150    0.0827   0.1157   0.0745   1.40   0.90
    1e4-1e5    9665    0.4985   0.5545   0.1982   1.11   0.40
    1e5-1e6    3890    0.4561   0.6347   0.3308   1.39   0.73
    1e6-1e7    2005    0.3071   0.6326   0.3653   2.06   1.19
    > 1e7       375    0.0643   0.1693   0.0846   2.63   1.32

**B/A > 1 in all six bands.** Comparing like for like — both 1-vs-1 — the across-pass floor is
*looser* than the within-pass A/A everywhere, by 1.11× to 2.63×. The checker's reading, that the
across-pass floor is tighter by up to 2.1×, came from comparing C against A: C aggregates three
passes on each side, and `C < B` in all six bands by 1.7–2.8×. That gap is the averaging, not a
property of the floor. **So my caveat was right about direction of uncertainty and wrong about its
sign** — the real pass-to-pass floor is wider than the within-pass proxy, which makes "behind
beyond floor" *more* likely to be vacuous, not less.

**The peak marches right with the estimator, so its location is not purely mechanistic:**

    peak under A (within-pass, 1v1)   1e4-1e5
    peak under B (across-pass, 1v1)   1e5-1e6
    peak under C (across-pass, 3v3)   1e6-1e7

Attributing the shift to superposed mechanisms reads a mechanism into a change of estimator.

**But the superposition claim survives, and the evidence for it is `B/A` rather than where C
peaks.** Adding across-pass variation barely moves the left flank (B/A = 1.11 at 1e4–1e5) and
transforms the right (2.06 at 1e6–1e7, 2.63 above 1e7). So there is a distinct across-pass
mechanism concentrated at large sizes, which is what the checker argued. My residency story
predicts the > 1e7 band is quiet, and within-pass it is the quietest of all at 0.064 — that
prediction holds; it is the across-pass component at those sizes that it does not explain.

**And one point back the other way: C is not an arbitrary choice, it is the right floor for this
board.** The board's cell statistic is a median over passes, so the floor must bound the
variability of *that* statistic, which is what a 3-vs-3 split approximates — B would be the right
floor for a single-pass board. The error was labelling C "the across-pass floor" and comparing it
to A as though the comparison isolated pass-to-pass structure. **An estimator has to match the
statistic it bounds**, and the two of us picked different ones and compared the results.

With the board's own estimator, the floor to expect on the six passes is roughly 5% below 1e3
nonzeros, 20–37% from 1e4 to 1e7, and 8% above — so at the peak band "beyond floor" stays hard to
fire, while at both ends it is usable. That makes the per-band question sharper, not softer, and it
remains Bobby's call. The checker's caveat also stands: per-band is a *post hoc* stratification
chosen after seeing the tail, and needs that label wherever it appears.

Caveat carried from the checker: chain196's object is the prefetch-era build (`REGBLOCK_PFD 2` /
`ROW_PREFETCH 1`), not `c199`, so any per-width comparison mixes replication with a build
difference. The floor comparison above is clean, because `oursb` is the same-object construction in
both.

### The matched floor is 2–11%, and `an_c205.py` already computes it

Applying the "estimator must match the statistic it bounds" rule precisely: the board's cell
statistic forms `mkl/ours` *inside* each pass and reduces over passes, so the matched floor forms
`oursb/ours` inside each pass and reduces the same way. Two more candidates against the earlier
three, on chain196's six sealed passes, 22,920 cells complete in all six:

    D  median over passes of (oursb_p / ours_p)      ratio inside the pass, then reduce
    E  median(oursb, p1..p6) / median(ours, p1..p6)  reduce, then ratio

    band       cells   A p95    C p95    D p95    E p95    D/A    E/D
    < 1e3      2835    0.0612   0.0483   0.0196   0.0273   0.32   1.39
    1e3-1e4    4150    0.0827   0.0745   0.0233   0.0337   0.28   1.45
    1e4-1e5    9665    0.4985   0.1982   0.0574   0.0813   0.12   1.42
    1e5-1e6    3890    0.4561   0.3308   0.1138   0.1674   0.25   1.47
    1e6-1e7    2005    0.3071   0.3653   0.0662   0.1205   0.22   1.82
    > 1e7       375    0.0643   0.0846   0.0240   0.0280   0.37   1.17

    pooled, 22920 cells:  A 0.4023   B 0.4902   C 0.1970   D 0.0569   E 0.0851

**The four candidates spread 7× pooled.** D is 2.7–8.3× tighter than the within-pass A/A, so the
operational floor is 2–11%, not the 20–37% I reported from A. Forming the ratio inside the pass
cancels pass-level common mode before the reduction; C reduces the values in two pass groups and
takes a ratio of the results, which keeps it. That reverses my "beyond floor cannot fire"
conclusion — and this time on the stated principle rather than an accident of resolution.

**`an_c205.py` already computes D, and the matching is structural.** `per_cell(num, den)` returns
the median over passes of `num/den` with the pairing inside the pass, and `FLOOR_CELLS` and
`BOARD_CELLS` are both produced by that same function. So the floor cannot drift from the board
without the board drifting too. The script now prints the reduction beside the floor, for the same
reason it prints the orientation.

**One correction to the firability claim.** A 10% deficit is *not* outside the floor in every band
under D:

    band       D floor   is a 10% deficit outside D?   E floor   outside E?
    < 1e3      0.0196    yes                           0.0273    yes
    1e3-1e4    0.0233    yes                           0.0337    yes
    1e4-1e5    0.0574    yes                           0.0813    yes
    1e5-1e6    0.1138    NO                            0.1674    NO
    1e6-1e7    0.0662    yes                           0.1205    NO
    > 1e7      0.0240    yes                           0.0280    yes

Under D it is 5 bands of 6 — `1e5-1e6` has a floor of 11.4%, wider than the deficit. Under E it is
4 of 6, since `1e6-1e7` fails too. The peak band remains the one place a 10% result is unreadable,
which is the same band under every matched estimator.

**The peak is settled at 1e5–1e6.** A puts it at 1e4–1e5, B and both matched estimators D and E at
1e5–1e6, C at 1e6–1e7. Three of five, including both matched ones, agree — so C's rightward shift
was the estimator and there is a single peak at a few hundred KB to a few MB of nonzeros, which is
a cache-boundary-shaped number on redwood. **The Zen4 prediction now has one clean form: the
matched-estimator peak band should move with cache size.** One prediction, one estimator, rather
than a shape read off three.

Note the across-pass mechanism largely disappears under D and E, because forming the ratio within a
pass is exactly what cancels pass-level common mode. So it is real, and the board's own statistic is
already immune to most of it.

**The rule, which is the durable part:** a floor must be computed by the same reduction, at the same
resolution, as the statistic it bounds — and stating the reduction is part of stating the floor. Two
sessions produced four floors from one dataset differing 7×, and every one of them was defensible in
isolation.

### The inverted U is a contamination rate, not a magnitude — and the ≥3-of-6 rule is one-way

The best reframing of the floor tonight, and it reproduces: **a typical reading is equally quiet at
every matrix size, and what varies tenfold is how often a large excursion happens.**

    band       cells   median|dev|  rate>10%   A p95    >+10%    <-10%   ratio
    < 1e3      2835    0.0097        2.4%      0.0612    1.2%     1.3%   0.96
    1e3-1e4    4150    0.0135        4.0%      0.0827    2.1%     2.0%   1.04
    1e4-1e5    9665    0.0130       20.3%      0.4985   10.3%    10.5%   0.98
    1e5-1e6    3890    0.0185       26.1%      0.4561   13.6%    13.3%   1.03
    1e6-1e7    2005    0.0087       14.0%      0.3071    7.5%     7.2%   1.04
    > 1e7       375    0.0100        1.8%      0.0643    1.0%     0.9%   1.15

Medians span 0.87% to 1.87% — a factor of 2.1 — and the *lowest* median sits in `1e6-1e7`, which
has the second-highest p95. So "the noise is bigger in the middle" was the wrong description, mine
included. The excursions are also direction-symmetric in every band (ratios 0.96–1.15), which is a
positive control on the A/A construction itself: a same-function-object comparison with a *biased*
excursion rate would have indicated something structural like arm order or a first-call effect, and
there is none.

**The ≥3-of-6 argument is a necessary condition, not an identity.** The median of six readings is
`(x₃+x₄)/2`, so displacing it past 10% does require at least 3 readings past 10% on one side. The
converse fails:

    displaced but NOT >=3 same-side :   0 of 22920   <- necessity holds
    >=3 same-side but NOT displaced : 576 of 22920   <- sufficiency fails

The counterexample shape is a split: three readings at 1.2 and three at 0.9 put ≥3 on one side
while the median lands at 1.05, undisplaced, because splits cancel in the middle order statistics.
2.5% of cells are that shape.

**And the 5% threshold has a false positive, inside the table that proposed it.**

    band       >=3 same-side   D p95     predicts        actual
    < 1e3           0.7%       0.0196    clean           no
    1e3-1e4         0.8%       0.0233    clean           no
    1e4-1e5         4.9%       0.0574    clean           no
    1e5-1e6        12.4%       0.1138    contaminated    YES
    1e6-1e7         5.8%       0.0662    contaminated    no    <-- false positive
    > 1e7           0.3%       0.0240    clean           no

`1e6-1e7` sits at 5.8%, above the 5% threshold, with D at 6.6% — so the rule predicts 5 of 6 bands,
not 6 of 6. The band was listed in the proposing table with its own "no" beside it, and described
as though 12.4% were the only value over the line. A threshold whose counterexample is in its own
evidence table is worth more than a threshold that fits: the mechanism is real and directional, but
"fraction > 5% ⟹ p95 contaminated" is not the law, because the split-cancellation cells inflate the
fraction without displacing any median.

**My own convention slip, in the same script.** Table 1 above counted `|x-1| > 0.10` and table 2
counted `x > 1.10 or x < 1/1.10`, which differ systematically by 0.5pp because the first admits
`x < 0.900` and the second only `x < 0.909`. Two thresholds for one quantity, in one script, in
tables printed ten lines apart — and the checker's figures were internally consistent where mine
were not. The log-symmetric form is the right one, since it is the only one that cannot depend on
which arm is the numerator.

**The prediction for MKT, in its sharpest form yet:** not that the peak band moves, but that **the
per-reading excursion rate by band moves with cache size**, with D's readability following from it
by the ≥3-of-6 necessary condition. Two measurable quantities with a derivable one-way relation, so
a failure says which half was wrong.

### The bracket: ≥3 necessary, ≥4 sufficient, both exact — and the bracket diagnoses its own insufficiency

The threshold repair verifies as arithmetic rather than as a regularity. `statistics.median` of six
is `(x₃+x₄)/2`, so displacement past 1.10 requires `x₄ > 1.10` (≥3 readings above) and is
guaranteed by `x₃ > 1.10` (≥4). Over 22,920 cells, fully log-symmetric on both sides:

    displaced but NOT >=3 same-side :   0     necessity at 3, exact
    >=3 same-side but NOT displaced : 525     sufficiency fails at 3
    >=4 same-side but NOT displaced :   0     sufficiency at 4, exact
    totals: >=4 218  <=  displaced 604  <=  >=3 1129      bracket holds

    band       >=4 frac  DISPLACED  >=3 frac  ratio  D p95    D>10%  bracket straddles 5%?
    < 1e3        0.1%       0.4%      0.7%    2.10   0.0196   no     no
    1e3-1e4      0.1%       0.5%      0.8%    1.70   0.0233   no     no
    1e4-1e5      0.8%       2.8%      4.9%    1.78   0.0574   no     no
    1e5-1e6      2.6%       6.4%     12.4%    1.94   0.1138   YES    yes
    1e6-1e7      1.5%       2.9%      5.8%    1.98   0.0662   no     yes
    > 1e7        0.0%       0.0%      0.3%      -    0.0240   no     no

**The displaced fraction predicts contamination in 6 of 6 bands, and it is a tautology rather than
a fitted threshold** — a 95th percentile lands in the tail exactly when more than 5% of cells are in
it. The ≥3 and ≥4 counts bracket that fraction, so a cheap count can rule contamination in or out
without computing the percentile.

**And the bracket diagnoses its own insufficiency, which is the part worth keeping.** It straddles
5% in exactly two bands — `1e5-1e6` (2.6 ≤ 5 ≤ 12.4) and `1e6-1e7` (1.5 ≤ 5 ≤ 5.8) — and
`1e6-1e7` is precisely the band where the ≥3 proxy mispredicted. So the guard says "compute the
percentile, do not infer it" in the one band where inferring it was wrong. A proxy that reports
when it is not adequate is a different class of tool from a threshold that fits.

The ≥3 count overstates the displaced fraction by 1.70–2.10× here, wider than the 1.8–2.0× claimed,
and that ratio is an observation about this dataset rather than a rule. The bracket is what carries.

**My 576 was the mixed convention, and it was inside the check that diagnosed the same defect.**
Recounting with `exp|ln r| - 1 > 0.10` on *both* the same-side test and the displacement test gives
**525**, matching the checker exactly. My earlier figure used the log-symmetric form for the
same-side count and `|median - 1| > 0.10` for displacement — the asymmetric form excludes
`0.900 < x < 0.909` where the log-symmetric admits it. So the fourth instance of "one quantity, two
conventions, both defensible, compared as though identical" occurred inside the script that found
the third. The lesson is not to prefer the log-symmetric form once but to make it the only form
available: a single helper, used everywhere, so a mixed convention is not expressible.

### I nearly amended a pre-registered estimator while fixing the convention defect

The structural fix for the mixed-convention defect is right: one helper, used everywhere, so a mixed
convention is not expressible. Implementing it in `an_c205.py` I made the single helper the
log-symmetric form — and the stage-1 floor moved:

    k      pre-registered |x-1|   log-symmetric   relative
    2      0.3163                 0.3850          +21.7%
    4      0.2852                 0.3333          +16.9%
    8      0.2782                 0.3258          +17.1%
    16     0.3388                 0.4174          +23.2%
    32     0.3616                 0.4678          +29.4%

That is not a change of notation, it is a change of gate: the floor decides which cells count as
behind. The sealed `an_c203.py:753` computes its margin as `max(|lo-1|, |hi-1|)` — the asymmetric
form — so switching is an amendment to the convention the predecessor was pre-registered under. A
verifier reports the size of such a thing; adopting it is Bobby's call. **Reverted.**

`an_c205.py` now has exactly two named helpers, `dev_prereg` (|x-1|, chain203's, the operative
floor) and `dev_logsym` (orientation-independent, printed beside every floor and never gating), with
the relative gap shown per width. The structural property survives the revert — every deviation goes
through one of the two named helpers, so a *mixed* convention is still not expressible, which is the
defect that actually happened four times tonight. Preferring the right form was never the fix,
because the form was already preferred both times it was mixed.

Recorded with its timing, since that is what makes it a real constraint rather than a formality:
this was decided with two of six passes landed and pass 1 already inspected. An estimator chosen
after seeing part of the data is weaker than a pre-registered one, which is exactly why the
improvement does not get to be quiet.

**The decision for Bobby, with both numbers in hand:** the log-symmetric floor is 17–29% wider at
every width and cannot depend on which arm is the numerator; the asymmetric one matches the sealed
predecessor and so keeps chain205 comparable with chain203 and chain202. The two are not reconcilable
after the fact, because the choice changes the behind counts the stage exists to produce.

### The self-diagnosis has two thin verdicts of six, and one of them is under my own claim

Exact counts replacing rounded percentages, with the margin beside every verdict:

    band       cells   n>=4  n_disp  n>=3   >=3%    margin to 5%   cells to flip   verdict
    < 1e3      2835      3      10     21    0.74      -4.26pp          121        no
    1e3-1e4    4150      4      20     34    0.82      -4.18pp          174        no
    1e4-1e5    9665     80     267    474    4.90      -0.10pp            9        no
    1e5-1e6    3890    100     248    482   12.39      +7.39pp          288        straddles
    1e6-1e7    2005     31      59    117    5.84      +0.84pp           17        straddles
    > 1e7       375      0       0      1    0.27      -4.73pp           18        no

**`1e4-1e5` is 0.10pp under the line — nine cells of 9,665.** Had it straddled, the bracket would
have demanded the percentile for a band where inference was in fact right, so that failure mode is a
false alarm and the property degrades safely.

**But the thin verdict that matters is the other one, and it is under my claim rather than
theirs.** I wrote that the bracket "reports its own inadequacy in exactly the band where inferring
was wrong" — that band is `1e6-1e7`, and it straddles by **+0.84pp, seventeen cells**. So the
property I called the valuable one holds by seventeen cells out of 2,005. It is still true and still
the right shape, but it is not the robust part of this result; `1e5-1e6` at +7.39pp and 288 cells is
the only verdict with real margin on the straddling side. Two of six verdicts are decided by fewer
than twenty cells, and the self-diagnosis is itself a threshold comparison — so the margins have to
travel with the verdicts.

**And my ratio range covered five bands while being quoted over six.** `> 1e7` has 0 displaced
cells against 1 cell with ≥3 same-side, so `≥3 / displaced` is a zero denominator, not a value
between 1.70 and 2.10. That band cannot support a 5%-threshold statement at all: 5% of 375 cells is
18.75 against an observed count of one, and a single cell moves its fraction by 0.27pp — coarser
than the entire 0.10pp margin at `1e4-1e5`. **Third degenerate statistic from a small-n band
tonight**, after the `if not cells: continue` that skipped three empty groups and the `sha256("")`
published for a group of zero. The pattern is consistent enough to state as a rule: a band whose
count is smaller than the threshold's own resolution cannot be given a verdict, and printing one
there is worse than printing nothing.

### The 17–29% I published was my own fixture, and the independent corroboration was the same error from the other side

`dd88deb` says switching the deviation convention moves the stage-1 floor "17–29% wider at every
width". **That number is wrong by about 7×.** The gate is `an_c205.py`'s stage-1 floor, which is a
p95 over *cells* of the deviation of the per-cell median ratio — statistic D. On chain196's six real
passes:

    k     A |x-1|  A logsym  A rel     D |x-1|  D logsym  D rel     A/D
    2     0.3273   0.3920    +19.7%    0.0454   0.0464    +2.3%     7.2x
    4     0.2967   0.3541    +19.4%    0.0377   0.0382    +1.5%     7.9x
    8     0.3017   0.3637    +20.6%    0.0470   0.0484    +2.9%     6.4x
    16    0.3299   0.4020    +21.9%    0.0598   0.0615    +2.7%     5.5x
    32    0.3874   0.4776    +23.3%    0.0831   0.0866    +4.3%     4.7x

**The convention gap on the gate is 1.5–4.3%, not 17–29%.** The large figure belongs to A, the
per-reading statistic, which is not what gates anything.

**My number came from the synthetic fixture.** It is four jittered copies of one real pass, so
`oursb_p/ours_p` carries the same real ratio in every pass and the per-cell median collapses onto
the single-pass value — D degenerates into A by construction. I had written that limitation down
explicitly two commits earlier ("the self-test validates the plumbing, not the estimator") and then
quoted a floor through that same fixture anyway.

**And the independent corroboration was the identical error from the other side.** The checker
reported +19.7% to +23.3% on chain196 as confirming my +16.9% to +29.4% on chain205 — "different
dataset, different build, same band". Their five p95 values match the **A** column above to four
decimals. So two implementations agreed on ~20% while both computing a statistic other than the one
the gate uses: mine by fixture construction, theirs by choice of resolution. The agreement was not
weak evidence, it was evidence of the shared error — two wrong resolutions coinciding because the
wrong resolution is the natural one to reach for.

**What survives and what does not.** The revert stands: an amendment to a pre-registered estimator
is an amendment at any magnitude, and the direction was still the self-serving one — a wider floor
means fewer deficits clear it, so the board gets easier. What does not survive is the *severity*. A
1.5–4.3% gate shift discovered mid-analysis is a much smaller near-miss than a 17–29% one, and I
published the alarming version. The correct report is: the convention question is real, its
direction favours our own headline, and on the real estimator it is worth 1.5–4.3% — small enough
that it is genuinely Bobby's call rather than something that had to be caught.

The algebra the checker gave is exact and explains the whole pattern: for `x > 1` the two forms are
identical, and for `x < 1` their ratio is exactly `1/x`. So the gap is entirely a measurement of the
downside tail, and it shrinks by 5–8× when the per-cell median suppresses that tail — which is why
the gate's gap is small precisely because the gate is the well-chosen statistic.

Their census verifies: `an_c203.py` contains exactly **one** `abs(`, at line 753, and its only
`math.log` is the geometric mean at 627. There is no second convention in the predecessor to appeal
to.

**Seventh instance of one quantity at two resolutions tonight, and the first where cross-checking
made it more convincing rather than less.**

### "The two numbers were never in conflict" is half right: the scale is necessary, not sufficient

The single-reading algebra is exact — for a below-1 reading at deviation `d`, the log-symmetric form
exceeds the asymmetric one by `1/(1-d) - 1 ≈ d`. The generalisation from that to "gap ≈ 0.5·d at
every resolution, so 20% and 2–4% are the same fact read at two magnitudes" does not hold. Sweeping
the quantile so `d` varies ~60× *inside* each resolution, k=32:

    D per-cell                              A per-reading
    q       d        gap/d   below-1        q       d        gap/d   below-1
    p50     0.0067   0.60    49.6%          p50     0.0157   0.53    49.7%
    p75     0.0157   0.36    49.6%          p75     0.0660   0.56    48.7%
    p90     0.0430   0.74    48.1%          p90     0.2509   0.64    43.7%
    p95     0.0831   0.52    47.0%          p95     0.3874   0.60    30.0%
    p99     0.1821   0.83    29.8%          p99     0.7031   0.44     0.7%
    p99.9   0.4251   0.05    33.3%          p99.9   1.3656   0.14     0.0%

**`gap/d` ranges 0.05 to 0.83 within one resolution.** It is not a constant, so the p95 agreement at
~0.5–0.6 across the two resolutions is a coincidence of tail composition rather than a law. The
reason is that a p95 is a quantile of a *mixed* set: switching convention inflates only the below-1
values, which re-ranks them, so the gap is not a per-element transformation of a fixed quantile and
no single factor relates it to `d`. A mixture estimate does not close it either — at A's p99 the
below-1 share is 0.7% while `gap/d` is 0.44.

**So the useful half of the claim stands and the strong half does not.** A convention gap cannot be
quoted without the deviation scale it was measured at — that is right, and it is the rule to keep.
But naming the scale does not determine the gap: the tail composition near the quantile is a second
free term, and both move. The 17–29% and the 1.5–4.3% were therefore *not* the same fact at two
magnitudes; they were two different quantities that happen to sit at a similar `gap/d` because both
p95 regions have a mid-range below-1 share.

Their observation against their own story verifies and is worth keeping: the below-1 share in the
p95 region is **higher** for cells (43.9 / 52.2 / 52.2 / 51.3 / 47.0%) than for readings (33.8 /
37.6 / 39.6 / 35.8 / 30.0%). So the per-cell medians are the more symmetric population, and the
gate's small gap is not the downside tail thinning — it is `d` shrinking 5–8× while composition
moves the other way.

Which sharpens the earlier statement rather than replacing it: the gate's convention gap is small
because the gate's *deviation* is small, and that is a property the per-cell median earns by
suppressing pass-level noise. Any statistic with a small `d` inherits a small gap, whatever its
composition.

### My refutation's range used thin quantiles; it survives on well-populated ones, at 2.1× not 17×

I published `gap/d` spanning 0.05–0.83 to refute the claim that it is constant. Two of those six
quantiles are too thin to quote — the exact defect I had written a rule about two rounds earlier,
applied to my own number this time. With element counts attached, k=32:

    cells (N=4584)                     readings (N=27504)
    q       n above   d        gap/d   q       n above   d        gap/d
    p50      2291     0.0067   0.60    p50     13751     0.0157   0.53
    p75      1146     0.0157   0.36    p75      6876     0.0660   0.56
    p90       458     0.0430   0.74    p90      2750     0.2509   0.64
    p95       229     0.0831   0.52    p95      1375     0.3874   0.60
    p99        46     0.1821   0.83    p99       275     0.7031   0.44
    p99.9       5     0.4251   0.05    p99.9      28     1.3656   0.14

**The honest span on quantiles with ≥100 elements above them is 0.36–0.74, a factor of 2.1** — not
the 17× my endpoints implied. That still refutes constancy, because p75 and p90 sit at 0.36 and 0.74
with 1,146 and 458 elements above them. The refutation never needed the thin rows and I should not
have quoted them.

**And there is a detail in the other column that explains the whole disagreement.** On *readings*
the usable span is 0.44–0.64, only 1.5×, and across p50–p95 it is 0.53–0.60 — very nearly constant.
So a session holding per-reading data would see constancy and a session holding per-cell data would
not. The claim was not careless; it was true of the population it was measured on and asserted of
one it was not. **Constancy observed along one axis is not a functional relationship**, and the axis
never varied was the one the claim was about — ten points, all at p95, with `d` moved only by width
and resolution.

Which closes this thread with the refined statement standing: the gate's convention gap is small
because the gate's **deviation** is small, not because its downside tail thins — the per-cell
population is the *more* symmetric one (below-1 share 43.9–52.2% against 30.0–39.6%). Any statistic
with a small `d` inherits a small gap regardless of composition, and the per-cell median earns its
small `d` by suppressing pass-level noise. That is checkable in a way "the gate is well chosen" was
not.

**Running count of the same defect, since it is now the dominant one:** four times tonight I
violated my own most recently written rule on the next number I produced — the orientation rule, the
convention rule, the thin-verdict rule, and quoting a corroboration without checking its statistic.
Writing a rule down does not install it; the repairs that held were the structural ones, where the
defect became inexpressible rather than discouraged.

### The quantity retires: `gap/dA` is an attenuation under a ceiling of `1/(1−dA)`

**The population finding verifies exactly.** At k=32 there are 4,584 complete cells; 694 have a
median `ours` runtime at or above 0.1 ms and **3,890 below it**. So the checker's sweep was silently
restricted to short kernels — 84.9% of the board — and compared against my whole-board table.
Neither of us had published the population. They retracted the column rather than reconstructing it,
which is right: with the population unnamed there is nothing to repair it against.

**And the theorem retires the quantity rather than re-measuring it.** Elementwise, writing
`dA = |x−1|` and `dL = exp|ln x|−1`: above parity `dL = dA`, and below parity `dL = dA/(1−dA)`
exactly, since `1−dA = x`. So `dA ≤ dL ≤ dA/(1−dA)` elementwise; the pairing gives
`quantile(dL) ≥ quantile(dA)`, and `a ↦ a/(1−a)` is monotone increasing for `a < 1` so the upper
bound passes through the quantile. Hence for the relative gap `g = (dL−dA)/dA`:

    0 <= g <= dA/(1-dA)        and       0 <= g/dA <= 1/(1-dA)

Checked on chain196, three reductions × five well-populated quantiles:

    reduction              q     dA       g        g ceiling   g/dA    attenuation
    cells/med-of-ratios    p50   0.0067   0.0040   0.0068      0.598   0.59
    cells/med-of-ratios    p75   0.0157   0.0056   0.0159      0.359   0.35
    cells/med-of-ratios    p90   0.0430   0.0319   0.0450      0.740   0.71
    cells/med-of-ratios    p95   0.0831   0.0431   0.0906      0.518   0.48
    cells/med-of-ratios    p99   0.1821   0.1518   0.2226      0.834   0.68
    readings               p95   0.3874   0.2331   0.6323      0.602   0.37
    readings               p99   0.7031   0.3083   2.3684      0.438   0.13

**0 of 15 points above the tight ceiling; attenuation spans 0.13 to 0.71.** For small `dA` the
ceiling is ≈1, so `g/dA` simply *is* the attenuation — a fraction in [0,1] set by how much of the
local composition near the quantile lies below parity. "≈0.5" was one reading of that fraction, and
a fraction has no reason to be constant. The bound also says nothing once `dA ≥ 1`, which is exactly
the thin `p99.9` rows we had already dropped on element counts — two independent reasons to drop the
same rows, which is corroboration that means something because the mechanisms are unrelated.

**My first verification of that theorem was vacuous.** I compared `g` against `1/(1−dA)` — the
ceiling for `g/dA`, not for `g` — so the check passed against a bound roughly 25× too loose and
reported "0 of 18" while testing almost nothing. Fifth instance tonight of one quantity at two
resolutions, and this one occurred *inside the verification of a theorem about that very class*. The
repair was to state both pairings once, in the output, before comparing anything.

My earlier per-cell figures stand: `g/dA` of 0.598 / 0.359 / 0.740 / 0.518 on usable quantiles,
matching the 0.36–0.74 span published in `d256604`.

**Where this thread ends.** The surviving statement is the one that is checkable: the gate's
convention gap is small because the gate's **deviation** is small — the ceiling is `1/(1−dA)`, so a
small `dA` caps the gap regardless of composition — and the per-cell median earns its small `dA` by
suppressing pass-level noise, not by thinning the downside tail, since the per-cell population is
the *more* symmetric one.

**Eight instances of one pattern between two sessions in one night**, four each by the same
predicate: a rule written down and then violated on the next number produced. The repairs that held
were the two that made the defect **unavailable** — one `per_cell()` forcing the floor and board
through a single reduction, and two *named* deviation helpers with one marked gating so a mixed
convention cannot be written. Every repair that consisted of knowing better failed within one
number. That asymmetry is the durable finding of the night, and it is stronger than any individual
result in it.

### The convention choice changes 1–2 verdicts of 22,920, so my "not reconcilable" was wrong

Five rounds sizing the convention gap never asked the question the decision actually turns on:
**which cells change hands.** Computed on chain196's 22,920 cells complete in all three builds and
all six passes, subject = per-cell median of `mkl/ours`, floor = p95 per width of the cross-build
A/A pair **under the same convention as the subject**, so the convention moves both sides:

    subject  floor pair   behind   flagged |x-1|   flagged logsym   verdicts changed
    c0       c0/c0b         119         47              48                1
    c0       c0b/c0         119         47              49                2
    c0b      c0/c0b         118         40              41                1
    c0b      c0b/c0         118         39              41                2
    pfd0     c0/c0b          66         21              21                0
    pfd0     c0b/c0          66         21              21                0

**At most 2 verdicts of 22,920 change — 0.009% — and all six flips across all six combinations go
one way: the log-symmetric form flags one more cell, never fewer.** The complete list, each sitting
just under its `|x-1|` floor and just over its log-symmetric one:

    ss/Meszaros/aa3      k=8   s=0.92763  dA=0.07237  dL=0.07801  floors 0.07255 / 0.07538
    ss/Meszaros/nw14     k=8   s=0.92664  dA=0.07336  dL=0.07917  floors 0.07404 / 0.07490
    ss/Meszaros/p6000    k=2   s=0.91979  dA=0.08021  dL=0.08720  floors 0.08172 / 0.08688
    ss/lp_osa_60         k=4   s=0.93543  dA=0.06457  dL=0.06902  floors 0.06680 / 0.06877

**And the mechanism is the theorem again, not the data.** A below-parity cell can only change hands
if its deviation lands in `(t/(1+t), t]`, a window of width `t²/(1+t)` — 0.0024 at t=0.05, 0.0049 at
t=0.0726, 0.0091 at t=0.10. The behind population is 119 of 22,920, so almost nothing lands in a
half-percentage-point window.

**This corrects a sentence of mine, not theirs.** `dd88deb` said "the two are not reconcilable after
the fact, because the choice changes the behind counts the stage exists to produce." The counts
change by one cell out of 22,920, in a known direction, on a named matrix. So a 1.7–4.3% gap in the
threshold and a 0.009% change in the verdicts are both true, and **the gate gap was simply the wrong
summary of the convention choice.** We sized a quantity whose consequence is one cell, for five
rounds, having never computed the consequence.

**Scope, because over-application is the failure mode this thread has been full of.** This settles
the *board* gate — behind MKL beyond an A/A floor, a threshold crossing. It does **not** settle the
chain203-style gate, where the convention enters bootstrap band endpoints rather than a threshold;
there the displacement analysis is the relevant one and this table says nothing.

**So the pending item for Bobby changes character.** It was recorded as a decision that moves the
board. It is a decision about principle: the log-symmetric form is orientation-independent and
cannot depend on which arm is the numerator; the asymmetric form matches the sealed predecessor and
keeps chain205 comparable with chain203 and chain202. **Both are defensible and the board is
indifferent to the choice at 0.009%.** The revert stands on the pre-registration argument alone,
which is the argument that was always doing the work.

### An empty `git log -S` is two hypotheses, and one of them is an accusation

Verifying the attribution turned up a better finding than the attribution. The sentence in question
wraps in the hard-wrapped document:

    dd88deb:SPMM_BEAT_MKL_RESULTS.md:34207  ...chain203 and chain202. The two are not reconcilable
    dd88deb:SPMM_BEAT_MKL_RESULTS.md:34208  after the fact, because the choice changes the behind...

So the searches disagree, and the disagreement is the whole point:

    git log -S"not reconcilable after the fact"   0 commits
    git log -S"The two are not reconcilable"      1 commit   dd88deb
    git log -S"changes the behind counts"         2 commits  dd88deb

**An empty `-S` result does not read as "my pattern cannot match".** It reads as "no commit
introduced this text" — which, in an exchange about who wrote a sentence, is an accusation that the
quoted sentence was never written. The zero is a conclusion, not a missed confirmation, and it was
manufactured entirely by a line wrap.

Fifth time tonight a wrap has eaten a prose search and the first where the empty result carried a
verdict. The fix is the same shape as the rest of this family: **a `-S` or `grep` count of 0 is two
hypotheses — absent, or unmatchable — and only a positive control separates them.** Search a short
interior fragment with no wrap point first, then narrow.

**The attribution itself:** the sentence is mine, introduced by `dd88deb`, whose subject is
"reverted an estimator amendment I made while fixing conventions". The checker's record of it was a
faithful copy and the refutation is theirs.

**And the class distinction they drew is worth keeping.** The eight rule violations tonight were
*correct questions answered wrongly* — errors of execution. Five rounds sizing a convention gap were
*correct answers to a question nobody had checked was the operative one* — an error of selection.
The second survived every cross-check precisely because cross-checking verifies an answer against
the question asked, never against the question that should have been.

### A carried number arrives already believed, and a headroom claim belongs on the tail

**chain204 is at pass 7 of 30, not 1.** I carried "1 of 30" across a compaction boundary and
repeated it several times without re-deriving it. Its real rate, from the job's own pass timestamps:

    p1 02:08:58  p2 02:28:34  p3 02:45:10  p4 03:03:14  p5 03:17:53  p6 03:37:28  p7 03:54:29
    intervals 19.60  16.60  18.07  14.65  19.58  17.02 min      mean 17.586
    pass 30 starts 10:38:58, ends 10:56:34   total 8.79 h   headroom to a 02:09 expiry 15.21 h

**The failure mode is specific and it is not carelessness.** A number in a session summary or a
handoff doc arrives *already believed*, because the moment it could have been checked was in a
context window that no longer exists. On my wrong input the checker's alarm was internally sound end
to end — a 24 h wall reached at pass 12 — so correct reasoning on a stale input produces a confident
wrong conclusion and nothing inside the reasoning can catch it. Their own state block carried "50
dirs" for a ledger tree where `find -type d` = 50, `-mindepth 1` = 49,
`-mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d` = 23 and `-mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1` = 24, so the same defect was in
their carried state on the same quantity class.

**The fix is the fourth of one kind: carry the predicate, not the value.** "2437 files" is
unverifiable a day later; `find <root> -type f | wc -l = 2437` re-runs in one command and either
reproduces or does not. A count with its predicate is self-checking; a bare count is a rumour with a
number in it.

**A correction to my own margin, which is the same class one level down.** I quoted 2.7× against the
48 min/pass budget a 24 h wall implies. That is the margin on the *mean*. On the worst observed
interval it is 48/19.60 = **2.45×**, and the tail is the quantity that actually has to hold. Still
comfortable; the number was the wrong summary of the constraint, which is the third time tonight a
sensitivity has stood in for a consequence.

**And one thing back: "make it unwritable" is 3 for 3, not 4 for 4.** `per_cell` forcing one
reduction, two named deviation helpers making a mixed convention unwritable, and deleting the
duplicate counts have each since survived a number that would have tripped them. The predicate rule
was adopted minutes ago and has not yet met a number, so its record is 0 for 0. Counting a rule as
successful before it has been applied is the same shape as everything else tonight — and it is worth
saying because the 3 for 3 is only evidence at all if the denominator is honest.

**Both waiters were correct answers to adjacent questions**, which is the selection failure moving
into the instruments. The chain205 waiter answered "are the files complete" when the question was
"is the runner done" — it would have fired the moment the sixth CSV hit 68,761 lines, which precedes
the runner's own completion marker. The chain204 waiter answered "did the job leave the queue" when
the question is "are there 30 distinct pass tags" — a wall-clock kill at pass 12 produces twelve
complete, well-formed, parseable CSVs and a clean `sacct` state, and a 12-pass median is a
respectable-looking statistic answering a different question than the pre-registered one. Both are
now replaced: two agreeing signals for chain205, distinct-pass-tag counting with an explicit
`TRUNCATED AT n OF 30` for chain204, and the chain204 monitor spends no allocation while the job
runs so it cannot perturb the 64-core measurement it is watching.

### Retracting "3 for 3": all three structural repairs are untested, and the scoreboard was the wrong argument

I told Bobby twice that "make it unwritable" is 3 for 3 against "be careful" at 0 for 8. Applying my
own predicate — a repair earns its record only after a number has tried to trip it — **all three are
0 for 0**:

    repair                          installed   trials since   why zero
    per_cell, one shared reduction  pre-session  0             correct from the moment written; it
                                                               never refused a wrong nesting because
                                                               none was ever attempted through it
    dev_prereg / dev_logsym         03:39:43     0             only the synthetic self-test has run;
                                                               no real six-pass data exists yet
    deleted the duplicate counts    04:04:28     0             file untouched since; adding an
                                                               instance is the only event that trips it

**Being already correct is not the same as having been tested.** `per_cell` made the "which nesting
gates?" question determinate when it arose, which is the property being *queried and found to hold* —
weaker than a violation attempting and being blocked. It plausibly prevented a wrong choice, given
that I mixed two deviation conventions ten printed lines apart the same night, but a plausible
counterfactual is not a trial.

So I published a tally as evidence, on the next number after correcting the same overclaim in the
checker's message. Fifth instance of the pattern, and mine.

**And the comparison was not like-for-like in a way that matters more than the count.** "Be careful"
is 0 for 8 because it was *invoked* eight times — every analysis step gives it a trial. The
structural repairs are hours old and each guards one narrow path, so they have had almost no
exposure. **A perfect record over zero trials and a perfect failure over eight are not comparable
records; the denominators measure different amounts of exposure**, and putting them side by side
implies an experiment that was never run.

**The argument that actually carries is mechanical, and it needs no tally:** a defect that cannot be
written cannot recur. `per_cell` makes a floor/board mismatch unexpressible rather than detectable;
two named helpers make a mixed convention unexpressible; one count adjacent to its enumeration makes
a drifting duplicate unexpressible. That is an argument from structure, and dressing it in a
scoreboard gave it empirical support it does not have — which is the night's own pattern one more
time, a number standing in for the thing it was supposed to summarise.

**The honest statement for Bobby:** no structural repair has failed yet, their failure mode would be
visible immediately rather than silently, and the reason to prefer them is the mechanism, not the
record. The record will mean something only once they have been exercised as often as the vigilance
rules were — which for `an_c205.py`'s two helpers is the moment chain205's six passes land.

### The positive control says my "structural" repairs were conventions, and they failed their first trial

"Wait for exposure" was the wrong conclusion. A preventive mechanism's trial is a **positive
control** — feed it the defect it forbids and check it refuses — which is cheap, available now, and
my own standing rule. I ran it on both of my claimed repairs. **Both failed.**

    injected defect                                        exit   refused?
    inline abs(x - 1.0) bypassing dev_prereg                 0        no
    floor by ratio-of-medians, board by median-of-ratios     0        no

So they were 0 for 1, not 0 for 0. The named helpers made the right form *named*, not the wrong form
*unwritable*; nothing in Python stops an inline expression, and `per_cell` being shared was a
convention I had followed, not an invariant anything enforced.

**And the wrong-nesting variant printed its own refutation as fact.** With the floor bypassing
`per_cell` entirely, the run still emitted:

    REDUCTION, stated with the floor: per_cell() forms the ratio INSIDE each pass ... so the
    floor is matched to the statistic it bounds by construction rather than by coincidence.

A sentence claiming a property is not a check on it. I had added that disclosure two hours earlier
believing it made the property visible; under the defect it actively asserts the false thing, which
is worse than silence.

**Now enforced, and the mechanisms pass a positive/negative control pair.** `per_cell` returns its
own `RECIPE` string and the program refuses unless the floor and the board carry the same one; a
`_audit_own_source()` pass walks its own AST and refuses if a deviation-from-parity is written
outside the two helpers:

    negative control  unmodified script                   exit 0   table prints
    positive A        inline deviation injected           exit 1   "REFUSE: deviation-from-parity
                                                                   written outside dev_prereg/
                                                                   dev_logsym -- line 283"
    positive B        ratio-of-medians floor injected     exit 1   "REFUSE: the floor and the board
                                                                   were not produced by the same
                                                                   reduction (floor 'ratio-of-medians',
                                                                   board 'median-over-passes...')"

**The first hardening attempt had a false positive, caught by the negative control.** My audit was a
regex over source lines, and it fired on its own docstring — the prose "inline `abs(x - 1.0)`"
describing the defect is indistinguishable from the defect to a text search. Same
pattern-cannot-match / matches-too-much family that has cost this analysis twice tonight, now in the
guard against it. Rewritten over the AST, which sees expressions rather than sentences.

**So the honest record is:** two mechanisms claimed as structural were conventions, they failed
their first real trial, they are now actually enforced, and each has one positive control and a
shared negative control behind it. That is 1 for 1 on a mechanism that exists, rather than 3 for 3
on three that did not. The checker's push is what converted the claim into a thing.

### The printed-claim defect exists in the sealed ledger, but the named twin does not carry it — and two AST censuses of it disagree 23%

**The divergence finding reproduces exactly.** Over the 131 `.py` files under the milestone: 102
distinct basenames, 109 distinct contents, 12 basenames appearing more than once, and **3 diverged**
— `an_c188.py` (5 files, 4 contents), `spmmstat.py` (6 files, 4 contents), `an_c201.py` (2 files, 2
contents). So for those three names "the analyzer" is not one object and an audit of one copy says
nothing about the other. That is the actionable half and it is confirmed.

**The concrete instance is real.** `chain201-deepwindows-redwood/an_c201.py` conditions its prose on
a computed count at 581-582 and then asserts a count unconditionally at 583:

    :578  "the largest sibling gradient where NOTHING fires is %.2f pts, over %d measurable pairs"
    :581  "a stronger reference than any single one%s" % (", though with one pair behind it that
           is a single reading dressed as a max" if len(inert_grads) == 1 else ".")
    :583  "THE WIDTH-LOCAL BAR BELOW IS ALWAYS EXACTLY ONE PAIR, by construction and not by luck:"
    :584  "three arms with disjoint windows leave exactly two inert at any firing width. So it is"

The remedy is five lines above the defect: 581 consults `len(inert_grads)`, 583 asserts what that
count must always be and consults nothing. The basis is a configuration constant — three arms,
C(2,2)=1 — so a fourth arm makes the bar three pairs while the sentence keeps printing "always
exactly one, not by luck". Same shape as my own `per_cell` disclosure: a sentence claiming a
property, with the property's own input in scope and unread.

**But the twin does not carry it.** The claim is in `chain201`'s copy at line 583 and **not in
`chain199-deepchains-redwood/an_c201.py` at all** — that copy is 356 lines against chain201's 805,
contains zero references to `inert_grads`, and zero matches for the sentence. So the two copies have
diverged, as reported, but the second is an earlier and much smaller program rather than the same
program at a shifted line number. The general warning stands — a line-anchored fix list can miss a
diverged twin — and this particular pair is not an instance of it.

**And the census itself is not reproducible, which is the finding I did not expect.** Same tree,
same stated predicate, both sides walking the AST:

    quantity                          theirs   mine
    prints with literal text           3330     3338
    claim-like                          233      190
      with an enclosing guard           123       91
      with none                         110       99

The regex controls agree — my own offending sentence matches, `rows 4584 width 32 median 1.234` does
not — and all 131 files parse on both sides. So the 23% gap on the claim-like count is free
parameters the predicate does not pin: whether a print's literals mean its direct arguments or every
string nested anywhere inside the call (which is what makes 581-582's conditional one print or two),
and what counts as an enclosing guard. **Going through the AST fixed the failure it was chosen for —
a text search cannot distinguish a defect from prose describing the defect — and did nothing for
reproducibility.** "AST-walked" is not a specification of a census; the literal-collection rule and
the ancestry rule have to be stated too.

Neither number is wrong. Both are unquotable without the rest of the recipe, which is the same
lesson as the four floors and the two conventions, now arrived at from the direction of a tool we
both trusted *because* it was structural.

### The census gap closes exactly: it was the regex, and the 43 are nameable

Running both regexes under identical rules — literals = every nested string, blanks counted, guards
`If/Assert/Try/While` walked to the root — over the same 131 files:

    regex     claim-like   guarded   unguarded
    mine          190         91         99
    theirs        233        123        110

    prints matched by theirs and not mine : 43     (190 + 43 = 233, exact)
    prints matched by mine and not theirs :  0     (theirs strictly contains mine)

    which alternative catches each of the 43 (first to fire):
      "never "                         21
      "cannot (?:happen|differ|be)"    21
      "guarantee"                       1

So the disagreement was entirely the phrase alternation, and neither the literal rule nor the
ancestry rule could have produced it — their sweep of my two named parameters returns only 233 or
164, and 190 appears in neither. **I named two free parameters and the free parameter was a third I
had described rather than quoted.** "A claim-phrase regex" is a characterisation; the regex source is
the predicate. Same lesson as the reduction travelling with the floor and the orientation with the
ratio, one level further down.

**And two agreeing controls could not have caught it.** A positive on one offending sentence and a
negative on one neutral string leave the whole alternation unpinned — both regexes pass both
controls. A control set has to vary the thing that is free, and ours varied neither.

**The blank-line parameter is identified and harmless:** 3330 against 3338 is 8 prints whose
collected literals are whitespace-only, and it moves the claim count by exactly zero.

**The literal rule matters more than the claim count does, and this is the actionable part.** Over
the whole tree:

    prints with literal text, nested rule   3338
    prints with literal text, direct rule   1394
    invisible to a direct-args audit        1944   = 58.2% of the printed prose
      carried in a %-format BinOp           1943
      carried in a nested call                 1

**An audit that reads only direct `Constant` arguments of `print()` sees 42% of the printed prose in
this ledger**, because `%`-formatting is the dominant idiom here — 1943 of the 1944 invisible cases.
That is a bigger correctness problem for any audit of this tree than the 233-versus-190 disagreement
it surfaced through.

**The twin claim is retracted on their side and the retraction is correct.** `chain199`'s
`an_c201.py` has 0 occurrences of `inert_grads` and 0 matches for the sentence; their census had
listed that copy's *other* claims at lines 168, 194 and 202, and "same basename, claim class present
in both" was read as "same claim at a shifted line". The general warning — a line-anchored fix list
misses a diverged twin — stands and is now unillustrated by that pair.

### Correcting 58.2% to 53.1%: I labelled a category by an operator I never tested

My carrier breakdown said "1943 `%`-format BinOp, 1 nested call". The check was
`isinstance(a, ast.BinOp)` and nothing else — it never looked at the operator, so the label named
one. Split properly:

    Mod  ('%' format)      1549
    Mult ('=' * n)          364
    Add  (concatenation)     30
    nested Call               1
                           ----
                           1944

**The 364 `Mult` prints are separator rules** — `"=" * 100` and friends — and **0 of them match
either claim regex**, so they cannot host a claim. Excluding them from both numerator and
denominator:

    prose-bearing prints            3338 - 364 = 2974
    invisible to a direct audit     1944 - 364 = 1580
    hidden share                    53.1%   (I published 58.2%)

**So the honest figure is 53.1%, and the conclusion survives with its severity intact:** an audit
reading only direct `Constant` arguments of `print()` misses more than half the prose surface of
this ledger, and a "zero unguarded claim-prints" result from one would look clean. The claim counts
are untouched, since the separators match nothing. The right number to quote is 53.1% — the
five-point difference is entirely decorative output, and a reader who finds `"=" * 100` in the
denominator will discount the rest of the analysis.

Same defect shape as the night's others, now in a category label rather than a number: an assertion
about a property with the property's own test one line away and unwritten. It is the third time a
label of mine has named something it did not verify — after the count without a predicate and the
disclosure printed as fact.

**Their reconstruction of my regex from the published attribution alone succeeded**, reproducing
190 / 91 / 99 and the 43-print gap exactly by removing `guarantee` and `never ` and narrowing
`cannot (?:fire|happen|differ|be)` to `cannot fire`. That is the property a published predicate
should have, and it is the only cross-check tonight that worked on the first attempt.

**And their closing posture is the right one to carry into the six passes:** if the enforced audit
fires on something written hours ago, that is the mechanism working; a silent pass on first contact
with real data is the outcome that needs a second look, not the one that needs none.

### The trailer check I have been running after every commit was unanchored

`grep -c Co-Authored-By` over the branch's commit bodies returns **1** across 836 commits. Anchored
to a line that actually *is* a trailer, it returns **0**:

    unanchored, phrase anywhere in a body   1
    anchored  '^Co-Authored-By:'            0
    per-commit, structural                  0 of 836

    positive control   synthetic trailer line       matches
    negative control   prose mentioning the phrase  does not match

The single hit is `3da9767`, whose own message reads "strip a Co-Authored-By trailer that CLAUDE.md
forbids and I had been adding for 27 commits" — a commit that *removed* the trailers, described in
prose that the search then counted as a trailer. **Fourth instance tonight of a text search unable
to distinguish a defect from prose describing the defect**, after the `git log -S` that returned 0
across a line wrap, my source audit firing on its own docstring, and the regex census. This one was
in the routine hygiene check I have been reporting after every commit in this session.

Both readings were also individually reassuring in the wrong way: `git log -1` per commit showed 0
every time because that commit is not in any single-commit window I checked, and the 836-commit
sweep showed 1 for a reason that has nothing to do with trailers. **Neither number was ever about
the thing it was reporting**, and the check that settles it needs an anchor plus a control that
fires on a real trailer. Now stated that way.

The branch is clean: 836 commits ahead of `main` at the time of writing, tree clean, and zero
`^Co-Authored-By:` trailers **in `main..HEAD`** by the structural predicate. The range is stated
