because the range is what the next section is about: the same sentence without it reads as a claim
about the repository, which is false — 30 anchored trailers exist on other refs, and one of them is
an ancestor of both `main` and `HEAD` and so lies outside any `main..HEAD` range by construction.

### The trailer census scoped to `main..HEAD` could not fail in the direction it claimed to check

Every commit reachable from any ref, tested structurally for a `^Co-Authored-By:` line: **30
trailers on 30 commits.** The three-way split, verified:

    27  refs/backup/pre-trailer-strip AND refs/heads/perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel-pretrailer
     1  b606b30 (2026-03-05) -- ancestor of HEAD and of main
     2  bbfa606, e7673a2 (Nov 2025) -- refs/remotes/origin/exp only

**`b606b30` is an ancestor of HEAD and no `main..HEAD` census can see it**, because that range
excludes main's own history by construction. I have reported "anchored trailers: 0" after commits all
session on exactly that range. The scope made the check unable to fail in the direction it claimed to
check — a range reading 0 because the only mainline candidate lies outside it.

**And it is already published, which settles what to do about it: nothing.** `b606b30` is on
`refs/remotes/origin/main` — pushed six months ago, before this work — along with `origin/bench` and
six other remote branches. Removing it would mean rewriting published history. The accurate claim is
**"0 new trailers on the 837 commits this branch adds, and 1 pre-existing and already-published
commit on mainline history that no `main..HEAD` census can see."**

**The one live item, stated precisely.** The 27 are reachable from a normal local branch, not only
from the `refs/backup/` ref:

    perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel             local + origin   0 anchored trailers   (the stripped one)
    perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel-pretrailer  local only      27 anchored trailers

and enumerating every local branch with no `origin/` counterpart, that is **the only unpushed branch
carrying trailers**. So `git push --all` would publish exactly one branch of trailers, whose stripped
sibling is already on the remote. Recorded as a fact about the repository; I do not touch refs and am
not proposing anything.

**Also: the unanchored count is 2 now, not 1, and the range is 837.** `d16e695` — the commit
documenting this finding — added a second prose mention of the phrase. That check's reading is a
function of how much has been written about it, which is a property worth naming on its own: a
text-matching metric over a corpus that includes commentary on the metric.

**The sub-family is complete at four and they share one control gap.** A `git log -S` returning 0
across a line wrap; a source audit firing on its own docstring; two claim-print censuses disagreeing
on an unquoted regex; and this scope defect. Prose about a defect lives in the same text the search
reads — and **the control set must include prose that mentions the defect without being it.** None of
the four had such a case, and one would have caught all four.

### The branch denominator differs by one ref, and it is the ref that decides the action

Our branch censuses disagree — 29 local / 9 on-origin / 20 local-only here against 30 / 11 / 19 —
and the parameter is identified:

    git for-each-ref refs/heads                29
    git branch --list                          29
    refs/heads + refs/backup                   30   <- their denominator
    same-named origin/<branch> exists           9
    has an upstream configured                  9

So the extra ref is `refs/backup/pre-trailer-strip`, counted as a local branch. **That is precisely
the parameter that decides the actionable claim**, because `git push --all` pushes `refs/heads` only
— a ref under `refs/backup/` does not go out with it. Under their denominator two refs carry the 27
trailers and one of them is publishable; under mine one ref carries them and it is the publishable
one. Same 27 commits, and the count of *refs* is what changes.

**The conclusion is invariant under every predicate tried**, which is what makes it reportable:
exactly one ref under `refs/heads` carries anchored trailers above `main`, and it is
`perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel-pretrailer` with 27, local-only, whose stripped sibling
`perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel` is already on origin with 0.

**And the two censuses are complementary rather than redundant**, which is the useful structural
point: a per-branch table counting trailers *above* `main` cannot see `b606b30`, which sits below it;
a `main..HEAD` sweep cannot see it either. The below-`main` count was established separately and is
1, already on `origin/main` since March. Two checks with complementary blind spots add to coverage —
either alone reads clean, and neither alone is evidence.

    27  above main, one publishable ref (-pretrailer), unpushed   -> the only actionable set
     1  below main, ancestor of origin/main since March           -> nothing, it is published
     2  on origin/exp only, published Nov 2025                    -> nothing
    ---
    30  no residue

**Two rules out of this, and neither was written down before tonight.** First: **when two forms of
one check disagree, the disagreement is the finding, and neither number is reportable until it is
explained.** My per-commit and unanchored trailer readings disagreed 0 against 1 on the same screen,
and I reported the one that matched what I expected. Second: the anchored form is not merely more
accurate, it is **stable** — its reading does not depend on how much has been written about it, where
the unanchored count went 1 → 2 because the commit documenting the finding mentioned the phrase.
Stability is a stronger argument for structural matching than accuracy, because accuracy can be
argued about and stability cannot.

### A complete consistent copy of a run passes every consistency check, because agreement is what a copy has

While waiting for chain205's six passes, `/scratch/bobbyy/c205an/` turned up on redwood — two
characters from the live `/scratch/bobbyy/c205/`, sorting adjacent to it — holding **six CSVs at
exactly 68,761 lines**, three arms (`mkl`/`ours`/`oursb`), 22,920 cells per pass, 22,920 shared
across all six, slice tags `corpusp1`…`corpusp6` agreeing with their own filenames, and `build` =
`c0` exactly as the live run stamps. All six are timestamped **02:20:15**, seven minutes *before*
the live run wrote its first row (p1 started 02:27:32), and `c205an/p1` differs from `c205/p1`.
Nothing names that directory: not `rw_s_chain205.sh`, not `c205_stage.log`, not any script on
either host.

**It is not the jittered fixture either.** Per-cell `oursb/ours` spread across the six passes reads
p05/p50/p95 = 0.020 / 0.126 / 0.860, and **0 of 22,920 cells are identical across passes** — the
signature that made the earlier synthetic fixture useless is absent, so this is real measured data
from a run that no log accounts for.

**And it defeats every guard in `an_c205.py`, by construction.** The filename-versus-`slice`
cross-check, the rows/nnz single-value guard, the shared-reduction stamp, the duplicate-row check —
all of them compare the inputs *against each other*. **A complete, internally consistent copy
agrees with itself on all of them.** The missing predicate was never consistency; it is provenance.
The strongest available identification is a single row: the same cell `1138_bus` k=2 arm `mkl` reads
ms 0.014163 / batch 36 in the live pass 1 and ms 0.017659 / batch 29 in the copy — a
six-significant-figure float plus an independent integer, which no coincidence supplies.

**The binding that was added, with its controls.** `--stage-log` is now required, and every input
CSV must match its own pass's `pass pN of M done HH:MM:SS (R rows)` line on **both** the row count
and the file mtime, within 120 s:

    1  real log, 4 of 6 closed, matching dir   REFUSE  "the run is INCOMPLETE -- not a provenance
                                                        failure, it is 'not finished yet'"
    2  six files all stamped 02:20:15          REFUSE  names all six, 2260s..11429s apart
    3  mtimes matching the log                 PASS    "6 of 6 passes bound ... tolerance 120s"
    4  one file at 24271 rows                  REFUSE  "24271 data rows, the log says 68760"

Case 1 carries as much weight as case 2. **"Not finished yet" and "wrong run" are different
refusals and must print different messages** — one generic refusal for both is how an incomplete run
gets read as a substitution and a substitution gets waved through as impatience. The controls were
built from metadata alone (six local files of the right line count, `os.utime` to set the stamps), so
none of it read a byte on the host running the live bandwidth-bound pass.

**Its limitation, stated because it is real: mtime is mutable.** `cp -p` or a `touch` forges the
binding. This catches an accidental substitution — the thing that actually happened — and not a
deliberate one. The content-based version requires the producer to publish a digest as each output
closes, which chain205's runner does not do, and the runner is not being changed mid-run. Stated as
a requirement rather than a suggestion: **a run that does not publish a digest per output cannot
afterwards be bound to its outputs by anything stronger than a timestamp.**

### Two bugs, one wrong answer, and it was the maximal one

A census of "which local branches would `git push --all` actually publish" returned **29 of 29**.
The correct answer is **3**. It was wrong twice, by unrelated causes:

    REM=$(git for-each-ref ... refs/remotes); for r in $REM   # zsh does NOT word-split unquoted
                                                              # params -- one iteration, 17 refs
                                                              # as a single string, every
                                                              # --is-ancestor fails
    bash -c 'mapfile -t REM < <(...)'                          # macOS bash 3.2 has no mapfile --
                                                              # empty array, inner loop runs zero
                                                              # times

**The defect that matters is neither bug: the failure mode of a containment census is its maximal
answer.** "No remote ref contains this branch" is exactly what gets printed when there are no
remote refs to check, so a broken census and a repository with nothing pushed are indistinguishable
from the output. 29 of 29 should have stopped the report on sight, and `main` — whose tip is
demonstrably on `origin/HEAD` — was sitting in the output one line from the top.

The fix that holds is not a better loop. It is `git for-each-ref --count=1 --contains=<branch>
refs/remotes`, which has no splitting step for a dialect to disagree about, **printed beside a
control that must fail**: `main` must be excluded, and the run is unreadable without it.

    heads total                                  29
    tip contained in NO remote ref                3
      perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel                  0 trailers above main
      perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel-pretrailer      27 trailers above main
      refactor/compiler-ir-phase3-std-move-call   0 trailers above main
    positive control: main contained in refs/remotes/origin/HEAD  (correctly excluded)

**And the predicate that decides an action must be the one the action uses.** "Local-only by name"
(20 branches) was standing in for "would publish something"; the real answer is 3, because 17 of
the 20 have tips already contained in some remote ref under a different name. Three predicates,
three answers — 20, 20, and 3 — and only the last answers the question the number was being used
for. `git push --all` publishes every `refs/heads`, but what it *adds* is only commits no remote ref
already reaches.

The trailer conclusion is unchanged and now rests on the right denominator: **exactly one branch
would publish trailers**, `perf/spmm-probe-and-kernel-pretrailer` with 27, whose stripped sibling is
already on origin. Recorded as a fact and not a proposal: the third member of the would-publish set
is `refactor/compiler-ir-phase3-std-move-call`, the branch checked out in the main worktree, so a
`push --all` from this repository would also publish that in-progress refactor. No refs were
touched.

### Identified: it was chain196's `c0` set, and it replicates chain205 to 0.19%

The unprovenanced six-pass dataset in `/scratch/bobbyy/c205an/` is **chain196's `c0` six-pass
full-collection set**, copied at 02:20:15 and renamed `sh_*` → `fc_*` into chain205's convention.
The one-row probe hit the first candidate and md5 over full file bytes confirmed **6 of 6**:

    c205an/p1..p6   06f49552 8f24f38f d888e022 6917e0e7 bd65394d 8b4cb946
    chain196 c0     identical, all six          (sealed, sha256 in chain196's SHA256SUMS)
    chain196 c0b / pfd0, twelve files           match nothing
    one byte flipped in c0/p1                   matches nothing

So the identification is **unique, not merely consistent** — the negative controls are in the same
run. chain196 uses `corpusp1`…`corpusp6` as well, which is precisely *why* the filename-versus-
`slice` guard passed: after the rename the two identifiers genuinely agreed. "Real measured data from
a run I cannot account for" resolves to **real measured data from a run that is fully accounted for,
just not this one** — not fabricated, not synthetic, not corrupt.

**And this is the finding, not the forensics: chain196 replicates chain205's pass 1 to 0.19% pooled,
every width inside 0.7%.** Had the copy been analysed as chain205, the full-collection board would
have come out **within a fifth of a percent of the true answer**. No plausibility check on the
result could have caught it — not the pooled ratio, not the per-width table, not the floor, not the
behind counts, not the worst-cell list. **When the substituted input is a near-replicate of the
right one, the output is indistinguishable from the correct output at every resolution anyone
inspects.** Provenance is not a belt-and-braces check here; it is the only defence that exists.

**The corollary inverts, in the binding's favour.** "A run that does not publish a digest per output
cannot afterwards be bound to its outputs by anything stronger than a timestamp" is true of
chain205 — but **chain196 did publish one, and that is what identified the intruder.** The mechanism
is not a proposal for a future chain, it is a precedent one chain back. Write it as: **seal each
output as it closes, as chain196 did.** And note what it bought, because integrity is not what was
asked of it: **a per-output digest is an identity check, not only an integrity check.** It answered
*which run this was*. No integrity check is ever asked to do that.

Two consequences taken up now. First, chain205's six passes get sealed from outside the producer,
the instant the run's completion marker lands — the earliest sealing point reachable without editing
a live runner. Second, `c205an` stops being an intruder and becomes an asset: chain196's `c0` and
chain205 are two independent six-pass runs over the same 22,920 cells on the same host, so the pair
supports a **cross-chain replication of the full-collection board** at no measurement cost. That is
worth more than the 0.19% pass-1 figure it started from, and it is reported as a replication, never
as a second confirmation of the same run.

### The binding gets a content mode, and nine controls of which six must refuse

chain196's sealed digests make the stronger binding reachable, so `an_c205.py` now takes two modes
and requires at least one:

    --expect-sha256 FILE   binds to CONTENT      sha256 over full file bytes, per pass
    --stage-log FILE       binds to the run log  row count + mtime, 120 s tolerance
    neither                REFUSE                "an analysis that cannot name the run that
                                                  produced its inputs must not print a board"

Content is strictly stronger and is preferred wherever the producer sealed: **an mtime is mutable
and a digest is not.** The refusal says so in place — "a digest names the run; a timestamp only
names a moment, and an mtime can be forged by `cp -p`."

    1  real log, 4 of 6 passes closed            REFUSE  "INCOMPLETE -- not a provenance failure"
    2  six files all stamped 02:20:15            REFUSE  names all six, 2260s..11429s apart
    3  mtimes matching the log                   PASS
    4  one file at 24271 rows                    REFUSE  "24271 data rows, the log says 68760"
    5  neither binding given                     REFUSE  cites the chain196 substitution by name
    6  digests matching the bytes                PASS
    7  one digest corrupted in the first nibble  REFUSE  names the pass and both prefixes
    8  content and log, both agreeing            PASS    both lines print
    9  chain196's real sealed digests vs other   REFUSE  names all six expected/got pairs
       bytes
    ---
    6 of 9 controls must REFUSE, 3 must PASS, and all 9 do.

Six failing controls to three passing is the ratio that makes the set worth anything. A guard whose
controls all pass has been described rather than tested.

### The same shell bug a third time, and this time it failed loud

The control harness above first reported **4 of 4 mtime-mode controls as REGRESSIONS**. The script
was fine. `set -- $a` does not split in zsh either:

    a="bound LOG 1"
    set -- $a      ->  $# = 1,  $1 = "bound LOG 1",  $3 = ""
    set -- ${=a}   ->  $# = 3,  $1 = "bound",        $3 = "1"

so every invocation got one malformed `--dir` and exited 2 on argparse, against an expected code
that was the empty string. **Third instance of one root cause tonight** — the containment census,
its bash "fix", and now the harness checking the fix.

**The instructive part is the direction.** In the census the bug was silent: it printed 29 of 29,
which is a well-formed answer that a reader accepts. In the harness it was loud: it printed
REGRESSION four times for a script that had not regressed, and a false alarm gets investigated
within a minute. Same defect, opposite consequence, and the difference is entirely whether the
broken path's output is *indistinguishable from a real answer*. That is the same property that made
the chain196 substitution dangerous at 0.19% and the 02:20:15 timestamp harmless — **what matters is
never how wrong the mechanism is, it is whether being wrong looks different from being right.**

### Correction: the 0.19% was published before its provenance was asked for, and it is withdrawn

Two sections up, the near-replication of chain196 and chain205 is stated as **0.19% pooled, every
width inside 0.7%**, and the whole framing rests on it. **That number is withdrawn as a
measurement.** Re-derivation on the side that can be provenanced shows:

    chain196 c0, 22920 complete cells, subject = per-cell median over passes of mkl/ours
                                      PASS 1 ONLY   ALL SIX PASSES
      geomean of per-cell medians       2.2605        2.2915
      median of per-cell medians        2.4596        2.5452
      geomean over all readings         2.2605        2.2695
      total-time ratio                  2.1067        2.1200

The pair of figures behind the 0.19% were **not the same reduction** — one was geomean of per-cell
medians, the other geomean over readings — and **at pass 1 those two reductions coincide by
construction**, since one reading per cell makes the median the reading. That identity is exactly
what hid the mismatch. The other side of the comparison was a chain205 figure quoted from a report
with its reduction unstated, compared across two programs: the shape that produced the earlier
17–29% overstatement.

**The defect that is mine is the order of operations.** The number arrived, it went into this
document as the headline of a finding, and *then* its provenance was requested. The rule already
written down says to ask provenance when a number drives an action — and **publishing a number as
the load-bearing claim of a finding is the action.** Asking in the next breath is asking one step
too late; the commit had already been made. See `carried_state_numbers_are_claims`: a number that
crosses a boundary arrives already believed, and a peer message is a boundary.

**What replaces it is derivable and stronger, because it needs neither chain205 nor a cross-program
comparison.** From chain196 alone — same corpus, same host, same build tag, different run:

    pooled board, geomean over 22920 cells, ONE PASS AT A TIME
      build   p1     p2     p3     p4     p5     p6     spread
      c0     2.2605 2.2811 2.2817 2.2595 2.2556 2.2785   1.16%
      c0b    2.2773 2.2769 2.2697 2.2599 2.2574 2.2755   0.88%
      pfd0   2.3326 2.3388 2.3542 2.3337 2.3420 2.3439   0.93%

    across builds at fixed pass
      p1   c0 2.2605  c0b 2.2773  pfd0 2.3326    spread 3.19%
      p6   c0 2.2785  c0b 2.2755  pfd0 2.3439    spread 3.01%

**Run-to-run movement of the pooled board is under 1.2%; swapping the object entirely moves it 3%.**
So the statement the argument actually needs is an a priori one: **a substituted full-collection
dataset from the same corpus and host cannot move the board by more than the pass-to-pass spread,
about 1%, which is below the resolution at which anyone reads it.** No cross-chain difference
required, and no reduction that cannot be seen.

The conclusion is unchanged and now rests on something checkable: the timestamp is why the copy was
noticed, near-replication is why noticing was the only thing that could have worked, and provenance
is the only defence. **This table is itself a number received across a boundary** and has not been
independently computed here; chain196's `c0` set is on redwood in `c205an`, so the per-pass pooled
board will be recomputed locally after the run closes, in the same program as chain205's, under one
named reduction. If it does not reproduce, the disagreement is the finding.

### The pooled board and the behind-count have opposite sensitivities, demonstrated not asserted

The substitution bound in the previous section is a statement about the **pooled board**, and the
pooled board is the statistic *least* sensitive to a substituted near-replicate: a geometric mean
over 22,920 cells moves by about the pass-to-pass spread by construction. But the standing goal is a
**cell-count** goal — scorch beats MKL everywhere — so the operative statistic is the count of cells
below parity, which is a threshold-crossing count concentrated at 1.0 and has no such stability.

Asserting that is cheap, so it was put on a fixture instead: twelve keys × two widths × six passes,
with two keys clearly behind, **two keys placed at parity + 0.1%** so they change hands between
passes, and eight ahead.

    dataset    pass       pooled      behind         n
    behindy    p1         1.6552           7        24
    behindy    p2         1.6371           6        24
    behindy    p3         1.6523           7        24
    behindy    p4         1.6466           4        24
    behindy    p5         1.6382           8        24
    behindy    p6         1.6459           5        24
    behindy    SPREAD             spread 1.10%   behind 4..8 over 6 passes

**The pooled board moves 1.10% across the six passes while the behind-count runs 4 to 8 — it
doubles.** Same readings, same cells, same passes; one statistic is stable to a percent and the
other is not stable to a factor of two. The magnitude here is designed in, so this demonstrates the
mechanism and not its size on real data; the size comes from chain205 and chain196 once both are
bound. The consequence for reading a substituted dataset is the part that transfers: **a near-
replicate is undetectable in the pooled board and may be very detectable in the behind-count**, and
if it is, the behind-count is a provenance signal — a statistic that separates two near-replicate
datasets is exactly what every consistency check lacked.

The replication script invokes `an_c205.py --provenance-only` rather than restating the binding, so
there is one implementation and this harness cannot drift from the one the board uses. Controls: the
matching-digest case passes for both sides, binding one side with the other's digests refuses and
names the offending passes, and the differing-cell-set path prints its NOTE and runs on the shared
set rather than absorbing the difference.

Two more shell-dialect defects caught in the test harness rather than the code, both mine and both
in the *checking*: `set -- $a` does not split in zsh, and `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is a bash name — zsh
spells it `$pipestatus[1]`, so `${PIPESTATUS[0]:-$?}` silently reads the exit status of the last
command in the pipe, which after `| head` is always 0. **A negative control whose exit-code check
always reads 0 reports every refusal as a pass.** Re-checked without the pipe: rc=1, as required.

### Correction: the fixture's transfer claim is wrong, and the caveat attached to it was the wrong caveat

The section above concludes that "a near-replicate is undetectable in the pooled board and may be
very detectable in the behind-count, and if it is, the behind-count is a provenance signal."
**Measured on 22,920 real cells, it is not detectable there.** chain196 `c0`, six real passes,
behind = per-cell `mkl/ours < 1` within a single pass:

    pair      |A|   |B|   entered   left    net   |net|/|A|
    p1->p2    431   410      329     350    -21     4.9%
    p2->p3    410   402      323     331     -8     2.0%
    p3->p4    402   435      338     305    +33     8.2%
    p4->p5    435   398      323     360    -37     8.5%
    p5->p6    398   410      325     313    +12     3.0%

    mean entries per consecutive pair 328,  mean |net| 22  -- churn is ~15x the net movement

**About 328 cells cross the parity line every pass and the total moves by 22.** Entries and exits
balance, so the count is stable to 9% while the membership is almost entirely reshuffled: Jaccard
0.10–0.13 against p1, 1,707 cells behind in at least one pass, **13 behind in all six.**

**The fixture had the right marginal fraction and still gave the opposite answer.** Two marginal
cells of 24 is 8.3%; the real marginal population is 1,694 of 22,920, or 7.4% — near enough that
sizing was not the problem. **The stability is a cancellation over the churn, and cancellation
cannot occur at n=2 by construction**: with two marginal cells each crossing is 25% of a base of 4,
while with 1,694 of them the in-and-out flows average out and the residual is ±5%. So the caveat
attached to that fixture — "the magnitude here is designed in, so this demonstrates the mechanism and
not its size on real data" — **was the wrong caveat.** It hedged on size when the error was in kind:
the mechanism itself is different at scale. **A fixture can prove that a mechanism exists and say
nothing about whether it operates**, which is the same defect as the jittered-copy fixture that
collapsed a per-cell median onto a single pass, arriving from the opposite direction.

So the transfer sentence is replaced, not resized: **neither the pooled board nor the behind-count
nor the behind set is a provenance signal.** The count moves 9%, the same order as the pooled board's
1.2%, so it cannot separate two runs; the set churns 90% *between two passes of one run*, so it
cannot either. That strengthens the digest-only conclusion rather than qualifying it.

**What was verifiable here without touching the measuring host, and what was not.** The churn table
above and the separately-reported Jaccard figures are mutually consistent: `|B| = |A| − left +
entered` balances in **5 of 5 rows**, the means reproduce (327.6 → 328, 22.2 → 22), and the p1/p2
Jaccard implied by the churn counts is 81/760 = 0.1066 against 0.107 reported from a different
computation. Two separately-produced tables agreeing on a derived quantity is a real check and it is
the check that was skipped earlier tonight on a branch table whose own split did not sum to its own
total. **It is necessary and not sufficient** — the night's theme is that consistency does not
establish correctness, and two tables from one wrong computation agree just as well. The independent
recomputation runs when chain205 closes, in one program, over both datasets, under one named
reduction.

### The milestone's own number depends on a reduction nobody has named

The goal is stated as a cell count — scorch beats MKL everywhere — and that count is:

    single pass                          398 - 435   (spread 9% across six passes)
    per-cell median over six passes            119
    behind in ALL six passes                    13
    gated by a single-pass A/A p95 floor    15 - 52   (a 3.5x swing on the noise-corrected one)

**33× between the loosest and the tightest, and the goal does not say which.** A single-pass behind
list is about 97% churn — 1,707 cells appear on one at least once and 13 survive every pass — so
"everywhere except N" read off one pass is a list of the cells that happened to be behind during
that half hour. This is the same argument that forced the floor and the board to share a reduction,
arriving at the scoreboard: **the behind count and the goal it is measured against must share a
reduction, and the gated count needs its floor computed at the resolution of the count it gates** —
a single-pass floor is about twice as wide as a per-cell one, which is why the gated version swings
more than the ungated one it was meant to clean up. All three counts go in the report with the
reduction named on each, and a statement of which one the milestone is stated in. That last part is
Bobby's to decide, not ours.

### chain204 acquired 48 CPUs of co-tenant 2h34m into a bandwidth-bound timing run

Read from the SC login node only, spending no allocation, so none of this perturbed the job it
describes:

    mkt1   CPUTot=128   CPUAlloc=128   ThreadsPerCore=2   CPULoad=44.84
      17439864  c204_rungconf    64 CPUs   started 2026-09-15T02:08:58   limit 24h
      17443267_0..5 ptbench-pred  8 CPUs each = 48        started 2026-09-15T04:43:04, limit 10h
                                                          task _6 PENDING
      17418470  bash (alexh06)   16 CPUs   started 2026-09-13T13:28  -- constant, predates the run

chain204 therefore ran with 16 CPUs of unrelated work beside it for **02:08:58 → 04:43:04**, and
with 64 from 04:43:04 on, and the array outlives chain204's projected finish so no later pass is
clean.

**Mechanism, not worry.** `OverSubscribe=OK` shares the *node*, not the CPUs: with
`CPUAlloc=128=CPUTot` each job holds a disjoint cpuset, so no CPU is stolen. But **memory bandwidth
and the memory controllers are not partitioned by any cgroup**, and SpMM is bandwidth-bound, so
absolute times after 04:43:04 are contaminated whatever the pinning guarantees. The co-tenant
requested **no GPUs** — `ReqTRES=cpu=8,mem=64G` on a node carrying `gres/gpu:l40s=8` — so it is
CPU-side work and the contention is real rather than assumed. Wall clock is not at risk: elapsed
2:47 against a limit of 2026-09-16T02:08:58.

**The attribution, and the limit of it.** Every Slurm identity field returns the same value for
every job on this allocation — `squeue -u bobbyy -O username,account | sort -u` is one row,
`bobbyy mkt` — so Slurm metadata **cannot** attribute a job to a session, which is precisely why the
standing rule is to cancel only job IDs one's own `sbatch` returned rather than any name pattern or
`-u` sweep. What does attribute it is the submit path: `Command=/sailhome/bobbyy/ptbench/
pred_array.sbatch`, `WorkDir=/sailhome/bobbyy/ptbench`, submitted 04:42:11 — a different project,
not scorch. Nothing was cancelled and nothing of that project was read beyond its Slurm record.

**What the within-pass reduction buys, and the control that makes it a claim.** The recipe already
in use — `median-over-passes of (num/den)`, the ratio formed *inside* each pass — means every arm in
a pass sees the same environment, so ratios survive what absolute times do not. chain204 has thereby
acquired an unplanned natural experiment with a step change at a known timestamp. **The immunity is
only demonstrated if the step is demonstrated first:** absolute `ms` must jump at 04:43:04 and be
quantified, and only then does the ratio's flatness mean anything. Without that positive control
there was nothing to be immune to, and the result would be an A/A comparison reported as robustness.
The scale for "the ratio did not move" comes from passes 1–8, which contain no environment change
and so supply the null distribution.

**Two open items stated before the data lands rather than after.** First, the clean block is 8
passes, not 9: pass 9 straddles 04:43:04 on the clean-period 17.586 min mean. That mean is only
valid inside the regime it was measured in, which covers the boundary but **not** the projected
10:56 finish — the contaminated passes will be slower, so the pass→time map does not extend past the
boundary it was used to locate. Second, whether the 8/1/21 split costs anything depends on a design
detail that is unreadable from the login node, because `StdOut` is on `/scr` (node-local to mkt1)
and the AFS-side `sbatch` is a nine-line wrapper:

    if every pass carries every arm (chain205's shape: 3 arms x 22920 cells every pass)
        8 clean passes are 8 COMPLETE passes, divisibility over arms never arises,
        and pass 9 drops as straddled at no cost beyond n=8
    if arms rotate by pass
        the clean block is unbalanced 3/3/2 -- excluding pass 9 loses balance,
        including it imports ~24% of a contaminated pass. Report both and disclose
        the imbalance: an imbalance is measurable, a contamination is not.

And the contaminated block is **not one condition**: array task `_6` is PENDING and starts when one
of `_0..5` finishes, so the co-tenant load changes again at a time readable from `sacct` at no
allocation cost. Treating passes 10–30 as a single level would be the same defect as pooling a
per-band statistic across bands.

by a program written for this purpose. Every figure reproduces:

      build       p1      p2      p3      p4      p5      p6   spread      n
      c0      2.2605  2.2811  2.2817  2.2595  2.2556  2.2785    1.16%  22920
      c0b     2.2773  2.2769  2.2697  2.2599  2.2574  2.2755    0.88%  22920
      pfd0    2.3326  2.3388  2.3542  2.3337  2.3420  2.3439    0.93%  22920

      pair      |A|   |B|   entered   left    net
      p1->p2    431   410       329    350    -21
      p2->p3    410   402       323    331     -8

      union 1707   intersection 13   ratio 131x   marginal 1694 = 7.39% of 22920

**Exact agreement on every value, from different code over the same bytes.** That rules out
computational error and it does **not** rule out a data problem: this is two implementations, not
two measurements. What it does establish is that the milestone statement can now be made without
carrying anyone's number — 2.2605 at pass 1 against 2.2915 over six passes is the reduction
mismatch itself, visible in one table, and 431 / 119 / 13 is the goal's count under three
reductions.

### A census that returned zero, for the third shell reason tonight

Before that recomputation, a census of the ledger for full-collection CSVs printed **0 files**, and
the conclusion drawn from it — "chain196's CSVs are not in my local cache" — was reported to the
peer. There are **34** of them.

    find ... -name "*_float32_p*.csv" | while read -r f; do
      n=$(wc -l < "$f"); [ "$n" = "68761" ] && echo "HIT $f"      # 0 hits
      n=$(wc -l < "$f"); [ "$n" -eq 68761 ] && echo "HIT $f"      # 34 hits
    done

**macOS `wc -l < file` pads its output to width 8**, so `n` is `"   68761"` with length 8 and the
string comparison never matches, while `-eq` strips whitespace for arithmetic and does. Two
compounding errors, actually: the first search also globbed at `maxdepth 1` when the milestone
directories live one level down under `spmm-beat-mkl/` — the same depth assumption that moved a
ledger-local count 33 → 1669 → 3 earlier in this milestone.

Third distinct shell semantic tonight to produce a plausible wrong count, after zsh's
non-splitting of unquoted parameters (twice) and `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` being a bash-only name. **And
the failure mode is the family's signature again: zero files found is indistinguishable from zero
files existing**, and it was caught only because an unrelated search by file *size* contradicted it.
The 34 also matches the peer's independently-run survey exactly, which is the cross-check that
should have been the first thing asked for rather than the last.

The general form, now stated for the fourth time in this document and apparently needing it: **a
count must be printed beside something that proves the count could have been non-zero.** Here that
would have been the number of files the `find` produced before filtering — 127 CSVs over 2 MB in
the same tree.

## Open decisions, consolidated

Tonight's work produced a number of questions that are not a session's to answer. They are collected
here because they are otherwise spread across thirty commits, ranked by whether they block the
milestone claim.

**Blocking the milestone claim.**

1. **Which reduction the goal's cell count is stated in.** "scorch beats MKL everywhere" resolves to
   431, 119, or 13 cells behind on the same 22,920-cell dataset depending on whether it means a
   single pass, the per-cell median over six, or behind-in-all-six. 33× apart. Default if unanswered:
   report all three with the reduction named and lead with the per-cell median over six passes, since
   that is the reduction the floor and the board already share.
2. **Whether the gated count is used at all.** Gating by a single-pass A/A p95 floor swings 15–52
   across passes — worse than the ungated count it was meant to clean up, because a single-pass floor
   is about twice as wide as a per-cell one. Either compute the floor at the resolution of the count
   it gates, or drop gating from the headline. Default: compute at matching resolution.
3. **The deviation convention.** `|x−1|` matches the sealed predecessor and keeps chain205 comparable
   with chain203/202; `exp|ln x|−1` is orientation-independent. The board is indifferent — it changes
   1–2 verdicts of 22,920, 0.009%. Default: keep `|x−1|` as the gate, print the log-symmetric beside.
4. **Per-width or per-size-band floor.** Per-band is ~5× tighter at the ends but is a post hoc
   stratification chosen after seeing the tail. Default: per-width, with per-band reported as
   exploratory.

8. **Which A/A defines the floor for the headline count — and this is the only one of the five
   convention parameters that changes a number.** Measured one at a time, the deviation scale, the
   p95 estimator and the orientation each move the gated count by **zero** cells and the per-cell
   reduction by **one**; the A/A choice moves it by **nineteen**. It is answerable only by running
   two identical-source build pairs, which no existing chain has. Arm identity (`oursb/ours`, one binary
   twice) gives 66 behind and 115 indeterminate; build identity (`c0/c0b`, two compilations of one
   source) gives 47 and 203. A wider floor lowers the behind count and raises the indeterminate one
   by construction, so the count alone cannot choose. Default if unanswered: report the three-way
   partition under both, lead with arm identity, and state that 131 wins sit inside build variation.

**Not blocking, but decided better now than later.**

5. **chain204's clean-block choice**, which is a pre-registration and therefore expires: excluding
   the straddled pass 9 breaks (arm, position) balance at 8 passes with 3 arms; including it imports
   ~24% of a contaminated pass. Default: report both, disclose the imbalance — an imbalance is

6. **Whether `/scratch/bobbyy/c205an` stays where it is.** It is chain196's `c0` set under a

7. **Whether to push.** 849 commits ahead of `main` as of `72d4f8f` (`git rev-list --count main..72d4f8f`; a bare "commits ahead" numeral is wrong within a second, because recording the count increments it) on a single copy with no bundle or mirror, which

**Carried from earlier chains and still open:** the deferred k=4 equivalence test from chain191;
chain191's `9f50a83` revert decision; whether a ledger should record dependencies satisfied elsewhere
in the codex; what should happen when a sealed analysis publishes a number from an artefact that
exists nowhere; what quantity the stage-4 pre-registered bar bounds; whether amendment 4's floor of 8

**And a correction inside that list, three minutes after writing it.** Item 7 above first read "852
commits ahead of `main`". The measured value is `git rev-list --count main..HEAD` = the number now in
place; 852 was written from memory in a section whose entire subject is that numbers must carry their
provenance. That is the fourth instance in this milestone of a rule being violated by the next number
its author produced, and the mechanism is always the same: the rule governs *received* numbers and
feels satisfied once it has been applied to someone else's. **A number you generate crosses the same
boundary as a number you receive**, because the version of you that measured it is not the version
writing it down. The predicate is now in the text beside the value, which is the only form that
self-checks.

### The rotation's balance claim, verified here rather than accepted

The chain204 pre-registration rests on what chain203's rotation protects, so it was recomputed from
the sealed orders file at `~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl/chain203-rungwise-redwood/
orders_idx11x22.txt` (528 bytes, read-only):

    22 rows x 11 entries, 22 distinct, every row a permutation of 1..11
    (arm, position) coverage     22 passes -> every cell exactly 2, 0 unfilled   BALANCED
                                 11 passes -> every cell exactly 1, 0 unfilled   BALANCED
                                  9 passes -> 22 unfilled                        NOT
                                  8 passes -> 33 unfilled                        NOT
    generated by +1 mod 11 from the previous row                                 False

So the rotation protects **(arm, position)** balance — the ordinal slot in which each arm is measured
inside a pass — and not arm presence. Every pass carries every arm, which is what makes the
within-pass ratio available at all; the rotation exists to neutralise measurement order, and that is
the quantity a truncated pass count breaks. Applied to chain204 with three arms:

    8 clean passes   remainder 2   position balance BROKEN
    9 / 21 / 30      remainder 0   intact

And the design intent is legible in the pass counts: chain203 ran 22 passes for 11 arms and chain204
runs 30 for 3 — both exact multiples of the arm count, which is what a balanced rotation requires
rather than a coincidence. The generator is **not** a `+1 mod 11` cyclic shift, checked across all
21 transitions; balance holds anyway because it was measured on the coverage table instead of
inferred from a generator, which is the only reason that reading cost nothing.

Same directory tree confirms the survey the identification rested on: **34** sealed CSVs at 68,761
lines, **18** in chain196 (`c0`/`c0b`/`pfd0` × passes 1–6) and **16** in chain197
(`c0`/`c0b`/`pfd0`/`stream` × passes 1–4 only). Six-pass sets exist only in chain196, so the copy
could only have come from there — the elimination is exhaustive over the ledger rather than a lucky
first guess.

### A commit count written into a commit is off by one by construction

The correction two sections up replaced 852 with 848 and **848 was also wrong**, for a reason
re-measuring cannot fix:

    git rev-list --count main..72d4f8f^   848   <- what was written
    git rev-list --count main..72d4f8f    849   <- true once the commit recording it landed

848 was true at the instant it was measured and false at the instant the commit containing it
existed, because **the act of recording a commit count increments it.** No amount of re-measuring
converges; the measurement is its own invalidating event. It is the validity-domain shape with the
shortest possible domain — valid until the next line of work, and the next line of work was the
same line.

So the durable half of that fix was the whole of it: **the command in the text self-checks and the
numeral beside it cannot.** Either drop the value or stamp it. "849 as of `72d4f8f`" is verifiable
forever; "848 commits ahead" is wrong within a second. Corrected to the stamped form.

**And one site the earlier correction did not reach**, found by the verifier rather than by me: a
summary line read *"the branch is clean: 836 commits ahead of `main`, tree clean, zero
`Co-Authored-By` trailers by the structural predicate"* — asserting a clean trailer state **with no
range**, directly above the heading that documents the range as the defect. Naming the predicate
does not name the scope, and the scope was the whole finding. Now reads *"zero `^Co-Authored-By:`
trailers in `main..HEAD`"*, with the reason the range is stated given in place.

**The mechanism, which covers every instance on both sides tonight.** The provenance rule governs
*received* numbers, and it feels discharged once it has been applied to someone else's. But **a
number you generate crosses the same boundary as a number you receive, because the version of you
that measured it is not the version writing it down.** That is why "ask provenance" kept failing
while "put the predicate in the text" keeps working: the first is addressed to a reader who may not
be suspicious, the second is addressed to the document and re-runs on demand.

**66 cells of 22,920 are behind MKL beyond their own width's noise floor — 0.29% of the
collection** — and that is the **first gated count computed at matched resolution**: the floor and
the count come out of the same `per_cell()` reduction, the ratio formed inside each pass and the
median taken over the six. The single-pass gated version of the same quantity swings 15–52 across
passes, because a single-pass floor is about twice as wide as a per-cell one, so gating at the wrong
resolution adds more noise than it removes. This is the version to state the milestone in.

**Three independent programs now agree on this dataset**, which is worth recording because they were
written for different purposes:

    geomean of the five per-width board gms   2.2915
    verify_c196.py six-pass pooled            2.2915
    an_c205.py behind (per-cell median)         119
    verify_c196.py behind (same reduction)      119

Agreement across three implementations excludes computational error and says nothing about the data
— the same limit as before. What it does buy is that the 05:30 analysis is not being run for the
first time on the data it has to report.

**The shape by width is the finding under it.** The deficit is concentrated at the narrow widths —
56 of the 66 beyond-floor cells are at k=2 and k=4, and only 3 are at k=16 and k=32 combined — while
the pooled ratio rises monotonically with width, 1.73 → 2.91. Narrow-k is where MKL is still
competitive, which is consistent with everything this milestone has found about short kernels, and it
is the opposite of a shape that could be tuned away by a threshold: the cells are spread across
degree bands rather than clustered in one.

For orientation: this is chain196's `c0`, the **predecessor** object. chain205 measures the current
one over the same 22,920 cells, so the pair answers whether the current build improved on these 66
— and it answers it as a replication with both sides computed in one program under one named
reduction, never as a second confirmation of one run.

### The 66 are at most 47 independent problems, and the three-population account covers 59% of them

Two things the count alone hides, both computed from the same sealed chain196 `c0` set.

**First, 66 cells are not 66 problems.**

    66 cells beyond floor
      -> 52 distinct matrix keys          11 keys appear at more than one width
      -> 47 distinct (rows, nnz) shapes    4 shapes carry more than one key

    keys at multiple widths   connectus x4, nw14 x3, and x2 each: FX_March2010, air04,
                              bibd_17_8, boyd1, kl02, mycielskian11, raefsky1, rail507, us04
    shapes with >1 key        case9 / case9_A_01 / case9_A_11   (rows 14454, nnz 147972)
                              aa03 / aa3                        (rows 825,   nnz 70806)
                              Pd_b / Pd_rhs                     (rows 8081,  nnz 6323)
                              heart2 / heart3                   (rows 2339,  nnz 680341)

A matrix that is behind at four widths is **one** structural problem observed four times, not four;
and three near-duplicate `case9` variants at identical `(rows, nnz)` are not three problems either.
So the honest statement of the deficit is **at most 47 independent problems**, and this is the same
question as the open item about whether a pre-registered floor of 8 counts cells or independent
problems — arriving at the milestone's own headline. The corpus-duplication issue recorded earlier in
this milestone (an 89-key list being at most 87 distinct problems) recurs here at 22,920 cells.

**Second, the three-population account does not cover the set.** The populations on record are
mostly-empty rows at k=2, fewer rows than workers, and long rows with enough of them. Classified
with the thresholds as stated (`deg < 1`, `rows < 24` for redwood's 24-way affinity, `deg >= 100`):

    C  long rows (deg >= 100)                  35   53%
       UNCLASSIFIED                            27   41%
    A  mostly-empty rows (deg < 1)              4    6%
    B  fewer rows than workers (rows < 24)      0    0%

**Population B is empty** — no cell in the beyond-floor set has fewer rows than redwood has workers —
and 41% of the set falls outside all three. The unclassified cells are mid-degree and mid-size:
`raefsky1` k=2 at 0.7398 (rows 3242, deg 90.5), `msc00726` k=4 at 0.7480 (deg 47.5), `boyd1` k=4 at
0.7840 (rows 93279, deg 13.0), `rajat25` k=2 at 0.8478 (deg 7.0), the three `case9` variants at
deg 10.2.

**The thresholds were deliberately not moved.** Several unclassified cells sit just under `deg = 100`
— `raefsky1`/`raefsky2` at 90.5, `mycielskian11` at 87.8, `aa03`/`rat_A_3` at 85.8 — so dropping the
cut to 50 would absorb most of the 27 and make the account look complete. That is the overfitting
this milestone is explicitly constrained against: a classification whose boundary is chosen after
seeing which points are outside it explains nothing, and a threshold with no mechanism behind it is
not a finding. **The reportable result is that the three-population account was built on 33 cells
from an 89-key corpus and covers 59% of the beyond-floor set on 4,584 matrices**, which is a
finding about the account rather than a reason to widen it.

What would earn a fourth population is a mechanism first and a boundary second — the unclassified
group is concentrated at k=2 and k=4 (20 of 27), where the earlier narrow-k work already implicates
three loads per nonzero rather than any row-geometry effect, so that is where to look.

### Correction: the unclassified 27 are two groups with an empty band, and 89% are narrow-k

Three corrections to the section above, all verified here, and two of them strengthen its conclusion.

**The narrow-k share was understated.** The unclassified cells by width are `{k=2: 12, k=4: 12,
k=8: 3}` and **nothing at k=16 or k=32** — so **24 of 27, or 89%**, are at the two narrowest widths,
not the 20 of 27 stated. The conclusion that a mechanism would have to come from the narrow-k work
is stronger than it was written.

**The cell that makes the threshold argument unanswerable was missing from the list.** `cegb2802` at
k=4 sits at **deg 98.99** — one hundredth of a degree unit below a cut at 100. The examples given
(raefsky1/2 at 90.5, mycielskian11 at 87.8, aa03 at 85.8) all reproduce, but the nearest cell to the
boundary was absent. One cell at 98.99 against a cut at 100 demonstrates that the classification is
doing arbitrary work at its margin more sharply than three cells at 85–90 do.

**And the 27 are not one residual.** Sorted by mean degree, the largest gap in the sequence is
**34.56**, between **12.99 and 47.55**, and nothing lies inside it:

    deg 47.55 - 98.99   14 cells   cegb2802 99.0, raefsky2 90.6, raefsky1 90.5 x2, air04 88.7 x2,
                                   mycielskian11 87.8 x2, aa03 85.8, aa3 85.8, rat_A_3 85.8,
                                   comsol 65.1, GT01R 54.0, msc00726 47.6
    deg  2.04 - 12.99   13 cells   boyd1 13.0 x2, case9 family 10.2 x3, ASIC_100k 9.5, p6000 9.5,
                                   Chebyshev3 9.0, ins2 8.9, rajat25 7.0, adder_dcop_04 5.8,
                                   ASIC_680k 3.9, poli 2.0

**So lowering the degree cut to 47 would absorb exactly 14 of the 27 and leave 13 that no
row-geometry threshold can reach** — the low group's maximum degree is 3.7× below the high group's
minimum. That makes the refusal to move the threshold stronger rather than merely principled: the
move would be **visibly partial**, buying half the residual and leaving a group an order of magnitude
away in the one variable being thresholded.

The low group is where the interesting thing is. **12 of its 13 cells are at k=2 or k=4** (only
`ins2` at k=8 is not), and it contains the two largest matrices in the whole beyond-floor set —
`ASIC_680k` at 682,862 rows and `ins2` at 309,412 rows, at degrees 3.9 and 8.9. Very large, very
sparse, very narrow k. That is a different regime from long rows, and it is the one the earlier
narrow-k work already implicates through three loads per nonzero rather than any row-geometry effect.

**The boundary here is an observation about the distribution, not a chosen cut**, and the difference
matters: 12.99/47.55 is where the data has a hole, reported with its width, whereas 50 would be a
number picked to make a classification look complete. It is offered as a description of the residual
and **not** as a fourth population — a population needs a mechanism first and a boundary second, and
no mechanism is being claimed for either group yet.

Confirmed unchanged: `deg < 1` catches 4 cells, and the minimum row count over all 66 is **50**, so
nothing falls in the fewer-rows-than-workers class on any plausible worker count.

### A floor alone cannot be a gate on a board that is winning

The gate producing the 66 is `x < 1.0 − floor(k)`, one inequality rather than a conjunction, so it
cannot lose its direction test. But it is worth recording what the other reading would do, because
the failure would not look like a bug:

    cells                                        22920
    |x-1| > floor   (the FLOOR ALONE)            22805   99.5%
      of which ahead,  x > 1 + floor             22739
      of which behind, x < 1 - floor                66   <- the gate
    x < 1           (direction alone)              119

    119 behind      -> 66   the floor removing 53
    22805 beyond    -> 66   the direction removing 22739

**A gate written as "beyond the floor" without the direction would flag 99.5% of the collection** —
because the board sits at 1.73–2.91 and almost everything clears a 4–8% floor on the *winning* side.
The output would be "22,805 of 22,920 cells are beyond the noise floor", which reads as a
catastrophic result rather than as a mistake, and a reader checking it against the pooled ratio of
2.29 would find nothing wrong with either number.

Both conditions are load-bearing and they remove very different populations: the floor takes 53 of
the 119 behind cells, and the direction takes 22,739 of the 22,805 beyond-floor cells. **Beside a
gate, report what each conjunct removes** — this is the same discipline as reporting the number that
shows a count could have been non-zero, applied to a filter with two terms instead of one.

### The convention audit fired on its author, on its first real trial

A new stage was added to print the goal's count under every reduction. It was written with a fresh
`abs(x - 1.0)` for the single-pass floor, and the analyzer refused to run:

    REFUSE: deviation-from-parity written outside dev_prereg/dev_logsym -- line 515:
            abs(x - 1) in <module>. One helper per convention, used everywhere, so a mixed
            convention is not expressible rather than merely discouraged.

**That is the trial this mechanism had not had.** Its record was 1 for 1 against an injected
positive control and 0 for 0 against anything real; it is now 2 for 2, and the real violation was
written by the same author who installed the guard, in the same session, minutes after publishing
it. A convention that had been merely *documented* would have produced a mixed-convention floor and
a plausible number — the single-pass gated count, which nothing downstream would have flagged. Fixed
by routing through `dev_prereg`, with the incident recorded at the line so the next reader knows the
call is not stylistic.

(Recorded once more because it recurred within the same hour: the first check of the exit code read
`rc=0` through a pipe to `tail`. The real code was 1. That is the `$?`-after-a-pipe defect again,
now four times in this session, and it briefly hid the refusal entirely.)

### The goal's count under every reduction, printed together

    reduction                                       behind   gated at matched resolution
    a SINGLE pass (6 passes, range shown)          398-435       46-71     <- ~97% churn
    per-cell MEDIAN over passes  (the RECIPE)          119          66     <- floor and count matched
    behind in EVERY pass                                13         n/a
    behind in ANY pass                                1707         n/a
    -> the count moves 131x between the loosest and the tightest reduction

The analyzer now prints all four with the reduction named on each and states in place that **which
one the milestone is stated in is not a session's decision.** The per-cell gated count, 66, sits
inside the single-pass gated range 46–71, as it must.

**And a discrepancy that is itself the finding: 46–71 here against 15–52 reported by the verifier,
for the same quantity.** The cause is not resolution — both are single-pass — it is *which A/A
defines the floor*:

    oursb / ours   one binary, two labels        the arm-identity floor   -> 46-71
    c0 / c0b       two builds of the same source the build-identity floor -> 15-52

The build-identity floor is wider, so it admits fewer cells, which is consistent with the layout
artefact already measured in this milestone: two objects with identical decisions differ 1–2.6% on
narrow-k SpMM while identical-source rebuilds differ 0.3%. **So a gated count needs its floor named
by A/A as well as by resolution** — "beyond the noise floor" is under-specified in two dimensions,
not one, and the two choices move the count by a factor of three. Neither is wrong; they bound
different things. The arm-identity floor answers "is this cell's deficit larger than the same code
measured twice", and the build-identity floor answers "larger than two compilations of the same
source". The milestone's claim is about the kernel, so the arm-identity floor is the matched one for
it, and the build floor belongs beside any claim that compares two objects.

### A wider floor lowers the behind count by construction, so the behind count alone cannot choose a floor

Two corrections and one result, all on chain196's `c0` with `c0b` supplying the build-identity A/A.

**First, my "factor of three" was range-extreme against range-extreme.** Per pass, both floors:

    pass          p1   p2   p3   p4   p5   p6      range
    arm identity  52   71   46   63   68   55      46-71
    build         15   52   35   35   50   45      15-52
    ratio        3.47 1.37 1.31 1.80 1.36 1.22

The per-pass ratio runs **1.22× to 3.47×**; quoting 71 against 15 gives 4.7× and describes no pass.
Comparing the maximum of one range to the minimum of another is the same error as reading a span off
thin quantiles.

**Second, at the resolution the headline uses the gap is 1.40×, not 3×.**

    k      arm floor  build floor  ratio   beyond(arm)  beyond(build)
    2       0.0451     0.0817      1.81x        20            16
    4       0.0376     0.0668      1.78x        36            24
    8       0.0470     0.0725      1.54x         7             4
    16      0.0598     0.0867      1.45x         1             1
    32      0.0830     0.1233      1.49x         2             2
    ALL                                         66            47

The 3× lives only at single-pass resolution where both floors are noisy. And the floor ratio falls
monotonically from **1.81× at k=2 to 1.45× at k=16** — the layout artefact's own signature, largest
at the narrowest width, matching the 1–2.6%-on-narrow-k measurement already on record. **The
per-cell gated count is also robust to the floor's exact value where the per-pass one is not:** the
verifier's independently computed build floors differ from mine by 2–3% (0.0838 vs 0.0817 at k=2)
and the per-cell counts agree exactly at 16/24/4/1/2, while the per-pass counts differ by up to 8
cells. That is a third argument for the per-cell resolution, independent of the two already made.

**Now the result, which inverts the case for the tighter count.** The argument for the
build-identity floor is that Scorch is compiled on the user's host, so build-to-build variation is
variation a user is exposed to, and 47 is therefore a *harder* claim than 66. That is right about
the behind list and incomplete, because **the same variation that removes 19 cells from the behind
list puts 131 currently-winning cells inside it**:

    floor            behind   indeterminate   ahead    not-certainly-ahead
    arm identity         66             115   22739     181   (0.79%)
    build identity       47             203   22670     250   (1.09%)

**A wider floor moves cells out of both tails into the middle, so it necessarily lowers the behind
count and necessarily raises the indeterminate count.** Reporting only the first is favourable by
construction — "all but 47" reads as better than "all but 66" while the set that is *not safely won*
grows from 181 to 250. Choosing a floor to minimise the behind count is therefore not a neutral
methodological preference; it is a direction, and the only report that cannot be gamed this way is
the three-way partition.

So both floors belong, with the partition attached to each rather than a single count:

    beyond MEASUREMENT noise (arm identity)   66 behind, 115 indeterminate
      "we really measured this deficit"
    beyond BUILD variation (build identity)   47 behind, 203 indeterminate
      "this deficit survives recompilation -- and 131 of our wins may not"

The 19 in between — beyond measurement noise but inside build variation — are a named, checkable
category rather than a rounding, and so are the 131. Which floor the milestone's claim is stated
against is a decision about what is being promised to a user, and it is Bobby's, not a session's.
It is now item 8 in the open-decisions list.

**And a constraint that decides which of the two floors chain205 can even report.** chain205 wrote
one build — `fc_c0_float32_p1..p6` and nothing else — so it has `oursb/ours` and no second object.
**The build-identity floor is not computable from chain205's data at all.** chain196 ran three
objects (`c0`, `c0b`, `pfd0`) and therefore supports both floors; chain205 supports one.

So the 66-versus-47 question is answerable only on chain196, and chain205's board will carry the
arm-identity floor alone unless it is compared against chain196's `c0` — which the cross-chain
replication does, but across chains rather than within one. That is a weaker pairing: two chains
differ by more than a recompilation.

**Whether the harder claim is computable is a property of the experiment's design, not of the
analysis**, so it is a decision that has to be made before a run rather than after. Noted for the
next chain: a run intended to support a claim about the shipped kernel rather than about one binary
needs a second compilation of the same source in the arm set, and it costs one more build and no
extra measurement time per pass beyond that arm's own.

**Resolved: the whole discrepancy is one parameter acting on one side.** Two implementations
reported the build-identity partition as 47/203/22670 and 47/211/22662. Widening the build floor by
2.5% — the size of the difference between the two implementations' p95 — changes the counts like
this:

    floor x1.000   behind  47   band below parity  72   band above parity 131
    floor x1.025   behind  47   band below parity  72   band above parity 141

**The behind tail does not move at all and neither does the below-parity half of the band; every
cell the wider floor picks up is above parity.** So the 203-vs-211 disagreement, and the 131-vs-139
one inside it, are the same 2.5% floor-width residual landing entirely on the winning side. Behind
agrees exactly at 47 under both.

The reason is a density asymmetry that is worth stating on its own: **there are more cells just above
parity than just below it**, so the indeterminate count is sensitive to the floor's exact value in a
way the behind count is not. That is a fourth, mechanical argument for reporting the behind count at
per-cell resolution — and simultaneously a reason the middle column of the partition needs its floor
stated to 3 significant figures, since it is the column that moves. The 2.5% itself is unresolved;
cross-build pass pairing and the p95 index convention are both candidates, and it is recorded as an
open residual with its size rather than left implicit.

And the monotonicity is a **theorem, not an observation**: the band is symmetric about parity, so
widening the floor moves cells out of both tails into the middle and never out of it. `behind` is
non-increasing in floor width and `indeterminate` is non-decreasing, for every floor and every
dataset. Therefore **a behind count alone is not a measurement of the collection's state** — a free
parameter moves it in a known direction, no bad faith required, and a reader cannot detect it from
the number. The three-way partition is the only form in which widening the floor has a visible cost,
because the cost must appear in the middle column.

**The theorem, with its positive control.** The analyzer now prints the three-way partition, and the
claim attached to it — that `not-certainly-ahead` is the number a wider floor cannot shrink — is
provable and was also checked by sweeping the floor width over a 6× range on chain196 `c0`:

    floor mult   behind   indeterminate   ahead    not-certainly-ahead
    x0.5             87              65   22768     152
    x1.0             66             115   22739     181
    x1.5             49             177   22694     226
    x2.0             44             261   22615     305
    x3.0             29             819   22072     848

`behind` falls monotonically and `not-certainly-ahead` rises monotonically, as it must:
`not-certainly-ahead = total − ahead`, and `ahead` is non-increasing in floor width, so the sum can
only grow. **At a floor 3× wider the behind count is 29 — less than half of 66 — while 848 cells are
no longer safely won.** That is the demonstration the argument needed: a reader shown only "29 cells
behind" would take it for a better kernel, and the dataset is identical.

So the partition is printed with its floor named and its identity stated — arm identity bounds
measurement noise, build identity bounds what survives recompilation, the latter is wider and is not
computable from a single-build run. This is the form chain205's board will carry.

### The floor residual was the A/A's orientation, which my own analyzer already warns about

The 2.5% build-floor disagreement is fully explained, and it is neither the p95 index nor the pass
pairing nor the cell population (the cell sets are identical — all 22,920 in all three builds):

    definition              k=2      k=4      k=8     k=16     k=32   behind  indet  above-band
    c0 / c0b               0.0817   0.0668   0.0725   0.0867   0.1233     47     203     131
    c0b / c0               0.0838   0.0666   0.0738   0.0884   0.1273     47     211     139
    MAX of the two         0.0871   0.0706   0.0755   0.0931   0.1430     45     226     152
    log-symmetric          0.0869   0.0693   0.0752   0.0917   0.1364     46     222     149

**It is the orientation of the A/A ratio.** `median(y/x) ≠ 1/median(x/y)` at an even pass count —
six here — because averaging two order statistics does not commute with inversion. `an_c205.py`'s
stage 6 states exactly this, about the board, in the text it prints; the same fact was then walked
into on the floor. **A rule published in one program about one quantity does not transfer itself to
the adjacent quantity in the same program**, which is the fifth instance of that pattern in this
milestone and the first where the rule and the violation were in the same file.

**And for an A/A neither orientation is privileged**, because both arms are the same code — so a
single-orientation floor is making an arbitrary choice that moves the middle column by 8 cells.
chain203's sealed convention is `max(abs(lo − 1), abs(hi − 1))`, which is **orientation-symmetric by
construction**; that is the property an A/A floor needs and the reason the sealed analyzer took a max
rather than a side. It reads 0.0871 / 0.0706 / 0.0755 / 0.0931 / 0.1430 — wider than either side, as
it must be.

**The behind count spans 45–47 across all four definitions and the indeterminate count spans
203–226.** Two cells against twenty-three: the same robustness asymmetry as before, now measured
against four definitions of one A/A rather than a perturbation of one. (A line in the script that
produced this table asserted "47 under all four" and "203 to 217"; both were written before the
numbers existed and both are wrong. Corrected here — an assertion typed ahead of its output is not
a measurement, which is the same defect as counting off one's own printed list.)

Against the arm floor's genuine replicate, the headline is steadier still: `oursb/ours` measured
inside `c0` gives 66 behind and inside `c0b` gives 65, while the floors themselves differ by up to
**14.1%** at k=4 (0.0376 against 0.0429). **A 14% floor disagreement buys one cell.**

**And the design point this exposes runs against the build floor.** chain196 supports exactly one
identical-source build pair (`c0`/`c0b`) and two arm-identity replicates. The `pfd0` pairs are not
spare build replicates — their p95 runs to 0.176, up to 3.7× the arm floor at k=8, because `pfd0`
carries a real code difference. **So the build-identity floor is the one estimate in the design with
n = 1 and no way to attach an uncertainty to it**, while the arm floor has a replicate that agrees
to one cell on the headline. That is a reason to report the arm-gated partition as the primary and
the build-gated one beside it, and it is a requirement for the next chain: **two identical-source
build pairs, not one**, if a build-identity floor is to carry an uncertainty rather than a value.

### And 61 is not distinguishable from chain196's 66

The comparison against chain196 `c0` was computed in one program under one named reduction, both
sides bound to content:

    per-pass pooled   c196c0 2.2605 2.2811 2.2817 2.2595 2.2556 2.2785   spread 1.16%
                      c205   2.2649 2.2860 2.2704 2.2744 2.2929 2.2693   spread 1.24%
    six-pass pooled   c196c0 2.2915   c205 2.2978   -> 0.28% apart
    behind (per-cell) c196c0 119      c205 106      -> 13 cells apart

**The control that settles it is chain196's own second build of the same source.** Each board gated
by its own arm floor:

    build   k=2  k=4  k=8  k=16  k=32   beyond   behind   pooled
    c0       20   36    7     1     2      66      119    2.2915
    c0b      29   34    8     0     1      72      118    2.2909
    c205     18   31    9     2     1      61      106    2.2978

**Recompiling the same source moves the gated count from 66 to 72 — a 6-cell spread — and the
pooled board by 0.03%.** chain205's 61 is 5 below `c0` and 11 below `c0b`, so it sits inside the
band that recompilation alone produces. The pooled difference, +0.28%, is also inside the 1.16–1.24%
pass-to-pass spread.

So the honest statement is: **chain205 reproduces chain196 and does not beat it.** 61 against 66 is
not an improvement that this design can resolve, and saying otherwise would be reading a 5-cell move
against a 6-cell noise band. The two-cell agreement of the arm floor's replicate (66 vs 65) does not
help here, because that replicate holds the *board* fixed and varies only the floor; varying the
object moves the count six.

**What the pair does establish** is that the board is reproducible across chains at the pooled level
to 0.28% and at the gated-count level to within build noise — which is what makes a future
improvement measurable, and is the first time this milestone has had a two-chain baseline at full
collection scale.

### An mtime binding cannot survive the transfer it exists to protect

The close-out refused at step 5. The six real chain205 passes had been sealed on redwood, pulled,
and verified byte-for-byte against that seal — and the mtime binding then rejected them:

    fc_c0_float32_p1.csv: mtime 05:32:52, the log closed p1 at 02:57:55 (9297s apart)
    ...
    fc_c0_float32_p6.csv: mtime 05:33:02, the log closed p6 at 05:30:23 (159s apart)

**`scp` does not preserve mtime**, so a transferred copy of the *right* run fails exactly as a copy
of the *wrong* run does. The board was then run on the content binding alone, which is not a bypass:
the seal was taken on the producing host and the local copy verified against it, so provenance rests
on the stronger of the two mechanisms. But **a binding that cannot survive the transfer it is meant
to protect is half a mechanism**, and it was designed only hours after the substitution it was
designed for — which is how the limitation "mtime is mutable" got written down while the sharper
limitation "mtime is *not carried*" did not.

The refusal now distinguishes the two cases instead of merging them:

    EVERY input is NEWER than the log's last close and no row count is wrong. That is what a
    TRANSFERRED COPY looks like (scp does not preserve mtime) and also what a substituted copy
    looks like -- this check cannot tell them apart. If these files were copied from the
    producing host, bind to CONTENT with --expect-sha256 against a seal taken THERE, which is
    stronger, and drop --stage-log. Do not widen the tolerance.

The last sentence is the load-bearing one. **The tempting repair is to widen the tolerance until the
transfer fits, and that destroys the check** — a tolerance large enough to admit a 9,297-second
transfer admits every copy ever made. The correct repair points at a different mechanism rather than
a looser version of this one.

### The MKL deficit and the register-block prefetch are largely the same question

chain196 carried a third object, `pfd0`, with the register-block prefetch deleted. Gated by its own
arm floor it reads **37 cells beyond floor against `c0`'s 66**, with a pooled board 3.0% higher —
and its floor is *narrower* (0.0405/0.0288/0.0353/0.0465/0.0669 against c0's
0.0451/0.0376/0.0470/0.0598/0.0830), so the improvement is not a gating artefact.

    per-width beyond-floor count, each build gated by its OWN arm floor
      build   k=2  k=4  k=8  k=16  k=32   ALL
      c0       20   36    7     1     2     66
      c0b      29   34    8     0     1     72
      pfd0     20   10    3     2     2     37
      c205     18   31    9     2     1     61

**Deleting the prefetch removes 26 of the 36 beyond-floor cells at k=4 and 4 of the 7 at k=8** —
which is most of the narrow-k deficit that the population analysis identified as the place a
mechanism would have to come from.

**And it cannot ship as it stands.** Against the orientation-symmetric build-identity floor
(`max` over both orientations of `c0` vs `c0b`; 0.0871/0.0706/0.0755/0.0931/0.1430):

    k     faster>floor   slower>floor   inside floor    gm       worst regression
    2           138             74           4372    1.0040   Delor64K @ 0.593
    4          1273             44           3267    1.0456   LargeRegFile @ 0.710
    8          1560             30           2994    1.0597   wiki-topcats_Categories @ 0.600
    16          794             48           3742    1.0395   sgpf5y6 @ 0.484
    32          149             53           4382    1.0119   sx-superuser_C2A @ 0.556
    ALL        3914            249          18757

**3,914 cells faster beyond the floor against 249 slower, a 15.7:1 ratio — and `sgpf5y6` at k=16 is
2.07× slower.** The project's standard is neutral-or-better everywhere with no regressions, so a
15.7:1 ratio is not a licence; it is a finding to report. Consistent with what chain197 already
recorded for this change ("deleting it wins 2.9–14.2% but harms 115 matrices at width 32" — a
different predicate from the 53 measured here, and the difference between those two numbers is
itself unresolved).

The convention for this situation is already in the repository: gate a sub-regime win behind a
runtime condition that **provably cannot fire** on the shapes it would hurt. So the next question is
whether a mechanism separates the 3,914 from the 249 — and it has to be a mechanism, not a boundary
fitted to the 249, or it is the special-case pile the standing instruction forbids. The named worst
regressions span k=2 through k=32 and include both a 64K-row FEM matrix and two large power-law
graphs, which is not an encouraging start for a single geometric predicate.

### Retraction: `max(|lo−1|, |hi−1|)` is not orientation-symmetric, and neither is the log-symmetric form

Two sections up, chain203's `max(abs(lo − 1), abs(hi − 1))` is called "orientation-symmetric by
construction" and offered as the principled resolution of the A/A orientation problem. **That is
wrong**, and it takes no data to show:

    band      [1.0722, 1.3002]  ->  max dev 0.3002
    inverted  [0.7691, 0.9327]  ->  max dev 0.2309
    symmetric only when the band is GEOMETRICALLY CENTRED on 1:
      [0.5000, 2.0000]  1.0000 vs 1.0000   symmetric
      [0.8000, 1.2500]  0.2500 vs 0.2500   symmetric
      [1.0722, 1.3002]  0.3002 vs 0.2309   NOT

The band used is chain203's own published one. **And the error was a conflation of two different
objects**: `max` over the two *endpoints of a band* is not `max` over the two *orientations of a
per-cell ratio*. The second one *is* symmetric — swapping orientations swaps the arguments of `max`
— and it is the estimator that was actually computed and used for the `pfd0` comparison. So the
analysis used the right thing for the wrong stated reason, which is the more dangerous way to be
right.

**The log-symmetric form does not fix it either, and it fails silently.** `exp|ln r| − 1` is
symmetric under `r → 1/r`, but the orientation choice happens **upstream of it**, inside the median
over six passes, so `m₁ ≠ 1/m₂` and the transform inherits the asymmetry it was brought in to
remove: 0.0869/0.0693/0.0752/0.0917/0.1364 one way against 0.0866/0.0686/0.0748/0.0908/0.1375 the
other — different at all five widths, while the partition lands on 46/222/149 both ways. **Agreeing
on the counts while differing on the floors is worse than disagreeing**, because a counts-based check
passes it.
