computed **on redwood** before transfer (`c205.sha256`, 7 of 7 verify here), so custody reaches the
producing host rather than starting at this machine.

### The substitution was a symlink farm, not a renamed copy

The finding previously recorded as "chain196's sealed six-pass set sat in chain205's analysis
directory, byte-identical and renamed" now has its mechanism. `/scratch/bobbyy/c205an/` contains six
**symlinks**:

    fc_c0_float32_p1.csv -> /scratch/bobbyy/c196/sh_c0_float32_p1.csv        (p2..p6 likewise)

created 2026-09-15 **02:20**, whereas the real chain205 run wrote its own outputs into
`/scratch/bobbyy/c205` between **02:57 and 05:30**. So the substitution predated the data it
displaced. It was not a copy that drifted in; it was a deliberate symlink set, which is why
byte-identity held exactly and why every consistency check passed. A symlink farm is strictly harder
to catch than a copy: it has no independent bytes, no independent mtime on the data, and `ls`
shows the intended names.

### Both published counts recount correctly from their own bytes

The open question this raised is whether the published 63 was read off the symlinks. It was not, and
that is settled by recount rather than by argument. Recomputed under the sealed estimator --
per-cell `exp(median(log ratio))` over the 6 passes, deviation `exp|ln x|-1`, floor = per-width
`sorted(d)[int(0.95*(len(d)-1))]` of `dev(oursb/ours)`, behind iff `dev(S) > floor` and `S < 1`
with `S = mkl/ours`:

    source                           k=2    k=4    k=8   k=16   k=32    TOTAL   published
    genuine chain205  behind          20     31      9      2      1       63        63
                      band            45     33     20      7      8      113
                      ahead         4519   4520   4555   4575   4575    22744
                                                             sum = 22920
    chain196 c0       behind          21     37      7      1      2       68        68

Both reproduce exactly. Had `c205an/` been read, chain205 would have printed 68. The three classes
are each counted from their own predicate and sum to 22920, so the partition is a check rather than
an identity.

The two behind-sets overlap in only **30** cells -- 33 chain205-only, 38 chain196-only. Two runs of
the same source disagreeing on more than half of their gated cells is why the analysis moved off
single-chain counts onto replication.

### The sealed analyzer could not run in the layout it was sealed into

A second session found this and it is the same silent-null shape the analyzer's own copy check was
written to catch. `an_c206.py:30` reads `C206 = os.path.join(D, "c206final")`, where `D` is the
script's directory. In the ledger layout the CSVs sit directly in the chain directory and no
`c206final` subdirectory exists, so the glob returns zero files and the comparison set is empty.
Run in place, the filed artefact prints:

    IDENTITY: 0 chain206 outputs; 18 other CSVs on disk compared by content
      no chain206 output matches any other set's bytes -- this is not a renamed copy
      builds: [] ; cells each: {}

It asserts the outputs are not a renamed copy having compared **nothing**, with no error and no
warning, and then prints an empty table. This is the fourth harness in this milestone to hardcode a
ledger-relative path instead of taking the tree root as `$1`.

`an_c206.py` is kept unmodified, because it is the artefact that produced the published numbers and
editing it would break that binding. Added beside it: `an_c206_ledger.py`, which takes the tree root
as `argv[1]`, asserts 18 input files and 22920 cells per build and refuses otherwise, and reports
the **size-eligible candidate count** beside the match count. All three guards were fed the defect
they forbid and refused: an empty directory, a 17-of-18 partial input, and the as-ran copy's own
failure reproduced above. Its output reproduces every published figure and uses the corrected
median-of-three denominator.

Against the whole ledger it now reports 1290 other CSVs, **25 size-eligible**, 0 byte-identical --
and the eligible count is the number that makes the zero mean something.

### One consequence of filing, recorded because it inverts a check

Before chain206 was filed, the only copy of its outputs was the scratchpad, so the correct answer to
the renamed-copy scan was 0 matches. Two known-good copies now exist, so a scan that includes the
scratchpad correctly finds 18 matches; when the scratchpad is reaped the answer returns to 0 for a
third reason. The raw count is therefore uninformative in both directions, which is why the
size-eligible count and `PROVENANCE.md`'s record of how many known-good copies exist are the parts
that carry the meaning.

### Tree-level attestation, verified and left alone

The ledger root's `spmm-beat-mkl/SHA256SUMS` is cksum/CRC-32 despite its name: `shasum -a 256 -c`
on it emits **0 lines, 0 OK, 0 FAILED** -- it verifies nothing while appearing to verify 1123
entries. Anchoring on the path component, it names **4** chain directories (chain185 x2,
chain187 x2) of the 22 present, so chain188 through chain206 have no tree-level attestation.
Nothing it names is missing, so this is omission, not rot. Per-directory `SHA256SUMS` carries the
load. Not repaired here: regenerating a manifest at the ledger root changes shared evidence
infrastructure and is Bobby's call.

### Fifth instance of the hardcoded-path defect, in a script filed minutes after writing that section up

`recount205.py` — the recount above, filed into the chain205 directory — opened with
`L = os.path.expanduser("~/.cache/scorch-codex/spmm-beat-mkl")` and both chain directory names
hardcoded. That is the same defect the preceding section reports as the fourth instance, committed
into the ledger immediately after the write-up criticising it. Recorded rather than quietly fixed,
because the pattern is that a rule gets broken by the very next artefact its author produces.

Fixed: takes the ledger root as `argv[1]`, defaulting to the script's parent so it is correct in
place, and refuses on a wrong-sized input.

**The positive control found something the guard design had wrong.** Fed a 2-of-6-pass subset, the
cell-count guard **passed** — all 22920 cells are present, each with fewer passes — and what caught
it was the separate per-arm reading count (45840 against an expected 137520). So asserting the cell
count does not detect a partial-pass input, which is the likelier corruption when a run is
interrupted. Both assertions are needed and only one of them fires on this case. This is the
argument for feeding a guard the defect it forbids rather than reasoning that it covers it.

### Attribution: the symlink farm is a report from redwood, its consequence is independently verified

Stated because a reader would otherwise assume both halves were confirmed the same way. The
verifying session is instructed never to touch redwood, so the **mechanism** — six links in
`/scratch/bobbyy/c205an/` created 02:20 against a real run writing 02:57-05:30 — rests on this
session's reading of that host and is not independently checked. What is independently checked, by a
session that reimplemented the gating rule from the prose description alone, is the **consequence**:
the filed bytes are chain205's own and print 63, chain196's bytes print 68, per-width vectors match
digit for digit (20/31/9/2/1 and 21/37/7/1/2), both partitions sum to 22920 with 4584 cells at every
width, and the intersection/only/only split reproduces at 30/33/38. Their independent floors for
chain196 also matched a figure they had computed an hour earlier for an unrelated purpose.

Their identity scan over both roots: **0 exact size matches, 913 files within 5% of the range, 0
byte-identical.** The near-miss population is large, so the zero is informative — and it is only
informative because chain196's `sh_*` family exists, which is the family the vacuity claim had
written off.

### The surviving-cell count, and an honest note on which guard actually fires

`recount205.py` filtered cells to those with all six passes (`if len(rs)==6`) while printing
`len(T)`, the cells *loaded*. A dataset missing a pass, or one key absent from one pass, would
therefore board a confident count over a quietly smaller denominator with the printed cell count
still looking right. Fixed: the post-filter surviving count is now printed per width for both the
floor arm and the board, and it reads 4584 at every width for both chains, so nothing was dropped
here — but it is now the printed number rather than an inferred one.

**The assertion behind it has not been shown to fire, and that is worth saying rather than
implying.** Both positive controls — deleting a whole pass, and deleting one key's 15 rows from one
pass — were caught **upstream** by the per-arm reading count (114600 and 137515 against an expected
137520) before the surviving-cell check was reached. For these corruptions the reading count is
strictly stronger, so the surviving-cell assert is unreachable defence-in-depth. Being already
covered is not being tested; what the fix genuinely delivers is the printed value the peer asked
for, not a demonstrated guard.

### And one in my own verification line, immediately after writing the section about it

Reporting the two new seals, this session printed `OK 0` for both manifests. Cause:
`shasum -a 256 -c $D/SHA256SUMS` was run from a different working directory, and the manifests hold
relative paths, so it found no files and emitted **0 lines, 0 OK and 0 FAILED** — byte for byte the
same failure mode as the ledger root's CRC-32 manifest reported two sections earlier, and the same
shape as the analyzer that certified nothing. Verified from inside each directory: chain205 11 of 11
and 7 of 7 against the redwood-side digests, chain206 26 of 26 and 18 of 18. The peer's figures were
right and this session's were vacuous.

The general form, now on its fourth appearance in one day: **`shasum -c` reports success and failure
on the same channel it reports "I could not find the file", and the third case prints as silence.**
Any use of it must assert the emitted line count against the manifest line count.

### The seal-through-a-symlink assumption, closed on the producing host

A digest computed *through* a symlink records the target's content, so a seal can verify 18 of 18
while the bytes belong to another run — every layer agreeing and every layer wrong together. Given
that a symlink farm existed one directory away, this was the strongest claim in both filings resting
on its one unexamined assumption. It is a fact about redwood, so it is checkable here even though the
verifying session cannot reach that host:

    /scratch/bobbyy/c205   regular files  7   symlinks 0
    /scratch/bobbyy/c206   regular files 20   symlinks 0

Both producing-host digest files were therefore computed over regular files. On the filed copies,
`find -type l` returns nothing and every entry's `realpath` stays inside its own directory. The
general point, which the symlink farm makes concrete: **"the bytes match what the host hashed at that
path" is not "the path was a regular file when it hashed it."** A content check had been standing in
for a provenance check.

Also recovered while checking: `c206_run.log`, 10,218 bytes and 90 lines — the run's own log on
redwood, distinct from and larger than the staging record filed earlier. Now sealed.

### Content binding: strong for chain206, absent for chain205, and one instrument whose obvious reading is wrong

chain206's `build` column is self-identifying. Across all 18 files the value matches the filename
with **0 disagreeing rows out of 1,237,680**, so a link to another run's bytes would have to carry
that run's build label.

chain205 gets nothing from this, and that is the reason the substitution survived: chain205 and
chain196 are **schema-identical**, both writing `build=c0` and `slice=corpusp1` over 68,760 common
rows per pass with the same keys, widths and arms. No column labels chain205 as chain205.

The `batch` column — repeat counts a run re-derives from its own timings — was proposed as the
missing content-level cross-check. It works, but **not in the way the raw number suggests, and a
negative control is what separates the two readings**:

    chain205 vs chain196, all 6 passes   batch identical  30,268 / 412,560   7.34%
    within-run baseline, chain205 p1-p2  batch identical   4,857 /  68,760   7.06%
    within-run baseline, chain196 p1-p2  batch identical   4,496 /  68,760   6.54%

The cross-run figure sits **inside** the within-run baseline, because `batch` is re-derived per
*pass* from that pass's own timings and so varies between two passes of one run as much as between
two runs. So 7.34% is not positive evidence of independence; it is the null.

**The power is one-sided, and that is the claim worth keeping.** A literal substitution — symlink or
copy — makes `batch` agree on 100% of rows. Against a 6.5-7.1% baseline, an observed 7.34% rules
substitution out decisively while saying nothing in the other direction. The informative comparison
is the gap to 100%, not the distance from zero. A right instrument with the wrong denominator reads
as evidence when it is a baseline.

### Correction: the surviving-cell assertion is reachable, and finding the reaching case turned it into a theorem with a missing premise

The preceding section called the surviving-cell assertion "unreachable defence-in-depth" on the
evidence that two positive controls were caught upstream. **That verdict was wrong**, and a peer was
right to challenge it, though not by the route they proposed. Their two constructions were run here
against the actual script:

    construction                          raw rows   cells loaded   per-arm readings   what fires
    1. path prefix on one key, pass 1      412,560         22,925            137,520   cell count
    2. relabel key A's rows to existing
       key B, pass 1                       412,560         22,920            137,515   reading count

Construction 2 was predicted to pass every upstream guard. It does not: the relabelled rows
**overwrite** key B's existing pass-1 entry in the dictionary, so five readings per arm are lost and
the reading count lands at 137,515. Their prediction counted raw CSV rows, which really are
unchanged; the guard counts post-insertion `(cell, pass, arm)` entries, which are not.

**Why every deletion- and relabel-shaped corruption fires upstream — the argument is pigeonhole, and
it is worth stating because it says exactly when the assertion becomes reachable.** 22920 cells,
each contributing at most one reading per arm per pass, with the pass index drawn from at most 6
values, gives at most 137,520 readings per arm. So `readings == 137,520` **forces** exactly six
passes for every cell. The surviving-cell count cannot then differ from 4584.

**The premise is "at most 6 values", and nothing asserted it.** `load()` globbed the pass files
without checking how many it found. With a seventh file, a cell carrying seven passes compensates
for one carrying five and every upstream count sits exactly at expectation. Constructed and
verified: key A's 15 rows removed from pass 1, a `_p7.csv` added carrying key B's 15 rows.

    raw data rows            412,560  = expected      does not fire
    cells loaded              22,920  = expected      does not fire
    per-arm readings         137,520  = expected      does not fire
    surviving cells / width    4,582 vs 4,584         FIRES, alone

So the assertion is the unique guard for that case and is now a demonstrated guard rather than an
untested one. Two details from the construction: the dropped count is **two** cells, not one,
because `len(rs) == 6` is an equality — the cell with *seven* passes is discarded too, so the check
catches over-coverage as well as under-coverage. And the corruption alters the estimate rather than
merely shrinking the denominator, since one key's pass-1 weight is doubled while another's is
dropped.

Fixed at the source as well, which is cheaper than relying on the downstream check: `load()` now
asserts the input file count and explains in place that the reading-count argument depends on it.
The seven-file construction now fails at the file count instead. Both assertions are kept — the
file count closes the class, the surviving-cell count is the backstop if a future caller widens the
glob.

**The general lesson, which is the reason this is recorded at length.** "Guard B is unreachable
because guard A catches everything" is a proof obligation, not an observation, and here the proof
existed and rested on an unasserted premise. Two controls firing upstream is evidence about those
two controls. What settles reachability is the pigeonhole argument — and writing it down is what
exposed the hole, because the argument names its own premise.

### The `batch` baseline, resolved over all 66 pairs: the separation is a pass-index effect, and the population was selected on it

Two successive claims about the `batch` column were both wrong, in opposite directions, and the full
enumeration settles it. The earlier section sampled **two** within-run pairs (7.06% and 6.54%) and
concluded the cross-run 7.34% "sits inside the within-run baseline". A peer then enumerated all 15
within-run pairs per chain, found the cross-run value above the within-run maximum 6 times out of 6,
and reported the two populations as separated. Both were computed here:

    population                               n    min      max     median
    chain205 within-run, all pairs          15   6.61%    7.06%    6.82%
    chain196 within-run, all pairs          15   6.54%    7.01%    6.78%
    pooled within-run baseline              30   6.54%    7.06%    6.78%
    cross-run, MATCHED index p_i vs p_i      6   7.17%    7.48%    7.37%
    cross-run, ALL 36 pairs                 36   6.51%    7.48%    6.80%
    a file against itself (symlink/copy)     1              100.0%

**Over all 36 cross-run pairs the two populations overlap almost exactly** — median 6.80% against
the within-run 6.78%, ranges 6.51-7.48% against 6.54-7.06% — and only **6 of 36** exceed the
within-run maximum. Those six are precisely the matched-index pairs.

So the separation is not a property of the two runs. It is a property of **comparing passes at the
same index**, and the peer's population was selected on exactly that feature. `p1` against `p1`
agrees more than `p1` against `p4` because the pass index is a real covariate — same position in the
run, same slice ordering, same state the repeat counts are re-derived from. Selecting the six
matched pairs and comparing them to an unmatched baseline measures the index alignment, not the
provenance.

**Corrections, in both directions.** The earlier "sits inside the baseline" was right for the
unrestricted comparison and was reached from a two-point baseline that happened to bracket the
value — a correct conclusion from an inadequate sample, which is not the same as a correct
argument. The peer's separation is arithmetically right and does not mean what it appears to; it
also does not revive their retracted claim, since the excess is in the direction of **more**
agreement, and more agreement cannot evidence independence.

**What survives is the one-sided framing, now with both ends measured.** A file against itself —
which is what a symlink or a copy delivers — gives **100.0%**. On a scale from 6.5-7.5% for any pair
of genuinely separate passes to 100% for a substitution, the observed 7.34% is unambiguously at the
separate end. The gap to 100% carries the conclusion; nothing in the third significant figure does.

**The transferable point is the selection, not the statistic.** A population chosen on the feature
that causes the effect will separate from a population that was not, and the separation will look
like the thing being tested for. The check that catches it is to enumerate the comparison class
completely — 36 cross-run pairs, not the 6 that share an index — and here that turned a reported
clean separation into a 6-of-36 overlap.

### The guard set closes by proof, and the file-count premise is exactly the right strength

Carrying the pigeonhole argument through its remaining degree of freedom closes the class. Given
(a) exactly 6 input files, (b) cells == 22920, and (c) per-arm entries == 137520 for each of the
three arms, every cell necessarily carries all six passes for every arm:

- 6 files contribute at most 6 distinct pass indices, so each `(cell, arm)` holds at most 6 entries,
  giving at most 22920 x 6 = 137520 per arm. **Equality forces exactly six for every cell.**
- The cell count cannot be low: 22919 x 6 = 137514 falls short of 137520, so (c) forces
  cells >= 22920, and (b) pins it.
- The cell count cannot be high: with cells == 22925 and per-arm == 137520, 22920 cells at full
  depth would consume every entry and leave none for the five phantom cells, so a phantom key must
  cost completeness — and (b) fires on 22925 first.

Verified on the filed data: 6 files, pass indices exactly `[1,2,3,4,5,6]`, 22920 cells, 137520
entries for each arm, pass-depth distribution `{6: 22920}`, and zero cells short of six passes for
any arm.

**The surviving-cell check is therefore redundant-by-proof against the current guard set**, which is
the backstop role it was assigned — it earns its place only for a future caller that widens the
glob, since the proof's first premise is the file count. The earlier "uniquely necessary" reading
was correct only against the guard set as it stood *before* the file count was asserted.

One case neither of us named, and it shows the premise is exactly the right strength rather than
merely sufficient: **six files need not mean six distinct pass indices.** `..._p1.csv` and
`..._p01.csv` both parse to 1, giving five distinct indices from six files. The file-count assertion
passes. What catches it is the per-arm count, since the maximum drops to 22920 x 5 = 114600 and the
equality fails. So the file count bounds the index set from above, which is all the pigeonhole needs,
and the per-arm equality detects any shortfall inside that bound. Neither assertion covers the case
alone.

### The mirrored failure, recorded because both halves are instructive

The two errors that produced this exchange are duals, and each reached a defensible conclusion by a
route that did not support it.

- **Mine:** a two-point baseline for the `batch` agreement rate, reaching a verdict that survived
  full enumeration for the unrestricted comparison. Right answer, inadequate sample.
- **The peer's:** a harness that incremented once per **CSV row** while the guard counts once per
  **dictionary insertion**, then predicted the guard's behaviour from the wrong quantity. On the
  relabel construction those differ — 137520 raw rows against 137515 distinct `(cell, pass, arm)`
  entries — so the prediction failed while the underlying instinct (that a reachable case exists)
  was correct.

The second is a harness measuring something other than what production computes, which this
milestone has on record from three other directions. The operational form: **before predicting what
a guard will do, check that your instrument counts the same quantity the guard counts.**

### The file count is not redundant: the two assertions are orthogonal, shown both ways

A peer proposed replacing the file-count assertion with `len(set(indices)) == 6`, on the reasoning
that six files cannot yield more than six distinct indices and fewer cannot yield six, so the file
count adds nothing. The first half is right and the conclusion is wrong, because **more than six
files can yield exactly six distinct indices.** Constructed and measured:

    case                          files  distinct idx   file==6  distinct==6  cells   per-arm   depth
    unmodified                        6  [1,2,3,4,5,6]    pass      pass      22,920  137,520   {6:22920}
    _p6 -> _p01  (collision)          6  [1,1,2,3,4,5]    pass      FIRES     22,920  114,600   -
    extra _p06   (7th, collides)      7  [1,..,6,6]       FIRES     pass      22,920  137,520   {6:22920}
    _p6 -> _p7   (benign relabel)     6  [1,2,3,4,5,7]    pass      pass      22,920  137,520   {6:22920}

Row 3 is the decisive one. A seventh file whose name parses to an existing index overwrites that
pass for every cell and arm, so one file's data is **silently replaced by a duplicate of another** —
and cells, per-arm readings and pass depth all land exactly at expectation. With only the
distinct-index assertion it passes every check. That is the substitution failure mode this milestone
has already had once, reached by a filename.

So each assertion catches exactly what the other misses, and together they force a bijection between
files and pass indices, which is the real requirement. Both are kept.

**The peer's actual point was right and is adopted separately: the diagnosis was misattributed.** On
the collision the per-arm count fires at 114,600 against 137,520, which reads as *missing data* —
one pass short. The fault is a filename collision with all six passes present and readable, and
re-running the "missing" pass does not fix it, because the new file lands under the same colliding
name. The distinct-index assertion now names that fault at the point of loading, before any count is
derived from it. A guard that fails closed and a guard that fails closed *and* points at the cause
are different objects.

Row 4 is why the weaker assertion is the right one: `_p6 -> _p7` is a correct dataset with one
filename changed, and asserting the index set equals `{1..6}` would reject it. For a single-build
script the pass label is only a grouping key. **That is not true of the cross-build analyzer**, where
`floor_of` intersects pass indices between two builds: relabelling one build's `_p6` to `_p7` leaves
all three builds at six distinct indices, so a cardinality check passes, while the intersection drops
to five and every cross-build row reads `nan` with `n=0` — the within-build rows still printing
normal values, and exit status 0. There the requirement is that all builds share the same index set,
which cardinality cannot express.

## chain207: the full DLMC board, and why it was the missing half (2026-09-29)

### The gap

Every full-collection board to date is **SuiteSparse only** — chain196, chain205 and chain206 all
measure 4584 matrices x 5 widths and nothing else. DLMC is cached on both hosts at **3820
matrices** and has never been boarded at that scale. What the results doc records about DLMC comes
from a sample of roughly **24 matrices** (15 rn50 + 9 transformer), and that sample is where Scorch
is documented to *lose*:

- "we lost 30 of 36 cells on the dlmc transformer family"
- "every one of the worst cells is a dlmc transformer or pruned-ResNet layer, 512-2048 rows"
- "the dlmc transformer family -- 512 rows, 105-138k nonzeros, mean degree 205-269, **all at k=4**"
- "84 of the shipped gate's 121 cells are the dlmc rn50 pruned-ResNet family, rows 64-128"

**A loss family characterised on 24 of 3820 matrices is the sampling problem running in the
opposite direction.** The overfitting instruction warns against generalising a *win* from a few
cells; a deficit generalised from 24 cells is the same error with the sign flipped, and it is
currently load-bearing — it is the stated reason k=4 matters.

The k=4 detail is the reason this board comes before any kernel change. 14 of the 24 replicated
SuiteSparse core cells are at k=4, and the DLMC transformer losses are reported as "all at k=4".
Two unrelated matrix populations failing at one width is either a real property of the kernel at
half the AVX2 vector, or an artefact of a 24-matrix sample. Those have different fixes, and only a
full board separates them.

### Design: one binary, two collections, one estimator

chain207 boards all 3820 DLMC matrices with **build `aa` from `/scratch/bobbyy/det1`** — the
chain206 object whose `.text` was verified byte-identical to `bb`, `.so` digest `7f8f78d5...`.
That choice is what makes the comparison sound: **aa's own SuiteSparse board is already inside
chain206's sealed CSVs**, so the same binary's behind-MKL count can be computed on both collections
under one estimator with no build difference to argue about. Same widths (2,4,8,16,32), dtype
(float32), `--reps 4 --target-ms 6`, 6 passes and 24-thread pool as chain206.

Rows per pass = 3820 keys x 5 widths x 3 arms + header = **57301**, asserted per pass with resume.

Pre-flight, all asserted before any timing: 3820 keys; resolution **exact 3820, 0 unresolved** via
the sealed `csrresolve` (the defect that silently dropped 50 of 298 keys for months); torch pool 24
equal to `OMP_NUM_THREADS`; built `.so` present and digested.

### The baseline this will be measured against, computed from sealed bytes

Build `aa` on SuiteSparse, same estimator — per-cell `exp(median(log ratio))` over 6 passes,
`S = mkl/ours`, floor = per-width p95 of `dev(oursb/ours)`, behind iff `dev(S) > floor` and `S < 1`:

                      k=2      k=4      k=8     k=16     k=32     TOTAL
    A/A floor      0.0483   0.0410   0.0436   0.0575   0.0851
    behind MKL         30       34       10        4        1        79
    in the floor       36       34       23        6        9       108
    ahead of MKL     4518     4516     4551     4574     4574     22733
                                                    sum = 22920, checked

So **79 cells behind MKL, 0.345% of the collection**, and **34 of the 79 (43%) are at k=4** — the
width concentration reproduces on this binary independently of the core analysis.

**This is also a third count on one collection, and it widens the known spread.** chain196 c0 gave
68, chain205 gave 63, and build aa gives **79**. Three measurements of the same 22920 cells
disagreeing across 63-79 is a 25% spread in the headline number, which is the replication
instability already on record and the reason the analysis moved onto the core of 24 rather than any
single chain's count. Every DLMC figure from chain207 must be read against that spread, not against
a point value.

### Correction and redesign: chain207 restarted as a replicated pair, because one object is not enough

**My attribution in the launch note was wrong.** I reported the headline spread as 63 / 68 / 79
across chain196 c0, chain205 c0 and build aa, and called it a 25.4% disagreement between
measurements. A second session boarded chain206's other two objects on the same collection with the
same estimator, and the numbers are worse in a way that changes the diagnosis. Recomputed here from
the sealed bytes, with the three-axis input guard passing on each set and the `build` column
self-identifying on all 412,560 rows:

    object   behind by width k=2..32      total   band   ahead
    aa       30   34   10    4    1          79    108   22733
    bb       21   31    8    1    1          62    113   22745
    aax      25   33   10    3    3          74    107   22739
                                     each class from its own predicate, each sum = 22920

**aa and bb have byte-identical `.text`.** chain206's `det_diff` established it and the driver now
re-asserts it with full SHA-256. So 79 against 62 is a **27.4% spread with zero bytes of code
differing** — wider than the 25.4% I attributed to build differences. The spread is a property of
the process boundary, not of three builds, and the null is available on the exact object chain207
uses. Reported correctly it is **62-79 on aa/bb**, not a c0-versus-aa comparison, which would
smuggle in a build difference the effect does not need.

**And the behind-set barely replicates.** Union over the three objects is 139 cells; **22 (15.8%)
appear in all three, 32 in exactly two, and 85 (61%) in exactly one.** Pairwise Jaccard is 0.356
(aa/bb), 0.275 (aa/aax), 0.259 (bb/aax). Three-fifths of a single object's behind-set would not
appear in a rerun of the same machine code.

That is decisive against the design I launched. A one-object DLMC board would have produced a
number, and 61% of its content would have been churn.

**chain207 restarted with two objects, `aa` and `bb`, as a pure replication pair.** Identical
machine code in `.text`, distinct object files at same-length build paths, so two independent
process boundaries and no code difference to confound. A DLMC cell behind MKL on **both** is behind
for a reason that survives the process boundary; behind on **one** is churn. That is the distinction
a single board cannot draw, and it is what makes a deficit a finding rather than a number.

The rotation is balanced — two objects over six passes, each in each position exactly three times —
because the sliced-three-build result showed an unbalanced order makes the later object read
systematically differently. 12 object-passes at 57,301 rows each. The partial output of the
single-object run was discarded rather than reused.

The driver now asserts the premise before timing anything: `objcopy --only-section=.text` on both
objects, refusing if `.text` differs (not a replication pair) **or** if the whole-file digests match
(the same file twice, so no second process boundary). Both printed, both hold.

Two smaller corrections from the same check:

- **The core-by-width profile reproduces on a different arm set.** Cells behind in all three
  objects: `{k=2: 8, k=4: 12, k=8: 2, k=16: 0, k=32: 0}`; union `{51, 57, 20, 7, 4}`. This is the
  earlier 8/14/2/0/0 profile obtained from aa/bb/aax rather than the c0/c0b measurements, so
  **nothing at k >= 16 survives replication** on either arm set. Practical consequence: a k >= 16
  DLMC deficit from chain207 is unreplicated by construction and is not reportable from one object.
- **"43% at k=4" is a point inside a band.** The share is 43.0% (aa), 50.0% (bb), 44.6% (aax). What
  is robust is that k=4 carries the largest replicating core — 12 of the 22 — and moves least in
  absolute terms (34 / 31 / 33, range 3) while k=2 is the noisiest (30 / 21 / 25, range 9, which is
  9 of the 17-cell total spread on its own). The percentage should travel with all three values.

One provenance note resolved in passing: chain206's stage log records `aa whole 7f8f78d5...` and
`.text a79b5d20...` as bare 64-bit labels that do not name their function, which was flagged as
adequate for a run label but not as an integrity claim. Recomputing full SHA-256 over both objects
reproduces exactly those prefixes, so **they are SHA-256 prefixes** — the label was sound and is now
independently confirmed rather than assumed.

### What the aa/bb disagreement actually is: every pass tilts the whole collection, and pooling does not fully cancel it

The natural hypothesis for the aa/bb spread was that the two objects occupy separated time windows
inside each pass, so ambient drift between the windows inflates the difference. chain206's stage log
contains a natural experiment for it — the aa and bb windows are about 30 minutes apart in p1/p3/p5/p6
and about 61 minutes apart in p2/p4 — and **the hypothesis is refuted**: the far pair is *less*
dispersed than the near four (p95 dev of the per-cell ratio 0.4580 against 0.4854, ratio 0.9436;
on mean `|ln|` it is 1.0050, half a percent the wrong way). Weak design, 2 passes against 4, and only
a 30-versus-61-minute contrast, so this bounds the effect rather than excluding a larger one at
longer separations. Consequence: finer slice-level interleaving would buy nothing on this axis.

**The test found something more consequential instead.** Fraction of the 22,920 cells where
`aa.ours > bb.ours`, per pass — under paired noise with no systematic difference this should sit at
0.5 in every pass, and the binomial SE at n=22,920 is 0.0033:

    pass      p1       p2       p3       p4       p5       p6
    fraction  0.4908   0.3795   0.5789   0.4283   0.5160   0.4593
    SE from   -2.8    -36.5    +23.9    -21.7     +4.8    -12.3

**These are collection-wide level shifts between two objects with byte-identical `.text`.** p2 tilts
12 percentage points one way, p3 8 points the other. A whole-window ambient effect that does not
average out inside a pass, on 22,920 paired cells.

**Pooling over six passes reduces it but does not cancel it, and here the verifying session's figure
and mine disagree in a way that matters.** They reported the pooled sign fraction as 0.469-0.479.
Computed here on the six-pass reduced statistic — per-cell `exp(median(log(aa/bb)))` over all six
passes:

    width            k=2      k=4      k=8     k=16     k=32
    median ratio  0.9974   0.9981   0.9982   0.9971   0.9978
    sign fraction 0.4313   0.4496   0.4533   0.4398   0.4531

So the residual is **4.7 to 6.9 points below one half, not 2.1 to 3.1**, and the median ratio says
`aa` reads **0.18% to 0.29% faster than `bb` at every width** — consistently, with identical machine
code. Balanced rotation takes the per-pass tilt from +-12 points down to a ~5-point residual with a
sub-0.3% median offset. **It does not remove it.** That residual is the same size and sign as the
layout artefact already on record, where two objects with identical decisions differ 1-2.6% on
narrow-k SpMM.

Two consequences for chain207, both now load-bearing:

- **The "behind on both objects" test must be computed on the pooled six-pass reduced statistic and
  never on a per-pass board.** One pass can tilt the entire collection by 12 points of sign
  fraction, which is far larger than any gated effect.
- **The intersection test must be symmetric between `aa` and `bb`.** Since `aa` reads ~0.2% faster
  pooled, any procedure that privileges one object — using it for the floor, or breaking ties toward
  it — imports that offset. Behind-on-both is symmetric by construction; a one-object floor would
  not be.

### A loose citation, corrected

The restart commit justified the balanced rotation by citing "the sliced-three-build requirement".
That citation is wrong in its particulars. The sliced-three-build result is about rotating builds
*inside* 25-matrix slices, and chain206 and chain207 rotate at **pass** level, with one object
sweeping the whole corpus per window. The balance argument still applies at pass level — each object
in each position an equal number of times, so a monotone ambient trend cancels to first order, and
the arithmetic checks (2 objects x 6 passes = 12 object-passes, 2 positions x 3 slots each; chain206's
3 x 6 = 18, 3 positions x 2 each). But the requirement I named was written against a finer
granularity than the one being used, and per the refuted drift hypothesis above the coarse
granularity is measured to be harmless here rather than assumed to be.

### What the floor is made of

Worth printing beside the floor, because it says what the reduction buys:

    width                              k=2      k=4      k=8     k=16     k=32
    unreduced p95 dev, single pass  0.4493   0.3979   0.4055   0.4807   0.6027
    six-pass reduced arm floor      0.0483   0.0410   0.0436   0.0575   0.0851
    shrink                             9.3x     9.7x     9.3x     8.4x     7.1x

k=32 is widest on both scales and k=4 narrowest, and the median-of-six reduction buys roughly an
order of magnitude. The gated numbers live on the bottom row; the top row is what a single pass
would have offered.

### An open axis on the replication-pair premise, deliberately not closed yet

The driver refuses if `.text` differs (not a pair) or if the whole-file digests match (same file, no
second process boundary). Those are irredundant, but irredundant is not complete: `.text` identical
plus whole-file differing means the difference lives in some **other section, and the assertion does
not name which**. If it is `.comment`, `.note.gnu.build-id` or debug/relocation content, then "zero
bytes of code differing" is exact and the pair is clean. If any of it were in `.rodata` or `.data`, a
tuning constant could differ while `.text` stayed byte-identical, and "identical machine code" would
be true of the instruction stream but not of behaviour.

**Not measured yet, and deliberately so: chain207 is timing on redwood right now, and running
`objdump` over multi-megabyte shared objects on the measuring host is the perturbation-next-to-a-live-run
mistake.** The reasoning that it is debug and comment content — both objects built from byte-identical
source at same-length paths, so every constant originates in identical source — is strong but is
reasoning, not measurement. This is recorded as a **gate**: the section enumeration runs when the
board finishes, and the replication-pair claim is provisional until it does.

### The floor question is worth 3 cells, the data difference 20, and behind-on-both is robust to the choice

The verifying session found its own estimand error — its 0.469-0.479 pooled sign fraction was over
27,504 **raw** ratios, six per cell, not over the 4,584 per-cell reduced values. Reducing first
strips the within-cell symmetric noise that was pulling the raw fraction toward one half, so the
reduced statistic is *further* from 0.5, not closer. Both sides now agree on
0.4313 / 0.4496 / 0.4533 / 0.4398 / 0.4531, at -9.3 / -6.8 / -6.3 / -8.2 / -6.4 SE. The median agreed
under both estimands, which is why checking only the median missed it.

**Orientation control passes**, so the residual is not the median-of-even artefact: `aa/bb > 1` plus
`bb/aa > 1` sums to 1.0000 at k=4/8/16/32 and 0.9996 at k=2, where exactly 2 cells have a log-median
of precisely zero. Log-space median-of-six negates exactly — the orientation trap lives in
median-of-ratios, not median-of-logs.

**The 2x2, whose data against whose floor**, which separates the two things the published gap
conflated:

    data  floor    k=2  k=4  k=8 k=16 k=32   TOTAL
    aa    aa        30   34   10    4    1      79
    aa    bb        31   36   10    4    1      82
    bb    aa        20   29    8    1    1      59
    bb    bb        21   31    8    1    1      62

The pure floor effect is **exactly +-3 cells** on each object. Holding the floor fixed, the data gap
is **20 either way**. A common midpoint floor gives aa 80, bb 59, gap 21. So the 17-cell gap first
published is a **20-cell data gap partially masked by a 3-cell floor offset pointing the other
way** — using each object's own floor *understates* the spread between them.

**And the behind-on-both test barely moves with the choice**, which is the design result:

    floor convention        intersection   union   Jaccard   by width k=2..32
    each object's own            37         104     0.356     12, 20, 4, 1, 0
    common midpoint              36         103     0.350     12, 19, 4, 1, 0

One cell. The free parameter that consumed a long argument moves the headline statistic by a single
cell on the intersection, against 3 cells on a single-object board. **That is the SuiteSparse prior
chain207's DLMC intersection must be read against** — 37 of 104, concentrated at k=2 and k=4, with
k=32 at zero and k=16 at one, consistent with the three-object core {8, 12, 2, 0, 0}.

**A reduction-free confirmation of the residual**, no estimator and no floor involved. Cells where
one object is faster in **all six** passes: aa 98/93/85/94/78 = **448**, bb 55/56/54/54/43 = **262**.
Equal in expectation under the null; the difference of 186 at SE 26.6 is **7.0 SE**, same direction
as the median. And only **710 of 22,920 cells (3.1%) are unanimous across six passes, so 97% flip
sign at least once** — an independent argument for "behind on one object is churn" that routes
through no reduction at all.

### The mechanism, with one correction: it holds where the effect is large, not at every width

The proposed resolution of why `aa` has *more* behind cells while being *faster* is that the behind
count is a tail statistic, so it tracks dispersion rather than level, making aa's higher floor and
its higher behind count one fact rather than two. Checked per width against a common floor:

    width                    k=2      k=4      k=8     k=16     k=32
    arm floor aa          0.0483   0.0410   0.0436   0.0575   0.0851
    arm floor bb          0.0454   0.0367   0.0416   0.0578   0.0863
    floor aa - bb        +0.0029  +0.0043  +0.0020  -0.0003  -0.0011
    behind aa - bb            +10       +6       +2       +3       +0

**The signs agree at 3 of 5 widths, not 5 of 5.** They agree at k=2, k=4 and k=8 — which carry 75 of
aa's 79 cells — and disagree at k=16 and k=32. But the two disagreeing widths have floor gaps of
-0.0003 and -0.0011 against +0.0029 / +0.0043 / +0.0020 for the agreeing ones, so those are ties
rather than counterexamples and the sign carries no information there. Stated properly: the
dispersion account is supported wherever the floor gap is larger than a rounding, and is untested
where it is not.

The substantive conclusion survives and is worth keeping. **The 27.4% spread between two objects
with identical machine code is a difference in noise, not in speed**, and the ~0.2% median offset is
a separate and much smaller effect riding on top of it. Both systematic effects — aa faster on the
median, aa's floor higher — point toward aa having *fewer* behind cells, and on a fixed floor it has
20 more.

## chain204's contamination: no regime change in the duration series (2026-09-29)

The deferred `/scr` read is done. mkt1 was fully idle (0 of 128 CPUs allocated) and nothing was
timing on it, so this cost no perturbation — which is why it was worth waiting for.

**What the logs settle first, before any timing question.** The requeued job 17649043 prints pass
headers `p1` through `p23` all stamped `18:40:05`, its own start time. Those are the resume logic
*skipping* already-complete passes, not running them. The original run 17439864 completed **p1
through p24** and was cancelled during p25 (started 09:14:39 for p24, 09:31:14 for p25). So the
requeue added p25-p30 on top of 24 complete passes, exactly as intended.

**Per-pass wall duration, all three arms, original run:**

    p1  19.60   p2  16.60   p3  18.07   p4  14.65   p5  19.58   p6  17.02
    p7  26.28   p8  21.20   p9  14.07   p10 17.57   p11 20.65   p12 17.68
    p13 19.32   p14 17.52   p15 16.47   p16 15.12   p17 19.55   p18 18.35
    p19 17.05   p20 21.82   p21 20.82   p22 14.15   p23 22.57   p24 16.58   (minutes)

The reported contamination event is 04:43:04, which falls inside **p9** (04:41:58-04:56:02), so p9
is the one straddling pass.

    segment              n    mean     sd     range
    pre-event  p1-p8     8   19.12   3.54   14.65-26.28
    straddling p9        1   14.07
    post-event p10-p24  15   18.35   2.42   14.15-22.57

    post - pre = -0.78m  (-4.1%)   Welch t = -0.56
    best changepoint over ALL cuts: after p4, t = 1.15

**Post-event passes are 4.1% faster, not slower, and no cut in the series produces a t above 1.2.**
A 48-CPU co-tenant arriving on a 128-CPU node, with this job pinned to 64 CPUs, would be expected to
lengthen subsequent passes. Nothing of the kind is present. p9 itself — the straddling pass — is
14.07m, the second-shortest of all 24.

**Consequences, and they revise two earlier positions including my own.**

- The verifying session's inference that "the clean subset is the first eight passes", so the six
  added passes do not repair the run, is **not supported**. It was a reasonable inference from a
  known co-tenancy event, but the wall-clock observable does not show the event mattering.
- My own straddled-pass framing was right in kind and far too pessimistic in degree. I bounded the
  damage at "at most 9 of 24 straddled" from 9 regime changes. The duration series locates exactly
  **one** straddling pass, p9, and shows no level shift on either side of it.
- So **all 24 original passes plus the 6 added are usable**, with p9 the only candidate for
  exclusion — and dropping it leaves 29 of 30.

**The caveat, stated because absence of evidence is being used as evidence here.** This bounds the
contamination rather than excluding it. With a pre-segment sd of 3.54m over n=8 and a post-segment
sd of 2.42m over n=15, the difference detectable at 2 standard errors is about 2.8m, i.e. roughly
**15% of pass duration**. A co-tenancy effect smaller than that is invisible to this instrument. What
makes the bound useful anyway is that pass duration is an aggregate over all three arms, so a
co-tenant stealing memory bandwidth would slow every arm at once — which is both why arm-versus-arm
comparison survives a shifted ambient level, and why duration is the right observable for asking
whether the ambient level shifted at all. It says it did not, to within 15%.

### chain204 filed, and the matched instrument finds a regime change the duration test could not

**Filed.** chain204 had no ledger entry and its duration series existed only on mkt1's `/scr` and in
a commit message — a number across a boundary with no bytes to recompute from, which is the exact
shape this milestone has been correcting all day. Now at `chain204-k32gate-mkt`: 90 CSVs, 4 logs,
84 MB, 102 files under `SHA256SUMS`. Digests were computed **on mkt1** before transfer, staged
through `/matx` because `/scr` is node-local, and checked twice on arrival — the tarball digest
matched and then **95 of 95 files verified, 0 failed, 95 lines emitted**, with the emitted count
asserted because `shasum -c` reports "not found" as silence.

**Two corrections to how the duration result was stated**, both in the strengthening direction:

- The right form is a **containment bound**, not a detectability floor. With df = 10.6 the critical
  value is 2.211, so the 95% CI on the post-event shift is **[-3.86, +2.32] minutes** — the data
  **exclude a slowdown larger than +2.32 min = +12.2%** of the pre-event mean (90%: +9.2%). The
  earlier "an effect below 15% would be invisible" says what the instrument cannot see; this says
  what the data rule out, which is the statement matched to the question.
- The changepoint number must be reported **as a maximum with its cut count**: max |t| = 1.15 over
  **22 cuts**. The null distribution of a maximum over that many correlated statistics runs near 2,
  so 1.15 actively supports no level shift rather than merely failing to contradict one. Written
  bare it reads as a single-cut t and undervalues the result.

**And the limitation that mattered.** Duration is an average, so it is blind to the tail — and
tonight established that the board count moves on the *tail* of per-cell dispersion, not the level:
two objects with byte-identical `.text` give a 27.4% spread in behind counts while their dispersion
base rate is 0.5019. A co-tenant could hold mean duration inside the ±12% bound while inflating
dispersion, and the board would follow the dispersion. So the question was re-asked with the matched
observable — per-pass A/A dispersion and sign fraction of `oursb/ours`, tested across p9 exactly as
duration was:

    object   p95 dev pre -> post      t       sign fraction pre -> post      t
    ov64     0.1098 -> 0.1432      +0.74      0.5028 -> 0.4892           -1.41
    ov64b    0.0670 -> 0.0683      +0.06      0.4981 -> 0.4958           -0.23
    ovp      0.0865 -> 0.0835      -0.20

**Nothing at p9 on the matched instrument either, on all three objects.** The no-contamination
conclusion now rests on the observable that can see the failure mode, not only on the one that
cannot.

**But the matched instrument found a large regime change elsewhere, and the duration test at p9
could not have found it:**

    object   best cut      max|t|   cuts
    ov64     after p24      4.08     25
    ov64b    after p24      4.14     25

Same cut, both well above the null maximum. Per-pass dispersion for p25-p30 is **0.0145-0.0283 on
all three objects** against 0.03-0.60 for p1-p24 — **3 to 5 times tighter and far more stable**.
That boundary is not the contamination event. It is the boundary between job 17439864 (2026-09-15,
contended node) and job 17649043 (2026-09-28, node fully idle).

**So chain204's 30 passes are two regimes and must not be pooled, and the split is at p24/p25 rather
than at p9 — neither of the places either session was looking.** Two homogeneous segments exist:
p1-p24 (24 passes, noisier, contended) and **p25-p30 (6 passes, 3-5x tighter, idle node)**. The
second is better data by every available measure, and six passes is exactly the count chain196,
chain205 and chain206 use, so it is directly comparable to the sealed SuiteSparse boards. Any
chain204 number must declare its segment.

**An open question left open.** p9 is the second-shortest of the 24 original passes (14.07m against
a 19.12m mean). An *arriving* 48-CPU co-tenant should make the straddling pass longer, so p9's
shortness is evidence against an arrival at 04:43:04 — which supports the no-contamination reading —
but it does not explain what made p9 short, and a *departure* would still be a regime change in the
favourable direction that breaks comparability for that pass. p9 is excluded from the p1-p24 segment
regardless, leaving 23.

### Six corrections to the chain204 filing, five of them mine

**1. The p9 test's post window spanned both regimes — my own straddling rule, broken one level up.**
The window was `p10..p30`, which includes the six tight passes of the other regime, and they drag the
post mean down and cancel the effect being tested for. Restricting the post window to `p10..p24`, so
the comparison stays inside the noisy regime:

    object   p9 dispersion pre -> post      t (post p10..p30)    t (post p10..p24)
    ov64     0.1098 -> 0.1925                    +0.74                +1.46
    ov64b    0.0670 -> 0.0872                    +0.06                +0.80
    ovp      0.0865 -> 0.1101                    -0.20                +1.67

**All three overrides are positive inside one regime**, where the spanning window gave one negative
and one near-zero. Not individually resolvable, but 3-of-3 sign agreement is 1-in-8 by chance alone.
So "nothing at p9 on the matched instrument" was too strong. The honest statement: **within the noisy
regime the p9 dispersion increase is positive on all three objects and not individually
resolvable** — weaker than a finding, and weaker than "found nothing". My own commit set the rule
that any chain204 number must declare its segment, and this number straddled the boundary my own
scan had just located.

**2. I under-reported my own strongest result by a factor of 2.5.** The regime scan gives max|t| =
4.08 (ov64), 4.14 (ov64b) and **10.53 (ovp)**. I quoted the two smaller ones because the output
filter I used to read the results cut off the third object's line — a selection artefact in my own
reporting, not in the analysis. Against a null maximum near 2 over 25 cuts, 10.53 is the decisive
number and I omitted it.

**3. "3-5x tighter" understated it.** The segment-mean ratios are **8.19x (ov64), 6.04x (ovp), 3.75x
(ov64b)**. Both stated ranges were also too narrow at the low end: p1-p24 dispersion spans
**0.0222-0.6012** (stated 0.03-0.60) and p25-p30 spans **0.0125-0.0283** (stated 0.0145-0.0283).

**4. A positive control that came free, and it is the matched null for tonight's main result.**
chain204's per-pass A/A sign fraction over all 90 object-passes runs **0.4419 to 0.5693, mean
0.4929** — against chain206's **0.3795 to 0.5789**. chain204's A/A is `oursb` against `ours`
**within one process**; chain206's `aa`/`bb` spanned **two**. So the absence of a per-pass tilt here
is direct evidence that the chain206 tilt is a **process-boundary** effect rather than an ambient
property of the host or the harness — measured on data collected for an entirely different purpose.
And at the p24/p25 boundary the sign fraction does *not* move (t = -1.47 / -0.28 / -0.32) while
dispersion moves by 4-10 SE: **only dispersion shifts, which is the signature of a contention change
and not of a systematic one.**

**5. The filed analyzer could not run where it was filed — the third instance.** `c204_matched.py`
hardcoded `D = "/scr/bobbyy/c204"`, so run inside the sealed directory it globbed nothing, printed
`builds: []` and `passes per build: {}`, and **exited 0**. A silent vacuous pass, after
`an_c206.py`'s `c206final` and `recount205.py`'s hardcoded ledger root. I had already fixed this
exact defect twice in this milestone and filed a third instance of it hours later. Rewritten to take
the tree root as `argv[1]`, refuse on an empty glob, and assert the shape (3 builds x 30 passes x 267
cells) before computing. It now runs in place and reproduces every figure above.

**6. Both manifests covered outputs only, so the inputs that define what the outputs mean were
sealed zero times.** My seal used an extension glob (`*.csv *.log *.sbatch *.sha256 *.py *.md`), which
left **49 of 151 files unattested** — including the corpus `c198_keys.txt`, the rotation order
`orders_idx3x30.txt` (i.e. the balance premise), all four harness scripts, the pinned `tree/` with
`spmm.h` and `scorch_policy.h`, and **both built `scorch_ops*.so` files**. A changed corpus, rotation,
harness or binary would have left both manifests verifying perfectly at 95/95 and 102/102.

That is pointed rather than pedantic because **chain207's entire design rests on binding a binary to
a board by `.so` digest**, and chain204's binary was the one thing not bound. Re-sealed with
`find -type f` instead of an extension glob: **149 files, 149 manifest lines, coverage gap 0**, 149
OK, 0 failed, 149 emitted. A stale `__pycache__/*.pyc` was deleted rather than attested, being a
build artefact and not evidence.

The binary is now bound: both `.so` copies digest to `83ff79d7...` and are **the same object at two
paths**. Corpus `d9184eb9...`, rotation `f72f3fe5...`, and the two harness bodies are distinguishable
at `fa3441af...` (5,580 bytes) and `2b19eb1b...` (5,879 bytes).

**One thing I could not determine.** Which harness body ran which segment. Both job logs open with
the identical header line, and neither records the body version or its digest. So the two bodies are
now pinned by digest but **not attributed to jobs**, and the segment claim rests on the pass
numbering in the logs rather than on knowing which script produced it. Recorded as a gap rather than
guessed: a harness that does not record its own digest cannot be bound to its output after the fact.

### A seal and a last edit can race, and the file that failed was the one rewritten to fix a defect

Verification of the re-sealed chain204 directory read **148 OK, 1 FAILED**, and the failing file was
`c204_matched.py` — the analyzer rewritten to close the vacuous-pass defect. Cause pinned by mtime:

    SHA256SUMS        22:48:59
    c204_matched.py   22:49:43

The manifest was computed **44 seconds before** the script was rewritten, so it sealed the old copy.
`find -newer SHA256SUMS` confirms that file was the only one newer. Re-sealed: **149 files, 149
manifest lines, 149 OK, 0 failed, and 0 files newer than the manifest.**

**The general form belongs next to the harness-digest rule, because it is the same failure at a
different timescale.** A verification result is evidence about the moment it was run, not about the
filed state — so "149 OK, 0 failed" was true when I printed it and false by the time anyone read it.
The check that closes it is cheap and now part of the procedure: **assert that no file in the
directory is newer than the manifest.** Digest equality alone cannot distinguish "sealed and
unchanged" from "sealed, then changed, then re-verified against a stale manifest" — only the
timestamp ordering can, and it costs one `find`.

This is the same family as a commit count written into the commit that makes it wrong: a measurement
whose own subsequent action invalidates it. Sealing is not idempotent with respect to editing, and
the ordering has to be stated rather than assumed.

**Two smaller precisions.**

- The claim that "the `__pycache__/*.pyc` was deleted rather than attested" was true of one of two
  entries and read as though it covered both. The top-level `__pycache__/csrresolve.cpython-312.pyc`
  was deleted. `tree/__pycache__/scorch_build.cpython-312.pyc` (2026-09-15 01:43:38, 7,605 bytes) is
  still present and **is** attested — which is the better call for that one, since it dates from the
  original build rather than from later analysis, and so is part of the pinned tree rather than an
  artefact of inspecting it.
- The emitted-line count differs between the two sessions' readings — 149 here against 150 there —
  because `shasum`'s `WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match` summary goes to stderr, which my
  `2>/dev/null` discarded. So an emitted count taken with stderr suppressed cannot see the warning
  line, and the honest form of the emitted-count assertion has to say whether stderr was kept.

**And the quantitative form of the positive control, which is stronger than the qualitative one.**
chain206's per-pass sign fraction spans **0.1994 across two process boundaries**; chain204's spans
**0.1274 across one** — a cross-process spread **1.57x** the within-process spread. The levels
separate the same way: chain204's within-process A/A sits essentially at one half (mean 0.4929,
median 0.4906, n=90) while chain206's cross-process reduced statistic sits at 0.4313-0.4533. One
caution on testing 0.4929 against 0.5: the 90 passes share the same 267 cells, so a per-pass
binomial standard error is optimistic and the honest test uses the empirical scatter of the 90
values. The control does not need a significance test — the contrast in both spread and level
carries it.

## chain204 CLOSED: the k=32 override fails its second-host gate, and the failure locates a real defect in the worker-count rule (2026-09-29)

chain203 found on redwood that at k=32 an override setting the worker count equal to the caller's
pool ran **14.4% to 21.2% faster** than the ambient policy on the 25 cells where it raises the
resolved count. chain204 is the MKT gate on that, and its body script pre-registered three
predictions and a falsification condition before any timing:

- **P1 the floor** — `ov64` against `ov64b`: same object, same argument, so whatever it reads is the
  instrument.
- **P2 the claim**, direction fixed in advance and one-sided — on cells where `resolved[ov64] >
  resolved[ovp]`, `ov64` is faster.
- **P3 the built-in null** — on cells where `resolved[ov64] == resolved[ovp]` the override changes
  nothing the kernel can see, so the arms must agree inside the floor.
- **Falsifier** — "ov64 null against ovp on the raise group with the floor tight, or a sign flip."

Run on the clean `p25-p30` segment (6 passes, idle node, the segment identified earlier as
homogeneous), at k=32, 89 cells:

    P1 FLOOR   ov64 / ov64b                    p95 dev 0.0312   median dev 0.0040     <- tight
    P2 CLAIM   raise group, ov64/ovp           n=38  median 1.0367                    <- SIGN FLIP
               faster beyond floor 5   slower beyond floor 21
    P3 NULL    equal group                     n=32  p95 dev 0.2850                   <- fails

**The falsification condition is met: a sign flip with the floor tight.** The override is 3.5%
*slower* on MKT where chain203 measured 14.4-21.2% faster on redwood, faster on only 8 of 38 cells,
and slower beyond the floor on 21 against 5.

### P3's failure is a grouping defect, not an instrument defect

Splitting the equal group by whether a worker count was actually resolved:

    equal subgroup            n   p95 dev (ov64/ovp)   same cells on the floor arm
    resolved > 0             26         0.0378                  0.0312
    resolved = -1             6         0.2850                  0.0103

**The built-in null passes on the 26 cells where the kernel resolved a count** — 0.0378 against a
0.0312 floor. All of the failure is the six `resolved = -1` cells, and on the floor arm those same
cells are *quieter* than average (0.0103), so they are not intrinsically noisy: they differ
specifically between `ov64` and `ovp`. So `resolved = -1` does not mean "the override changes
nothing the kernel can see"; it means no count was recorded, and the pre-registered partition
mis-specified those cells as argument-identical when they are not. Excluding them, P3 holds and P2's
verdict stands on the narrow floor.

### A mechanism I proposed and then refuted

The obvious explanation for a host-dependent sign flip is team-width cost: MKT's pool is 64 against
redwood's 24, OpenMP team cost is paid per worker, so "raise to pool" should cost proportionally
more on the wider pool and only repay itself when each worker gets enough nonzeros. That predicts
**fewer nonzeros per worker gives a larger slowdown**.

Measured, on the 19 raise-group cells where both arms resolve a real count: Pearson r between
`log(nnz per worker)` and `log(ov64/ovp)` is **+0.734**. Positive. **More nonzeros per worker gives a
larger slowdown** — the opposite of the prediction. The mechanism is refuted, and the cells with the
most starved workers (99-628 nnz each) are exactly where the override wins biggest.

### What the data actually say: the effect is bimodal in the ambient policy's own choice

    ambient chose    n   median ov64/ovp   faster   slower   median nnz
    1-8 workers      5       0.6591           5        0        14,209    ov64 FASTER by 52%
    9-30 workers     7       1.3517           1        6        99,147    ov64 slower by 35%
    31-63 workers    7       1.0654           1        6       206,670    ov64 slower by 7%

Pearson r between `log(ambient resolved count)` and `log(ov64/ovp)` is **+0.734**: the lower the
ambient policy set the worker count, the more the override wins.

    ambient badly under-provisions            ambient is already well tuned
    t3dl_e        4 workers   +95%            comsol       20 workers   -52%
    m3plates      1 worker    +82%            vsp_c-30     26 workers   -42%
    case39_b1_06  8 workers   +52%            aa03         15 workers   -40%
    Pd_rhs        1 worker    +48%            lp_osa_07    30 workers   -35%
    TSOPF_b300_c2 3 workers   +33%            case9_A_11   31 workers   -28%

**So the median -3.5% is the average of a bimodal distribution, and the blanket override must not
ship**: it would trade a 33-95% win on the under-provisioned cells for a 28-52% loss on the
well-tuned ones. That is a regression, and per the standing convention a regression is a finding to
report rather than a shape to tune around.

### The finding worth acting on, and why it is not an if-case

The override is the wrong instrument, but it exposes a real and structurally describable defect:
**the ambient worker-count rule resolves 1 to 8 workers out of a 64-wide pool on matrices with
roughly 6,000 to 40,000 nonzeros, where 64 workers run 33% to 95% faster.** That is not a tuning
coincidence on a few matrices — it is one end of the rule's domain, it is monotone in the rule's own
output (r = +0.734), and the rule is demonstrably *correct* on the adjacent band, which is what
makes the low end a defect rather than a preference.

**And it predicts why chain203 saw a blanket win on redwood.** redwood's pool is 24, so the
over-provisioning band that costs 28-52% on MKT barely exists there — there is little room above the
well-tuned range to push into. If chain203's redwood win is also concentrated on its low-ambient
cells, then both hosts are showing **one** mechanism: the rule under-provisions at the low end
everywhere, and the apparent host disagreement is an artefact of pool width truncating the loss
band. That is a testable prediction against chain203's sealed data and it is the next thing to check,
because a single mechanism explaining both hosts is the difference between a generalizable fix and
two host-specific rules.

## RETRACTION of parts of cf9a0a2: the resolved column was read wrong, and the floor was the wrong floor

An independent session recomputed chain204 from the sealed bytes without my analyzer and found four
defects. All four reproduce here. The ship verdict survives and is stronger; three of the supporting
claims do not.

### The root defect: `resolved = -1` is the mkl arm, not a property of a cell

`mrgate_ov.py:176` writes `resolved=(resolved if arm != "mkl" else -1)`. Checked directly:

    arm mkl    24030 rows   resolved == -1 on 24030  (100.0%)
    arm ours   24030 rows   resolved == -1 on     0  (  0.0%)
    arm oursb  24030 rows   resolved == -1 on     0  (  0.0%)
    cells whose non-mkl resolved is multi-valued across 30 passes: ov64 0, ov64b 0, ovp 0

My loader assigned `RES[build][cell]` on **every** row, so it kept whichever arm was written last —
and `mrgate_ov.py:166` shuffles arm order by `crc32(key|k|pass_tag|build)`. So the `resolved` value I
partitioned on was a deterministic coin flip on a CRC seed, carrying **zero** information about the
override. Non-mkl `resolved` is in fact single-valued across all 30 passes, so the correct read is
trivial and I did not do it.

**Consequences, in order of how badly they hurt:**

- **The population was wrong.** Correct: 89 k=32 cells split **raised 40, declined 49, lowered 0**. I
  reported raised 38, equal 32, lowered 19 — and **19 "lowered" cells are structurally impossible**,
  since the override asks for 64 and the pool is 64, so it can never resolve below ambient. A
  partition containing an impossible class should have stopped me; it did not.
- **P3's "rescue" was noise.** I split the equal group by `resolved = -1` versus `> 0` and reported
  that the null passes on the 26 resolved-positive cells. That split was the mkl-arm coin flip, so
  **the gate's third prediction currently passes on a random partition.** P3 is withdrawn as a
  passing prediction. The verifying session reports making the identical error an hour earlier and
  getting 29 of 89, which is the same 1-in-3 draw.

### The floor was the wrong floor, and the right one was free in my own data

The 49 cells where the override **resolved identically** are a declined-argument A/A across the exact
build pair under test — same code, same effective argument, same process structure as ov64-vs-ovp.
That is the matched null, and I used the relabelled-object floor instead:

    ov64b / ov64  (relabelled same object)    p95 dev 0.0312   median 0.0040   n=89
    DECLINED-argument A/A, ov64 vs ovp        p95 dev 0.3122   median 0.0070   n=49
                                              ratio 10.0x

**And the narrow floor fails its own A/A**: 10 of the 49 declined cells sit beyond it on the slow
side and 0 on the fast side. Re-gating P2 against the correct floor:

    floor                    population   median    beyond floor
    narrow ov64b/ov64        raised 40    1.1346    27 slower,  9 faster
    declined A/A (correct)   raised 40    1.1346    10 slower,  8 faster
    declined A/A (correct)   all 89       1.0162    13 slower,  8 faster

**The median sign flip survives; my "21 against 5" per-cell asymmetry does not.** Against its own
free A/A it is 10 against 8. I have the rule for this written down — a declined argument is a free
A/A — and did not apply it to the case that hands it over directly.

### A mechanical confound in the harness that the win figure rests on

`batch_ours` is shared across arms within a build+pass but **not across builds**: equal on only
**27 of 534** cell-passes (5.1%). The harness's own docstring records that a small batch reads
systematically slower and once put two identical-code arms up to 3x apart, which is why it was fixed
*within* a process. Across builds it is unfixed, and it predicts the effect:

    r[log batch ratio, log ms ratio] on the 40 raised cells   -0.6770
    batches agree within 1.1x    n=13   median ms ratio 1.0901
    batches diverge  >1.1x       n=27   median ms ratio 1.2820
    of the 11 ambient-1-8 cells, 9 sit in the diverging-batch group

**So the 33-95% win that the rule-defect finding rests on is confounded with batch size**, and the
figure cannot be quoted until a batch-matched re-measurement: pin the batch per (cell, k) in a
pre-pass and hand the same integer to every build, which the harness already does across arms.

### One regression used twice

I reported r = +0.734 for `log(nnz per worker)` and again for `log(ambient resolved count)` as if
they were two findings — refuting team-width cost with the first and installing the ambient-choice
mechanism with the second. The two predictors correlate with **each other at +0.9913**. On this
population they are the same variable, so the refutation is not independent evidence for the
replacement. Neither figure reproduces as +0.734 either: here they are +0.6410 and +0.6589.

The refutation of team-width cost stands on its own terms — a fixed per-worker cost should amortise
*better* on bigger matrices, and the sign is wrong for that. What does not follow is that the ambient
policy's choice is a **distinct** mechanism this data can resolve.

### What survives

- **The k=32 blanket override must not ship.** The median is slower on every population, window and
  estimator tried: all 89 cells 1.0162, raised cells 1.1346. The pre-registered falsifier — a sign
  flip with the floor tight — is met.
- **The bimodal shape is real**, though my counts were wrong. On the correct population: ambient 1-8
  gives median 0.6766 (9 faster of 11), ambient 9-30 gives 1.2880 (1 of 17), ambient 31-63 gives
  1.1346 (1 of 12).
- **Restricting to p25-p30 was right, for a stronger reason than dispersion.** In p1-p24 `ovp`'s MKL
  arm is displaced 70-210x with a median calibrated batch of 1 against 139 and 176 for the other two
  objects, so any ours-versus-MKL number from that segment is **invalid rather than merely wide**.

**The low-ambient win is now a hypothesis awaiting a batch-matched measurement, not a finding.** It
is the right thing to measure next and the design is already specified.

### The retraction's own follow-ups: a filed analyzer, and one claim that gets worse on inspection

`an_c204_resolved.py` is now in the chain204 ledger and reproduces every figure above from the
sealed bytes. It takes the tree root as `argv[1]`, and its guards assert the things that went wrong
rather than printing them: that `resolved < 0` holds on all 24,030 mkl rows and none of the 48,060
non-mkl rows, that non-mkl `resolved` is single-valued across all 30 passes, and that the `lowered`
class is empty. **A contaminated read announces itself through an impossible class**, so the
partition is now checked against the mechanism that makes it impossible. Ledger re-sealed at
151 of 151 with nothing newer than the manifest; the producing-host seal still verifies 95 of 95.

**The conventions, named, because every disagreement on this chain resolved to an unstated one.**
Ratio-then-reduce: per-pass ratio first, then `exp(median(log .))`. Reduce-then-ratio is a different
quantity — it reads 1.0189 / 1.1386 against 1.0162 / 1.1346 and moves the gated count by one cell
(9-against-8 rather than 10-against-8), with the verdict invariant. Ratio-then-reduce is preferable
on a mechanism rather than on taste: the three builds inside one pass run close together in wall
clock, so pass-to-pass machine drift is common-mode within a pass and pairing at the index removes
it. Both orders are inversion-equivariant to 2.2e-16 over the 89 cells, so neither carries the
even-count asymmetry that bit the board's A/A. **The same estimator must be used for the `batch`
column as for the timings** — ratio-of-medians there reads r = −0.9289 against −0.6770.

**The collinearity finding is worse than collinearity.** The worker count under the override is the
constant 64, so the predictor I called "nnz per worker" is `log nnz` shifted by a constant and
contains **no worker variation at all**. It is matrix size. The ambient policy picks its thread count
from matrix size, which is why it and `log(ambient resolved)` correlate at **+0.9978**. The
per-worker load that actually varies is `nnz / ambient`, and it correlates **−0.6800** — the
opposite sign. So the team-width refutation and the mechanism installed in its place rest on one
regression on matrix size, and the predictor named "per worker" was not per worker.

**The window restriction broke the rotation's own guarantee.** Over all 30 passes the build rotation
is exactly balanced, 10/10/10 per position for each build, read from the landed write order in
`c204_run.log` rather than from `orders_idx3x30.txt`. Inside p25-p30 it is ovp 3/2/1, ov64 2/3/1,
ov64b 1/1/4 against the 2/2/2 a balanced six-pass window needs. Two defences in tension, and
invisible if balance is certified from the schedule instead of from the passes that landed. Bounded
rather than asserted away: the measured position effect on the k=32 `ours` arm is −0.790% / −0.427%
/ +0.067% (n=534 each, every reading over its own cell's window median), and pushing the actual
imbalance through it gives **+0.0608% on ov64/ovp**, the comparison every conclusion rests on — 27x
below the all-89 median and 221x below the raised median. The larger +0.3092% lands on ov64b/ov64,
the narrow floor this analysis discards anyway. No conclusion moves, and the next window selection
checks balance on the landed passes. **This carries to chain207**, where any segment restriction has
the same exposure.

### Which floor is correct is OPEN: the 10x gap is neither population nor batch

I called the declined-argument A/A "the correct floor" two commits ago. That was over-claimed. The
evidence that the narrow floor is too tight stands; the identification of the declined A/A as its
replacement does not survive its own diagnostics.

**The population explanation is dead, which is the good news.** If the 49 declined cells were simply
the small noisy ones, their wider A/A would be a size artefact. They are not: the relabelled-object
floor is flat across all three populations.

    pair                     population     n    p95 dev   median |batch dev|   median nnz
    ov64b/ov64  relabel      all            89    0.0312   0.0128               99147
    ov64b/ov64  relabel      declined       49    0.0312   0.0119               135135
    ov64b/ov64  relabel      raised         40    0.0295   0.0133               98559
    ov64/ovp    test         all            89    0.5913   0.0554               99147
    ov64/ovp    test         declined       49    0.3122   0.0178               135135
    ov64/ovp    test         raised         40    0.8164   0.2584               98559

**Batch is a mediator on the raised cells, not a confound.** Batch divergence on the raised cells is
25.84% against the relabel pair's 1.33%, and the causal order is fixed by the harness: the override
changes the kernel's speed, calibration observes the new per-call time, and it therefore picks a
different batch. The override *causes* the batch change. That path runs from treatment to
measurement through an artefact the harness documents, so pinning the batch blocks an artefact path
rather than removing real effect — the fix is still right, and the reason is better than the one I
gave.

**But batch divergence does not explain the declined pair's width.** On the declined cells the two
pairs diverge in batch by 1.78% and 1.19% — nearly equal — while their floors are 0.3122 and 0.0312,
a factor of ten. So whatever makes the declined A/A wide is not the thing I said it was.

**It is concentrated on small matrices.** By nnz quartile, the test pair reads 0.5913 / 0.8164 /
0.4215 / 0.0361 while the relabel pair reads 0.0079 / 0.0287 / 0.0117 / 0.0380. **They agree on the
largest quartile and differ 75-fold on the smallest.** A floor that is 0.008 for one argument pair
and 0.59 for another on the same 22 matrices is not measuring the hardware.

**And "declined" is a reconstruction, not an observation.** The `resolved` column is
