`scorch_spmm_nthreads()` called by the harness with arguments rebuilt from outside the timed call,
and `mrgate_ov.py`'s own comment records that the zero-row term spmm.h adds to `work` is not
reconstructed, so the column is a **lower bound** wherever a matrix has empty rows. The declined set
is therefore declined according to a model of the policy, not according to the kernel. `ov64b/ov64`
is argument-identical by construction and needs no model. That is a real asymmetry in favour of the
narrow floor, and it points at small matrices — exactly where the reconstruction is least reliable
and where the gap lives.

**So both of these stand and they do not pick a winner:** the narrow floor fails its own A/A (10
declined cells beyond it slower, 0 faster), so it is too tight; and the declined floor is ten times
wider for reasons that are not population, not batch divergence, and not yet named. P2's verdict is
unaffected — the median sign flip survives under either floor — but **no per-cell gated count from
this chain should be quoted until the floor question is settled by measurement**, which is what the
batch-pinned re-run is now designed to do.

### The position effect I published does not exist, and neither does the opposite one

I reported a position effect of −0.790% / −0.427% / +0.067% one commit ago and used it to bound the
window's rotation imbalance. **That was a normalisation artefact and the number is withdrawn.** So
was the opposite-signed estimate reached independently by the verifying session. Both of us
normalised, and normalising cannot separate position from build in an imbalanced window: dividing by
a build's own window median centres position *within* each build and absorbs the effect; dividing by
the median of the three builds at one pass centres *across* builds and imports the build difference
wherever build and position are correlated — and ov64b sits at position 3 in 4 of the 6 passes, which
is exactly that correlation. One denominator hid it, the other manufactured it, and the opposite
signs were the signature.

The right instrument is a fit, because the imbalanced table is not proportional and the main effects
are therefore separable. `log ms ~ cell + pass + build + position` on the k=32 `ours` arm over
p25-p30, n=1602, rank 98:

    position 2 vs 1     -0.1391%   (SE 0.6900%, t -0.20)
    position 3 vs 1     -0.1628%   (SE 0.7628%, t -0.21)
    build ov64 vs ovp   +5.619%    (SE 0.690%)
    build ov64b vs ovp  +5.683%    (SE 0.763%)

**No detectable position effect at |t| ≤ 0.21.** What should be published is the bound, not a point
estimate: 0.690% SE per position step times the 0.167-position ov64-versus-ovp imbalance gives 95%
bounds of **±0.23% on ov64/ovp** — an order below the 1.62% all-89 median and two below the 13.46%
raised median. The conclusion I drew from the wrong number happens to be the conclusion the bound
supports, which is luck rather than method.

The build row is the more useful output: **ov64 and ov64b agree with each other to 0.06% while both
sit about 5.6% above pure policy.** Two same-argument objects landing together is what a floor is
supposed to show, and it is a cleaner statement of the override's cost than either position estimate.

**The tension this exposes carries to chain207.** Over all 30 passes the rotation is balanced and
build and position are orthogonal by design — and that window is unusable: position 3 reads +13.674%
at t +3.43 and the ov64 build +80.022%, because p1-p24 holds whole-pass catastrophes. The balanced
window is contaminated and the clean window is imbalanced, and **there is no window with both**. So
for chain207: certify balance on the landed passes of whatever is analysed, and if a restriction is
needed, **fit position as a factor rather than normalising it away** — normalising is what produced
two confident estimates with opposite signs here.

Three smaller corrections from the same exchange, all verified against the sealed bytes:

- **`resolved[ov64]` on the raised cells is {25: 1, 51: 2, 64: 37}, not the constant 64.** So "the
  predictor contains no worker variation at all" was too strong — it contains a little, on 3 of 40
  cells. The consequence is exact: substituting the literal 64 reads the collinearity as +0.9978
  while **the pair I actually named reads +0.9913**. Same conclusion, wrong pair; the analyzer now
  quotes the named one.
- **`nnz/ambient` is a better-posed predictor, not a re-description.** A joint fit loads log nnz at
  **−0.9852** (SE 0.4671, t −2.11) and log ambient at **+1.0610** (SE 0.4280, t +2.48) — nearly
  (−1, +1), so the data picks out `log(ambient/nnz)` as the direction that matters. VIF is 226.7, so
  the individual coefficients are not identified but **that contrast is**. Its spread is a ninth of
  its components (sd 0.133 against 1.161 and 1.267), and since nnz and the resolved count are exact
  integers with no measurement error, the narrow spread is real structure rather than residual. The
  refutation-is-unsupported conclusion is on firmer ground than I claimed.
- **The batch rule is about the reduction *statistic*, not the reduction order.** On the batch
  column the order is worth nothing: ratio-then-reduce with `exp(median(log .))` reads −0.6770 and
  reduce-then-ratio with the same geometric reduction reads −0.6747. It is the **arithmetic** median
  that moves it to −0.9289 (and the mean to −0.9262). `exp(median(log .))` is not `median`.
  Separately, the "10 of 11 low-band" figure I quoted was not a slip: that group is *defined* by
  whether the batch ratio diverges past 1.1x, so it does depend on the batch estimator — it is 9, 10,
  10, 9 across the four conventions, and 10 under the arithmetic-median one I was describing.

### The floor question CLOSES: the narrow floor was right, and the 10x gap is the batch on 7 cells

Two commits ago I said the narrow floor fails its own A/A and the 10x gap was "not batch, not
population, and not yet named". The population half stands. The rest was my own error, and it was a
specific one: **I compared a median batch divergence to explain a p95 width.** On the declined 49:

    pair                  mean |log batch dev|   median   p95
    ov64/ovp    test              13.78%          1.76%   24.52%
    ov64b/ov64  relabel            3.04%          1.19%   12.08%

Median to median says "nearly equal", which is what I reported. The mean is 4.5x apart and the p95
2x apart — and the quantity I was explaining is a p95.

**Conditioning on the batch is legitimate here, and my own causal argument is what licenses it.** I
wrote that batch is a mediator on the raised cells: the override changes the kernel's speed,
calibration observes it, so the treatment causes the batch change and conditioning would remove real
effect. That is right. But on the **declined** cells the override changes nothing the kernel can see
by construction, so a batch difference there is not caused by the treatment at all — it is
calibration noise, a pre-treatment nuisance, and conditioning on it is valid. The same causal
ordering forbids conditioning on one subset and permits it on the other. I stated the premise and
did not draw the consequence.

Splitting the declined cells by batch agreement:

    batch agreement      n    test p95   relabel p95   ratio     median nnz
    within 1.02x         27     0.0228      0.0380      0.6x        297538
    1.02-1.10x           15     0.0374      0.0242      1.5x        135135
    beyond 1.10x          7     0.5930      0.0101     58.7x           756

**The entire 10x gap lives in 7 cells, and where the batch agrees the test pair is TIGHTER than the
relabelled-object floor.** It is also not the small-matrix effect I proposed: inside the smallest nnz
quartile of the declined set, batch-matched cells read 0.0074 at median nnz 174 and batch-diverged
cells 0.5913 at median nnz 131 — **the same size, 80x apart, with batch agreement the only
difference.** My small-matrix quartile row was additionally computed over all 89 cells while the
sentence attached it to the declined pair, so the evidence for a claim about the declined set
included the raised cells where the override genuinely fires. On the declined 49 alone the
concentration survives in direction and not in magnitude.

**So the narrow floor does not fail its own A/A.** Beyond it: all 49 declined gives 10 slower / 0
faster, but batch-matched cells give **1 slower / 0 faster** and batch-diverged cells 9 / 0. The
failure was the artefact, not the floor.

**Both floors now agree, and the gated count is not in doubt.**

    floor                                    p95 dev    raised 40 beyond it
    relabelled object ov64b/ov64              0.0312     27 slower,  9 faster
    batch-matched declined A/A (n=27)         0.0228     27 slower,  9 faster
    unconditioned declined A/A (n=49)         0.3122     10 slower,  8 faster

Two independently constructed floors give the same count; the one that disagreed was carrying the
artefact. **The correct per-cell figure for chain204's k=32 override is 27 slower against 9 faster on
the raise group**, gated by the relabelled-object floor. cf9a0a2's "21 against 5" was wrong for the
population reason already retracted, and my "10 against 8" was wrong for this one. My "no per-cell
gated count should be quoted" was over-cautious and is withdrawn; 27/9 is quotable with the floor
named.

**What still genuinely needs the batch-pinned re-run is the low-ambient win magnitude**, where batch
*is* a mediator and conditioning is not available — that is the 0.6766 median on the 11 raised
ambient-1-8 cells, 9 of which sit in the diverging-batch group.

One finding about the corpus rather than the kernel: **four of the 89 shared keys are degenerate at
k=32.** `ss/S10PI_n1/S10PI_n1_C` has nnz = 1, `ss/M20PI_n1/M20PI_n1_B` has 3,
`ss/bips07_1998/bips07_1998_B` has 4, and `ss/Pajek/Tina_AskCog/Tina_AskCog` has 36 — all timed at
7 to 23 microseconds and all resolving to a single worker. They are not measuring SpMM, the nnz = 4
one was the single largest deviation in the declined set, and they are in the corpus that chain202,
chain203 and chain204 all share.

### chain203 re-verified: the "21.2%" endpoint does not exist, and the lever is mostly cold-start

An independent recomputation of chain203 from its sealed bytes, checked here against the same data.
Its mechanism claim and point estimate are exactly reproducible. Two published numbers are wrong and
one new finding is larger than the headline.

**What reproduces to the cell.** 242 CSVs, 11 builds x 22 passes, 801 rows each. Population at
k=32: ov24 raises the resolved count on 25 cells, is null on 64, and **lowers on 0** — the theorem
`an_c203.py:412` states. `resolved[ov24]` is 24 on all 25 raised cells while `resolved[ovp]` spans
1 to 23. Point estimate 1.1805 against the filed 1.1806.

**The rotation is perfect here, and it is the counter-case to chain204.** All 22 passes landed all
11 builds with every build occupying each of the 11 positions exactly twice, verified from the
`wrote` lines in `c203_rw.log`. Because the analysis used all 22 passes and 22 = 2 x 11, nothing was
windowed and nothing broke. The constraint that follows is worth stating: **with 11 builds the only
position-balanced windows are 11 and 22 passes**, so any segment restriction on this design
necessarily breaks balance. chain204 got unlucky with a 6-pass window; chain203 did not.

**The +21.2% endpoint is not reachable by any nesting.** Crossing the two named reductions with the
two reduction orders gives four, and all four:

    ratio-then-reduce + geometric mean over cells   1.1805   +18.05%
    ratio-then-reduce + median over cells           1.1441   +14.41%
    reduce-then-ratio + geometric mean over cells   1.1783   +17.83%
    reduce-then-ratio + median over cells           1.1449   +14.49%

**The range is +14.4% to +18.1%.** The lower endpoint is real; the upper one does not exist, and it
is not the bootstrap CI either ([1.0768, 1.2949]). The sealed artefacts contain no 1.212 anywhere —
only 1.1806, twice — so the range was computed at session time, never filed, and its upper endpoint
is wrong. Note also that the spread is **entirely the across-cells statistic** (geometric mean
against median, 3.6 points) and not the reduction order (0.2 points), so the reduction pair has to
be named beside the number.

**The batch exposure is worse here than on chain204 and cannot be conditioned away.** On the
headline 25, `ov24/ovp` batch divergence is mean |log| 164.53% / median 196.60% / p95 230.58%
against the duplicate pair `ov24b/ov24` at 3.47% / 1.75% / 9.06% — a factor of 47. And the mediation
split that closed chain204's floor question cannot run: **1 of 25 cells is batch-matched within
1.02x, 0 in the middle band, and 24 of 25 beyond 1.10x.** There is no overlap to condition on.

**Two things say the effect is not merely the artefact.** The sign is wrong for a small-batch bias:
`r[signed log batch ratio, log(ovp/ov24)] = -0.4882`, where the documented bias predicts positive.
And the mediator argument applies in full — ov24 really is faster on the adoption group, so the
calibrator picks a larger batch for it, putting the divergence downstream of the effect. Conditioning
would be wrong even if there were cells to condition on.

**But the two instruments inside each cell disagree by 5.70x, and that is the real finding.** Since
`batch = target_ms / single_call_time`, the batch ratio measures the speedup that *calibration* saw
on isolated calls, and the timed ratio measures it in back-to-back batches of hundreds:

    median batch_ov24 / batch_ovp   6.5230    what calibration saw on isolated calls
    median timed ovp / ov24         1.1441    what the batched timing saw
    disagreement                    5.70x

So **the override looks about 6.5x better on an isolated call and about 1.14x better in warm batched
steady state.** `calibrate()` times five single calls; `timeit()` times batches. The honest reading
is that most of the lever is per-call team spin-up, not steady-state throughput — a production caller
issuing many SpMM calls back-to-back gets the 1.14x, and only a caller issuing isolated calls gets
anything like the rest. That is consistent with the caller-path cold/warm split already on record and
it makes the +18% a steady-state number sitting beside a much larger cold one. It is directly
measurable and it changes what the lever is for.

**chain204's floor result replicates here independently** — different host, different pool, different
rung set, data collected sixteen days earlier for another purpose. The declined-argument A/A on the
64 null cells reads p95 dev **0.1304** against the duplicate pair's **0.0398**, a 3.3x gap; split by
batch, the matched half (n=32) reads **0.0209** against 0.0256 — the declined pair *tighter*, as on
chain204 — while the diverged half (n=32) reads 0.1433 against 0.0463. Same finding, same direction,
same mechanism, on independent data. That is the cross-chain confirmation the floor conclusion needed.

**And chain208's calibration pre-pass prices the unpinned batch directly**, before anything is timed:
across 267 cells of the shared corpus, `batch_ours` is identical under the two configurations on only
**7 cells (2.6%)**, median ratio 1.0363, p95 1.5440. Tail-concentrated, which is the shape that
caught me out once already.

Corrections owed: the memory file carrying "14.4% to 21.2%" needs its upper endpoint fixed to 18.1%
with the reduction pair named, and `headroom_c204.py`'s docstring quotes the same wrong "14-21%".
That file is inside a sealed ledger and is not edited; the error is recorded here instead.

### chain208 pre-registration, AMENDED while the run is in flight (2026-09-29 23:52 local)

Recorded before any chain208 **timed** output has been read. What I have read from the running job is
its calibration map comparison, which times nothing: across 267 cells `batch_ours` is identical under
the two configurations on 7 (2.6%), median ratio 1.0363, p95 1.5440. The run's own body script is
**not** edited — it is a live measurement, and the amendment goes in the record with a timestamp
instead.

**P1's pass band was narrower than the uncertainty of the value it tests against.** I pre-registered
"the pinned unconditioned declined A/A must fall to 0.023-0.031", taken from the two agreeing floors.
But 0.0228 is a p95 over 27 cells and 4000 bootstrap resamples put its own 95% CI at **[0.0083,
0.0361]** — my entire pass band sits inside the CI of its target, so P1 could pass or fail on
sampling alone and a failure would not license "the batch was not what widened it". **Corrected pass
band: [0.008, 0.036].** And the power stated rather than implied: at this n the test cannot
distinguish 0.023 from 0.036, so only a reading above about 0.06 is evidence against the batch
explanation. The comparison that actually carries weight is against the **unpinned 0.3122**, which is
an order outside the band either way — P1 is a strong test of "the batch widened it" and a weak test
of "it fell to exactly the floor".

Two worries about P1 that I checked and killed, so the run is not spent on them:

- **The population substitution is benign.** 0.0228 is a p95 over the 27 matched cells while chain208
  pins all 49, and a p95 over 49 reaches further into the tail. Resampling the matched distribution
  to n=49 gives median **0.0228**, CI [0.0123, 0.0361] — the nearest-rank index moves from 24-of-27
  to 45-of-49, nearly the same quantile. Use 0.0228 for both.
- **The four degenerate keys do not carry the gate statistic.** A p95 over 49 lands 2-3 cells from the
  top and the nnz = 4 matrix was the largest deviation in the *unconditioned* declined set, so this
  was the obvious way for the anti-selection decision to cost something. It does not: the p95
  excluding all four is **0.0228**, identical to four decimals, and the top three deviations among the
  matched cells are `cegb2919` (nnz 321543), `us04` (297538) and `bas1lp` (587775) — all large.

**P3 now carries a pre-registered predicted value, which is what makes it falsifiable.** The batch
slope is measurable from chain204, so the pinned value is predictable from chain204. Regressing
log(ms ratio) on log(batch ratio) and reading the intercept at batch ratio = 1:

    population            n    slope              r        intercept at batch=1        cells near 1
    c204 raised 40        40   -0.4306 (0.0759)  -0.6770   1.0945 [1.0186, 1.1759]     13 of 40
    c204 ambient 1-8      11   -0.9717 (0.0855)  -0.9669   1.0866 [0.9979, 1.1833]      2 of 11

The observed **unpinned** median on those 11 low-ambient cells is **0.6766** — the 32% win the
rule-defect finding rests on. **The prediction is that it inverts to about 1.087, i.e. 8.7% slower**,
and r = −0.967 on 11 cells is as tight a relationship as anything in this milestone. If chain208
returns those cells near 0.68 the slope story is dead and the win is real; near 1.09 and the
rule defect evaporates.

**The diagnostic that says how much to trust each intercept is how many cells sit near batch ratio
1.** For the raised 40 it is 13 of 40, so the intercept is an interpolation. For the ambient 1-8 band
it is **2 of 11** — the line is tight but only two points anchor the intercept, so that band is
optimistic and the point prediction should be read as a direction with a wide band, not as a value.
On chain203's headline 25 it is 1 of 25, a pure extrapolation resting on one influential point, so
**no prediction is pre-registered there at all** — that population can only be settled by pinning,
which is the same argument that built chain208.

**P5, new: the two calibration maps must bracket the pinned value by about 5.5%.** The same slope
predicts it — |−0.4306| x log(1.1346) = **5.59%** using chain204's own median speedup (about 6.5% if
the chain203 figure is used instead, so the pre-registered magnitude is 5 to 7%). If the observed
bracket is much wider, the two maps differ in something other than the batch integer and the
single-manipulated-variable claim has failed. This is the failure `batch_local` was added to catch,
and until now nothing predicted a size for it.

### The board's headline survives a second, independent instrument — and the cold/warm story does NOT generalise

chain203's override looked 6.52x better on isolated calls than the 1.14x it showed batched, which
raised a question about the whole milestone: is our ~2.6x advantage over MKL a property of batched
timing? The board data answers it for free, because every row carries a `batch` column and
`batch = target_ms / single_call_time`, so **the batch ratio between two arms measures the same
comparison at isolated-call granularity.** Run over chain206's sealed board — 4,584 SuiteSparse
matrices x 5 widths, 22,920 cells, six passes, redwood at pool 24.

    build aa    batched median   isolated median    behind-MKL batched   behind-MKL isolated
    k=2         0.6637           0.7232              42 (1.0%)            296 (6.7%)
    k=4         0.5609           0.5501              49 (1.1%)             44 (1.0%)
    k=8         0.3662           0.3603              15 (0.3%)             43 (1.0%)
    k=16        0.3231           0.3094               5 (0.1%)             19 (0.4%)
    k=32        0.3089           0.3015               2 (0.0%)            171 (4.2%)
    POOLED      0.3840           0.3785             113 (0.5%)           573 (2.7%)

**The two instruments agree at the centre.** Pooled 0.3840 batched against 0.3785 isolated, and the
per-cell median of isolated/batched is **0.9938** — within 0.7%. It replicates on build `bb`
(0.3842 / 0.3769, median 0.9937), which is a separate process with byte-identical `.text`.

**The sign test needs no floor and says the same thing.** The isolated instrument reads *worse* for
us on only **46.15%** of the 21,535 usable cells (9,939 of 21,535), which is 11.3 SE *below* half —
it reads better for us more often than worse. And this is conservative by construction: `int()`
truncation in `batch = int(target/t)` biases the isolated time **upward**, so the true single-call
time is at most what this reads, and it still does not read slower than batched.

**So the milestone's headline is not a batching artefact**, and chain203's 5.70x cold/warm divergence
is a property of *that override comparison*, not of our kernel. Restricting the earlier finding
accordingly.

Three things that had to be got right for that conclusion to mean anything:

- **Quantisation, stated and enforced.** `batch` is an integer, so relative error is 1/batch. Cells
  count only when every pass has batch >= 10 on both arms; that keeps 21,535 of 22,920 and the
  excluded count is reported per width (170 to 524, largest at k=32).
- **The within-process A/A gives this instrument no floor at all.** The harness hands one batch to
  `ours` and `oursb` inside a process, so `batch_oursb / batch_ours` is exactly 1 **by construction**
  — a floor of zero that would have made every behind cell look significant. The only A/A available
  is across builds, `aa` against `bb`, and it reads **0.2603** against the timed floor's **0.0876**.
  The isolated instrument is 3.0x cruder, which is the whole explanation available for its larger
  behind-MKL count (400 cells beyond its own floor against 43 for the timed one) in the absence of
  any systematic tilt, and the sign test says there is none.
- **A fixed per-call cost is refuted, and the number it produced must not be quoted.** Modelling
  `t_isolated = t_batched + C` gives a no-intercept line in 1/t whose slope is C. Fitted per width on
  our arm alone it returns C = 2.85 / 0.78 / 0.92 / 0.61 / 4.21 us — a 6.9x spread where a fixed cost
  predicts one constant — and **r ranges from −0.077 to +0.099 at every width**, so the line explains
  nothing and the slope is an artefact of forcing a fit through an unrelated cloud. The same fit on
  MKL's arm returns 32 to 68 us. **I nearly reported that as MKL's per-call overhead.** It is not a
  cost; it is what a no-intercept fit returns when there is no relationship, and printing `r` beside
  the slope is the only reason it was caught.

One correction to my own framing above: I checked the behind-MKL counts against the p95 floor's 5%
false-positive budget (1,076 cells) and read them as "below budget, no deficit". **That comparison is
a category error** — the budget applies to a population whose true effect is zero, and these cells
sit at a true ratio near 0.38, far enough from parity that 26% noise cannot push them past it. The
conclusion stands on the sign test and the replication, not on that budget.

### The 25 remaining behind-MKL cells have no structural signature except width

With the board confirmed by a second instrument, the actual remaining work for "faster than MKL on
all of SuiteSparse" is small and now enumerated. Taking chain206's two byte-identical builds and
requiring a cell to be behind MKL on **both**, beyond the cross-build floor at its own width:

    k       arm A/A   build A/A   behind aa   behind bb   BOTH
    k=2     0.0483    0.0818      19          13           6
    k=4     0.0410    0.0747      23          22          14
    k=8     0.0436    0.0756       7           7           4
    k=16    0.0575    0.0909       2           1           1
    k=32    0.0851    0.1387       1           1           0
    total                         52          44          25

**25 cells of 22,920 (0.109%), 22 distinct matrices, and none at k=32.** The width distribution is
{2: 6, 4: 14, 8: 4, 16: 1, 32: 0}, which reproduces the core-by-width shape already on record from a
different chain and floor. Median excess over MKL is 1.1461 on `aa` and 1.1408 on `bb`.

**I then proposed two structural regimes off the sorted head of that table and they are wrong.** The
top entries are arresting — `nw14` has 73 rows at degree 12,396, `connectus` 512 rows at degree
2,202, `bibd_17_8` 136 rows at degree 5,005, and at the other extreme `Pd_b` and `m3plates` sit at
degree 0.78 and 0.60. So I named row-parallelism starvation and empty-row overhead as the two
regimes. **Those five cells are 5 of 25.** Reading a mechanism off the visible extremes of a sorted
list is selection on the head, and the test below is what it costs.

Four predicates, each derived from a mechanism and written down before its coverage was computed,
against a base rate of 0.109%:

    predicate (mechanism)                                     fires   core hit   precision   lift
    rows < 2 x pool (48): the row loop cannot fill the team      860         0      0.000%     0x
    rows < 4 x pool (96)                                        1380         2      0.145%     1x
    rows < 8 x pool (192)                                       1975         3      0.152%     1x
    rows < 32 x pool (768)                                      4125         5      0.121%     1x
    deg x k x 4B > 0.5 MB: the row's B-panel gather exceeds L2     16         0      0.000%     0x
    deg x k x 4B > 1.0 MB                                         10         0      0.000%     0x
    deg x k x 4B > 2.0 MB                                          5         0      0.000%     0x
    deg < 1: more rows than nonzeros, row overhead dominates    2135         3      0.141%     1x
    nnz x max(k,16) < 150000 (the shipped grain)                6567         4      0.061%     1x

**Every one of them has a lift of about 1, which is to say none of them discriminates at all.** The
cache predicate fires 5 to 16 times on the whole board and catches nothing. Splitting the core by the
two named mechanisms leaves **20 of 25 cells in "neither"** — median nnz 501,111, 2,337 rows, degree
120, 13 of the 20 at k=4. The bulk of the deficit is unremarkable mid-size, mid-degree matrices.

**The only predictor that works is the width.** k=4 holds 14 of 25 core cells from 20% of the board —
0.305% against the 0.109% base rate, a lift of 2.8 — and k=32 holds none.

That is a useful negative for the standing constraint that optimizations must generalize. **A
runtime-gated rule cannot be built for these cells out of rows, nnz, or degree**, because no
threshold on those features selects them. So closing the k=4 half of the core requires a change that
makes k=4 faster *generally*, not a condition that fires on 14 matrices — which is the outcome the
no-overfitting rule was there to force, arrived at by measurement rather than by preference.

### The 25 needs its predicate in the sentence; the per-call diagnostic is confirmed as non-vacuous

**The count is criterion-sensitive and I published it without its predicate.** All seven rows below
require the cell to be behind MKL on *both* byte-identical builds; they differ only in how the floor
is applied. Floors are p95 over cells at that width of `dev(exp median log(ms_bb_ours / ms_aa_ours))`
requiring all six passes in both builds — cross-build 0.0818 / 0.0747 / 0.0756 / 0.0909 / 0.1387, and
the arm-identity floor on `oursb/ours` within `aa` at 0.0483 / 0.0410 / 0.0436 / 0.0575 / 0.0851.

    criterion                                  k=2/4/8/16/32   cells   matrices   k=4 lift
    both beyond cross-build floor (published)  6/14/4/1/0        25       22         2.8
    aa beyond cross-build floor               12/18/5/2/0        37       31         2.4
    both beyond arm floor                     12/19/4/1/0        36       32         2.6
    mean beyond cross-build floor             11/23/4/2/0        40       33         2.9
    either beyond cross-build floor           14/25/5/2/1        47       38         2.7
    either beyond arm floor                   17/29/6/2/1        55       45         2.6
    no floor at all                           21/37/8/2/1        69       56         2.7

**So "the remaining work is 25 cells" moves between 25 and 69 on the criterion alone**, and the
sentence has to carry the predicate: *25 cells are behind MKL on both builds beyond the cross-build
A/A floor at their own width.* The published 6/14/4/1/0 reproduces exactly under that criterion.

**What survives every construction is the part the conclusion rests on:** the k=4 lift is **2.4 to
2.9 in all seven**, and none at k=32 under the two strictest. So "width is the only predictor" and
"no runtime-gated rule on rows, nnz or degree selects these cells" hold whichever criterion is
chosen.

An independent recomputation agrees with this board cell-for-cell — applying its ratios to my floors
returns 400 against my 400 on the isolated instrument and 44 against my 43 on the timed one — while
reporting different floors (k=8 at 0.1493 against my 0.0756, a factor of two). **The whole count
discrepancy is in the floor, not the data.** My floor definition is stated above; the source of the
difference is not yet identified and the number should be read with its floor attached until it is.

**The per-call-cost diagnostic: which two vectors the correlation is between.** My `r` is
`corr(1/t_batched, t_isolated/t_batched − 1)` — the regressor against the response, not the residual
against the regressor. It is not zero by construction, and the check is one line of simulation:

    model                                    corr(1/t, ti/t-1)   corr(t, ti)
    additive, ti = t + C exactly                  +1.000000        +1.0000
    multiplicative, ti = 1.05 t + 15% noise       +0.012057        +0.9848
    mixed, ti = 1.02 t + C                        +1.000000        +1.0000

**Under a perfect additive model it is exactly 1.** My measured −0.077 to +0.099 sits precisely where
the multiplicative simulation lands, so it is evidence against a fixed per-call cost rather than an
artefact — the diagnostic did its job.

And `corr(t_batched, t_isolated)` reads **0.985 under pure multiplicative noise**, so it cannot
discriminate the two models at all: both quantities are driven by cell size. A reported 0.986 for it
is not evidence that a fixed cost explains the data. The refutation therefore has two independent
legs — the 6.9x spread in fitted C where a constant is predicted, and `r ≈ 0` on the statistic that
would read 1 if the model held. Both say the same thing, and neither C value should be quoted.

One external correction worth recording because it confirms my numbers: the board harness sets
`--target-ms 6` (`rw_s_chain206.sh:121`), not `mrgate_ov.py`'s default of 25. Taking the default
inflates every isolated time by 4.17x. My C values were computed with 6 and stand; the lesson is that
a constant has to come from the harness that produced the data, not from the harness that was read.

MKL's cross-build variation by construction through

### The reduction order is decidable by measurement, and the mechanism we assumed is absent in the clean window

The ratio floor has two constructions and they differ by up to 17%:

    A   reduce each build's S over passes, then one ratio    dev(S_aa / S_bb)
    B   ratio the two builds at each pass, then reduce       dev(reduce_p(S_aa,p / S_bb,p))

    k         2        4        8       16       32
    A    0.0896   0.0951   0.1493   0.1349   0.1689
    B    0.1046   0.1081   0.1439   0.1470   0.1821
    B/A    1.17     1.14     0.96     1.09     1.08

**B is larger at four of five widths, so pairing at the pass index is adding variance rather than
removing it.** A is the floor to use, and the count of 14 rests on A.

**The premise is directly measurable and it fails.** Pairing helps only if the two builds' per-pass
deviations are positively correlated at that index. Centring each build's six log values on its own
median and correlating the two six-vectors per cell, then averaging over 22,920 cells:

    k=2 +0.0063   k=4 +0.0102   k=8 +0.0119   k=16 +0.0114   k=32 -0.0044      SE 0.0148

**Every width is within 0.8 SE of zero.** There is no common-mode at the pass index across runs, which
is why pairing recovers nothing.

**This undercuts the justification I adopted for `ratio-then-reduce` on chain204 an hour ago.** The
mechanism I wrote down — three builds inside one pass run close in wall clock, so drift is
common-mode and pairing at the index removes it — is testable on chain204 itself, and in the p25-p30
analysis window it is absent:

    pair                p25-p30 (clean)              all 30 passes (contaminated)
    ov64  vs ovp        -0.062 / -0.075 / -0.097      +0.091 / +0.123 / +0.133
    ov64b vs ov64       +0.066 / +0.071 / +0.041      +0.250 / +0.294 / +0.311
    ov64b vs ovp        -0.085 / -0.040 / -0.084      +0.108 / +0.104 / +0.120
    (k = 2 / 4 / 32, n=89 per cell-set, SE 0.1060)

In the clean window every entry is inside ±0.9 SE of zero and four of six pairs are **negative**. Over
all 30 passes there is real positive correlation — up to **+0.311 at +2.9 SE** on the same-argument
pair — and that is coherent rather than contradictory: p1-p24 contains the whole-pass catastrophes,
which are genuine shared disturbances and do correlate. **Common-mode exists exactly when there is
something in common to remove, and a clean window has nothing.**

So the convention, stated as a test rather than a mechanism: **pair at the pass index only where the
within-cell cross-build correlation at that index is measurably positive; otherwise reduce each side
first.** One line of arithmetic decides it per dataset. Nothing published turns on this — the choice
was worth one gated cell on chain204 with the verdict invariant — but the *justification* I gave was
an assumption dressed as a mechanism, and it is the same error as certifying rotation balance from the
schedule instead of from the landed passes.

The cancellation figures also verify against the corrected A column: S's floor is 0.62 / 0.65 / 0.82 /
0.74 / 0.68 of the naive sum of its component floors. **A ratio's floor is neither the sum of its
factors' floors nor bounded by either one, and has to be measured.**

### Correction: my SE was 2.24x too large, and the mechanism is sign-dependent rather than absent

The previous section said the cross-build per-pass correlation was "within 0.8 SE of zero at every
width" and concluded the common-mode mechanism is absent. **The SE was wrong and the conclusion does
not follow.** I used `SE = 1/sqrt(n)`, which assumes the per-cell correlations have sd 1. Measured sd
is **0.42 to 0.45** — the textbook `1/sqrt(n-1) = 0.447` for a correlation on six points — so every
`t` I quoted was understated by 2.24x.

chain204, p25-p30, correct SE:

    pair            k      r        sd       SE       t        t I published
    ov64/ovp        2   -0.0622   0.4202   0.0445   -1.40        -0.59
    ov64/ovp        4   -0.0747   0.4308   0.0457   -1.64        -0.70
    ov64/ovp        32  -0.0973   0.4229   0.0448   -2.17        -0.92
    ov64b/ov64      2   +0.0664   0.3917   0.0415   +1.60        +0.63
    ov64b/ov64      4   +0.0707   0.3480   0.0369   +1.92        +0.67
    ov64b/ov64      32  +0.0406   0.4503   0.0477   +0.85        +0.38
    ov64b/ovp       2   -0.0851   0.3943   0.0418   -2.04        -0.80
    ov64b/ovp       4   -0.0397   0.4299   0.0456   -0.87        -0.37
    ov64b/ovp       32  -0.0843   0.4165   0.0442   -1.91        -0.80

And my all-30 figure was understated four-fold: `ov64b/ov64` reads **+10.03 / +12.29 / +12.01**, not
the +2.4 to +2.9 I reported.

**The structure I missed is the finding.** Ignore significance and read the signs: the
**same-argument** pair is positive at all three widths (+0.041 to +0.071) and **both cross-argument**
pairs are negative at all six (−0.040 to −0.097). **Nine of nine entries track argument identity.**

So the mechanism is not absent — it is sign-dependent, and for the cross-argument pairs it runs
backwards. That gives `B > A` an actual mechanism rather than an absence of one, and the mechanism is
algebra: the paired datum is `log S_aa,p − log S_bb,p` with variance `var_a + var_b − 2cov`, so a
**negative** covariance inflates it. Anti-correlation at the pass index makes pairing strictly worse,
not merely useless.

**And it reshapes my own replacement rule.** "Pair where the correlation is measurably positive" is
right, but it does not return one answer per dataset — it returns one per pair, and **the pair
carrying the floor (same-argument, +1.92 SE at k=4) and the pair carrying the effect (cross-argument,
−2.17 SE at k=32) want opposite treatment.**

**A further error of mine: I reported a median-centred cosine and called it a correlation.** Pearson
centres on the mean, and on n=6 they are different statistics that disagree about significance. On
chain206 at k=32 the median-centred version reads t = −0.72 and Pearson reads **t = −2.35**:

    k              2         4         8        16        32
    median-cos  +0.0063   +0.0102   +0.0119   +0.0114   -0.0044
    Pearson     -0.0031   +0.0028   +0.0057   +0.0027   -0.0156

The first row is what I published; the second is what an independent recomputation produced, and the
gap between us was entirely the centring rather than the data.

**What the decision actually needs is the bound, not the detection** — which is a rule already in
this document and which I violated by framing this as a significance test at all. No correlation is
required to decide it:

    floor A (reduce each side, then ratio)   0.0896  0.0951  0.1493  0.1349  0.1689
    floor B (pair per pass, then reduce)     0.1046  0.1081  0.1439  0.1470  0.1821
    B/A                                        1.17    1.14    0.96    1.09    1.08

**Pairing moves the floor by at most 17% and the gated count by one cell.** That claim survives every
choice of correlation statistic, centring convention and standard error, and it is the one to quote.
A is still the floor and the count is still 14; the reasoning behind it is what needed fixing.

### The correlation table, one estimator throughout (superseding the mixed one above)

The table two sections up pairs Pearson means with median-centred-cosine standard deviations and
`t` values. That is the mixed-estimator slip I identified on the `batch` column, one level down, and
the third instance tonight. **Pearson throughout, on the log times, with the empirical sd** —
chain204, p25-p30, n=89 per row:

    pair          k     Pearson r    sd       SE       t        cosine t
    ov64/ovp      2      -0.0692   0.4430   0.0470   -1.47       -1.40
    ov64/ovp      4      -0.0876   0.4591   0.0487   -1.80       -1.64
    ov64/ovp      32     -0.1259   0.4511   0.0478   -2.63       -2.17
    ov64b/ov64    2      +0.0765   0.4010   0.0425   +1.80       +1.60
    ov64b/ov64    4      +0.0519   0.3679   0.0390   +1.33       +1.92
    ov64b/ov64    32     +0.0518   0.4666   0.0495   +1.05       +0.85
    ov64b/ovp     2      -0.1030   0.4065   0.0431   -2.39       -1.16
    ov64b/ovp     4      -0.0560   0.4536   0.0481   -1.16       -0.87
    ov64b/ovp     32     -0.0831   0.4395   0.0466   -1.78       -1.91

**Four of nine beyond 1.8 SE and two beyond 2.3** under Pearson, against two beyond 2.0 on the
cosine — the mixed table understated, since the cosine `|t|` is smaller at seven of nine. The
qualitative conclusion is unchanged and slightly stronger. **The sign pattern is identical under both
estimators: same-argument positive at 3 of 3, cross-argument negative at 6 of 6.**

One technical point in my favour, recorded because it bears on how to use the robust variant: the
`t` above divides by the **empirical** sd of the per-cell values, not by the theoretical
`1/sqrt(n-1)`. That makes it a valid test of "is the mean of these per-cell statistics zero" for
*either* statistic — the theoretical value was only ever quoted as a sanity check that Pearson's
measured sd matched what n=6 predicts (0.447, and it does). So the defect was mixing two estimators
in one table, not the standard error of the robust one. **Pearson is still the right default** because
it is the standard and its sampling distribution is known; the cosine needs no separate SE derivation
when the sd is measured, but it does need to be named.

The decision is unaffected. The surviving claim is still the bound rather than any of these
correlations: `B/A` = 1.17 / 1.14 / 0.96 / 1.09 / 1.08, so **pairing at the pass index moves the floor
by at most 17% and the gated count by one cell.** A is the floor, the count is 14, and the
correlations explain why pairing does not help rather than establishing whether it does.

### The 89 cells are not independent: an exact permutation test retracts every significance claim above

`sd/sqrt(89)` assumes the 89 cells are independent, and they share the same six passes. Measured
cross-cell correlation of the per-cell pass vectors, within a single build, at k=2/4/32:

    ovp     +0.0673  +0.0830  +0.0674
    ov64    +0.1396  +0.1641  +0.1643
    ov64b   +0.0384  +0.0184  +0.0376

**Positive at all nine build x width combinations**, so the direction is signed before the magnitude
is known: positive dependence can only inflate the true standard error.

**The magnitude is exact rather than bounded.** Centre and unit-normalise each cell's six-vector per
arm to `Ahat`, `Bhat`; then the mean per-cell Pearson under a permutation `s` of arm B's pass labels
is `theta_s = (1/n) * sum_j M[j, s(j)]` with `M = Ahat.T @ Bhat` — so all 720 permutations of six
labels are one 6x6 product and a gather. Applying the **same** permutation to every cell destroys the
A-to-B pass alignment while preserving each arm's own cross-cell pass structure, which is precisely
the dependence that breaks the iid standard error.

    pair          k     mean r    iid SE   perm SE   ratio   perm t   exact p
    ov64/ovp      2    -0.0692   0.0470    0.0707    1.51    -0.98    0.3611
    ov64/ovp      4    -0.0876   0.0487    0.0740    1.52    -1.18    0.2778
    ov64/ovp      32   -0.1259   0.0478    0.0673    1.41    -1.87    0.0528
    ov64b/ov64    2    +0.0765   0.0425    0.0770    1.81    +0.99    0.3778
    ov64b/ov64    4    +0.0519   0.0390    0.0798    2.05    +0.65    0.4667
    ov64b/ov64    32   +0.0518   0.0495    0.0800    1.62    +0.65    0.5583
    ov64b/ovp     2    -0.1030   0.0431    0.0666    1.55    -1.55    0.1194
    ov64b/ovp     4    -0.0560   0.0481    0.0519    1.08    -1.08    0.2972
    ov64b/ovp     32   -0.0831   0.0466    0.0499    1.07    -1.67    0.0972

**"Four beyond 1.8 SE and two beyond 2.3" becomes zero of nine at exact p < 0.05.** The point
estimates are unchanged; only the standard error was wrong, by 1.07x to 2.05x. This is the third
successive widening of the same floor — `1/sqrt(n)`, then `sd/sqrt(n)`, now the permutation SE — and
each one moved against my significance claims while leaving the point estimates alone.

**The substantive finding survives pooling and is stronger than any single entry.** Cross-argument
pooled over its six entries: **−0.0875, exact p = 0.0042 (3 of 720)**. And the null it is measured
against is biased toward positive, because a shared ambient pass effect correlates *any* two arms
positively — that effect lives in the alternative here, not the null, so a negative result is
conservative for this direction.

**Two claims of mine that do not survive, and the second is the one that matters:**

- **"Same-argument positive at 3 of 3" carries no weight.** Pooled it is +0.0601 at exact
  **p = 0.3931** (283 of 720). Three agreeing signs over three non-significant numbers has a 1-in-4
  base rate, and the shared ambient effect already predicts positive between any two arms, so that
  half of the pattern needs no argument-identity story at all.
- **"The sign tracks argument identity" is a contrast and has to be tested as one.**
  `same − cross = +0.1476` at exact **p = 0.0778**, quantile 0.922 of its own null. Outside 0.05, and
  not sitting on a cliff — the adjacent |contrast| order statistics are 0.1484 / 0.1480 / **0.1476** /
  0.1468 / 0.1456.

**Instrument floor:** with six passes there are 720 permutations, so the smallest reachable two-sided
p is **1/720 = 0.00139**. The pooled 0.0042 is three permutations above that floor and must not be
quoted as if the instrument could separate it from 0.0014.

**A delete-one-pass jackknife is not a substitute and is recorded so nobody repeats it:** at G=6 it
has 5 degrees of freedom, matched the exact SE to 0.3% on one entry (0.0705 against 0.0707) and was
about 2x off on others (0.1512 against 0.0800, 0.0370 against 0.0519), with its SE swinging 4x across
entries at identical n. That spread is the 5 df, not the standard error. Use the permutation value; it
is exact.

**This is a floor correction, not a result inside a floor.** What moved is the sampling floor on the
mean per-cell correlation, 1.07x to 2.05x wider than quoted, and it moved toward leniency for the
null. The recorded statement is now: *different-argument arms in the same pass are anti-correlated,
pooled −0.0875 at exact p = 0.0042 over 720 permutations of the pass labels, measured and unexplained;
the same-argument positive is indistinguishable from the shared ambient effect (p = 0.39) and the
same-versus-cross contrast is p = 0.078, so the sign pattern is suggestive and not established.*

None of this touches the decision. `B/A` = 1.17 / 1.14 / 0.96 / 1.09 / 1.08 is a measured ratio of two
floors with no significance test in it: pairing moves the floor by at most 17% and the gated count by
one cell. A is the floor, the count is 14.

### The contrast null is skewed, so two-sided p is not twice one-sided — and my stated cause was wrong

I attributed the 0.9222-against-0.9444 quantile gap to tie handling at rank 56. **There are zero
ties.** The exact decomposition of the two-sided count of 56:

    upper tail (>= +|obs|, including the observed)      41
    lower tail (<= -|obs|)                              15
    sum                                                 56
    exact ties at |obs| other than the observed          0
    strictly above the observed SIGNED value            40

My figure was `1 - 56/720 = 0.9222`, the fraction of permutations with **|contrast|** below the
observed **|contrast|** — which is `1 - two-sided p`, not the quantile of the signed value. The
quantile of the signed value is `1 - 40/720 = 0.9444`. Both quantities are well defined; my label was
ambiguous and my diagnosis of the difference was simply wrong.

**And the reason that matters is the part worth keeping.** Tie handling would have been arbitrary and
small. This is neither: the tails split **41 against 15, a 2.7x asymmetry**, because the null is
skewed **+0.3234** with median **−0.0092** rather than 0. Percentiles 2.5 / 50 / 97.5 are
**−0.1374 / −0.0092 / +0.1750** — visibly off-centre. So on this null:

    two-sided p       0.0778   (56/720)
    one-sided p       0.0569   (41/720, counting the observed)
    2 x one-sided     0.1139   -- the two-sided value is 32% SMALLER

**Reconstructing either tail from the other is wrong here, in whichever direction one guesses.** A
permutation null on a contrast of two pooled correlations has no reason to be symmetric, and this one
is not. Any p quoted from it has to say which tail it counted.

The filed statement now reads: *the same-versus-cross contrast is +0.1476 at exact two-sided
p = 0.0778, quantile 0.944 of a null whose tails are asymmetric 41 against 15, so the two-sided value
is not twice the one-sided 0.0569.* The conclusion is unchanged — suggestive, not established.

**Two refinements to the lesson I recorded, both better than my version.** First, the tell was not
that the standard error was approximate; it was that **six passes is enumerable**, and "is this design
small enough to enumerate exactly" is a question askable *before* any estimator is chosen rather than
after three of them fail. Second, and this is the limit of the whole exercise: **an exact test buys
the uncertainty and never the estimate.** All three widenings — `1/sqrt(n)`, `sd/sqrt(n)`,
permutation — moved exactly one column and left all nine point estimates untouched. Getting the
interval right does not make a point estimate mean more than it did.

### Two free choices, not one — and the one I named pushes the wrong way

I said the 43%-versus-32% gap between two statements of the same asymmetry was the
observed-permutation convention. **It is two conventions, and mine was the minor one pointing
backwards.**

    observed conv.    percentage base      value
    exclude obs       two-sided p          42.9%      <- the other session's 43%
    exclude obs       doubled              30.0%
    include obs       two-sided p          46.4%
    include obs       doubled              31.7%      <- my 32%

One at a time, net −11.1 points:

    flip the observed convention, base held    42.9 -> 46.4    +3.6 pts
    then flip the percentage base              46.4 -> 31.7   -14.7 pts

**The observed convention is 3.6 of 11.1 points and pushes the wrong way** — holding the base fixed,
*including* the observed permutation makes the gap larger, not smaller. The percentage base is 14.7
points, **132% of the net gap.**

**And the decomposition is order-dependent, which is the part to keep.** Flipping the base first gives
42.9 → 30.0 (−12.9) then → 31.7 (+1.7). Same two factors, same endpoints, attributions of
+3.6/−14.7 against −12.9/+1.7. That is the ranked-one-at-a-time problem this document already records
for the board's five free parameters: **two non-orthogonal conventions have no unique per-factor
share, so the honest form is the 2x2 table and not an attribution.**

The fix is to quote no percentage at all. Two-sided **0.0778** against a doubled one-sided of
**0.1111** or **0.1139** depending on the convention — and doubling is simply the wrong operation on
a null skewed +0.3234. The four cells say everything the percentage was reaching for.

**This is the second consecutive instance of the same reflex**, and the pattern is worth more than
either instance: shown a numeric discrepancy, I reached for one plausible cause and stopped — tie
handling for the quantile gap (there were zero ties), then the observed convention for the percentage
gap (it was the base). Both times the explanation was mechanical-sounding and unverified, and both
times a two-line decomposition would have settled it. **Decompose a gap before naming it.**

### chain207 PRE-REGISTRATION: the analyzer exists and is bound by digest before its data does

`an_c207.py`, SHA-256 **`5207b0498db0dbc09e042df2c64d9c08fc55c7f9aba9c3733a065ed9c7c03a50`**, 14116 bytes, written while the run was on pass 4 of 6 with no
DLMC timing yet read. Every choice it makes provably predates the numbers it will produce. That is
not ceremony — the SuiteSparse count moved between 14 and 69 purely on a criterion chosen after
seeing the data, and choosing it first is the only fix available.

**What is fixed in advance.** The gated statistic is `S = ours/mkl` per cell, and the floor is
`dev(S_aa/S_bb)` — S's own cross-build reproducibility, reduce-each-build-then-ratio, p95 by
nearest rank, per width. A cell is behind MKL only if it is behind on **both** byte-identical builds
beyond that floor at its own width. The arm-identity floor is printed beside it for contrast and is
explicitly **not** the control. Estimator: per-cell `exp(median(log .))` over six passes,
deviation `exp|ln x| - 1`.

**The prior, stated so the result can disagree with something.** SuiteSparse under this exact
criterion: 14 of 22,920 cells (0.0611%), 13 matrices, 6/7/1/0/0 by width, none at k≥16, no predicate
on rows/nnz/degree above lift ~1, width the only predictor with k=4 at 2.4–2.9x. DLMC is pruned
neural-network weight matrices — far more structurally uniform than SuiteSparse — so a materially
different rate is the interesting outcome in either direction.

**The file will not report a single count.** It prints all seven readings of "behind on both builds
beyond the floor" and names the headline with its predicate in the same sentence.

**Five guards, each proven to fire on its own violating input** — built as synthetic trees and run:

    tree          violation introduced                                    result
    t_files       one object-pass absent (11 files)                       GUARD 1 fires: "found 11, expected 12"
    t_relabel     build bb's p6 renamed p7 (both still 6 indices)         GUARD 1b fires: pass-index sets differ
    t_partial     build aa pass 3 truncated to 51 of 60 rows              GUARD 2 fires: wrong row count
    t_dupcell     one key duplicated, another dropped                     GUARD 3 fires: 15 cells, expected 20
    t_ok          none                                                    all five pass

**`t_dupcell` is the orthogonality proof**: it carries the **correct** row count of 60 while holding
only 15 distinct cells, so the cell-count guard is not redundant with the row-count guard. And
`t_relabel` leaves both builds at six distinct pass indices while their intersection drops to five —
the case a cardinality check cannot see, which would otherwise print `nan` at n=0 and exit 0.

**My first version of that self-test was itself vacuous** and is worth recording as the reason to run
it rather than describe it: the `t_partial` generator compared a 2-tuple to a 3-tuple, so the
condition never fired, the tree was written complete, and the guard "passed" by having nothing to
catch. The test reported exit 0 and I read it as a missing guard. Fixed, and the guard fires.

Shape constants are overridable by environment variable **only** so the self-test can build a small
tree, and any override prints `!! SHAPE CONSTANTS OVERRIDDEN` on the first line — so a real run
cannot quietly assert the wrong shape.

**The section above was committed with five words silently deleted, and the cause is the trap already
recorded in this session's notes.** I needed `$DIG` interpolated into the document, so I used an
unquoted heredoc — which enables backtick command substitution as well as variable expansion. Every
backticked identifier in the prose ran as a shell command and was replaced by its empty output:
`t_dupcell`, `t_relabel`, `nan`, `t_partial` and the `!! SHAPE CONSTANTS OVERRIDDEN` banner all
vanished, leaving grammatical sentences with the subject missing. The shell printed
`command not found` for each, which I read as harmless noise from the commit rather than as the
document being rewritten.

The note I had already written said to use a quoted heredoc. It did not say what to do when a value
has to be interpolated, which is the case that bit: **quote the heredoc and substitute the value
afterwards in a language that does not run backticks.** An unquoted heredoc is not a weaker version
of a quoted one — it is a different tool with command execution enabled, and a document full of
inline code spans is the worst possible input to it.

It also failed silently in the direction that survives review: deleting a word leaves prose that
still parses. Five sentences read as complete English with their subjects removed.

**The repair is verified complete on four axes, and three of them were needed.** No two of the

    axis                       bc5c0a9   bb7e5b2   e669216
    mid-sentence gap             114       117       114
    broken emphasis span           0         1         0
    leading-space lowercase        1         2         1

The series localises the damage to `bb7e5b2` and shows the repair removed exactly what it added. The

**The check that catches a deleted word is never reading the prose; it is asserting the tokens are

**And a backtick-parity check is vacuous by construction**, confirmed rather than argued:

### The token assertion had an enumeration premise; the span check is now mechanical

The repair of the unquoted-heredoc deletion was verified by asserting that six named
tokens were present in the committed file: `t_dupcell`, `t_relabel`, `nan`, `t_partial`,
`t_files`, `t_ok` and the `!! SHAPE CONSTANTS OVERRIDDEN` banner. The peer session
identified the defect in that form, and it is real: the assertion can only catch the
deletion of a token the author thought to list, so "all six present" carries no
information about a seventh that neither party considered. The predicate's completeness
is an untested assumption sitting underneath a check that reports PASS.

`tools/spandiff.py` replaces it. It extracts the span set from the intended source,
set-differences it against the emitted file in both directions, and compares
multiplicities. There is no list left to be incomplete, because the list IS the source.

**Proven non-vacuous by replaying the repaired section through the original defect** --
an unquoted heredoc -- and requiring the tool to catch it. On that planted tree it
reports 15 under-represented spans and 1 EXTRA. The extra span is the part the old form
could not reach: `** is the orthogonality proof**`, the mangled bold run left behind
when the subject of the sentence vanished. A presence-only assertion over typed tokens
is blind to an ADDED span by construction, so that axis had no coverage at all.

**The shell's own stderr is mechanical but incomplete, and the incompleteness is
knowable.** It was tempting to treat the five `command not found` lines as the
mechanical enumeration, since they did in fact name the five deletions. Two measured
reasons they are not sufficient, both from the planted tree: stderr keys on the FIRST
WORD and deduplicates, so five spans that were each deleted twice produced one line
apiece and the multiplicity was lost; and a span that expands to nothing emits zero
diagnostics, which is what an unset `$DIG` does -- 1 of 13 missing code spans had no
diagnostic of any kind. The shell reports only the spans that FAILED, which is a
different set from the spans that were DELETED.

Scope, stated rather than implied: the tool is complete for "span present in the
intended source, absent or under-represented in the output". Reordering and relocation
are separate axes and are not covered by it.

### A flag divided by a count reads as a large, plausible effect

While checking that chain208's batch pinning was doing anything at all, the first
comparison used `batch_local` against `batch_pinned` and reported a median ratio of
589 with a maximum of 3506 -- a number that looks like a decisive effect. `batch_pinned`
is a flag: `batch_pinned=(1 if BIN is not None else 0)`. The comparison divided a batch
count by a boolean. The correct column is `batch`, the batch actually used.

Re-run against the right column, the pin verifies: 534 map entries, 16821 pinned rows,
`batch` used equal to the map value on 16821 of 16821 with zero lookup misses, and local
calibration would have chosen differently on 97.1% of rows. Median local/used ratio
1.002, p95 1.257, tails 0.003 and 363.5. So the pin is a TIGHT control that mostly
reproduces what local calibration would have picked; if the batch explanation is real it
lives in that few-percent tail, not in a gross across-the-board shift.

The error was caught only because a flag's value of exactly 1.0 on every row was too
clean to believe. A flag that happened to carry a mid-range value would have passed
unnoticed, which puts this in the same family as reading a sentinel without its row
type: the column name described the quantity loosely enough that the units were never
checked.

### WITHDRAWN: "median local/used is 1.002, so the pin is a tight control"

The claim was that chain208's batch pin mostly reproduces what local calibration would
have picked, so any batch explanation of the unpinned result must live in a few-percent
tail. **That does not follow, and the peer session identified why.** `batch_local/batch`
is a WITHIN-ROW quantity. The regressor the batch explanation was ever about is the
CROSS-BUILD ratio within a cell, `batch(ov64)/batch(ovp)`, and the two are independent:
a symmetric unbiased substitution can remove an arbitrarily large between-build
difference while leaving the within-row median at exactly 1.000. If local calibration
gives ov64 100 and ovp 150 and the pin gives both 120, the within-row ratios are 0.83
and 1.25 with median ~1.0, while the cross-build ratio collapses from 1.5 to 1.0.

So median 1.002 and "97.1% of rows differ" are both consistent with a pin that changes
everything and a pin that changes nothing. A number that cannot discriminate was used to
draw a directional conclusion. The correct statistic is below.

**What pinning actually does, verified:** under a fixed map, the batch USED is identical
across builds on 1602 of 1602 (cell, arm) pairs, 0 differing. The design is crossed --
3 builds (ovp, ov64, ov64b) x 2 maps, file stem `bm_<mapsrc>_<build>` -- so a fixed map
hands both builds the same batch and the cross-build ratio is 1 by construction. That is
the intended intervention, not an artefact.

### The regressor, with its own byte-identical A/A control

`ov64b` and `ov64` are byte-identical objects, so `ov64b/ov64` is the floor for this
exact statistic. Without it the raw reading "63% of cells more than 5% off 1" is mostly
floor, because the A/A is itself 19.3% off by that much. Deviation is `exp|ln x| - 1`,
p95 by nearest rank, per-cell estimator `exp(median(log .))` over landed passes.

    population      arm    A/A p95 dev   OVERRIDE p95 dev   ratio    override median
    ALL 267         ours      0.1638          0.6500        3.97x        0.9735
    ALL 267         mkl       0.1340          0.2367        1.77x        1.0380
    RAISED 120      ours      0.0738          0.7778       10.5x         0.8269
    RAISED 120      mkl       0.1078          0.2633        2.44x        1.0876
    DECLINED 147    ours      0.1790          0.3870        2.16x        0.9973
    AMBIENT 1-8     ours      0.1642          0.6500        3.96x        0.9993
    AMBIENT 1-8     mkl       0.1049          0.1767        1.68x        1.0310

**The lever was engaged.** On the raised cells the cross-build local-batch ratio for our
arm sits at median 0.8269 with a p95 deviation 10.5x its own byte-identical A/A. Since
`batch = target_ms / single_call_time`, a ratio of 0.827 means ov64's calibration chose
~17% fewer iterations, i.e. saw our kernel as ~1.21x SLOWER per isolated call -- a
64-wide team's spin-up cost appearing in calibration, the same direction as chain203's
6.52x calibration against 1.14x timed. MKL moves the other way (median 1.0876) at only
2.44x its A/A, which is correct: the override does not touch MKL's team.

This was reported to the peer BEFORE any timed ratio was read, at 25 of 36 object-passes,
because it decides which of their three pre-registered outcomes is live. Their outcome
that the lever was never engaged is ruled out, so on their own stated terms a null on the
raised subset now falsifies their slope rather than excusing it.

**Two negative controls inside the same table.** DECLINED sits at median 0.9973 --
centred on 1, as it must be where the argument changes nothing, which is the regressor
checking itself and passing. AMBIENT 1-8 is also centred at 1 (0.9993) but carries wide
tails at 3.96x its A/A, so it is a MIXTURE rather than a uniformly engaged population and

**Count predicates, since chain204 will be compared against this.** chain208's cell is

single-valued within each build on all 267 cells, all three builds are present on all
267, and `assert not lowered` fired clean at 0.

### CORRECTION: "the width-expanded analogue of 40/49" pooled three different 40-cell sets

chain208's RAISED 120 was described as the width-expanded analogue of chain204's raised 40.
The count is right and the description is wrong in the way that matters. Each width
independently gives exactly 40 raised / 49 declined / 0 lowered, and **it is not the same

contributing 5 raised cells at each width. 35x3 + 15 = 120. So the pooled 120 is three
