### The 89-key corpus is selected on the outcome, and the enrichment survives it anyway

The chain198 section records the selection rule verbatim: "89 matrices instead of 4584 --
the 49 carrying those 61 cells plus 40 controls we beat MKL by more than 2x at every
width". So the corpus is chosen ON the outcome and **bimodally** -- one group for being
behind MKL, one for being at least 2x ahead everywhere, nothing sampled from the middle.
Any within-corpus association between a structural property and being behind MKL can
therefore be induced by the selection rather than revealed by it.

The peer session reported that the 10 width-flipping keys contain 7 of the 10 board
behind-MKL matrices in this corpus, hypergeometric P = 1.89e-06. Conditioning on
proximity to parity does not remove it:

    reference set                             N    K   n   x   expected   P(X>=x)
    ALL 89 keys                               89   10  10  7     1.12     1.89e-06
    not >2x-faster at every width             61   10  10  7     1.64     2.84e-05
    behind MKL at >=1 width                   32    8   9  7     2.25     7.96e-05
    worst-width ratio within 20% of parity    27    6   5  4     1.11     0.00398
    inside the flippers' nnz range            51    8  10  7     1.57     7.8e-06

Two caveats kept attached. Reconstructing the control group as worst-width ratio below 0.5
yields 28 keys against the declared 40 -- a different host and era than the list was drawn
from -- so the conditioning is approximate. And conditioning inside a curated corpus
cannot undo selection that acted on the joint distribution; only the full collection
settles it. **My first version of this ladder was circular**: K was set to the 7 overlap
keys, making x = K by construction and every p-value an artefact of the definition.

### The flip has TWO opposite mechanisms, and they map onto the board by width

"Flipping means the resolved count crosses 64 as k varies, so the decision is marginal"
describes 5 of the 10. Ambient resolved per width tells both stories:

    FX_March2010   301899 nnz   32/32/64   raised at k=2,4    declined at k=32
    bas1lp         587775 nnz   62/62/64   raised at k=2,4    declined at k=32
    cegb2919       321543 nnz   34/34/64   raised at k=2,4    declined at k=32
    cond-mat-2005  351382 nnz   37/37/64   raised at k=2,4    declined at k=32
    lp_osa_14      317097 nnz   33/33/64   raised at k=2,4    declined at k=32
    Pd_b             6323 nnz    1/1/1     declined at k=2,4  raised at k=32
    Pd_rhs           6323 nnz    1/1/1     declined at k=2,4  raised at k=32
    TSOPF_RS_b162_c3_b 7645 nnz  1/1/1     declined at k=2,4  raised at k=32
    m3plates         6639 nnz    1/1/1     declined at k=2,4  raised at k=32
    poli             8188 nnz    1/1/1     declined at k=2,4  raised at k=32

The first five saturate the pool at k=32 so the override becomes a no-op -- that is the
marginality story. The last five sit at ambient 1 at every width, nowhere near 64; what
varies is whether the override is GRANTED, not where the ambient decision sits.

**And the two groups match the board's two width clusters.** Of the 6 board behind-MKL
cells at k=2, four are second-group matrices (Pd_b, Pd_rhs, m3plates, poli) at the width
where ambient resolved is 1. Of the 7 at k=4, three are first-group (lp_osa_14, cegb2919,
FX_March2010) at the width where ambient sits at 32-34. So a 6-8k-nonzero matrix running
SINGLE-THREADED at k=2 and a ~320k-nonzero matrix at half the pool at k=4 are two
different regimes, both computable at plan time, and neither is in the rows/nnz/degree
space where every predicate came back at lift ~1. A single-threaded 6323-nonzero SpMM
losing to MKL needs no exotic explanation.

Structural fact for any predicate written on this: `work = nnz*max(k,16)` while
`work_true = nnz*k`, so k=2, 4 and 8 share a work term. Only 3 of 89 keys change ambient
resolved between k=2 and k=4 against 50 between k=4 and k=32, so a predicate phrased on
"resolved varies with k" is nearly a k>=16 predicate unless it goes through `work_true` or
the row-axis ceiling.

**The decisive test and why it is cheap.** `scorch_spmm_nthreads` is already
pybind-exported at `ops.cpp:704` as (work, rows, nthreads_override, work_true, nnz) -- a
pure function, so resolved counts for all 4584 x 5 board cells are ~23k calls with no
timing attached. The rule is queryable, so no harness needs to restate it. It must run on
the host whose pool the claim concerns, because the base bound reads omp_get_num_procs()
internally. Not being added to chain207, which is live; pre-registered for the next
full-collection run with the predicate stated before the data.

### The unpinned override effect at all three widths, and 0.6766 is a k=32-only result

chain204's analyzer was run at each width by copying the sealed file and changing one line,
`K = 32` to `K = 2` and `K = 4`; `R()` already takes a width parameter so nothing else
moved. **Positive control: the K=32 copy is byte-identical to the sealed analyzer** (empty
`diff`) and reproduces 1.1346 / n=40 / 27 slower, 9 faster exactly, so the
copy-and-substitute procedure is faithful and the sealed artefact was not modified.

Estimand as filed: `ours(ov64)/ours(ovp)`, `exp(median(log .))` over passes 25-30, raised
set of that width, floor = p95 deviation of `ours(ov64b)/ours(ov64)` on two byte-identical
objects.

    width   n    unpinned ratio   outcome floor   beyond-floor split
    k=2     40      1.4239           0.0318       35 slower, 4 faster
    k=4     40      1.3452           0.0261       32 slower, 6 faster
    k=32    40      1.1346           0.0312       27 slower, 9 faster

**Asking for the whole pool costs more at narrow widths, monotonically.** The penalty falls
from 42.4% at k=2 to 13.5% at k=32, and the faster count rises 4 -> 6 -> 9. Every width is
far beyond its own floor, so the override being harmful on raised cells is not a k=32
artefact.

**But the one result that was framed as a win IS a k=32 artefact.** The ambient-1-8 band on
the raised cells:

    width   n    ambient 1-8 ratio   faster/slower   median nnz of the band
    k=2     11        1.3761              4 / 7           40215
    k=4     11        1.3580              4 / 7           40215
    k=32    11        0.6766              9 / 2           10899

The sign REVERSES. At k=32, raising the thread count on cells ambient leaves at 1-8 threads
wins 32%; at k=2 and k=4 the same intervention loses 36-38% with most cells slower. And it
is not the same population: `work = nnz*max(k,16)` makes the k=2 and k=4 bands identical
(n=11, median nnz 40215), while k=32's band is a different and much smaller-matrix set
(median nnz 10899). So 0.6766 carries an unstated k=32 predicate, and any claim that
"raising threads helps thread-starved cells" is false at the two narrow widths where it was
never checked.

**The batch confound is also strongly width-dependent**, which matters for what chain208
can resolve. chain204's own confound block gives r[log batch ratio, log ms ratio] on the 40
raised cells as -0.9547 at k=2, -0.9810 at k=4 and -0.6770 at k=32: the cross-build batch
difference accounts for an r-squared of 0.91-0.96 at narrow widths against 0.46 at k=32.
That is a slope-free reason to expect batch pinning to bite hardest at k=4, and it does not
require transporting a k=32-fitted slope across width.

**A label hazard worth recording.** At k=32 the raised-40 ratio is 1.1346 and the
ambient-31-63 band ratio is also 1.1346 at n=12. Recomputed independently: two different
populations landing on the same value. A reader moving between the headline and the band
table could take one for the other, so either figure must name its population.

**Floor discipline, applied against a peer's power calculation and in their favour.** The
peer computed effect-over-floor for the predicted pinning move using the A/A floor of the
REGRESSOR (the cross-build batch ratio, 0.1039 / 0.0668 / 0.0689). The question is whether
a move in the TIMED RATIO clears its own noise, so the floor is the timed ratio's own, above
(0.0318 / 0.0261 / 0.0312). Their k=32 verdict survives -- 2.06% predicted against a 3.12%
floor is 0.66x and cannot fire, so a k=32 null falsifies nothing. Their k=2 verdict flips
from 0.89x to 2.92x and becomes testable. Same principle as the two earlier instances in
this chain: measure the statistic the claim is about.

### WITHDRAWN: "the batch confound is strongest at narrow widths". Slope -1 is the null.

The r values -0.9547 / -0.9810 / -0.6770 at k=2/4/32 were read as the batch confound being
strongest where r is largest. That inverts their meaning, and the peer session supplied the
argument. `ms` is per-call and `batch = target_ms / t_calibration`, so
`log(batch_ratio) = -log(t_calib_ratio)` **by construction**, and a slope of exactly -1 in
`log(ms_ratio) ~ log(batch_ratio)` says the timed ratio EQUALS the calibration ratio. Slope
-1 is the null of no measurement bias, not evidence of one. A high r with slope near -1 is
two instruments agreeing.

The premise checks out on chain204's own rows: `ms * batch` clusters on the target in every
arm at every width -- ours 22.78 / 24.16 / 24.01, mkl 23.89 / 24.32 / 24.59, IQR 20.5-25.3,
p05-p95 17.3-27.8.

### A pass-level jackknife inverts which width the slope can speak about

Both sessions quoted OLS standard errors that assume 40 independent cells, when all 40 share
the same six passes. Leaving out one pass at a time and refitting:

    k      slope     OLS SE   jack SE   jack/OLS   |slope+1| in jack SE   verdict
    k=2   -1.1440    0.0578    0.0516     0.89x            2.79          distinguishable
    k=4   -1.0796    0.0347    0.0247     0.71x            3.22          distinguishable
    k=32  -0.4306    0.0759    0.8520    11.22x            0.67          NOT distinguishable

**The dependence does not always inflate.** At the narrow widths the pass-to-pass wobble is
smaller than the cell-to-cell residual scatter, so the jackknife SE comes in at 0.71-0.89x
the OLS one; at k=32 it is 11.2x. Assuming the correction must widen an interval is itself a
guess -- measure it.

**The k=32 slope is one cell measured cold, and it is non-robust to dropping a PASS, not just
a cell.** `rajat26` by width:

    k=2    batch ov64/ovp = 467.7 / 479.5 = 0.96x    ms ratio 1.2401
    k=4    batch ov64/ovp = 507.5 / 575.0 = 0.90x    ms ratio 1.1433
    k=32   batch ov64/ovp = 367.0 /  36.8 = 9.99x    ms ratio 0.9839

At k=32 the ovp build's calibration collapsed to batch 36.8 -- about 0.65 ms per call --
while its timed time came out equal to ov64's. The same cell at k=2 and k=4 is unremarkable.
Dropping it, the three slopes become -1.1498 / -1.0809 / -0.9385, so **every width sits near
-1** and "the instruments disagree at k=32" is a single cold calibration reading. The drop-1
fit is recorded, not adopted: choosing the fit one prefers after seeing the leverage is how a
result gets manufactured.

**Consequence for the registered test.** At k=4 the two competing models stay 37-40% apart
for any slope in [-1.15, -1.00] -- batch-as-cause predicts 0.959 to 0.983, batch-as-symptom
predicts 1.3452 -- against a 2.61% outcome floor, so at worst a 14x separation. The slope
dispute does not touch the discriminating power of that cell.

**Consequence at k=32.** The verdict that a pinning move "cannot fire" there rests on slope
-0.4306. Under a slope of -1, which the jackknife cannot distinguish from, the predicted
pinned value is 1.1346 x 0.9529 = 1.0811, a 4.72% move against a 3.12% floor, which is 1.51x
and marginally live. So k=32 is a LOW-POWER TEST rather than a pure bound, and will be
reported as both.

**An open question raised rather than asserted.** chain203's 6.52-against-1.14 cold/warm
figure has the same shape as what `rajat26` turned out to be: a calibration reading far from
the timed one. It is a different measurement so nothing follows automatically, but whether
that number carries comparable single-cell or single-pass leverage is not currently known,
and it is load-bearing in the memory record. To be checked with the same jackknife.

### CORRECTION to e68d0d1: a pass jackknife cannot license a TIGHTER interval

The section above concluded that the narrow-width slopes are distinguishable from -1 at
2.79 and 3.22 jackknife SE. **That is withdrawn.** The peer session supplied the argument
and it is decisive: a pass-level jackknife holds the CELL SET FIXED, so it estimates the
pass component of variance alone.

- Where the jackknife EXCEEDS the OLS SE, it reveals a component OLS missed and the larger
  value binds. That is k=32, and that conclusion stands.
- Where it FALLS BELOW, it says the pass component is small. It does **not** retire the
  cell component OLS was measuring. Taking the smaller of two estimates of DIFFERENT
  components is not a choice between estimators at all.

Combining in quadrature:

    k      slope     OLS SE   jack SE   combined   |s+1|/OLS   /jack   /combined
    k=2   -1.1440    0.0578    0.0516    0.0775       2.49      2.79      1.86
    k=4   -1.0796    0.0347    0.0247    0.0426       2.29      3.22      1.87
    k=32  -0.4306    0.0759    0.8520    0.8554       7.50      0.67      0.67

**No width is distinguishable from -1 at 2 SE**: 1.86 / 1.87 / 0.67. So the earlier claim
that the narrow widths reject slope -1 is wrong, and so was the peer's original 1.60 / 1.40
-- both overstated, in opposite directions, from different errors. Theirs was a reduction
order (reduce-then-ratio, which is the convention for a replication floor, applied to an
EFFECT whose two builds share a pass; ratio-then-reduce reproduces the sealed block to four
decimals at all three widths). Mine was the component confusion above.

**And the jackknife's magnitude is not trustworthy at G=6.** Five degrees of freedom means
0.8520 is a signal that a pass component EXISTS, not a measurement of its size. The caveat
travels with the number wherever it is quoted. The surviving k=32 conclusion depends only on
the sign of the comparison, not on the value.

What does NOT change: the `rajat26` decomposition, which is a separate instrument reaching
the same place -- the k=32 slope rests on one cell whose ovp calibration collapsed at that
width alone, and dropping it puts all three slopes near -1.

**The registered test is unaffected.** Model A's range over slopes [fitted, -1] against
Model B:

    k      worst-case A   B        gap      floor    gap/floor
    k=2      1.1351     1.4239   25.44%    3.18%      8.00
    k=4      0.9831     1.3452   36.83%    2.61%     14.11
    k=32     1.1113     1.1346    2.10%    3.12%      0.67

k=4 separates by at least 36.83% for any slope in [-1.08, -1.00], so the test is slope-free
in the range that matters. k=32 separates by less than one floor and is reported as
low-power with both model points printed. k=2 sits at 8.00 floors -- a test, not a bound,
but carrying the least robust slope of the three.

### A completeness message that certifies 267 rows in a file holding none

chain208's run log says, twice:

    wrote /scr/bobbyy/c208/cal_ovp.csv (267 rows)
    wrote /scr/bobbyy/c208/cal_ov64.csv (267 rows)

Both files are **107 bytes, one line, header only**. The counter behind the message counts
cells PROCESSED, not rows EMITTED, and in calibration mode no timing rows are written to
`--csv` at all -- only the batch map goes out, through `--batch-out`. So a completeness audit
conducted by reading the log would certify 267 rows in a file that contains none, and there
is nothing in the log that could reveal it. The fix is to increment the counter at the
`writerow` call or to make the message say "cells".

It does not touch the analysis: the map is `batchmap_*.csv`, both carry 267 cells, and the
batch actually used was verified against them on 16821 of 16821 rows with zero lookup
misses. The defect is in the attestation, not the data -- which is the worse half to have
wrong, because the attestation is what a later reader trusts.

**What the integrity check did establish, with its population stated:** 28 of 28 complete
object-pass files are exactly 802 lines = 801 rows = 267 cells x 3 arms. The one short file
is the newest by mtime and grew from 10 to 73 lines across a 20-second observation, so it is
the in-progress write rather than a silently truncated earlier pass. That was the thing worth
ruling out, since one truncated file among the completed ones would bias the analysis with
nothing in the log to show it.

**And a third count of mine without its predicate.** chain208 progress was reported as "31 of
36" and "32 of 36 object-passes" for an hour. The predicate was `grep -c "^wrote "` on the
run log, which also matches the two batch maps and the two calibration files. The true figure
was **28 of 36**, and the remaining time about 33 minutes rather than the 10 implied. The
earlier instances tonight were a leading-space count whose quantifier went unstated and a
board count published without its criterion; this one had a predicate that was simply wrong.

### Spot-check the LARGEST effect, not the most convenient one

Two convention errors were found tonight, and in both the width that agreed across the two
conventions was the width where the effect is smallest:

- reduce-then-ratio against ratio-then-reduce agreed at k=32 (-0.4317 against -0.4306) and
  differed at the narrow widths (-1.1063 against -1.1440).
- a log-scale gap-to-floor ratio against a dev-scale one agreed at k=32 (0.68 against 0.67)
  and diverged 16% at k=4 (12.17 against 14.11).

The general form: **a convention or scale error is proportional to effect size**, so
verifying against the cell with the smallest effect is verifying where the error is
definitionally invisible. Both times the one width that could be cross-checked cheaply was
the one that could not reveal the discrepancy. A spot-check has to name why the cell it
chose is capable of failing -- the same requirement as a guard firing on its own input.
